# Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons

###### Abstract

Attaching metallic contacts to transition metal dichalcogenide nanostructures
and in particular to MoS2 has posed significant challenges over the past
years. For MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons, a highly promising material for
field effect transistors as well as quantum electronic devices, this is even
more the case due to the small, curved surface. So far all attempts there have
led to a wide scatter of contact resistances on the same chip. Recently, for
quasi two-dimensional, flat MoS2 flakes, the use of semimetals has led to a
breakthrough, making transparent and Ohmic contacts possible. Here, we
demonstrate the steps required to reproducibly fabricate contacts to single,
vapor phase grown MoS2 nanotubes and nanowires. All devices display finite
room-temperature two-point resistances in absence of gating, with a median
value of 340 k​Ω340\text{\,}\mathrm{k\SIUnitSymbolOhm} in a large fabrication series. A detailed analysis
elucidates the impact of the different fabrication changes.

The isolation of few- and monolayer 2d materials such as graphene
[novoselov\_electric\_2004](#bib.bib1) or transition metal dichalcogenides
[novoselov\_two-dimensional\_2005](#bib.bib2) has led to an avalanche of research
regarding both classical semiconductor applications [das\_transistors\_2021](#bib.bib3); [dorow\_exploring\_2023](#bib.bib4); [chou\_status\_2023](#bib.bib5) and quantum electronics
[jing\_gate-controlled\_2022](#bib.bib6); [liu\_2d\_2019](#bib.bib7); [qiu\_recent\_2021](#bib.bib8). Nevertheless,
both commercial chip fabrication where integrated transistor channels become
narrower and narrower [hills\_modern\_2019](#bib.bib9); [si\_carbon-nanotube-based\_2024](#bib.bib10)
and quantum electronics with the manyfold focus on one-dimensional physics
[science-stern-2013](#bib.bib11); [science-frolov-2026](#bib.bib12) also point out the intrinsic
geometric advantage of quasi-1d nanostructures such as nanotubes, nanoribbons,
or nanowires. This has driven recent fundamental research on complex 1d
nanomaterials beyond carbon, including even so-called coaxial heterostructures
[xiang\_one-dimensional\_2020](#bib.bib13).

Molybdenum disulfide MoS2, mostly known as 2d material and semiconductor
[novoselov\_two-dimensional\_2005](#bib.bib2), also allows the growth of long,
straight, low-defect density nanotubes and nanoribbons via chemical vapor
deposition [remskar1996](#bib.bib14). These 1d nanomaterials of large aspect ratio
display outstanding optical properties [kazanov\_multiwall\_2018](#bib.bib15); [remskar2022](#bib.bib16) and have shown clear promise in first field effect transistor
devices [fathipour2015](#bib.bib17). The central challenge for electronic measurements
is however the reliable fabrication of Ohmic contacts. The formation of
Schottky barriers at the metal-semiconductor interface
[zphys-schottky-1939](#bib.bib18); [tung\_physics\_2014](#bib.bib19), often caused or enhanced by Fermi
level pinning [louie\_electronic\_1976](#bib.bib20); [monch\_valence-band\_1998](#bib.bib21); [tung\_physics\_2014](#bib.bib19), has required significant efforts to overcome
[nl-gong-2014](#bib.bib22); [kim\_fermi\_2017](#bib.bib23); [jpcc-sotthewes-2019](#bib.bib24).

For the 2d morphology of MoS2, i.e., multi- and monolayers, recently
breakthrough results have been achieved using semimetal contact layers, in
particular bismuth [shen2021a](#bib.bib25); [schock2023](#bib.bib26) and antimony [li2023](#bib.bib27). A
transfer of this technique to 1d morphologies was partially successful
[schock2023](#bib.bib26); [schock2025](#bib.bib28), with bismuth contacts leading to transparent
devices, but at relatively low yield and still a wide scatter of device
resistance values.

Here, we demonstrate the reproducible fabrication of MoS2 nanotube and
nanoribbon devices, by combining our experience from previous work
[schock2023](#bib.bib26); [schock2025](#bib.bib28) with several fabrication techniques developed in
other material systems. The results are characterized using room temperature
resistance measurements and demonstrate a reduction of the 2-point resistance
R2R\_{2} scatter by several orders of magnitude, with all measured nanotube and
nanoribbon segments displaying R2<30 M​ΩR\_{2}<$30\text{\,}\mathrm{M\SIUnitSymbolOhm}$. Given the extensive
interest world-wide in MoS2 integrated circuits, and the chance provided here
to reduce device dimensionality and with it the potential area footprint of
transistors, this development is not just interesting for quantum devices but
also of clear technological impact as well.

## Raw material and device fabrication

![Refer to caption](2606.28902v1/figure1-300dpi.png)

Figure [1](#Sx1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(a) shows the raw MoS2 nanomaterial, a mixture of
quasi-one dimensional and quasi-two dimensional structures, as deposited on the
wall of the growth quartz glass ampoule. The material synthesis via vapor phase
deposition is well-established and has been discussed in detail in published
literature [remskar1996](#bib.bib14); [schock2025](#bib.bib28). Detail optical and scanning electron
microscope (SEM) images in Figures [1](#Sx1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(b,c) demonstrate the
presence of long and crystalline one-dimensional morphologies, including
multiwall nanotubes, cf. Fig. [1](#Sx1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(d), and nanoribbons, i.e.,
nanotubes collapsed during growth. The nanomaterial is picked up using a
commercially available adhesive tape and deposited on the surface of a p++ Si /
SiO2 wafer with prefabricated grid markers [novoselov\_electric\_2004](#bib.bib1); [schock2023](#bib.bib26); [schock2025](#bib.bib28). Subsequently, the surface is imaged in an optical
microscope and the location of nanotubes and nanowires is recorded for contact
electrode design. As contact material, in either case a bilayer bismuth and
gold is deposited, as based on and described in previous work [shen2021a](#bib.bib25); [schock2023](#bib.bib26); [schock2025](#bib.bib28). An additional adhesion layer is not required, since
thermally evaporated bismuth bonds sufficiently to a silicon oxide or hBN
surface. The drawing of Fig. [1](#Sx1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(e) demonstrates an example of a
resulting chip geometry, with bond pads, leads, and nanotube regions. The
active device region between contacts is chosen to be between
100 nm to 500 nm100\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}500\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}.

As already discussed previously [schock2023](#bib.bib26); [schock2025](#bib.bib28), while highly
succesful and reproducible for 2d materials [shen2021a](#bib.bib25), this technique
leads for nanotubes and nanoribbons to a few good devices but overall a very
large scatter of two-point resistances, with overall insufficient device yield.
Consequently, a number of device fabrication optimizations have been developed
and tested in combination, listed in the following and discussed in detail
further below:

![Refer to caption](2606.28902v1/figure2-300dpi.png)

“spot anchoring”: in a small region of the nanotube contact
area, poly-methyl metacrylate (PMMA) electron beam lithography resist is
strongly overexposed, cross-linking the resist on top of and around the nanotube
and creating an effective glue droplet for mechanical stability and possibly a
smooth surface topology, see Fig. [1](#Sx1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(a–d)

deposition pressure: the ultra-high vacuum setup used for the
bismuth and gold deposition is pumped out overnight before each deposition,
with the substrate heated to 100 °C100\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius}, to remove adsorbates
and atmospheric contaminants; to further improve the chamber pressure of the
evaporation system, titanium is evaporated with a shutter in front of the
device, resulting in a final pressure of p≃5×10−8 mbarp\simeq$5\text{\times}{10}^{-8}\text{\,}\mathrm{mbar}$
instead of approximately 3×10−7 mbar3\text{\times}{10}^{-7}\text{\,}\mathrm{mbar} without these steps;

substrate heating: during the contact deposition process, the
heating of the chip substrate with the MoS2 nanotube to
100 °C100\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} is kept up, potentially enabling recrystallization of
the bismuth interface layer as discussed below; and finally

tilted-angle deposition: both materials bismuth and gold are
evaporated subsequently at two different angles each, i.e. with the substrate
rotated by ±15∘\pm 15^{\circ} from the orthogonal incident setting.

Subsequently a lift-off process in hot acetone is performed.

## Results

![Refer to caption](2606.28902v1/figure3-300dpi.png)

The two-point resistance characterization at room temperature of the tested
devices is shown in Fig. [3](#Sx2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(a), comparing the straightforward
contact deposition by evaporation with the procedure optimized using all the
steps as detailed above. A clear reduction in the scatter of resistance values
is observed, in conjunction with a decrease in median value. All devices tested
here with optimized fabrication display an unabiguous source-drain current upon
application of a bias voltage, with resistances below 30 M​Ω30\text{\,}\mathrm{M\SIUnitSymbolOhm} and a
median value of 340 k​Ω340\text{\,}\mathrm{k\SIUnitSymbolOhm}.

Since previous work has focused also on the effect of the substrate on the
device properties [schock2025](#bib.bib28), Figs. [3](#Sx2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(b) and
[3](#Sx2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(c) display a corresponding sorting of the data points.
Fig. [3](#Sx2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(b) focuses on the case of a bare, amorphous, and
thermally grown silicon oxide, while Fig. [3](#Sx2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(c) focuses on
devices where the nanotube has been transferred onto a hexagonal boron nitride
(hBN) flake [schock2025](#bib.bib28). While SiO2 based devices display
slightly lower resistances, same as in [schock2025](#bib.bib28), the effect of the
optimized contact fabrication is clearly visible in both cases, with
significantly smaller resistance scatter and a lower median value.

The data of Figure [3](#Sx2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(d) is part of a separate, subsequent
series of measurements designed to identify the impact of single optimization
steps on the device properties. Each column corresponds to a single chip with
several nanotubes and nanoribbons, fabricated with one of the optimizations
omitted. While the results have to be treated carefully due to fabrication
irregularities, this still enables us to draw some conclusions.

Omitting the substrate heating during contact deposition has a clear
detrimental effect, indicating that this is indeed a crucial detail. The same
to a slightly lesser degree is true of omitting the dual-angle evaporation.
A bad vacuum during contact deposition apparently still led to very
low-resistive devices, see the middle column in Fig. [3](#Sx2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(d);
unfortunately, large offsets in the data indicate ground loops that were
unnoticed at the time of measurement. This makes a quantitative analysis here
unreliable and more measurements would be required for a definite statement;
still, the overall trend indicates low two-terminal resistances.

![Refer to caption](2606.28902v1/figure4-300dpi.png)

Figure [4](#Sx2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons") displays typical further characterization results of
the chips α\alpha, β\beta, and γ\gamma of the second measurement series.
All devices on the chips were tested for Ohmic behaviour via recording the bias
dependence of the current I⁡(Vsd)I(V\_{\text{sd}}) at Vg=0V\_{\text{g}}=0. Predominantly, linear behaviour
was observed, see, e.g., the measurement of several nanotube segments on chip
γ\gamma in Fig. [4](#Sx2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(a). The only occurences of clear diode-like
response were on chip α\alpha, where the substrate was not heated during
contact deposition. This is demonstrated in Fig. [4](#Sx2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(b) with the
response of two neighboring segments; the curves nearly coincide when
mirroring, indicating that the central, shared contact limits the current here.

Fig. [4](#Sx2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(c-e) shows the gate voltage response I⁡(Vg)I(V\_{\text{g}}) of devices
on the three chips at fixed Vsd=20​mVV\_{\text{sd}}=20\,\textrm{mV}. While in the recorded range
−20​V≤Vg≤20​V-20\,\textrm{V}\leq V\_{\text{g}}\leq 20\,\textrm{V} a gate voltage dependence consistent with
electron conduction is visible througout, the response is by far strongest for
chip γ\gamma where no dual-angle evaporation was used.

## Discussion

### “Spot anchoring”

To ensure that the nanotubes adhere to the substrate surface, as well as to
avoid the formation of gaps in the contact material, poly-methyl methacrylate
(PMMA) electron beam resist is spun onto the chip and locally over-exposed by a
factor ∼200\sim 200. This leads to cross-linking of the PMMA molecules,
effectively turning the positive resist locally into a highly stable
negative-resist and polymer deposition [zailer\_crosslinked\_1996](#bib.bib29), see
Fig. [2](#Sx1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(b). Fig. [2](#Sx1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(c) shows an optical
microscope image of a device with the corresponding droplets (green arrow),
Fig. [2](#Sx1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(d) is a SEM micrograph of a corresponding contact
after metal deposition.

The cross-linked PMMA droplets glue the MoS2 nanomaterial to the chip
surface, significantly improving mechanical stability of the devices. This
resolves the challenge detailed in [schock2025](#bib.bib28) (cf. Fig. 8 there), where
the MoS2 nanostructure frequently tears off the chip during lift-off, taking
part of the contact metal with it. Furthermore, the polymer deposition can
assist a smooth surface transition between the chip substrate and the curved
nanotube surface, see the sketch of Fig. [2](#Sx1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(b), avoiding
shadowing effects and gap formation during contact material deposition and
leading to an unbroken contact film. The precise shape of the result depends
critically on the resist and contact deposition parameters; as visible in
Fig. [2](#Sx1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(d), thicker PMMA leads to mushroom-shaped polymer
structures.

Chips α\alpha, β\beta, γ\gamma of the second test series each contained
devices with and without PMMA droplets. Electronic characterization showed no
clear difference among devices with finite current. This confirms that the main
impact of the PMMA droplets is to provide mechanical stability and keep the
nanotube or nanoribbon in place.

### Deposition pressure

The contact material deposition is performed in an UHV chamber system via
electron beam assisted evaporation. In order to reduce contamination with
adsorbates and improve the interface quality, the devices are heated to
100∘​C100^{\circ}\text{C} inside the UHV system for >> 10 h10\text{\,}\mathrm{h} before
deposition. Additionally, a short Ti gettering step is performed to further
reduce the pressure of the evaporation system to p=5×10−8 mbarp=$5\text{\times}{10}^{-8}\text{\,}\mathrm{mbar}$.

Similar optimization steps were performed in early high-profile works on carbon
nanotubes that used comparable fabrication [nature-jarillo-herrero-2004](#bib.bib30); [nature-jarillo-herrero-2005](#bib.bib31); [private-pablo](#bib.bib32). Adsorbates or chemical surface
modifications can have a strong impact on the interface properties of
low-dimensional materials and the Schottky barrier [tung\_physics\_2014](#bib.bib19), as
also attested by a large body of complex and sometimes contradicting published
experimental results on 2d MoS2 devices. Recent studies have revealed that
the quality of Ni contacts to MoS2 depends heavily on the vacuum, with
typically ∼3\sim 3 times lower contact resistance going from HV to UHV
deposition conditions [sun\_hv\_uhv\_NiBi\_2024](#bib.bib33).

The authors of Ref. [sun\_hv\_uhv\_NiBi\_2024](#bib.bib33) could not identify any
significant improvement in contact resistance for Bi contacts for different
vacuum conditions. This is consistent with our observations when skipping the
vacuum optimization alone (chip β\beta), where this step turns out not to be
critical on a smaller test scale, but even led to surprisingly good contacts.
Further test would be required to confirm or refute whether a good vacuum has
advantages.

### Contact materials

The choice of a bismuth / gold bilayer as contact material for MoS2 was first
championed in [shen2021a](#bib.bib25) for flake-based 2d material devices, with
outstanding results. Many earlier attempts at Ohmic contacts to MoS2 had been
unsuccessful due to Fermi level pinning and Schottky barrier formation. Low
work function metals such as titanium or scandium are a possible solution
[das2013](#bib.bib34); [reinhardt2019a](#bib.bib35), however tend to react with the MoS2 surface
on deposition [wu2019](#bib.bib36), particularly detrimental in the low-dimensional
material case and for low-temperature applications. Doping with copper
[liu\_improvement\_2018](#bib.bib37) or yttrium [jiang\_yttrium-doping-induced\_2024](#bib.bib38)
has in general shown good results, but does not make much sense for nanotubes
due to the small surface area involved and the resulting electrostatic
potential irregularities.

Instead, bismuth as semimetal was chosen since its vanishing density of states
at the Fermi edge avoids the formation of metal-induced gap states and with it
Fermi level pinning [louie\_electronic\_1976](#bib.bib20); [monch\_valence-band\_1998](#bib.bib21); [shen2021a](#bib.bib25). Calculations indicate that the effective contact resistance results
from an interplay of the absence of interaction (leading to an absence of
metal-induced gap states) and the absence of tunneling (leading to a
suppression of current), close to the optimum for adjacent 2d layers
[lizzit\_ohmic\_2023](#bib.bib39). For nanotubes, the curvature of the surface as well
as the resulting more complex contact material deposition and morphology can
then easily explain the remaining resistance fluctuations.

While antimony delivers even better results for 2d material devices
[li2023](#bib.bib27), specifically for nanotubes and nanoribbons measurements have
demonstrated bismuth to be the best choice [schock2025](#bib.bib28). A detailed
explanation for this is still missing; one can speculate that a bismuth layer
may be less sensitive to the curved nanotube surface or the precise deposition
conditions, see also the discussion on recrystallization below.

### Deposition protocol

The contact materials, bismuth and gold, are deposited with 50 nm50\text{\,}\mathrm{nm} and
100 nm100\text{\,}\mathrm{nm} at rates of 0.03 nm s−10.03\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} and
0.05 nm s−10.05\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}, respectively. The substrate is kept heated at
100 °C100\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} and the incidence angle of the deposition is changed
from −15 °-15\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} to 15 °15\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} after half the layer thickness
has been reached for each material to improve coverage. After deposition, the
device is left inside the UHV chamber until reaching ambient temperature.

Thermal evaporation, while providing high quality thin films, is a directed
process. As a consequence, shadowing and capping effects can occur when surface
features such as the nanotubes here are of similar or larger scale as the film
thickness [schock2025](#bib.bib28), an effect that is in literature also deliberately
used for device structuring [chen\_gate-tunable\_2023](#bib.bib40). Dual angle
evaporation reduces this, with the material reaching into gaps and below
overhangs. Its specific advantage is confirmed by the measurement of chip
γ\gamma, where without dual angle evaporation clearly increased resistance
scatter and median value is observed, see Fig. [3](#Sx2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(d).
Additionally, without dual-angle evaporation, a stronger gate effect is
visible, see Fig. [4](#Sx2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(e). As unfortunate side effect, better
coverage of the nanotube or nanoribbon appears to lead to partial shielding of
the gate voltage.

Bismuth has comparatively low melting point of T=271∘​CT=271^{\circ}\text{C}. It tends
to form crystallites during thin film deposition [kumari\_effects\_2007](#bib.bib41);
this is visible in, e.g., Fig. [2](#Sx1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Raw material and device fabrication ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(d,h) both for the contact
surface away from the nanotube and for additional nucleation directly on top of
it, even with the additional gold capping layer. Early research has already
addressed the dependence of the crystal formation on the substrate temperature
[partin\_growth\_1989](#bib.bib42); [kumari\_effects\_2007](#bib.bib41), indicating that higher
temperature leads to better film quality. This is consistent with the
observation that chip α\alpha of the second test series, where substrate
heating was omitted, was the only one to display Schottky diode behaviour, see
Fig. [4](#Sx2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Results ‣ Reproducible Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons")(b). Furthermore, for our bismuth / gold bilayer, it is
likely that heating effects during the subsequent gold deposition lead to
(partial) melting and recrystallization, improving contact transparency
[private-ljl](#bib.bib43). The formation of the gold/bismuth intermetallic compound
maldonite (Au2Bi) at the interface [okamoto\_aubi\_1983](#bib.bib44) is
also possible and has likely been observed by us in a single device where the
contacts surprisingly displayed superconductivity phenomena at cryogenic
temperature [dehaas1931super](#bib.bib45), but seems to be the exception.

### Substrate

A surprising observation, here as already in [schock2025](#bib.bib28), is the
statistically clearly higher device resistance in case of a hexagonal boron
nitride (hBN) substrate. While the amorphous SiO2 is known for its dangling
bonds and surface charges, hBN has been the material of choice to precisely
avoid such effects. As a possible cause, the more complex fabrication of
hBN-based devices stands out: here, the hBN flakes have to be exfoliated and
deposited onto the chip substrate, and subsequently also the MoS2 nanomaterial has to be transferred again [schock2025](#bib.bib28). Each such step
increases the risk of surface contamination and structural damage.

## Conclusions and Outlook

We have managed to improve the fabrication of metallic contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons such that we consistently achieve Ohmic contacts,
with a median 2-point resistance of a segment of 340​k​Ω340\,\textrm{k}\Omega in a large
fabrication series. The impact of separate improvements is tested and
discussed. Decisive steps include local PMMA crosslinking for mechanical
stabilization, substrate heating to 100∘​C100^{\circ}\text{C} during contact
deposition, and dual-angle evaporation to improve coverage of the non-planar
nanomaterial. The precise impact of deposition pressure is so far unclear.

In previous work, the integration of MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons into
complex devices was challenging due to low fabrication yield. With reliable
contact formation, the path towards 1d MoS2 transistors as well as 1d MoS2 quantum electronics is now open.

What has not been adressed here is the intrinsic surface quality of the MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons as well as the impact of their geometry. Sulfur
vacancies have been reported to be beneficial for n-type contacts
[mcdonnell\_svacancy\_ndoping\_2014](#bib.bib46), but also modify the nanomaterial
properties in between them; fabrication in inert environment and
treatment with H2S [peto\_spontaneous\_2018](#bib.bib47) or thioles
[schwarz\_thiol-based\_2023](#bib.bib48) may help here. Wall curvature, inner
substructures, and deformation on substrate deposition modify the electronic
properties [malok\_edge\_2025](#bib.bib49); [malok\_electrical\_2025](#bib.bib50). A smaller number of
nanotube walls will likely improve reproducibility of device properties; free
single-wall MoS2 nanotubes are thermodynamically unstable
[khadiev\_misfit\_2024](#bib.bib51), but the recent development of coaxial
heterostructures provides a path to solve this problem
[xiang\_one-dimensional\_2020](#bib.bib13).

In the end, while challenges in nanomaterial chemistry and device technology
remain, the appeal of truly one-dimensional MoS2 for both traditional and
quantum electronics remains very much undiminished, and a significant step has
been made towards device implementation.

args.summary:
This arXiv paper (2606.28902) presents a method for reproducibly fabricating Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons—a key challenge previously hindering development of 1D field-effect transistors and quantum devices. The central problem was wide scatter in contact resistances on the same chip due to the small, curved surfaces of the 1D nanostructures. Building on recent breakthroughs using semimetals (bismuth, antimony) for flat 2D MoS2 flakes, the authors transferred this technique to 1D morphologies and developed an optimized fabrication protocol.

**Key Results:**
- All optimized devices displayed finite room-temperature two-point resistances with a median of 340 kΩ in a large fabrication series, with all measured segments below 30 MΩ—a reduction in resistance scatter by several orders of magnitude.
- Device active region between contacts: 100–500 nm.

**Fabrication Optimizations (tested in combination):**
1. **"Spot anchoring"**: PMMA electron beam lithography resist is locally overexposed (~200x), cross-linking it into a stable negative-resist/polymer droplet that glues the nanotube to the chip, improving mechanical stability and creating a smooth surface transition to prevent gap formation during metal deposition. Electronic characterization showed no electrical difference from droplets—their main role is mechanical stabilization.
2. **Deposition pressure**: UHV chamber pumped overnight with substrate heated to 100°C, plus a titanium gettering step, achieving final pressure of ~5×10⁻⁸ mbar (vs. ~3×10⁻⁷ mbar without). Vacuum quality proved NOT critical—chip β (skipping vacuum optimization) still gave surprisingly good contacts, consistent with earlier findings that Bi contacts are insensitive to vacuum conditions.
3. **Substrate heating** to 100°C during contact deposition: This was critical—omitting it (chip α) was the only case producing diode-like (Schottky) behavior. Higher temperature improves bismuth film quality (lower melting point 271°C, forms crystallites) and may enable recrystallization or formation of the maldonite (Au2Bi) intermetallic during gold deposition.
4. **Tilted-angle (dual-angle) deposition**: Bismuth (50 nm, 0.03 nm/s) and gold (100 nm, 0.05 nm/s) each evaporated at ±15° from orthogonal to improve coverage of the curved surface. Omitting this (chip γ) caused increased resistance scatter and median, plus a stronger gate effect (partial gate shielding from better coverage).

**Materials rationale:** Bismuth was chosen over antimony (better for 2D but not for nanotubes/nanoribbons), low-work-function metals (Ti, Sc) that react with MoS2, and doping approaches (Cu, Y) unsuitable for small nanotube surfaces. Bismuth's vanishing density of states at the Fermi edge avoids metal-induced gap states and Fermi level pinning.

**Substrate findings:** SiO2-based devices showed slightly lower resistances than hBN-based devices (surprising, since hBN normally avoids dangling bonds/charges), attributed to the more complex multi-step transfer fabrication of hBN devices increasing contamination/damage risk.

**Conclusions/Outlook:** With reliable Ohmic contacts now achievable, the path toward 1D MoS2 transistors and quantum electronics is open. Remaining challenges include intrinsic surface quality (sulfur vacancies, wall curvature, deformation) and reproducibility of single-wall nanotubes (which are thermodynamically unstable; coaxial heterostructures offer a path forward).

Funding: DFG grants Hu 1808/4-1 and Hu 1808/6-1, Slovenian Research Agency grants P1-0099 and PR-11224, DFG CRC/SFB 1277. Authors declare no competing interests. MoS2 nanomaterial grown at Jozef Stefan Institute (Ljubljana, Slovenia); project supervised by M. R. (Ljubljana) and A. K. H. (Regensburg, Germany).

## Abstract

Van der Waals (vdWs) stacking of two-dimensional (2D) materials can effectively weaken the Fermi level pinning (FLP) effect in metal/semiconductor contacts due to dangling-bond-free surfaces. However, the inherent vdWs gap always induces a considerable tunneling barrier, significantly limiting carrier injection. Herein, by inducing a sp 2 to sp 3 hybridization transformation in 2D carbon-based metal via surface defect engineering, the large orbital overlap can form an efficient carrier channel, overcoming the tunneling barrier. Specifically, by selecting the 2D carbon-based X 3 C 2 (X = Cd, Hg, and Zn) metal and the 2D MSi 2 N 4 (M = Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti, V, and Zr) semiconductor, we constructed 36 metal/semiconductor contacts. For vdWs contacts, although Ohmic contacts can be formed at the interface, the highest tunneling probability (_P_ TB) is only 3.11%. As expected, the _P_ TB can be significantly improved, as high as 48.73%, when MSi 2 N 4, accompanied by surface nitrogen vacancies, forms an interface covalent bond with X 3 C 2. Simultaneously, weak FLP and Ohmic contact remain at the covalent-bond-based surface, attributing to the protection of the MSi 2 N 4 band-edge electronic states by the outlying Si-N sublayer. Our work provides a promising path for advancing the progress of 2D electronic and photoelectronic devices.

args.summary:
This is a research article published in Nano Research (Springer) on August 1, 2024, titled "sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D metal-semiconductor contact interface suppresses tunneling barrier and Fermi level pinning simultaneously." The paper addresses a key challenge in 2D electronics: while van der Waals (vdWs) stacking of 2D materials weakens Fermi level pinning (FLP) in metal/semiconductor contacts due to dangling-bond-free surfaces, the inherent vdWs gap creates a considerable tunneling barrier that limits carrier injection.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers induced a sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D carbon-based metals via surface defect engineering, which enabled large orbital overlap to form an efficient carrier channel and overcome the tunneling barrier. They constructed 36 metal/semiconductor contacts by selecting:
- 2D carbon-based X3C2 metals (X = Cd, Hg, Zn)
- 2D MSi2N4 semiconductors (M = Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti, V, Zr)

KEY RESULTS: For vdWs contacts, although Ohmic contacts formed at the interface, the highest tunneling probability (PTB) was only 3.11%. However, when MSi2N4 with surface nitrogen vacancies formed interface covalent bonds with X3C2, the PTB was significantly improved to as high as 48.73%. Simultaneously, weak FLP and Ohmic contact were maintained at the covalent-bond-based surface, attributed to the protection of MSi2N4 band-edge electronic states by the outlying Si-N sublayer.

CONCLUSION: The work provides a promising path for advancing 2D electronic and photoelectronic devices by simultaneously suppressing tunneling barriers and Fermi level pinning through sp2-to-sp3 hybridization transformation enabled by surface defect engineering. The article is subscription content (paywalled) and has 771 accesses with 1 Altmetric mention. Authors include Wenchao Shan, Anqi Shi, Zhuorong Zhong, Xiuyun Zhang, Bing Wang, Yongtao Li, and Xianghong Niu from multiple Chinese institutions. The reference list cites 57 prior works spanning foundational studies on Fermi level pinning, Schottky barriers, van der Waals contacts, and MoSi2N4/WSi2N4 material systems.

However, the inherent vdWs gap always induces a considerable tunneling barrier, significantly limiting carrier injection."

Research Article sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D metal-semiconductor contact interface suppresses tunneling barrier and Fermi level pinning simultaneously Wenchao Shan1, Anqi Shi1, Zhuorong Zhong1, Xiuyun Zhang2, Bing Wang3 (✉), Yongtao Li1 (✉), and Xianghong Niu1,4 (✉) 1 School of Science, State Key Laboratory of Organic Electronics and Information Displays & Institute of Advanced Materials (IAM) and College of Electronic and Optical Engineering, Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Nanjing 210023, China 2 College of Physics Science and Technology, Yangzhou University, Yangzhou 225002, China 3 Institute for Computational Materials Science, Joint Center for Theoretical Physics (JCTP), School of Physics and Electronics, Henan University, Kaifeng 475004, China 4 Key Laboratory of Quantum Materials and Devices (Southeast University), Ministry of Education, Nanjing 211189, China © Tsinghua University Press 2024 Received: 16 May 2024 / Revised: 25 June 2024 / Accepted: 10 July 2024 ABSTRACT Van der Waals (vdWs) stacking of two-dimensional (2D) materials can effectively weaken the Fermi level pinning (FLP) effect in metal/semiconductor contacts due to dangling-bond-free surfaces. However, the inherent vdWs gap always induces a considerable tunneling barrier, significantly limiting carrier injection. Herein, by inducing a sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D carbon-based metal via surface defect engineering, the large orbital overlap can form an efficient carrier channel, overcoming the tunneling barrier. Specifically, by selecting the 2D carbon-based X3C2 (X = Cd, Hg, and Zn) metal and the 2D MSi2N4 (M = Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti, V, and Zr) semiconductor, we constructed 36 metal/semiconductor contacts. For vdWs contacts, although Ohmic contacts can be formed at the interface, the highest tunneling probability (PTB) is only 3.11%. As expected, the PTB can be significantly improved, as high as 48.73%, when MSi2N4, accompanied by surface nitrogen vacancies, forms an interface covalent bond with X3C2. Simultaneously, weak FLP and Ohmic contact remain at the covalent-bond-based surface, attributing to the protection of the MSi2N4 band-edge electronic states by the outlying Si-N sublayer. Our work provides a promising path for advancing the progress of 2D electronic and photoelectronic devices.
KEYWORDS two-dimensional (2D) material, metal-semiconductor contacts, tunneling-barrier, Schottky barrier, density functional theory 1 Introduction With the miniaturization of devices, the performance of semiconductor devices is increasingly dependent on interface characteristics rather than inherent material properties [1]. As a critical path of carrier injection in the device, the metal-semiconductor contact interface plays a crucial role in achieving high-performance electronic nanodevices. For conventional three-dimensional (3D) metal-semiconductor contacts, the interface generally suffers from a non-tunable Schottky barrier due to the strong Fermi level pinning (FLP) effect [2−9], resulting in high contact resistance [10], which presents great challenges for charge transport. The FLP mainly derives from metal-induced gap states (MIGS) or disorderly-induced gap states (DIGS) [9, 11−13].
Under the FLP effect, the Schottky barrier fails to reduce to the expected value by changing the work function of the metal, deviating significantly from the Schottky–Mott limit [14−16]. By contrast, two-dimensional (2D) metal-semiconductor contacts with the smooth planar surface can significantly weaken the FLP effect, inducing the obedience of the Schottky–Mott rule [17−19].
However, the vdWs gap inevitably leads to an additional tunneling barrier, increasing the interface barrier [20, 21]. How to suppress the FLP effect and the vdWs gap-induced tunneling barrier simultaneously is an excellent challenge for the high performance of the metal-semiconductor contact interface.
Recently, MSi2N4 (M = Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti, W, and Zr), a 2D septuple-layered semiconductor with unusual electronic properties, has received increasing attention [22−34]. One remarkable characteristic of MSi2N4 is that band-edge electronic states are mainly contributed by the M-N inner sublayer [35, 36].
Thus, the outer Si-N sublayer acts as a protective layer. Such a unique configuration makes MSi2N4 highly susceptible to surface manipulation for better carrier transport. For 2D electrode materials, X3C2 (X = Cd, Hg, and Zn), as a carbon-based metal material, possesses a graphene-like band structure that linearly crosses the Fermi level at the vertices of the hexagonal Brillouin zone [37]. This feature makes them excellent choices for electrode materials due to their high carrier mobility, conductivity, and thermal conductivity. When 2D MSi2N4 contacts X3C2 via the vdWs bonds, Ohmic contacts can be easily achieved by matching their work functions (WFs) due to Fermi level depinning [38, 39].
Unfortunately, as mentioned above, the performance of interface ISSN 1998-0124 CN 11-5974/O4 2024, 17(11): 10227−10234 https://doi.org/10.1007/s12274-024-6877-x Address correspondence to Bing Wang, wb@henu.edu.cn; Yongtao Li, liyt@njupt.edu.cn; Xianghong Niu, xhniu@njupt.edu.cn transport is limited by the vdWs gap-induced tunneling barrier.
Considering the unique electronic properties of MSi2N4, surface defects will not lead to FLP due to the outlying Si-N atomic layers acting as a natural buffer layer. Note that the corresponding electron density can be localized at the surface defect, which can have a chance to induce a transformation from the sp2 to sp3 hybridization of C atoms in the carbon-based X3C2. Thus, the vdWs gap is converted to covalent contacts, forming a carrier injection channel and suppressing the tunneling barrier. However, up to date, there is still a lack of corresponding exploration to suppress tunneling barriers and FLP for 2D metal-semiconductor contacts simultaneously.
In this work, we conduct a systematic analysis of the contact property based on 2D X3C2 carbon-based metal and 2D MSi2N4 semiconductor. Although Ohmic behavior can be observed in vdW-type contacts, the vdWs gap results in a large width and height of tunneling barriers, with the maximum value of tunneling possibility (PTB) being only 3.11%. Inspired by the band-edge electronic states of MSi2N4 protected by the outlying Si-N sublayer, defect engineering on the surface of MSi2N4 can be used to induce the transformation of carbon-based metal X3C2 from sp2 to sp3 hybridization, thus creating a charge injection channel and suppressing tunneling barriers significantly. This enables the PTB value to be up to 48.73%. Meanwhile, FLP is weak, and Ohmic contacts can be achieved easily. Furthermore, the I–V curves, exhibiting a rough linear relationship, further confirm the Ohmic contact characteristics for both vdW and covalent-type contacts.
Notably, covalent-type contacts present superior charge transport based on the higher current values under the same bias voltage. 2 Experimental Calculation method. This work used the VASP software to calculate the structure and electronic properties of the X3C2/MSi2N4 interface through density functional theory (DFT) [40, 41]. The Perdew–Burke–Ermzerhof (PBE) functional method was used for the exchange correlation functional [42]. The Brillouin zone of the system used a 2 × 2 × 1 K-space grid, and the cutoff energy of the plane wave was 500 eV. All atoms were fully optimized until the energy change of the system was less than 10−4 √ 7 √ 7 √ 7 √ 7 √ 3 √ 3 √ 13 √ 13 eV and the force change was less than 10−1 eV. The metal X3C2 was placed on the MSi2N4 to form a vdWs heterojunction. To minimize the lattice mismatch rate, a supercell mode was used for matching, and the matching modes were set as follows: (1×1) Cd3C2/( × ) MSi2N4, (1×1) Hg3C2/( × ) MSi2N4, and ( × ) Zn3C2/( × ) MSi2N4. In this way, the lattice mismatch rate between 2D metal materials and semiconductor materials was controlled to be within 5%. In addition, to avoid the interaction between adjacent layers, a 25 Å vacuum layer was used in the Z direction of the unit cell. Furthermore, a dipole correction was applied in the Z direction to mitigate errors in total energy, electrostatic potential, and atomic forces arising from the periodic boundary conditions [43].
For the electronic transport properties of the system, the non-equilibrium Green’s function (NEGF) method based on DFT in the Nanodcal software package was employed to investigate the electronic transport properties of heterojunctions [44, 45]. The Landauer formula for calculating the transport current is Eq. (1) [46] I(Vb) = −2q h w T(E,VL,VR)[fL(E,VL)−fR(E,VR )]dE (1) T(E,VL,VR) fL(E,VL) fR(E,VR) where represents the electron transmission coefficient, and respectively denote the Fermi distribution functions of the left and right electrodes. For studies on electron transport, the Z direction is typically set as the vacuum layer. In the calculation of transmission spectra, the k-point sampling for the x, y, and z directions is set as 1, 300, and 1, respectively. In the central scattering region, a semiconductor with a 1 × 2 supercell was used, forming two matched heterojunctions as the buffer layer, with an additional heterojunction selected as the electrode region. 3 Results and discussion Benefiting from the pristine interface of 2D materials, vdW-type contacts facilitate suppressing FLP and form Ohmic contacts (Fig.

If the surface carbon atoms undergo sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation by surface defect engineering, thus circumventing the vdWs gap and converting vdWs bonding to covalent bonding, this could provide an efficient channel by orbital overlap for carrier transport (Fig. 1(c)). However, in the case of most 2D semiconductors, the band-edge states are located in the outlying atomic layers (Fig. 1(d)). When the in-plane atoms form strong orbital overlaps with 2D metal acting as covalent bonds, the band-edge states of the semiconductor will be significantly affected via the generation of MIGSs, inducing the appearance of FLP. In contrast, if we select semiconductors with band-edge states located in the inner atom layer, the strong interfacial interaction will have a minimal influence on the band-edge states of the semiconductor (Fig. 1(e)). Therefore, it is possible to suppress the tunneling barrier and FLP, and achieve Ohmic contacts in 2D metal-semiconductor contacts simultaneously (Fig. 1(f)). 3.1 Geometric and electronic structure of X3C2 and MSi2N4 metal-semiconductor vdWs contacts Three types of carbon-based metals (Cd3C2, Hg3C2, and Zn3C2) were used for the X3C2/MSi2N4 vdWs contacts. The optimized structures are displayed in Fig. 2(a), with lattice constants of 7.26, 7.20, and 6.59 Å and WFs of 4.33, 4.33, and 4.58 eV, respectively.
The band structures of X3C2 are similar to that of graphene, exhibiting a Dirac cone structure, in agreement with previous reports (Fig. 2(b) and Fig. S1 in the Electronic Supplementary Material (ESM)) [50]. For the six types of monolayer MSi2N4 semiconductors, Fig. 2(c) and Table S1 in the ESM provide a summary of the lattice parameters, bandgap, work functions, ionization potential, and electron affinity. All MSi2N4 exhibit indirect band gap characteristics, ranging from 0.5 to 2.1 eV (Fig.
S1 in the ESM), in good agreement with previous report [51].
Taking MoSi2N4 as an example, according to the projected band structures in Fig. 2(b), the band edges are mainly contributed by the Mo-N inner sublayer, and the Si-N outer sublayer acts as a protective layer for the band edges. These features make MSi2N4 possess great potential to modify the surface for better metal-semiconductor contacts.

The interlayer distance varies from 3.12 to 3.36 Å, as typical vdWs interlayer distance. The stability of vdWs contacts was evaluated by binding energies (Eb) in Eq. All binding energies are negative, ranging from −0.01 to −0.02 eV, indicating that the vdWs contacts are energetically favorable and stable.
The Schottky barrier is a key indicator for evaluating the charge transfer properties at the metal-semiconductor interface. Two types of Schottky barrier exist in X3C2/MSi2N4 vdWs contacts: the n- or p-type Schottky barrier, defined by the energy difference between the Fermi level of X3C2/MSi2N4 vdWs contacts and the CBM/VBM of MSi2N4, as follows ϕn = ECBM −EF ϕp = EF −EVBM (3) where ECBM, EVBM, and EF are the energy of the CBM and VBM of the MSi2N4 monolayer and Fermi energy of the X3C2/MSi2N4 vdWs contact [52], respectively.
For the 18 types of vdWs contacts based on the 2D carbon-based metal X3C2 and 2D semiconductor MSi2N4, the value of Fermi level and CBM/VBM can be identified from the projected band structures of X3C2/MSi2N4 vdWs contacts (see Figs 3(b)−3(g) and Fig. S2 in the ESM). When Φn < Φp or Φn > Φp, the contact type is classified as an n-type Schottky barrier or a p-type Schottky barrier, respectively. If Φn or Φp is negative, the Schottky barrier height (SBH) is vanished and Ohmic contacts are formed, which facilitates the free transport of carriers between the metal and the semiconductor [53, 54]. The corresponding SBH values are summarized in Fig. 3(h). Most of the carbon-based metal X3C2 contacts with MSi2N4 do not exhibit energy state hybridization at the interface due to the weak vdW interaction. There are many n-type Ohmic contacts and quasi-Ohmic contacts due to the low metal work function (4.33–4.58 eV), indicating that FLP is weak and Ohmic contacts can be easily achieved by matching the different work function values of metals and semiconductors appropriately.
For vdWs contacts, although the SBH can be effectively reduced below the Fermi level, the interfacial vdWs gap can induce a large tunneling barrier, significantly impacting carrier transport efficiency. As shown in Fig. 5(a), the VBM and CBM electronic states of MSi2N4 are mainly contributed by the M-N inner sublayer. When the contact interfaces are linked by covalent bonds, the band edges of MSi2N4 remain undisturbed by the interface bonds due to the protection of the Si-N outer sublayer.
This intriguing behavior not only reduces the tunneling barrier but also ensures a weak FLP based on the protection for the band-edge electronic states of MSi2N4.

By generating the unsaturated bonds on the surface of MSi2N4, the carbon-based metal has a high possibility of forming stable C–Si bonds across the interface. Notably, the transformation of hybridization from sp2 to sp3 in 2D carbon-based metals will result in a large orbital overlap, which should lead to more geometric distortion for the thin X3C2 rather than MSi2N4. The effect will gradually weaken with the increase of 2D metal layer number. Once there are up to three layers, the interaction can be ignored (see Fig. S4 in the ESM). Hence, in order to suitably simulate the effect in the following section, we employ the bilayer of X3C2. Compared with vdWs contacts, the covalent-bond-based interface exhibits a strong interaction. S5 and S6 in the ESM, there is more charge accumulation and depletion occurring at the covalent interface. specifically, charge depletion states are present in the MSi2N4 interface, while charge accumulation states are observed in the Hg3C2 interface, indicating that the charge is transferred from the MSi2N4 to Hg3C2.
Next, we further investigated the covalent contact properties between X3C2 and MSi2N4. The projected band structures of monolayer MSi2N4 were calculated and the results are shown in Figs. 6(a)−6(c) and Fig. S7 in the ESM, and the VBM of MSi2N4 crosses the Fermi level. Thus, p-type Ohmic contacts are formed, in agreement with the charge density difference analysis mentioned above. The electronic states around the CBM and VBM are nearly unperturbed by defect states due to the Si-N outer sublayer protection, which avoids the metal-semiconductor interactions-induced interfacial gap states. Therefore, the FLP effect is still well restrained at the covalent interface, and Ohmic contacts can be easily formed by matching the appropriate work functions of X3C2 and MSi2N4.
To explore the covalent bonds at the interface, taking the Hg3C2/CrSi2N4 covalent contact as an example (Fig. 6(g)), the hybridization states of the 2s2p orbital of C in Hg3C2 and the 3s3p orbitals of Si in CrSi2N4 locate at the same energy around the Fermi level. Meanwhile, the 2s2p orbitals of the C atoms contribute more to the density of states (DOS) than the 3s3p orbitals of the Si atoms, indicating that Hg3C2 can form strong orbital overlaps with CrSi2N4. This result can also be further confirmed by the crystal orbital Hamilton population (COHP), where the negative and positive parts indicate the bonding and antibonding states, respectively. All bonding states are observed below the Fermi level, while antibonding states are detected solely above the Fermi level [57, 58]. This demonstrates a strong orbital hybridization between the C and Si atoms, resulting in the formation of a stable C–Si covalent bond (Fig. S9 in the ESM).
Importantly, when X3C2 forms the covalent bond with MSi2N4, the tunneling barrier can be effectively suppressed due to the overlap states. Thus, a lower ΦTB and narrower WTB of tunneling barrier can be obtained at the interface, as illustrated in Figs.
6(d)−6(f) and Fig. S8 in the ESM. The ΦTB (WTB) values of Hg3C2/CrSi2N4, Hg3C2/MoSi2N4, and Hg3C2/WSi2N4 covalent contacts are 2.35 eV (0.79 eV), 2.10 eV (0.74 eV), and 2.09 eV (0.73 eV), respectively, which significantly reduces compared with these of vdWs contacts. The PTB values of all X3C2/MSi2N4 covalent contacts are presented in Fig. 6(i), and all exceed 25%.
Among them, Zn3C2/MoSi2N4 exhibits the highest value, reaching 48.73%. Therefore, it is possible to achieve weak FLP and Ohmic contacts as well as suppress tunneling barriers simultaneously. 3.3 Quantum transport properties In order to further verify the feasibility of covalent-bond-based contacts, we constructed a dual-probe system with a central scattering region connecting two semi-infinite electrodes to explore the transport property (Figs. 7(a) and 7(b)). The contacts between Hg3C2 and CrSi2N4, MoSi2N4, WSi2N4 semiconductors are taken as examples.” in the manuscript. The transmission spectra under zero bias are presented in Figs. 7(c) and 7(d). For vdW-type contact, the Hg3C2/CrSi2N4 exhibits transport channels at the Fermi level, indicating good Ohmic contacts.
Hg3C2/MoSi2N4 and Hg3C2/Wsi2N4 show a transport gap, and the Schottky barrier is approximately 0.5 and 0.9 eV, respectively. In contrast, for covalent contacts, all of them exhibit transport channels at the Fermi level and completely Ohmic contacts.
Furthermore, the transmission coefficient of covalent contacts at the Fermi level is larger than that of vdWs contacts due to the greater charge transfer.

Therefore, for the interface linked by covalent bonds, tunneling-barrier-inhibition, weak FLP, and Ohmic contacts can be realized simultaneously, giving rise to better device performance. 4 Conclusions In conclusion, by inducing the 2D carbon-based metal X3C2 with a hybridization transformation from sp2 to sp3 through surface defect engineering onto the MSi2N4 semiconductor, the tunneling barrier can be suppressed by forming a large orbital overlap.
Simultaneously, weak FLP and Ohmic can be obtained. This significantly enhances carrier transport across the interface.
Specifically, although vdW-type contacts can exhibit weak FLP and Ohmic behavior, the vdWs gap at the interface leads to a large tunneling barrier, with the maximum value of PTB being only 3.11%. Inducing the transformation of the C atomic hybrid type from sp2 to sp3 in X3C2 and forming covalent bonds with MSi2N4 result in a narrower width and lower height of the tunneling barrier, which can increase PTB up to 48.73%. Meanwhile, the outlying Si-N protection layers of MSi2N4 semiconductors ensure that weak FLP and Ohmic contact are maintained at covalent contacts. Furthermore, the characteristics of Ohmic contact can be further confirmed by the I–V curves. Covalent-type contacts give rise to a better carrier injection than that of vdWs contacts due to the higher current. This work offers an effective strategy for advancing 2D metal-semiconductor contacts to higher-performance electronic devices. args.summary:
This is a research article published in Nano Research (2024, 17(11): 10227–10234) investigating a novel strategy to simultaneously suppress tunneling barriers and Fermi level pinning (FLP) in 2D metal-semiconductor contacts by inducing an sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D carbon-based metals via surface defect engineering.

**Study Design:**
- Authors: Wenchao Shan, Anqi Shi, Zhuorong Zhong, Xiuyun Zhang, Bing Wang, Yongtao Li, and Xianghong Niu (from Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Yangzhou University, and Henan University)
- Received 16 May 2024, revised 25 June 2024, accepted 10 July 2024
- Constructed 36 metal/semiconductor contacts using 2D carbon-based metals X3C2 (X = Cd, Hg, Zn) and 2D MSi2N4 semiconductors (M = Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti, V, Zr)
- Used density functional theory (DFT) via VASP software with PBE functional, and non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) method via Nanodcal for transport calculations

**Key Findings:**
1. **vdWs contacts**: Although Ohmic contacts can be formed with weak FLP, the inherent van der Waals gap induces large tunneling barriers. The highest tunneling probability (PTB) was only 3.11%. Tunneling barrier heights ranged from 4.11–5.00 eV with widths of 1.86–2.22 eV.

2. **Covalent contacts**: By inducing surface nitrogen vacancies in MSi2N4 and transforming carbon atoms in X3C2 from sp2 to sp3 hybridization, covalent C–Si bonds form across the interface. This creates large orbital overlap forming an efficient carrier channel. The PTB significantly improved to up to 48.73% (Zn3C2/MoSi2N4), with all covalent contacts exceeding 25%.

3. **Dual benefit**: The outlying Si-N sublayer of MSi2N4 protects the band-edge electronic states (contributed by the M-N inner sublayer), so weak FLP and Ohmic contacts are maintained even with strong covalent interfacial bonding.

4. **Transport properties**: Quantum transport calculations showed covalent contacts achieve completely Ohmic behavior with transport channels at the Fermi level, whereas some vdWs contacts exhibited Schottky barriers (0.5–0.9 eV). I–V curves confirmed Ohmic characteristics for both types, but covalent contacts produced higher currents (up to ~3 µA vs ~1 µA under 0.2 V bias for Hg3C2/CrSi2N4).

**Materials Properties:**
- X3C2 metals: lattice constants 7.26 (Cd3C2), 7.20 (Hg3C2), and 6.59 (Zn3C2) Å; work functions 4.33, 4.33, and 4.58 eV respectively
- MSi2N4 semiconductors: indirect band gaps ranging from 0.5 to 2.1 eV
- Lattice mismatch controlled within 5% using supercell matching modes

**Conclusions:**
The work demonstrates an effective strategy to simultaneously suppress tunneling barriers, maintain weak FLP, and achieve Ohmic contacts in 2D metal-semiconductor interfaces, offering a promising path for advancing 2D electronic and photoelectronic device performance.
args.key_excerpts: "For vdWs contacts, although Ohmic contacts can be formed at the interface, the highest tunneling probability (PTB) is only 3.11%. As expected, the PTB can be significantly improved, as high as 48.73%, when MSi2N4, accompanied by surface nitrogen vacancies, forms an interface covalent bond with X3C2."
