From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Type of electrical contact to semiconductors

| Ohmic contact |
| --- |
| [Component type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_component#Classification "Electronic component") | Connection |
| Working principle‍ | [electrical junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_junction "Electrical junction") |
| [Electronic symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_symbol "Electronic symbol") |
| Semiconductor region with one ohmic connection |

An **ohmic contact** is a non-[rectifying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifier "Rectifier") [electrical junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_junction "Electrical junction"): a junction between two conductors that has a linear [current–voltage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current–voltage_characteristic "Current–voltage characteristic") (I–V) curve as with [Ohm's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohm's_law "Ohm's law"). Low-resistance ohmic contacts are used to allow charge to flow easily in both directions between the two conductors, without blocking due to rectification or excess power dissipation due to voltage thresholds.

By contrast, a junction or contact that does not demonstrate a linear I–V curve is called non-ohmic. Non-ohmic contacts come in a number of forms, such as [p–n junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P–n_junction "P–n junction"), [Schottky barrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schottky_barrier "Schottky barrier"), rectifying [heterojunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterojunction "Heterojunction"), or [breakdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalanche_breakdown "Avalanche breakdown") junction.

Generally the term "ohmic contact" implicitly refers to an ohmic contact of a metal to a semiconductor, where achieving ohmic [contact resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_resistance "Contact resistance") is possible but requires careful technique. Metal–metal ohmic contacts are relatively simpler to make, by ensuring direct contact between the metals without intervening layers of insulating contamination, excessive roughness or [oxidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation"); various techniques are used to create ohmic metal–metal junctions ([soldering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soldering "Soldering"), [welding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welding "Welding"), [crimping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimp_connection "Crimp connection"), [deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thin-film_deposition "Thin-film deposition"), [electroplating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroplating "Electroplating"), etc.).

Stable contacts at semiconductor interfaces, with low [contact resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_resistance "Contact resistance") and linear I–V behavior, are critical for the performance and reliability of [semiconductor devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_devices "Semiconductor devices"), and their preparation and characterization are major efforts in circuit fabrication. Poorly prepared junctions to semiconductors can easily show rectifying behaviour by causing [depletion of the semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depletion_region "Depletion region") near the junction, rendering the device useless by blocking the flow of charge between those devices and the external circuitry. Ohmic contacts to semiconductors are typically constructed by depositing thin metal films of a carefully chosen composition, possibly followed by [annealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annealing_(metallurgy) "Annealing (metallurgy)") to alter the semiconductor–metal bond.

## Physics of formation of metal–semiconductor ohmic contacts

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ohmic_contact&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Physics of formation of metal–semiconductor ohmic contacts")]

Main article: [Metal–semiconductor junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal–semiconductor_junction "Metal–semiconductor junction")

Both ohmic contacts and [Schottky barriers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schottky_barrier "Schottky barrier") are dependent on the Schottky barrier height, which sets the threshold for the excess energy an electron requires to pass from the semiconductor to the metal. For the junction to admit electrons easily in both directions (ohmic contact), the barrier height must be small in at least some parts of the junction surface. To form an excellent ohmic contact (low resistance), the barrier height should be small everywhere and furthermore the interface should not reflect electrons.

The Schottky barrier height between a metal and semiconductor is naively predicted by the [Schottky–Mott rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schottky–Mott_rule "Schottky–Mott rule") to be proportional to the difference of the metal-vacuum [work function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_function "Work function") and the semiconductor-vacuum [electron affinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_affinity "Electron affinity"). In practice, most metal–semiconductor interfaces do not follow this rule to the predicted degree. Instead, the chemical termination of the semiconductor crystal against a metal creates electron states within its [band gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_gap "Band gap"). The nature of these [metal-induced gap states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal-induced_gap_states "Metal-induced gap states") and their occupation by electrons tends to pin the center of the band gap to the Fermi level, an effect known as [Fermi level pinning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi_level_pinning "Fermi level pinning"). Thus, the heights of the Schottky barriers in metal–semiconductor contacts often show little dependence on the value of the semiconductor or metal work functions, in stark contrast to the Schottky–Mott rule.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Different semiconductors exhibit this [Fermi level pinning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi_level_pinning "Fermi level pinning") to different degrees, but a technological consequence is that high quality (low resistance) ohmic contacts are usually difficult to form in important semiconductors such as [silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon "Silicon") and [gallium arsenide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallium_arsenide "Gallium arsenide").

The Schottky–Mott rule is not entirely incorrect since, in practice, metals with high work functions form the best contacts to p-type semiconductors, while those with low work functions form the best contacts to n-type semiconductors. Unfortunately experiments have shown that the predictive power of the model doesn't extend much beyond this statement. Under realistic conditions, contact metals may react with semiconductor surfaces to form a compound with new electronic properties. A contamination layer at the interface may effectively widen the barrier. The surface of the semiconductor may [reconstruct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_reconstruction "Surface reconstruction") leading to a new electronic state. The dependence of contact resistance on the details of the interfacial chemistry is what makes the reproducible fabrication of ohmic contacts such a manufacturing challenge.

## Preparation and characterization of ohmic contacts

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ohmic_contact&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Preparation and characterization of ohmic contacts")]

The fabrication of the ohmic contacts is a much-studied part of [materials engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_engineering "Materials engineering") that nonetheless remains something of an art. The reproducible, reliable fabrication of contacts relies on extreme cleanliness of the semiconductor surface. Since a *native [oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxide "Oxide")* rapidly forms on the surface of [silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon "Silicon"), for example, the performance of a contact can depend sensitively on the details of preparation. Often the contact region is heavily [doped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_(semiconductor) "Doping (semiconductor)") to ensure the type of contact wanted. As a rule, ohmic contacts on semiconductors form more easily when the semiconductor is highly [doped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_(semiconductor) "Doping (semiconductor)") near the junction; a high doping narrows the [depletion region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depletion_region "Depletion region") at the interface and allow electrons to flow in both directions easily at any bias by [tunneling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunneling_Effect "Tunneling Effect") through the barrier.

The fundamental steps in contact fabrication are semiconductor surface cleaning, contact metal deposition, patterning and annealing. Surface cleaning may be performed by sputter-etching, chemical etching, reactive gas etching or ion milling. For example, the native oxide of silicon may be removed with a [hydrofluoric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrofluoric_acid "Hydrofluoric acid") dip, while [GaAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GaAs "GaAs") is more typically cleaned by a bromine-methanol dip. After cleaning, metals are deposited via [sputter deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputter_deposition "Sputter deposition"), [evaporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaporation_(deposition) "Evaporation (deposition)") or [chemical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition") (CVD). Sputtering is a faster and more convenient method of metal deposition than evaporation but the ion bombardment from the plasma may induce surface states or even invert the charge carrier type at the surface. For this reason the gentler but still rapid CVD may be used. Post-deposition annealing of contacts is useful for relieving stress as well as for inducing any desirable reactions between the metal and the semiconductor.

Because deposited metals can themselves react in ambient conditions, to the detriment of the contacts' electrical properties, it is common to form ohmic contacts with layered structures, with the bottom layer, in contact with the semiconductor, chosen for its ability to induce ohmic behaviour. A diffusion barrier-layer may be used to prevent the layers from mixing during any annealing process.

The measurement of [contact resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_resistance "Contact resistance") is most simply performed using a [four-point probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-terminal_sensing "Four-terminal sensing") although for more accurate determination, use of the [transmission line method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmission_line_measurement "Transmission line measurement") is typical.

## Technologically important kinds of contacts

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ohmic_contact&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Technologically important kinds of contacts")]

[Aluminum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminum "Aluminum") was originally the most important contact metal for silicon which was used with either the n-type or p-type semiconductor. As with other reactive metals, Al contributes to contact formation by consuming oxygen from native silicon-dioxide residue. Pure aluminum did react with the silicon, so it was replaced by silicon-doped aluminum and eventually by silicides less prone to diffuse during subsequent high-temperature processing.

Modern ohmic contacts to silicon such as titanium-tungsten disilicide are usually [silicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicide "Silicide") made by CVD. Contacts are often made by depositing the transition metal and forming the silicide by [annealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annealing_(metallurgy) "Annealing (metallurgy)") with the result that the silicide may be [non-stoichiometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-stoichiometric "Non-stoichiometric"). Silicide contacts can also be deposited by direct sputtering of the compound or by ion implantation of the transition metal followed by annealing.

Formation of contacts to compound semiconductors is considerably more difficult than with silicon. For example, GaAs surfaces tend to lose [arsenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenic "Arsenic") and the trend towards As loss can be considerably exacerbated by the deposition of metal. In addition, the volatility of As limits the amount of post-deposition annealing that GaAs devices will tolerate. One solution for GaAs and other compound semiconductors is to deposit a low-bandgap [alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloy "Alloy") contact layer as opposed to a heavily doped layer. For example, GaAs itself has a smaller bandgap than AlGaAs and so a layer of GaAs near its surface can promote ohmic behavior. In general the technology of ohmic contacts for [III-V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/III-V "III-V") and [II-VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/II-VI_semiconductor_compound "II-VI semiconductor compound") semiconductors is much less developed than for Si.

Transparent or semi-transparent contacts are necessary for [active matrix LCDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LCD#Active_matrix_technologies "LCD"), [optoelectronic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optoelectronic "Optoelectronic") devices such as [laser diodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_diode "Laser diode") and [photovoltaics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaics "Photovoltaics"). The most popular choice is [indium tin oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indium_tin_oxide "Indium tin oxide"), a metal that is formed by [reactive sputtering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_sputtering "Reactive sputtering") of an In-Sn target in an oxide atmosphere.

## Significance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ohmic_contact&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Significance")]

The [RC time constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RC_time_constant "RC time constant") associated with [contact resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_resistance "Contact resistance") can limit the [frequency response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency_response "Frequency response") of devices. The charging and discharging of the leads resistance is a major cause of power dissipation in high-[clock-rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clock_rate "Clock rate") digital electronics. [Contact resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_resistance "Contact resistance") causes power dissipation by [Joule heating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joule_heating "Joule heating") in low-frequency and analog circuits (for example, [solar cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cells "Solar cells")) made from less common semiconductors. The establishment of a contact fabrication methodology is a critical part of the technological development of any new semiconductor. [Electromigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromigration "Electromigration") and [delamination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delamination "Delamination") at contacts are also a limitation on the lifetime of electronic devices.

This Wikipedia article defines and explains the physics, fabrication, and technological significance of ohmic contacts in semiconductor devices. An ohmic contact is a non-rectifying electrical junction between two conductors that exhibits a linear current-voltage (I-V) curve consistent with Ohm's law. Low-resistance ohmic contacts allow charge to flow easily in both directions without rectification blocking or excess power dissipation.

KEY PHYSICS: The formation of metal-semiconductor ohmic contacts depends on the Schottky barrier height. While the Schottky-Mott rule predicts barrier height based on the difference between metal work function and semiconductor electron affinity, most interfaces deviate from this rule due to Fermi level pinning caused by metal-induced gap states. Practically, high work function metals form the best contacts to p-type semiconductors, while low work function metals work best for n-type. High-quality ohmic contacts are difficult to form in important semiconductors like silicon and gallium arsenide due to Fermi level pinning.

FABRICATION: The fundamental steps are semiconductor surface cleaning (via sputter-etching, chemical etching, reactive gas etching, or ion milling), contact metal deposition (via sputter deposition, evaporation, or CVD), patterning, and annealing. Surface cleanliness is critical, with native oxide removal using hydrofluoric acid for silicon and bromine-methanol for GaAs. Heavy doping near the junction narrows the depletion region, allowing electron tunneling through the barrier in both directions. Layered structures with diffusion barriers are commonly used. Contact resistance is measured using a four-point probe or the more accurate transmission line method.

TECHNOLOGICALLY IMPORTANT CONTACTS: Aluminum was originally the most important silicon contact metal but was replaced by silicon-doped aluminum and eventually silicides (e.g., titanium-tungsten disilicide) made by CVD. Compound semiconductor contacts (GaAs, III-V, II-VI) are considerably more difficult due to arsenic loss and volatility. A table lists common contact materials for Si, Ge, GaAs, GaN, InSb, ZnO, CuInGaSe2, HgCdTe, and diamond. Transparent contacts (typically indium tin oxide) are needed for LCDs, laser diodes, and photovoltaics.

SIGNIFICANCE: Contact resistance creates RC time constants that limit device frequency response, causes power dissipation through Joule heating in low-frequency circuits and solar cells, and electromigration and delamination at contacts limit device lifetime. Establishing contact fabrication methodology is critical for developing any new semiconductor technology.

--- SOURCE 1: Contact Resistance Optimization in MoS2 Field-Effect Transistors through Reverse Sputtering-Induced Structural Modifications ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12022942

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces (March 11, 2025) by researchers from AMO GmbH, RWTH Aachen University, Eindhoven University of Technology, and AIXTRON SE. The study investigates the use of reverse sputtering (Ar+ ion bombardment via RF-generated plasma) to reduce contact resistance (Rc) in molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) field-effect transistors (FETs).

Key findings and methodology:
- MoS₂ FETs suffer from Schottky barriers at the metal-MoS₂ interface, causing high contact resistance. The study explores inducing a phase transition from semiconducting 2H-MoS₂ to metallic 1T-MoS₂ via reverse sputtering at the contact interface.
- Multilayer MOCVD-grown MoS₂ (~2.5 nm thick, ~4 layers) was transferred onto SiO₂/Si substrates. Devices were fabricated with nickel (Ni) top-contacts (TOP-FETs) where only the contact regions were sputter-treated, and bottom-contact (BOT-FETs) control devices where the entire MoS₂ was exposed.
- Characterization via PL, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS confirmed that reverse sputtering induces sulfur vacancies (VS) and a 2H-to-1T phase transition in MoS₂. XPS showed the S/Mo ratio decreasing from ~2.0 (pristine) to 1.80 (200 W treatment), with full 2H-to-1T conversion observed after sputtering.
- Optimal results were achieved at 75 W reverse sputtering for 10 s: Rc decreased from 1126 kΩ·μm (pristine) to 413 kΩ·μm (a reduction to less than 50% of untreated devices), and output current increased approximately 150-fold.
- Two-probe mobility (μ₂ₚ) nearly doubled for the 75 W sample (0.81 ± 0.20 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ vs. 0.48 ± 0.10 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ for pristine). On/off ratios of 10⁶ were maintained for pristine, 25 W, and 75 W samples, degrading to 10⁵ at 200 W.
- Excessive sputtering power (200 W) caused oxidation to MoOₓ and severe degradation. Insufficient power (25 W) produced too few sulfur vacancies and increased Rc. The 75 W condition represented the optimal balance between phase conversion and material damage.
- The mechanism involves sulfur vacancies creating heavily n-doped regions that narrow the Schottky barrier, plus the formation of conductive 1T-MoS₂ that enhances electron injection from Ni contacts.

The authors conclude that reverse sputtering is a scalable, CMOS-compatible, and clean method for optimizing contact resistance in MoS₂ FETs, with potential for broader application in 2D material-based microelectronics. Funding was provided by EU Horizon 2020/Horizon Europe programs, German BMBF projects (NEUROTEC, NEUROTEC 2, NeuroSys), and the German Research Foundation (DFG).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"MoS₂–FETs exposed to optimized reverse sputtering conditions in the contact area show Rc values reduced to less than 50% of their untreated counterparts."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Semimetal contacts to monolayer semiconductor ---
URL: http://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023JPhD...56w4001S/abstract

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper (published in Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics, June 2023) investigating electrical contact properties between semimetal electrodes (bismuth and antimony) and monolayer 2D transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) semiconductors. The study used first-principles density functional theory (DFT) simulations on six TMDC semiconductors (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2, MoTe2, and WTe2) with two semimetal contact materials (Bi and Sb).

Key findings:
- Bi and Sb work functions align well with TMDC conduction band edges, resulting in predominantly Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts.
- Semimetal/TMDC contacts have significantly larger interlayer distances than metal/TMDC counterparts, leading to only weak metalization of TMDC upon contact formation.
- This weak metalization generates semimetal-induced gap states (SMIGSs) extending below the conduction band minimum, providing an effective mechanism to reduce or eliminate n-type Schottky barrier height (SBH) while preserving the electronic structures of the 2D TMDC.
- The authors propose a modified Schottky-Mott rule accounting for SMIGS, interface dipole potential, and Fermi level shifting, which shows improved agreement with DFT-simulated SBH.
- Sb/TMDC contacts generally exhibit lower tunneling-specific resistivity than Bi counterparts, indicating better charge injection efficiency with Sb contacts.
- The findings highlight Bi and Sb as promising companion electrode materials for advancing 2D semiconductor device technology.

Paper details: Authors include Su Tong, Li Yueyan, Wang Qianqian, Zhao Weiwei, Cao Liemao, and Ang Yee Sin. DOI: 10.1088/1361-6463/acc53f; arXiv:2212.03003; 12 pages, 7 figures.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"As Bi and Sb work functions energetically aligns well with the TMDC conduction band edge, Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts are prevalent."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: [PDF] arXiv:2212.03003v1 [cond-mat.mtrl-sci] 6 Dec 2022 ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.03003

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) study investigating the electrical contact properties between semimetal electrodes (bismuth, Bi, and antimony, Sb) and six monolayer transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) semiconductors (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2, MoTe2, WTe2), covering 12 semimetal/TMDC contact heterostructures.

Key findings:
- Recent experiments showed semimetal Bi achieves ultralow contact resistance (as low as 123 Ω·µm) with monolayer MoS2, motivating broader investigation of semimetal contacts.
- The Fermi levels of Bi (-4.12 eV) and Sb (-4.25 eV below vacuum) align closely with TMDC conduction band edges (~4 eV), enabling Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts.
- Semimetal/TMDC contacts have significantly larger interlayer distances (>3 Å) than metal/TMDC counterparts, resulting in only weak metalization of the TMDC upon contact formation.
- This weak metalization creates semimetal-induced gap states (SMIGS) that extend below the conduction band minimum, providing an effective mechanism to reduce or eliminate n-type Schottky barrier height (SBH) while preserving TMDC electronic structures.
- A modified Schottky-Mott rule was proposed: Φ(e)SBH = Wmetal − EEA − ΔV + ΔεF − ΔM, incorporating interface dipole potential (ΔV), Fermi level shifting (ΔεF), and the SMIGS energy window (ΔM), showing significantly improved agreement with DFT-simulated SBH compared to the original Schottky-Mott rule.
- Contacts exhibit both physisorptive (Te-based TMDCs, larger interlayer distances, positive ΔV) and chemisorptive (S- and Se-based TMDCs, smaller interlayer distances, low/negative ΔV) interfacial interactions.
- Sb/TMDC contacts generally exhibit lower tunneling-specific resistivity (10^-9 Ω·cm² order) than Bi counterparts, suggesting better charge injection efficiency and better thermal stability, making Sb a potentially superior semimetal contact material.
- DFT-calculated SBHs for Bi/MoS2 (0.075 eV) and Bi/WS2 (0.13 eV) differ slightly from experimental values (zero/Ohmic and 0.040 eV, respectively), likely due to defects in experimental contacted regions.
- Computational methods: VASP with projector augmented wave method, PBE-GGA exchange-correlation, DFT-D3 vdW corrections, 500 eV kinetic energy cutoff, 6×6×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-sampling, and ≥15 Å vacuum spacing.

The work provides a theoretical foundation and design blueprint for semimetal-enabled high-performance 2D semiconductor nanoelectronics, with potential applications in valleytronics and multiferroics. Funding came from the Singapore Ministry of Education Academic Research Fund Tier 2 Grant and SUTD-ZJU IDEA Visiting Professor Grant.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Recent experiment has uncovered semimetal bismuth (Bi) as an excellent electrical contact to monolayer MoS2 with ultralow contact resistance."

--- SOURCE 4: Antimony Semimetal Contact with Enhanced Thermal ... ---
URL: https://hanwang6.github.io/Lab_Website/iedm_2021.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (IEDM 2021, DOI: 10.1109/IEDM19574.2021.9720608) from TSMC researchers studies antimony (Sb) semimetal as a novel contact material for two-dimensional (2D) MoS2 electronics, addressing the thermal stability limitations of previously studied semimetals like tin (Sn) and bismuth (Bi).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Sb contacts achieve near-zero Schottky barrier height and contact resistance of 0.66 kΩ·µm on monolayer (1L) MoS2
- Short-channel Sb-contacted MoS2 FETs demonstrate on-state current above 600 µA/µm at VDS=1V and 1000 µA/µm at VDS=2V
- Sb has a melting point of 630.6°C, substantially higher than Bi (271.5°C) and Sn (231.9°C)
- Sb-contacted devices remain fully operational after annealing at 400°C, versus only 300°C for Bi-contacted devices—a key advantage for back-end-of-the-line (BEOL) compatibility
- Sb-contacted 1L MoS2 FET retains 80% and 64% of pristine performance after annealing at 300°C and 400°C, respectively
- Bi-contacted devices decay significantly after 300°C annealing and fail completely at 400°C
- LCH=50nm devices show ION ~600 µA/µm at VDS=1V with nearly zero drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL)

METHODOLOGY:
- 1L MoS2 grown by CVD, transferred onto 100nm SiNx/Si substrate
- He-ion-beam lithography for S/D patterning; 20nm semimetal (Bi or Sb) capped with 15nm Au via e-beam evaporation and lift-off
- PMMA encapsulation with 200°C hard baking for 30 min in N2 glovebox
- Progressive thermal annealing at 200°C, 300°C, and 400°C
- Characterization via Raman spectroscopy, AFM, TEM, EDS mapping, UPS
- DFT simulations (VASP with PBE/PAW/GGA) for interface analysis and Bi-Sb alloy predictions

ALLOY STRATEGY (DFT-predicted):
- Bi-Sb alloy could balance thermal stability and low contact resistance
- BEOL compatibility requires melting point ≥400°C, needing >20% Sb ratio
- Preferred design space: 40%-100% Sb ratio (alloy remains semimetal; 4%-40% Sb makes it a semiconductor/topological insulator)
- Bi0.5Sb0.5 predicted to offer lower barrier height (0.10 eV) than pure Sb while maintaining good conductivity and 540°C melting point

CONCLUSION: Sb semimetal offers the best balance of thermal stability and low contact resistance among semimetals for 2D electronics, making it a promising BEOL-compatible contact solution for beyond-silicon technology. Funding from Ministry of Science and Technology (Grants MOST-109-2622-8-002-003; MOST 110-2119-M-A49-001-MBK).
</summary>

"Sb semimetal is studied as the contact metal for 2D materials for the first time, demonstrating one of the lowest contact resistance among previously reported approaches for MoS2 only second to Bi."

URL: https://physicsworld.com/a/reducing-the-contact-resistance-in-2d-semiconducting-transistors

SUMMARY:

This webpage from Physics World (IOP Publishing) features a scientific article about reducing contact resistance in 2D semiconducting transistors. --- SOURCE 6: Bismuth Confinement: A Strategy for Low Resistance and Good Thermal Endurance of Integrated Contacts to MoS2 ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13045353

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in ACS Nano (2026 Feb 24;20(12):9817, DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.5c19217) titled "Bismuth Confinement: A Strategy for Low Resistance and Good Thermal Endurance of Integrated Contacts to MoS2." The work was conducted by researchers from National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), Taiwan Semiconductor Research Institute, and the National Institutes of Applied Research in Taiwan. Corresponding authors are Iuliana P. Radu (TSMC) and Chao-Hsin Chien (NYCU).

**Core Problem:** Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are promising for advanced nanoelectronics due to atomically thin bodies enabling excellent electrostatic control. However, achieving low contact resistance (RC) requires semimetals like bismuth (Bi) or antimony (Sb), which have low melting points and are thermally unstable, limiting their compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) integration that requires annealing at 400°C in H2 environments. Refractory metals are thermally stable but induce prohibitively high RC (>1 kΩ·μm).

**Key Innovation:** The authors demonstrate a "confinement strategy" using AlOx and/or TiN barriers to encapsulate Bi contacts. This enables RC values below 200 Ω·μm while preserving device performance after forming gas annealing at 400°C for up to 10 minutes.

**Key Findings:**
- Unconfined Bi melts at ~273°C and forms spherical droplets when annealed; Sb rapidly sublimates at 400°C in forming gas within 1 minute.
- AlOx capping stabilizes Sb films up to 800°C (above its 671°C melting point) and Bi up to 450°C without outgassing, melting, or agglomeration.
- Device-level demonstration: Monolayer CVD MoS2 transistors with Bi contacts on 8 nm HfO2 gate dielectric (EOT~2nm) with TiN back gate, fully encapsulated in low-temperature ALD AlOx. After 400°C forming gas annealing (10 min), devices retained RC below 200 Ω·μm with nearly ohmic injection and ION over 60 μA/μm at LCH=100 nm.
- On-current after line-resistance subtraction exceeds 1 mA/μm at VDS=1V, ranking among the highest reported for monolayer MoS2.
- Intrinsic mobility improved slightly from 27 to 32 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹ after annealing (attributed to partial defect passivation).
- TCAD simulations extracted Schottky barrier height of 70 meV and van der Waals gap of 2 Å at the MoS2/Bi interface, confirming near-ohmic contact that did not degrade through annealing.
- Fab-relevant integration test: Bi deposited by PVD in SiO2 trenches (<40 nm wide), encapsulated by conformal 200°C ALD TiN barrier and W plug. Cross-sectional TEM/EDX confirmed Bi remains fully confined without diffusion or outgassing after 400°C annealing in N2, forming gas, and vacuum environments.
- A remaining grand challenge identified: selective dielectric etch that stops on 2D TMDs (to be addressed in subsequent publications).

**Keywords:** two-dimensional semiconductors, semimetal contacts, contact resistance, back-end-of-line (BEOL) integration, monolithic 3D integration, thermal stability
</summary>

"Using a Bi confinement strategy through AlOx and/or TiN barriers, RC values below 200 Ω·μm are demonstrated while preserving device performance after forming gas annealing at 400 °C for up to 10 min; this finding is validated through the characterizations of multiple devices."

This is a research paper published in Science China Information Sciences (Vol. 67, article 160402, published May 15, 2024) titled "Contact engineering for temperature stability improvement of Bi-contacted MoS2 field effect transistors."

Authors: Zizheng Liu, Qing Zhang (equal contribution), Xiaohe Huang, Chunsen Liu, and Peng Zhou, affiliated with Fudan University (State Key Laboratory of Integrated Chip and Systems, School of Microelectronics, Zhangjiang Fudan International Innovation Center; Frontier Institute of Chip and System) and Shaoxin Laboratory. --- SOURCE 8: Low contact resistance on monolayer MoS2 field-effect ... ---
URL: https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10531719

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article from ACS Nano (Manuscript ID nn-2024-07267z.R3, submitted 29-Jul-2024) by researchers from Purdue University and the University of Texas at Dallas, led by Zheng Sun, Seong Yeoul Kim, and Joerg Appenzeller. The study investigates contact engineering for monolayer MoS2 field-effect transistors (FETs) to achieve low contact resistance using CMOS-compatible metal contacts.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Ni Contacts (Covalent Type):** Ultra-high vacuum (UHV, 3×10^-11 mbar) deposited Ni contacts achieved a record-low contact resistance of ~500 ohm·μm for ML MoS2 FETs — 5 times lower than Ni deposited under high vacuum (HV, 3×10^-6 mbar) conditions. This was achieved across 60 UHV-Ni and 64 HV-Ni FETs fabricated with four channel lengths (85nm, 185nm, 385nm, 985nm) using the transfer length method (TLM). The best UHV-Ni device reached 470 μA/μm at VDS=1V, VGS=2.5V.

2. **Bi Contacts (van der Waals Type):** Contact resistance for Bi-contacted MoS2 FETs showed no dependence on vacuum deposition conditions (more than 150 Bi-contacted FETs tested: 40 UHV-Bi and 112 HV-Bi). Bi achieves high on-currents (~400 μA/μm) with on/off ratios of ~10^8, but does not chemically react with MoS2 regardless of vacuum conditions.

3. **Interface Chemistry (XPS Analysis):**
   - UHV-Ni deposition showed stronger Ni/MoSx bonding species (20% intensity vs 17% for HV-Ni) with more metallic properties
   - HV-Ni deposition resulted in MoO3 formation (thermodynamically favored due to ΔG°f,MoO3=-266.67 kJ/mol vs ΔG°f,MoS2=-112.95 kJ/mol), reducing Ni-MoS2 bonding
   - Bi showed no detectable chemical reaction with MoS2 under either condition; Bi2O3 was detected only for HV deposition
   - Thermodynamic data support these observations (ΔG°f,Bi2S3=-46.87 kJ/mol, higher than ΔG°f,MoS2)

4. **Thermal Stability:**
   - Bi/Au contacts showed excellent thermal reliability up to 400°C with no contact resistance degradation (Au capping prevented Bi evaporation; annealing in high vacuum prevented oxidation). This contrasts with prior reports of degradation at 200°C.
   - Ni contacts degraded after 100°C annealing (on-current dropped from 200 to 125 μA/μm; contact resistance increased from 2000 to 3000 ohm·μm), attributed to Ni diffusion into the channel and oxidation of diffused Ni
   - Bi remained concentrated at contact corners after 400°C annealing without chemical reaction with MoS2

**Methods:** CVD-grown ML MoS2 on SiO2 substrates, local bottom gate structures with HfO2 dielectrics (2.8nm and 5.5nm), e-beam lithography, monochromatic XPS (Al Kα, 1486.7 eV), STEM/EDS analysis, and annealing at 100-400°C in high vacuum.

**Conclusion:** The work demonstrates that interface engineering through UHV deposition of covalent-type metals (Ni) can achieve competitive contact resistance (~500 ohm·μm) comparable to vdW-type contacts, while Bi contacts offer superior thermal stability but no dependence on deposition vacuum conditions. The study provides the first statistically meaningful correlation (120+ FETs) between interface chemistry and contact resistance for ML MoS2 FETs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We achieved a low contact resistance for ML MoS2 FETs with ultra-high vacuum (UHV, 3×10-11 mbar) deposited Ni contacts, ~500 ohm·μm, which is 5 times lower than the contact resistance achieved when deposited at high vacuum (HV, 3×10-6 mbar) conditions."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Phase-engineered low-resistance contacts for ultrathin MoS2 transistors. | Semantic Scholar ---
URL: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Phase-engineered-low-resistance-contacts-for-MoS2-Kappera-Voiry/639d67e83ce5714200ebe21c69be72bbd5e553bf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Semantic Scholar record for the 2014 research paper "Phase-engineered low-resistance contacts for ultrathin MoS2 transistors" published in Nature Materials (DOI: 10.1038/nmat4080, Corpus ID: 16149935) by authors Rajesh Kappera, Damien Voiry, Sibel Ebru Yalcin, Brittany A. Branch, Gautam Gupta, Aditya D. Mohite, and Manish Chhowalla. Published on December 1, 2014, the paper demonstrates that the metallic 1T phase of MoS2 can be locally induced on semiconducting 2H phase nanosheets, decreasing contact resistances to 200-300 Ω·μm at zero gate bias. This work addresses a key bottleneck in ultrathin MoS2 transistor performance by providing low-resistance contacts.

The paper has accrued 1,684 citations and 62 references. Key citing works include:
- "Pushing the Performance Limit of Sub-100 nm Molybdenum Disulfide Transistors" (Nano Letters, 2016) by Yuan Liu, Jian Guo, and X. Duan, which demonstrated 2D semiconductor transistors offering comparable performance to the 2017 ITRS silicon transistor targets.
- "Low-Resistance 2D/2D Ohmic Contacts: A Universal Approach to High-Performance WSe2, MoS2, and MoSe2 Transistors" (Nano Letters, 2016) by Hsun-Jen Chuang, Bhim Chamlagain, and Zhixian Zhou, which presented a new device paradigm for overcoming TMD contact bottlenecks.
- "Approaching Ohmic Contacts for Ideal Monolayer MoS2 Transistors Through Sulfur-Vacancy Engineering" (Small Methods, 2023) by Jiankun Xiao et al., addressing unusually high contact resistances in monolayer 2D semiconductor FETs.
- "Dramatic Reduction of Contact Resistance via Ultrathin LiF in Two-Dimensional MoS2 Field Effect Transistors" (Nano Letters, 2021) by Hyunmin Cho et al.
- "Contact Resistance Optimization in MoS2 Field-Effect Transistors through Reverse Sputtering-Induced Structural Modifications" (ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, 2025) by Yuan Fa et al.

Key references cited by the paper include foundational MoS2 transistor research: "Single-layer MoS2 transistors" (Radisavljevic et al., Nature Nanotechnology, 2011, 13,272 citations), "How good can monolayer MoS₂ transistors be?" (Yoon et al., 2011), "High-mobility and low-power thin-film transistors based on multilayer MoS2 crystals" (Kim et al., Nature Communications, 2012), "Measurement of mobility in dual-gated MoS₂ transistors" (Fuhrer & Hone, 2013), "High-performance MoS2 transistors with low-resistance molybdenum contacts" (Kang et al., 2014), and "Switching mechanism in single-layer molybdenum disulfide transistors" (Liu et al., ACS Nano, 2014), which found contact resistivity for metal/MoS2 junctions is defined by contact area rather than contact width.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It is demonstrated that the metallic 1T phase of MoS2 can be locally induced on semiconducting 2H phase nanosheets, thus decreasing contact resistances to 200-300 Ω μm at zero gate bias."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Stable and scalable 1T MoS2 with low temperature-coefficient of resistance | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-30867-y

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Scientific Reports (volume 8, article number 12463, 2018) by Chithra H. Sharma, Ananthu P. Surendran, Abin Varghese, and Madhu Thalakulam. The paper demonstrates a controllable and scalable method for engineering the metallic 1T phase of MoS2 from the semiconducting 2H phase using forming-gas (10% H2 + 90% Ar) microwave plasma treatment on mechanically exfoliated samples. 

Key methodology and results:
- The technique allows lithographically defining 1T regions on 2H samples using aluminum masking, enabling monolithic integration of metallic and semiconducting phases.
- HR-TEM analysis confirmed extended 1T regions with areal coverage exceeding 70% over the 2H phase, with no signatures of distorted phases (1T′ or 1T″). The nearest Mo-Mo separation was measured at 3.19 Å.
- Raman spectroscopy showed characteristic J1, J2, and J3 peaks of the 1T phase, accompanied by photoluminescence quenching indicative of metallic phase formation. A new peak at 180 cm⁻¹ not previously reported was also observed.
- The phase transition occurs via gliding of Mo and S planes, induced by momentum transfer from plasma ions.
- Stability: 1T samples showed temporal stability exceeding 27-30 days at ambient conditions and thermal stability up to 300°C, well above standard device fabrication temperatures.
- Electrical transport: Two-probe and four-probe measurements on back-gated FET geometry from 4K to 300K showed Ohmic I-V characteristics with no gate voltage dependence (signature of metallic state). The 2H regions showed Schottky behavior and n-type FET characteristics with mobility of 16.4 cm²/V-s at 300K and 84 cm²/V-s at 4K.
- Extracted parameters for the 1T phase: sheet resistance of 108 Ω/□, carrier concentration of ~2.3 × 10¹⁵ cm⁻² (two orders of magnitude higher than 2H MoS2), and temperature coefficient of resistance α = −1.1057 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ (negligible temperature dependence from 4K to 300K).
- The sample satisfies the Ioffe-Regal criterion (kF·l ~ 239) confirming metallic conduction, ruling out hopping-mediated or activated transport.
- Stability verified over ~90 days post-processing (including ~30 days in ambient conditions) with minimal resistance variation.

The conclusion states this method enables extended, low-disorder 1T regions suitable for monolithic 2D circuits, unlike prior methods (intercalation, electron-beam irradiation, argon plasma) that yielded nanoscale patches or unstable phases.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The 1T samples show excellent temporal and thermal stability making it suitable for standard device fabrication techniques... The 1T samples exhibit Ohmic current-voltage characteristics in all temperature ranges without any dependence to the gate voltage, a signature of a metallic state."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Contact Resistance Optimization in MoS2 Field-Effect ... - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12022942

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces (March 11, 2025) by researchers from AMO GmbH, RWTH Aachen University, Eindhoven University of Technology, and AIXTRON SE. The study investigates the use of reverse sputtering (Ar+ ion bombardment via RF-generated plasma) to reduce contact resistance (Rc) in molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) field-effect transistors (FETs).

Key findings and methodology:
- MoS₂ FETs suffer from Schottky barriers at the metal-MoS₂ interface, causing high contact resistance. The study explores inducing a phase transition from semiconducting 2H-MoS₂ to metallic 1T-MoS₂ via reverse sputtering at the contact interface.
- Multilayer MOCVD-grown MoS₂ (~2.5 nm thick, ~4 layers) was transferred onto SiO₂/Si substrates. Devices were fabricated with nickel (Ni) top-contacts (TOP-FETs) where only the contact regions were sputter-treated, and bottom-contact (BOT-FETs) control devices where the entire MoS₂ was exposed.
- Characterization via PL, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS confirmed that reverse sputtering induces sulfur vacancies (VS) and a 2H-to-1T phase transition in MoS₂. XPS showed the S/Mo ratio decreasing from ~2.0 (pristine) to 1.80 (200 W treatment), with full 2H-to-1T conversion observed after sputtering.
- Optimal results were achieved at 75 W reverse sputtering for 10 s: Rc decreased from 1126 kΩ·μm (pristine) to 413 kΩ·μm (a reduction to less than 50% of untreated devices), and output current increased approximately 150-fold.
- Two-probe mobility (μ₂ₚ) nearly doubled for the 75 W sample (0.81 ± 0.20 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ vs. 0.48 ± 0.10 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ for pristine). On/off ratios of 10⁶ were maintained for pristine, 25 W, and 75 W samples, degrading to 10⁵ at 200 W.
- Excessive sputtering power (200 W) caused oxidation to MoOₓ and severe degradation. Insufficient power (25 W) produced too few sulfur vacancies and increased Rc. The 75 W condition represented the optimal balance between phase conversion and material damage.
- The mechanism involves sulfur vacancies creating heavily n-doped regions that narrow the Schottky barrier, plus the formation of conductive 1T-MoS₂ that enhances electron injection from Ni contacts.

The authors conclude that reverse sputtering is a scalable, CMOS-compatible, and clean method for optimizing contact resistance in MoS₂ FETs, with potential for broader application in 2D material-based microelectronics. Funding was provided by EU Horizon 2020/Horizon Europe programs, German BMBF projects (NEUROTEC, NEUROTEC 2, NeuroSys), and the German Research Foundation (DFG).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"MoS₂–FETs exposed to optimized reverse sputtering conditions in the contact area show Rc values reduced to less than 50% of their untreated counterparts."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Researchers find a way to reduce contact resistance with molybdenum disulphide nanosheets ---
URL: https://phys.org/news/2014-09-contact-resistance-molybdenum-disulphide-nanosheets.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Researchers from Rutgers University and Los Alamos National Laboratory have developed a method to reduce contact resistance in molybdenum disulphide (MoS2) nanosheets, a promising material for next-generation computer chips. Published in Nature Materials (September 5, 2014, DOI: 10.1038/nmat4080), the team developed a "lithiation" process that phase-shifts the semiconducting 2H phase of MoS2 into the metallic 1T phase by exposing it to n-butyl lithium. This enables wires to be easily connected to a fully conducting metallic contact, overcoming the high-resistance problem (0.7 kΩ μm–10 kΩ μm) typically caused when metals are deposited on the 2H phase.

Key results from the study include:
- Contact resistances decreased to 200–300 Ω μm at zero gate bias with 1T phase electrodes.
- Field-effect transistors (FETs) fabricated and tested in air exhibited mobility values of ~50 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.
- Subthreshold swing values below 100 mV per decade.
- On/off ratios of >10⁷ and drive currents approaching ~100 μA μm⁻¹ with excellent current saturation.
- The deposition of different metals had limited influence on FET performance, suggesting the 1T/2H interface controls carrier injection.
- Increased reproducibility of electrical characteristics was achieved through this phase-engineering strategy.

Remaining challenges include accurately phase-shifting only the desired portion of a sheet and the metastable nature of MoS2, which tends to revert to its semiconductor phase under certain (not yet fully understood) conditions. Possible solutions being explored include producing MoS2 flakes via exfoliation or chemical vapor deposition.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this study, we demonstrate that the metallic 1T phase of MoS2 can be locally induced on semiconducting 2H phase nanosheets, thus decreasing contact resistances to 200–300 Ω μm at zero gate bias."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Hydrazine Hydrate Intercalated 1T-dominant MoS2 with Long ---
URL: https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d31eb7f0-4ae1-4463-a873-71ce7531f355/download

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article describing a novel one-step hydrothermal method to synthesize 1T-dominant MoS2 nanosheets with long-term ambient stability for efficient electrocatalytic (hydrogen evolution reaction, HER) applications. The key innovation is the use of hydrazine hydrate (N2H4·H2O) as an intercalating agent that serves as an electron donor to stabilize the metallic 1T phase.

**Background:** Metallic 1T-phase MoS2 exhibits superior HER performance compared to the natural 2H phase due to higher electrical conductivity and more active sites, but previously reported 1T-MoS2 catalysts suffered from extreme instability, transforming back to 2H within ~2 hours at room temperature.

**Methods:** Samples were synthesized via hydrothermal treatment at 180°C for 48 hours using ammonium heptamolybdate and thioacetamide, with varying N2H4:Mo molar ratios (0:1, 1:1, 4:1, 12:1), producing samples labeled MoS2-0HZ, MoS2-1HZ, MoS2-4HZ, and MoS2-12HZ. Characterization used SEM, HR-TEM, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, and four-point-probe conductivity measurements. DFT calculations (PBEsol functional, VASP software, Tkatchenko-Scheffler dispersion correction, Hubbard-U=4.0 eV) were performed to understand the stabilization mechanism.

**Key Results:**
- The 1T phase proportion increased with hydrazine concentration: 0%, 31%, 69%, and 70% for MoS2-0HZ, MoS2-1HZ, MoS2-4HZ, and MoS2-12HZ respectively (saturation reached at N2H4:Mo = 4:1).
- The 1T-dominant MoS2-4HZ exhibited excellent ambient stability with no significant phase transformation over 3 months.
- Electrical conductivity was ~700 times higher than 2H MoS2 (sheet resistance decreased from 28.9 kΩ/square for 2H to 41.1 Ω/square for 1T-dominant).
- HER performance improved dramatically: onset potential reduced from 286 to 196 mV vs. RHE, Tafel slope decreased from 99 to 64 mV/dec, and current density was ~12 times larger than 2H MoS2 at overpotential 300 mV.
- ECSA increased with 1T phase content: 609.62, 787.23, and 970.66 cm² for 0%, 31%, and 69% 1T phase respectively.
- DFT calculations showed hydrazine intercalation is exothermic for 1T MoS2 (Eintercalation = -6.117 eV) but endothermic for 2H MoS2 (Eintercalation = +1.541 eV).
- Bader charge analysis revealed a Mo atom near the hydrazine docking position gets reduced by ~0.1 e⁻, donated from the N2H4 molecule, stabilizing the 1T phase by partially filling the 4dxy,yz,xz orbitals.
- An N-S bond forms between hydrazine and the MoS2 layer for the 1T polymorph but not for 2H.
- Hydrazine-intercalated samples showed enhanced suspension stability in water (remained suspended after 1 week vs. complete precipitation for 2H MoS2).

**Conclusions:** The one-step hydrazine-assisted hydrothermal method enables precise control of 2H/1T phase ratio with excellent stability, high conductivity, and superior HER performance, attributed to electron donation from hydrazine to adjacent Mo atoms. The strategy may be broadly applicable to developing highly efficient and stable 2D electrocatalysts. The work was conducted by researchers from the University of New South Wales, Macquarie University, The University of Newcastle (Australia), and the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (Spain).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"the as-synthesized 1T-dominant MoS2 sample demonstrates excellent ambient stability without significant degradation for 3 months. Additionally, the 1T-dominant MoS2 exhibits superior electrical conductivity (~700 times higher than 2H MoS2) and improved electrochemical catalytic performance (current density ~12 times larger than 2H MoS2 at overpotential 300 mV vs. RHE)"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Metallic contact induced van der Waals gap in a MoS2 FET. ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Semantic Scholar record for the scientific paper "Metallic contact induced van der Waals gap in a MoS2 FET" by Changsik Kim, Kwangyoung Lee, Inyong Moon, Sudarat Issarapanacheewin, and Won Jong Yoo, published in the journal Nanoscale on October 11, 2019 (DOI: 10.1039/c9nr04567h, PubMed ID: 31565703). The core finding of the paper is that electrical metal contacts formed with 2D materials strongly affect device performance and are strongly correlated with the electrical performance of 2D MoS2 field-effect transistors (FETs), providing practical guidelines for forming van der Waals contacts. These references collectively address the challenges of Fermi level pinning, contact resistance, and ohmic contact formation in 2D semiconductor devices.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Van der Waals contacts between three-dimensional metals and two-dimensional semiconductors - PubMed ---
URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30918403

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PubMed entry (PMID: 30918403) for a scientific paper titled "Van der Waals contacts between three-dimensional metals and two-dimensional semiconductors," published in Nature (2019 Apr; 568(7750):70-74, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-019-1052-3, Epub 2019 Mar 27). The paper reports the realization of ultraclean van der Waals contacts between 10-nanometer-thick indium metal capped with 100-nanometer-thick gold electrodes and monolayer molybdenum disulfide (MoS2). Key findings include: (1) indium and gold form a solid solution after annealing at 200°C; (2) the interface between gold-capped indium and MoS2 is atomically sharp with no chemical interaction, suggesting van-der-Waals-type bonding; (3) contact resistance is 3,000 ± 300 ohm·µm for monolayer MoS2 and 800 ± 200 ohm·µm for few-layered MoS2, among the lowest observed for 3D metal electrodes evaporated onto MoS2; (4) field-effect transistors achieved mobility of 167 ± 20 cm²/V·s; (5) low contact resistance of 220 ± 50 ohm·µm on ultrathin niobium disulfide (NbS2) and near-ideal band offsets in tungsten disulfide (WS2) and tungsten diselenide (WSe2) contacted with indium alloy. The work provides a simple method of making ultraclean van der Waals contacts using standard laboratory technology on monolayer 2D semiconductors. Authors include Yan Wang, Jong Chan Kim, Ryan J Wu, Jenny Martinez, Xiuju Song, Jieun Yang, Fang Zhao, Andre Mkhoyan, Hu Young Jeong, and Manish Chhowalla (corresponding author, mc209@cam.ac.uk), from institutions including University of Cambridge, Rutgers University, UNIST, University of Minnesota, California State Polytechnic University Pomona, Shenzhen University, and Princeton University.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here we report the realization of ultraclean van der Waals contacts between 10-nanometre-thick indium metal capped with 100-nanometre-thick gold electrodes and monolayer MoS2."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Ultraclean van der Waals contacts | Department of Materials Science & Metallurgy ---
URL: https://www.msm.cam.ac.uk/news-and-events/papers-month-archive/ultraclean-van-der-waals-contacts

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the Department of Materials Science & Metallurgy at the University of Cambridge, specifically highlighting a research paper published in May 2019 about "Ultraclean van der Waals contacts."

**Research Finding:** The researchers successfully demonstrated ultraclean van der Waals (vdW) contacts by evaporating indium and gold onto single-layer 2D semiconductors. This addresses a key technological challenge in field-effect transistors (FETs) using 2D semiconductors as channel materials, which offer excellent gate electrostatics to mitigate short-channel effects. In short-channel devices, transport through the semiconductor is ballistic, meaning virtually all power is dissipated at the contacts, making contact optimization critical. The team provided direct evidence using atomic resolution imaging and chemical analysis showing the interface between the metal and single-layer MoS2 is atomically clean with no chemical interaction, allowing the 2D semiconductor to remain pristine and lowering contact resistance to record levels.

**Publication Details:** The paper was published in Nature, volume 568 (2019), pages 70-74, authored by Y. Wang, J. C. Kim, R. J. Wu, J. Martinez, X. Song, Ji. Yang, F. Zhao, A. Mkhoyan, H. Y. Jeong, and M. Chhowalla. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-019-1052-3. The research is attributed to Manish Chhowalla FREng of the department.

**Department Information:** The Department of Materials Science & Metallurgy is located at 27 Charles Babbage Road, Cambridge, CB3 0FS, United Kingdom. Telephone: +44 (0)1223 334300. The department offers a comprehensive range of research disciplines (over 35 listed) including 2D & 3D Imaging, Battery and Fuel Cell Materials, Carbon Nanomaterials, Computational Materials Discovery, Electron Microscopy, and many others, plus undergraduate (Parts IA, IB, II, III) and postgraduate programs (MPhil and PhD).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"FETs using 2D semiconductors as the channel material offer excellent gate electrostatics, which allows mitigation of short channel effects. However, in short channel devices, the transport through the semiconductor is ballistic and virtually all of the power is dissipated at the contacts."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: The Contact Properties of Monolayer and Multilayer MoS2-Metal van der Waals Interfaces ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2079-4991/14/13/1075

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access scientific article published in Nanomaterials (MDPI) on June 24, 2024, titled "The Contact Properties of Monolayer and Multilayer MoS2-Metal van der Waals Interfaces" by Xin Pei, Xiaohui Hu, Tao Xu, and Litao Sun (Nanjing Tech University and Southeast University, China). The study investigates Fermi-level pinning (FLP) effects and contact types at MoS2-metal van der Waals (vdW) interfaces using density functional theory (DFT) calculations with the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP), employing PBE-GGA functionals, DFT-D3 dispersion corrections, PAW potentials, a 500 eV plane-wave cutoff, and an 11×11×1 k-mesh. 

Key findings: (1) Compared to monolayer MoS2-metal close interfaces, the FLP effect is significantly reduced at monolayer MoS2-metal vdW interfaces, with the pinning factor S increasing from 0.37 (close) to 0.49 (vdW); this is attributed to fewer metal-induced gap states (MIGS) and smaller interface dipoles. (2) As MoS2 layer number increases from 1L to 3L, the pinning factor rises from 0.49 to 0.54 to 0.65 (weakening FLP), but decreases to 0.47 at 4L (increased FLP), attributed to charge redistribution at MoS2-metal and MoS2-MoS2 interfaces. (3) P-type Schottky contacts can be achieved at 1L–4L MoS2-Pt, 3L MoS2-Au, and 2L–3L MoS2-Pd vdW interfaces, enabling low contact resistance and potential complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) logic applications. A low p-type Schottky barrier height of 0.11 eV was achieved in the 4L MoS2-Pt vdW interface. Metals studied included Al, Ag, Cu, Au, Pd, and Pt (111) surfaces with work functions ranging 4.15–5.65 eV. The study concludes that FLP and contact types can be effectively modulated by selecting the MoS2 layer number, providing a strategy for reducing contact resistance in MoS2-based devices.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The pinning factor S = 0.37 for 1L MoS2-metal close interfaces, indicating a strong FLP effect at the interface... The pinning factor S of 1L MoS2-metal vdW interfaces is 0.49, which is much larger than that of the 1L MoS2-metal close interfaces, suggesting a weak FLP at the vdW interfaces."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: [PDF] Van der Waals contacts between three-dimensional metals and two ... ---
URL: https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/bitstreams/14aa1559-2115-46f7-b66f-2dc8e8f3eaac/download

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper (preprint, Nature journal submission) reports the realization of ultra-clean van der Waals (vdW) contacts between three-dimensional indium metal electrodes and monolayer two-dimensional semiconductors (TMDs). Led by Yan Wang and Manish Chhowalla (University of Cambridge), the research demonstrates a simple method using standard laboratory thermal evaporation to deposit 10 nm indium capped with 100 nm gold on monolayer MoS2, NbS2, WS2, and WSe2.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Interface quality: STEM imaging shows the In/Au-MoS2 interface is atomically sharp with a vdW gap of 2.4 Å (monolayer) and 2.7 Å (multilayer), with no chemical reaction, oxidation, or indium sulfide formation detected (confirmed by XPS and EELS). The In and Au form a solid solution alloy after annealing at 200°C.
2. Contact resistance: ~3000 ± 300 Ω·μm for single-layer MoS2 (at n = 5.0 × 10^12 cm^-2) and ~800 ± 200 Ω·μm for few-layered MoS2 — among the lowest ever reported for 3D metal electrodes evaporated on MoS2. Contact resistance of 220 ± 50 Ω·μm was achieved on ultrathin NbS2 (among lowest reported for any metal on 2D TMD), and 2.4 ± 0.5 kΩ·μm for WS2.
3. Device performance: FETs with In/Au contacts on monolayer MoS2 achieved mobility of ~167 ± 20 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ and maximum current density of 196 µA/µm (multilayer). WS2 devices with In contacts achieved 83 ± 10 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ vs. only ~1 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ with Ti electrodes.
4. WSe2 contacts: Clean vdW interface (2.94 Å metal-Se spacing), ambipolar FET behavior with near-ideal band offsets (barrier heights 0.60 eV for electrons, 0.73 eV for holes), demonstrating defect-free interfaces without Fermi level pinning.
5. Work function tunability: Indium's soft nature allows alloying (e.g., In/Pd with work function 4.23 eV vs. 4.05 eV for In/Au) to tune injection barriers while maintaining clean interfaces.
6. Comparison: In/Au contacts outperform graphene contacts, ultra-high-vacuum-deposited Au, Co/h-BN contacts, and other strategies, especially on single-layer materials where clean interfaces had not previously been demonstrated.

METHODS: CVD growth of monolayer MoS2 using MoO3 and sulfur precursors; In deposited at 0.2 Å/s under <10^-6 Torr; devices annealed at 200°C in H2/Ar for 1 hour; Schottky barrier (110 meV for In/MoS2) extracted via thermionic emission/Richardson plot analysis; STEM/EELS performed at 200 keV with aberration-corrected microscope.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here, we report the realization of ultra-clean vdW contacts between indium metal (thickness = 10 nm) capped with gold (thickness = 100 nm) electrodes and monolayer MoS2."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: Low Resistance Metal Contacts to MoS2 Devices with Nickel-Etched-Graphene Electrodes ---
URL: https://www.academia.edu/101261979/Low_Resistance_Metal_Contacts_to_MoS2_Devices_with_Nickel_Etched_Graphene_Electrodes

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an Academia.edu paper page for the 2015 ACS Nano paper "Low Resistance Metal Contacts to MoS2 Devices with Nickel-Etched-Graphene Electrodes" by Khoong Hong Khoo. The paper reports an approach to achieve low-resistance contacts to MoS2 transistors while preserving the intrinsic performance of the MoS2 channel. Through a dry transfer technique and metal-catalyzed graphene treatment, nickel-etched-graphene electrodes were fabricated on MoS2 yielding contact resistance as low as 200 Ω·µm — a ~2 orders of magnitude improvement compared to pure nickel electrodes. This improvement is attributed to the smaller work function of nickel-graphene electrodes and the presence of zigzag edges in the treated graphene surface that enhance tunneling between nickel and graphene. Key methodological elements include a polymer-assisted dry transfer technique ensuring a clean graphene-MoS2 interface and a low-resistance nickel-graphene interface. The study demonstrates a two-order magnitude improvement in contact resistance, with graphene interlayers significantly lowering the Schottky barrier height and improving electron injection into MoS2. Extrinsic mobility increased threefold to 80 cm²/V-s in MoS2 FETs with Ni-treated graphene contacts. The transfer length method (TLM) was used to quantify contact resistance. The page includes 14 figures, 36 references, FAQs, related papers, and cited-by works. Related research covers topics such as phase-engineered low-resistance contacts for ultrathin MoS2 transistors, graphene/MoS2 lateral heterostructure contact resistance, nitrogen-doped graphene electrodes, and edge contacts to graphene using CMOS-compatible metals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We report an approach to achieve low-resistance contacts to MoS2 transistors with the intrinsic performance of the MoS2 channel preserved. Through a dry transfer technique and a metalcatalyzed graphene treatment process, nickel-etched-graphene electrodes were fabricated on MoS2 that yield contact resistance as low as 200 Ω.µm."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: Contact resistance at 2D metal/semiconductor heterostructures ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128214954000087

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a ScienceDirect chapter (Chapter 8) from the book "Frontiers of Nanoscience" Volume 17 (2020), titled "Computational Modelling of Nanomaterials" edited by Panagiotis Grammatikopoulos. The chapter is authored by Michel Houssa, Valery Afanas'ev, and André Stesmans, and is titled "Contact resistance at 2D metal/semiconductor heterostructures."

The chapter investigates contact resistance at metal/two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor heterojunctions, a major issue for integrating 2D materials in next-generation nanoelectronic devices. Using first-principles simulations based on density-functional theory (DFT) and the nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) method (implemented in the Siesta package), the authors compute contact resistance at graphene/MoS2 and 1T/2H-MoS2 heterostructures.

Key findings:
- Contact resistance (RcW) at graphene/MoS2 contacts strongly depends on edge contact symmetry/termination, varying between about 2×10² and 2×10⁴ Ω μm. This variation correlates with the presence or absence of dangling bond defects and/or polar bonds at the interface.
- A low contact resistance of ~200 Ω μm is computed at Mo-terminated zigzag edges.
- Contact resistance at pristine 1T/2H-MoS2 contacts is ~3–4×10⁴ Ω μm, largely independent of edge contact symmetry, due to a large electron energy barrier (~0.8 eV) at the interface.
- Functionalization of the metallic 1T-MoS2 contact with various adsorbates is predicted to decrease contact resistance by about two orders of magnitude, promising for device applications.

Computational details: DFT-GGA exchange-correlation functional, norm-conserving pseudopotentials, double-zeta polarized basis sets, 300 Ry energy cutoff, and (2×2×1) and (15×15×1) k-point grids. Large supercells (~250 atoms for graphene/MoS2) were used to minimize strain from lattice mismatch (graphene 2.47 Å, MoS2 3.17 Å), with residual strain ~1.5%. Four graphene/MoS2 lateral heterostructures with different edge symmetries (zigzag/armchair) and terminations (Mo and/or S) were studied, along with armchair and zigzag 1T/2H-MoS2 interfaces.

The chapter concludes that achieving contact resistances in the range of a few hundred Ω μm is critical for 2D material integration in nanoscale field-effect transistors, and first-principles simulations identify promising configurations (particularly Mo-terminated zigzag graphene/MoS2 edges and functionalized 1T-MoS2 contacts). The work was supported by KU Leuven Research Funds (project C14/17/080) and the European project "2DFun," with contributions from researchers at University of Oslo, AIST, IMEC, and University of Leuven.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>

- Multiscale simulation model treats diffusive transport horizontally and ballistic transport vertically across the van der Waals gap.

--- SOURCE 1: Tuning the Schottky barrier height in single- and bi-layer graphene-inserted MoS2/metal contacts | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-67150-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Scientific Reports (volume 14, article number 20905, 2024) titled "Tuning the Schottky barrier height in single- and bi-layer graphene-inserted MoS2/metal contacts." The study, authored by Xumei Zhao, Caijuan Xia, Lianbi Li, Anxiang Wang, Dezhong Cao, Baiyu Zhang, and Qinglong Fang, uses first-principle density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate how inserting single- and bi-layer graphene affects the electronic properties and Schottky barrier of MoS2/metals contacts (Mg, Al, In, Cu, Ag, Au, Pd, Ti, and Sc).

Key findings:
- Charge transfer occurs mainly at the graphene/metal interface, with smaller transfer at bi-layer graphene interfaces or graphene/MoS2 interfaces. Bader charge analysis shows weak interactions for Mg/Al/In (0.035-0.052 e), medium for Cu/Ag/Au (0.069-0.073 e), and strong for Pd/Sc/Ti (0.101-0.208 e) with graphene.
- A tunneling barrier exists at the graphene/MoS2 interface that hinders electron injection, but tunneling transmission probabilities remain high (88-97.8% for single-layer; 85.1-96.4% for bi-layer).
- The Schottky barrier height (Φ_SB,N) decreases upon graphene insertion. With single-layer graphene insertion: MoS2 contacts with Mg, In, Sc, and Ti achieve negative n-type Schottky barriers of -0.116 eV, -0.116 eV, -0.014 eV, and -0.116 eV respectively (indicating ohmic contacts); while Al, Cu, Ag, Au, Pd show positive barriers of 0.111, 0.146, 0.199, 0.462, and 0.332 eV respectively.
- With bi-layer graphene insertion: negative n-type Schottky barriers of -0.086 eV (Mg), -0.114 eV (In), -0.059 eV (Pd), -0.008 eV (Sc), and -0.0636 eV (Ti) are observed; while Al, Cu, Ag, Au show positive barriers of 0.492, 0.492, 0.230, and 0.359 eV respectively.
- Graphene preserves the intrinsic semiconductor properties of MoS2 (maintaining band gaps of ~1.3-1.6 eV with only band shifts), effectively isolating the MoS2 layer from the metal.
- Computational details: VASP code, PAW method, PBE-GGA functional with Grimme van der Waals correction, 450 eV cutoff energy, 11×11×1 k-mesh, 15 Å vacuum layer, energy convergence of 1.0×10^-5 eV, force convergence of 0.02 eV/Å.

The study provides practical guidance for designing high-performance transition metal dichalcogenide nanoelectronic devices by demonstrating that graphene insertion into MoS2/metal contacts can reduce or eliminate Schottky barriers, transitioning contacts to ohmic behavior.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results reveal that the charge transfer mainly occurs at the interface between the graphene and metal layers, with smaller transfer at the interface between bi-layer garphene or between graphene and MoS2. And the tunneling barrier exists at the interface between graphene and MoS2, which hinders electron injection from graphene to MoS2."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Research - 2D Materials - Schottky-barrier Injection ---
URL: https://www.purdue.edu/discoverypark/nanotechnology/membership/Appenzeller/research_2d_sbfet.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the Purdue University Appenzeller research group's Nanotechnology program, specifically describing their research on Schottky-barrier injection in 2D materials. The research focuses on making good electrical contacts to emerging 2D materials and separating contact effects from intrinsic material properties. Key findings include:

1. **MoS2 Schottky-barrier Transistor with Scandium Contact**: The group studied contacts to MoS2 using low work function metals (scandium ΦM=3.5 eV, titanium ΦM=4.3 eV) and large work function metals (nickel ΦM=5.0 eV, platinum ΦM=5.9 eV). They extracted Schottky barrier heights of ~230 meV (platinum), ~150 meV (nickel), ~50 meV (titanium), and ~30 meV (scandium). The work provided evidence that MoS2-to-metal interfaces are strongly impacted by Fermi level pinning near the conduction band, similar to III-V materials and silicon. Using scandium contacts on 10-nm-thick exfoliated MoS2 flakes covered by a 15 nm Al2O3 film, they achieved high effective mobilities of 700 cm²/(V·s) at room temperature (Nano Letters, 2013, 13, 100-105). Authors: Saptarshi Das and Ashish Penumatcha.

2. **Tunability of Short-Channel Effects in MoS2 Schottky-barrier Transistors**: MoS2 FETs show electrical performance governed by an unexpected dependence on effective body thickness, which depends on intercalated water molecules in the layered structure. The doping state of MoS2 FETs strongly depends on environment (air/vacuum). Device characteristics can be tuned by controlling the effective body thickness via intercalation and engineering the interlayer barrier (Nano Letters 15, 301-306). Author: Feng Zhang.

3. **Black Phosphorus Schottky-barrier MOSFET and Modeling**: Black phosphorus (BP) is a layered 2D material with phosphorus atoms in a puckered arrangement held together by weak van der Waals forces. BP has high mobility (200-1000 cm²/V-s) and a direct tunable bandgap, making it attractive for RF and optoelectronic applications, as well as tunnel FET development. The group used a Landauer model to fit transfer characteristics of BP Schottky-barrier MOSFETs and extracted both electron- and hole-Schottky barrier heights for Permalloy and Palladium contacts to black phosphorus. This model can be extended to other 2D-material SB-MOSFETs (Nature Communications 6, 6:8948). Authors: Ashish Penumatcha and Ramon Salazar.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Through analysis of experimental results, we found for many 2D materials of interest, such as transition metal dichacolgenides (TMDs) and black phosphorus, that the metal-to-semiconductor contacts are Schottky-barrier type."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Multilayer MoS2 Schottky Barrier Field Effect Transistor ---
URL: https://d-nb.info/1365289796/34

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific paper published in IEEE Open Journal of Nanotechnology (Volume 6, 2025, pp. 51-57, DOI: 10.1109/OJNANO.2025.3553692) by researchers from the University of Salerno (Italy) and Universität Konstanz (Germany). The paper was received December 21, 2024, revised in February and March 2025, accepted March 16, 2025, and published March 20, 2025. Corresponding author: Antonio Di Bartolomeo (adibartolomeo@unisa.it).

The study presents multilayer MoS2 Schottky Barrier Field Effect Transistors (SB-FETs) configured with back-gate and van der Pauw contacts. The devices were fabricated using a dry-transfer technique with MoS2 flakes (~16.7 nm thick, ~20 layers, ~137 μm² area) encapsulated between two hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) layers on a SiO2/Si substrate (300 nm SiO2 as gate oxide). Au(53nm)/Ti(7nm) contacts were patterned via e-beam lithography.

Key findings:
- IV characteristics showed non-linear, asymmetric, rectifying behavior across all six contact combinations, confirming Schottky barriers at Ti/MoS2 interfaces despite Schottky-Mott theory predicting ohmic contacts (due to Fermi level pinning from defects and metal-induced gap states).
- Rectification ratios varied from a few units to 10³ depending on the contact pair, attributed to local inhomogeneities from fabrication and different flake coverage areas.
- Transfer curves showed n-type behavior (electrons as majority carriers) with prominent "kinks" at a transition voltage (Vtr ~ -12V to -15V) marking the transition between thermionic emission and tunnelling conduction regimes.
- A hierarchy of Schottky barrier heights was established: φb,D < φb,E ≤ φb,G < φb,F.
- A band model combining thermionic emission and tunnelling (including Fowler-Nordheim tunnelling, confirmed by linear fits in Fowler-Nordheim plots) was developed to explain the device operation, which can be broadly applied to other SB-FETs.
- At negative gate voltages, thermionic emission dominates; at positive gate voltages, tunnelling dominates, causing barrier-height differences to become less influential and output curves to symmetrize.
- The higher the drain barrier, the slower the transition from sublinear to ohmic behavior in the IV curves.

The study concludes that lead local inhomogeneities and different flake coverage affect Schottky barrier heights, which critically determine conduction mechanisms in SB-FETs. The proposed band energy model aids in understanding and optimizing 2D material transistors with Schottky-type contacts.

Experimental equipment: Lake Shore probe station with Keithley 4200-SCS semiconductor characterization system, NaioAFM (Nanosurf AG) for height profiling, all measurements at room temperature, ambient pressure, and dark conditions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A hierarchy of the Schottky barrier heights at the contacts is established, and a band model is developed to elucidate the underlying conduction mechanisms. This model combines thermionic emission and tunnelling to explain the operation of the studied MoS2 devices and can be broadly applied to other SB-FETs."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Low-Temperature Ohmic Contact to Monolayer MoS2 by van ... ---
URL: https://pr.ibs.re.kr/bitstream/8788114/3821/1/Low-Temperature_NanoLetters_Young%20Hee%20Lee.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research letter published in Nano Letters (2017, Vol. 17, pp. 4781-4786, DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.7b01536) from researchers at Columbia University, Harvard University, Kyung Hee University, Yonsei University, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Sungkyunkwan University, and the National Institute for Materials Science.

**Main Topic:** The paper reports a new low-temperature Ohmic contact scheme for monolayer MoS2 using cobalt (Co) electrodes with a monolayer of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) inserted between the metal and the semiconductor.

**Key Findings:**
- The monolayer h-BN serves a dual function: it modifies the work function of Co (reducing it from ~5.0 eV to ~3.3 eV, confirmed by XPS) and acts as a tunneling barrier.
- This design breaks the metal-TMDC interaction, eliminating interface states that cause Fermi level pinning.
- A flat-band Schottky barrier of only 16 meV was measured (vs. 38 meV for Co directly on MoS2).
- Contact resistance of 3 kΩ·μm was achieved at a carrier density of 5.3 × 10^12/cm² at 1.7 K.
- Ohmic contacts were achieved at low carrier densities down to 3.5 × 10^12/cm², enabling observation of Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations at significantly lower carrier densities than previously possible.
- Hall mobility reached ~630 cm²/(V·s) at 5.3 × 10^12/cm² carrier density.

**Methodology:**
- Devices were fabricated using dry van der Waals transfer, with MoS2 and h-BN exfoliated from bulk crystals onto SiO2/Si substrates.
- 30 nm Co and 50 nm Au electrodes were evaporated under ultrahigh vacuum (~10^-10 Torr).
- Work function was verified via X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (XPS) showing Φ = 3.3 eV for Co/h-BN.
- Transport measurements included two-probe and four-probe resistance, Hall effect measurements, and magneto-transport up to 14 T at temperatures down to 1.7 K.

**Key Comparisons:**
- The h-BN/Co contact outperforms other schemes: few-layer graphene contacts (Rc ~10 kΩ·μm but only at ~10^13/cm²), Au contacts (only low resistance above 2 × 10^13/cm²), and low work-function metals like Sc and Al (non-Ohmic at low temperature).
- Co without h-BN showed nonlinear I-V behavior at low temperature.
- Other metals (Sc, Ti, Al, Ag) with h-BN tunnel barriers did not achieve low-T Ohmic contact, confirming the critical role of the strong h-BN/Co work-function interaction.
- Co evaporated under ordinary high vacuum (~10^-8 Torr) gave roughly 5 times higher contact resistance.

**Conclusions:** The Co/h-BN contact scheme provides the best reported contacts to monolayer MoS2 to date, particularly well suited for studies at low temperature and low carrier density, and may prove useful for electron injection in a wide range of other systems.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this work, we report a new contact scheme that utilizes cobalt (Co) with a monolayer of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) that has the following two functions: modifies the work function of Co and acts as a tunneling barrier. We measure a flat-band Schottky barrier of 16 meV, which makes thin tunnel barriers upon doping the channels, and thus achieve low-T contact resistance of 3 kΩ.μm at a carrier density of 5.3 × 1012/cm2."
