You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
Delft University of Technology Effects of alkali metal intercalation on structural and electronic properties of molybdenum disulfide Mádai, Eszter; Anusuyadevi, Prasaanth Ravi; Gonugunta, Prasad; Mohseni Armaki, A.; Mol, Arjan; Taheri, Peyman; Hartkamp, Remco DOI 10.1016/j.apsusc.2025.164284 Publication date 2025 Document Version Final published version Published in Applied Surface Science Citation (APA) Mádai, E., Anusuyadevi, P. R., Gonugunta, P., Mohseni Armaki, A., Mol, A., Taheri, P., & Hartkamp, R.
(2025). Effects of alkali metal intercalation on structural and electronic properties of molybdenum disulfide.
Applied Surface Science, 714, Article 164284. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apsusc.2025.164284 Important note To cite this publication, please use the final published version (if applicable).
Please check the document version above.
Copyright Other than for strictly personal use, it is not permitted to download, forward or distribute the text or part of it, without the consent of the author(s) and/or copyright holder(s), unless the work is under an open content license such as Creative Commons.
Takedown policy Please contact us and provide details if you believe this document breaches copyrights.
We will remove access to the work immediately and investigate your claim.
This work is downloaded from Delft University of Technology.
For technical reasons the number of authors shown on this cover page is limited to a maximum of 10. Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Applied Surface Science journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/apsusc Full length article Effects of alkali metal intercalation on structural and electronic properties of molybdenum disulfide Eszter Mádai a , Prasaanth Ravi Anusuyadevi a , Prasad Gonugunta a , Amirhossein Mohseni Armaki a , Arjan Mol a , Peyman Taheri a , Remco Hartkamp b,∗ a Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Delft University of Technology, Mekelweg 2, Delft, 2628 CD, South-Holland, The Netherlands b Department of Process and Energy, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Delft University of Technology, Leegwaterstraat 39, Delft, 2628 CB, South-Holland, The Netherlands A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Molybdenum disulfide Intercalation Hydration shell Electronic properties Phase transition A B S T R A C T 2D materials, characterized by their extensive surface area and customizable chemical and electronic prop-erties, offer compelling advantages as advanced materials. These unique attributes pave the way for the development of next-generation electronics and optoelectronics, photo- and electro-catalysis, energy storage and conversion devices, and sensors. The most prominent and commonly available 2D transition metal dichalcogenide, molybdenum disulfide (MoS2), has already shown its potential for advanced applications. However, its relatively unfavorable electronic structure and limited intrinsic conductivity lower its suitability for applications that require high conductivity, such as electrocatalysts. One way to enhance its conductivity is by electrochemically intercalating alkali metal ions, e.g., Na+ and K+, into its layered structure, potentially adjusting its electronic structure. Here, we present a comprehensive investigation into the atomic-scale intercalation mechanism using molecular dynamics simulations, complemented by experimental analysis of structural and electronic properties at the macro scale through various characterization techniques. It is demonstrated that the hydration shell of ions serves as an energy barrier to intercalation as it undergoes a structural change during the intercalation. When alkali metal ions are intercalated into MoS2, they introduce more defects and enhance conductivity. Notably, these effects are more pronounced for potassium than for sodium.
1. Introduction Meeting today’s technological and societal needs relies on advanced materials whose properties can be precisely tailored for high per-formance and demanding applications. A prominent and widely re-searched group of advanced materials is the family of 2D materials, due to their superior mechanical, electronic, and structural proper-ties [1]. The high surface-to-bulk ratio of 2D structures enhances their surface functionality, while their layered architecture allows for precise tuning of chemical and electronic properties [2]. These materials find applications across a wide range of fields, including electronics and optoelectronics (e.g., semiconductors, photodetectors), photo-, electro- (e.g., water purification, electrolyzers for water splitting, CO2 reduc-tion) [3] and thermal catalysis [4], energy storage and conversion (e.g., batteries, supercapacitors) [5,6], field emitters [7] and sensing (e.g., gas and biosensors) [8,9].
∗Corresponding author.
E-mail address: r.m.hartkamp@tudelft.nl (R. Hartkamp).
2D materials encompass a diverse range of classes, including transi-tion metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), MXenes, graphene and its deriva-tives, hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), and layered metal oxides, each offering distinct structural and electronic properties tailored for various applications [10]. Recently, 2D transition metal borides (MBenes) have also emerged as a promising class of 2D materials, exhibiting notable electrochemical and catalytic properties [11]. As a member of the (TMD) family, MoS2 is an abundant and cost-effective material that offers a tunable chemistry and bandgap, excellent chemical stability, and a layered structure, making it a promising choice for advanced applications [12].
A monolayer of MoS2 consists of a layer of molybdenum (Mo) atoms sandwiched between two layers of sulfur (S) atoms. These monolayers are held together by van der Waals forces, which then combine to form the bulk material [13]. The three major polytypes of bulk MoS2 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apsusc.2025.164284 Received 28 April 2025; Received in revised form 6 August 2025; Accepted 6 August 2025 Applied Surface Science 714 (2025) 164284 Available online 18 August 2025 0169-4332/© 2025 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V. This is an open access article under the CC BY license ( http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ ). E. Mádai et al.
are the metastable 1T-polytype with octahedral structure and exhibit-ing metallic properties, the 3R- and the 2H-polytypes with trigonal prismatic structure (see Figure S1) and displaying semiconducting prop-erties [14]. The 2H-polytype MoS2 is composed of a two-layer stacked unit cell that restores the otherwise broken inversion symmetry of the monolayer MoS2, while the 3R-polytype consists of a three-layer unit cell, where the inversion symmetry is broken [15,16].
Due to the broken inversion symmetry in the 3R-polytype, a strong spin–orbit coupling is possible based on the d-orbitals of the transition metals [17]. This provides the opportunity for the development of such applications as electronic and optoelectronic devices [18,19] and using properties such as valley- and spin-Hall effect and superconduc-tivity [20–22]. The 3R-polytype can be synthesized through chemical vapor deposition and via the mechanical folding and stacking of MoS2 monolayers [23,24]. Conversely, the 2H-polytype is the most com-monly and naturally available polytype [14]. The applications with this polytype include utilizing bulk or monolayer MoS2 as (electro-/photo-)catalyst both for hydrogen production in aqueous media [25–27] and for CO2 reduction in organic media [28–30]. Furthermore, the 2H-polytype MoS2 has demonstrated to be a suitable anode material for aqueous rechargeable batteries (ARBs) based on alkali earth met-als [31–36], earth metals [37–40], and earth-abundant materials [41– 43], as emerging competitors to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs).
As both the 2H and the 3R polytypes are semiconducting, the presence of the bandgap presents a challenge, but also an opportunity for tuning the electronic properties. The layered structure of MoS2 allows the intercalation of (alkali metal) ions, which then donate their valence electrons to the MoS2 and increase its conductivity and change the bandgap. If the intercalation occurs at high concentrations of intercalants, then a phase transition is induced from the 2H polytype phase to the metastable 1T-polytype phase by the gliding of the mono-layers [44]. The intercalation process of different alkali metal ions was studied through various experimental techniques [45,46]. Wang et al. imaged the intercalation process of Na+ ions in MoS2 with aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and they showed that the MoS2 structure undergoes complicated phase transitions due to the presence of the Na+ ions [45]. Attanayake et al. compared the intercalation of Na+, Ca2+, Co2+ and Ni2+ ions to MoS2 based on the efficiency of hydrogen production [47]. The intercalation of K atoms and K+ ions was studied by Andersen et al. using first-principle calculations [48]. Their calculations showed that the ions together with water molecules can be intercalated into the bulk MoS2 structure; however, based on measurements by Zak et al. [49] they only added one or two water molecules next to the ions, not a full hydration shell.
Controlling intercalation on the microscale can significantly impact the property changes of the 2D material. However, achieving such control requires a mechanistic understanding of intercalation and the factors that influence it, such as the role of the intercalant and the material and its electronic properties. While the effects of different in-tercalants have been studied in the literature, a holistic and systematic comparison that links the mechanisms at the atomistic level to changes in material properties at the macroscopic level is still lacking.
The electrochemical intercalation process, where the driving force of the intercalation can be controlled externally, presents a path for this systematic comparison. Hence, this article aims to bridge this gap by shedding new light on the intercalation mechanism influenced by external and internal parameters, such as the applied voltage and the inherent hydration shell of the alkali metal ions. We use molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to show the microscopic mechanisms of the intercalation, while the macroscopic mechanisms and changes in the material properties are studied experimentally.
2. Methods and materials 2.1. Molecular dynamics simulations All MD simulations were carried out in the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) simulation package [50] using the DelftBlue supercomputer. For the MoS2, the REBOMOS potential was used, developed by Jiang et al. [51]; the SPC/E water model was employed to describe the interactions between hydrogen and oxygen atoms in water molecules. The rigid structure of the water molecules was maintained using the SHAKE algorithm. A transferable ion force field, developed by Loche and co-workers [52], was used for KCl and NaCl. Packmol software was used to construct the simulation box. A detailed description of the MD simulations is provided in the Supplementary Information.
2.2. Electrode preparation MoS2 nanopowder (99% trace metal basis, Sigma Aldrich, for char-acterization see figures S7–S11) was mixed with Carbon Black (CB, Fischer Scientific) and poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) was mixed in a ratio of 90 wt%, 5 wt% and 5 wt%, respectively. Once the ingredients are measured and added to a 5 cm3 vial, the mixture is diluted with 2 mL of Deionized (DI) water, then the ink is sonicated in a water bath for 10 min for homogenization. The glassy carbon substrates (1 × 1 cm, Sigma Aldrich, redox.me) are cleaned with DI water and then sonicated in isopropyl alcohol for 5 min, then dried with compressed air. After the sonication of the ink, 25 μL is dropcasted on the glassy carbon substrates; afterwards, the samples are left to dry in air. Afterwards, the electrodes are prepared by connecting a copper tape to the substrate and then it is covered with tape, exposing only a circle of 10 mm in diameter. Then, the intercalation of the two different alkali metal ions (Na+ and K+) in the MoS2 was carried out to enhance its conductivity.
The intercalation of alkali metal ions into MoS2 is known to induce a phase transition from the semiconducting 2H-phase to the metallic 1T-phase, which is metastable and prone to reversion to the 2H-phase upon thermal treatment or over time [53,54]. In particular, Li+ and Na+ ions can intercalate reversibly and stabilize the 1T-phase to some extent due to their smaller size, while K+ ions, having a larger atomic radius, cause more pronounced lattice distortion and reduced reversibility [54]. The 1T-phase has been reported to transform back to the thermodynami-cally stable 2H-phase at temperatures as low as 95 ◦C [55]. To mitigate such phase relaxation, all sample processing and characterization steps were performed at room temperature or below.
2.3. Electrochemical techniques All electrochemical measurements were carried out on a BioLogic VMP-3e Multichannel Potentiostat with the software EC-Lab. For each measurement the prepared electrode was immersed in 40 mL of 1 mM KHCO3 (Sigma Aldrich, 99.99%) (K+-intercalation) or 1 mM NaHCO3 (Sigma Aldrich, 99.99%) (Na+-intercalation) in an electrochemical H-cell. The electrode was placed in the cathode compartment together with a saturated calomel electrode (SCE), while a Pt mesh electrode was put in the anode compartment. All electrodes were then connected to the potentiostat and the whole system was put into a Faradaic cage. For the electrochemical intercalation, an electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was first carried out from 1.0 MHz to 100 mHz, then a chronoamperometry (CA) measurement was set on for 1 h at a preset potential (the effect of potential was studied and an intercalation potential was defined for each ion). Afterwards, the working electrode was rinsed with DI water to remove any potential adsorbed layer and another EIS measurement was carried out to assess the conductivity of the sample.
2.4. Scanning electron microscopy Scanning Electron Microscopy was performed using a JEOL IT800SHL system equipped with a field emission gun, operating at 10.00 kV and a beam current of 42.20 nA. Energy Dispersive Spec-troscopy (EDS) analysis was conducted with an Oxford Instruments Maxim 100 detector.
Applied Surface Science 714 (2025) 164284 2 E. Mádai et al.
Fig. 1. Nquist plots for (a) unfavorable (−1.0 V vs RHE) and (b) favorable (−1.3 V vs RHE) conditions of electrochemical intercalation of sodium ions, (c) resistance change at different potentials due to (un)favorable conditions for the electrochemical intercalation of Na+ and K+ ions.
2.5. XRD The XRD patterns were measured in a Bruker D8 Advance diffrac-tometer with Bragg–Brentano geometry and Lynxeye position sensitive detector with Cu K𝛼 radiation, divergence slit V12, scatter screen height 5 mm, at 45 kV and at 40 mA. The Detector was set to LL 0.11 W 0.14. The measurement range was set between 5◦ to 80◦, with a step size of 0.03◦ (in case of the VS-MoS2 and K+-intercalated VS-MoS2) and 0.06◦ (in case of the Na+-intercalated VS-MoS2) with a counting time per step of 2 s.
2.6. Raman spectroscopy The Raman spectra were obtained using a WiTec Alpha300R Raman Imaging microscope with a 532 nm laser at 1 mW power to prevent sample damage. The integration time was set to 5 s with 10 accumula-tions, and a 63X/0.9 water-dipping objective was used. To ensure high spectral resolution, a 1800 g/mm grating was employed, providing a resolution better than 1 cm−1.
To accurately monitor structural changes induced by intercalation, in situ Raman measurements were performed at the exact same position on the sample surface before and after the electrochemical process. The sample was mounted in a beaker filled with the electrolyte, which was fixed directly on the Raman stage. The initial (pristine) Raman spectrum was acquired while the sample was immersed in the elec-trolyte. Following this, the objective was retracted in the Z direction to remove it from the solution, and the electrochemical intercalation process was carried out. After intercalation, the objective was carefully repositioned to the same coordinates (The spatial positioning resolution of the system was approximately 25 nm in XYZ directions, enabling precise repositioning of the measurement spot) and focus depth to acquire the post-intercalation Raman spectrum. This ensured that the layer number and measurement location remained constant, and that any observed spectral changes originated from structural modifications, such as defect formation, rather than sample drift, delamination, or layer number variation.
2.7. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy was carried out in a Physical Electronics (PHI) 5400 (Eden Prairie, USA) instrument. The XPS spectra were acquired by using non-monochromatic Al K𝛼 radiation produced from an X-ray source with an Al anode, operating at 200 W and 13.5 kV. The primary photoelectron lines for each element were captured with a step size of 0.1 eV and a dwell time of 1.25 s, employing a spherical capacitor analyzer configured with a pass energy of 71.55 eV. The MultiPak software was used to analyze and process the XPS data, where the acquired peaks were normalized and fitted using the iterated-Shirley background.
3. Results and discussions 3.1. Electrochemical intercalation The insertion of Na+- and K+-ions into MoS2 was achieved via electrochemical intercalation by applying a constant potential on the working electrode. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) mea-surements before and after the intercalation steps are used as an indicator of changes in conductivity, suggesting favorable conditions for intercalation. Figs. 1(a) and (b) show the Nyquist plots of unfa-vorable and favorable conditions, respectively, where Z0 is the charge transfer resistance belonging to the unexposed electrode and Z is the charge transfer resistance belonging to the electrode which was sub-jected to chronoamperometry for 1 h at the respective potentials. The position of Z with respect to Z0 determines if the potential of the chronoamperometry can be considered as a favorable or unfavorable condition for electrochemical intercalation. In Fig. 1(a), a case of unfavorable condition is presented, where it shows that the internal resistance (the sum of the electrolyte resistance and the charge transfer resistance [56]) of the intercalated electrode is higher than the unex-posed electrode, namely 𝑍> 𝑍0. On the other hand, Fig. 1(b) shows the favorable conditions for intercalation, where the internal resistance of the exposed electrode is smaller than that of the unexposed elec-trode, namely 𝑍< 𝑍0. This relation indicates favorable conditions for intercalation, which results in a lower charge transfer resistance and, therefore, a higher conductivity. The data from different measurements at different potentials are collected in Tables S1 and S2 for sodium and potassium intercalation, respectively.
Fig. 1(c) shows the averaged difference of the measured resistance of the electrode at different applied potentials. A negative difference indicates a drop in the internal resistance of the electrode due to intercalation. Where the Z-Z0 value is strongly negative, they were labeled as ‘intercalation potential’ for each ion, namely for potassium −1.4 V vs RHE, for sodium −1.3 V vs RHE, respectively.
3.2. MD simulations MD simulations with umbrella sampling were used to study the intercalation mechanism of the Na+ and K+ ions. A simulation box (19.3 nm × 9.4 nm × 4.4 nm) was created with 18 000 water molecules, 4 MoS2 sheets, containing 2700 atoms per sheet, and one cation (Na+ or K+) with one Cl− ion for charge neutrality. A description of simulation details and the cross-interaction parameter optimization to reproduce the correct wettability can be found in the Supplementary Information (Tables S3 and S4, Figures S2-S5).
The intercalation Gibbs free-energy curves are shown in Fig. 2(a). The hydration shell of Na+ and K+ in bulk water contains approx-imately 6 and 7 water molecules on average, respectively [57,58]. Intercalation of these ions into MoS2 requires the hydration shell to be perturbed, resulting in an energy barrier at the edge of the MoS2. This energy barrier for intercalation is almost twice as high for the K+ Applied Surface Science 714 (2025) 164284 3 E. Mádai et al.
Fig. 2. (a) Gibbs free-energy curves for non-biased (E=0 V/Å) and biased (E=-0.01 V/Å and E=-0.02 V/Å) intercalation. (b and c) Merged snapshots from MD simulations of Na+-intercalation and K+-intercalation, respectively, showing the deformation of the hydration shells of the ions upon intercalation (molybdenum atoms are represented with blue color, sulfur atoms are represented with yellow color, sodium ions are represented with pink color, potassium ions are represented with purple color).
Fig. 3. (a) Gibbs free-energy profiles when no electric field is present, (b) and (c) Gibbs free-energy profiles of sodium and potassium ions in a geometry of 50% hydrated MoS2 and different electric fields are present.
ion as for the Na+ ion, despite the larger hydration energy of the latter ion [59].
If an external electric field is applied to the system, in accordance with our experiments, then a force 𝐹 = 𝑞𝐸 acts on each charged atom, where q is the charge and 𝐸 is the electric field. The external electric field acts as an additional driving force for the ion insertion in the interlayers of the MoS2. By applying 0.01 V/Å, the intercalation barrier for Na+ and K+ ions is lowered by about half relative to the case without an external field applied. However, the barrier remains larger than the thermal energy 𝐸𝑡ℎ= R𝑇≈0.59 kcal∕mol, such that intercalation events are not likely to occur on the simulation time scale. At 0.02 V/Å, the intercalation barrier has vanished for Na+, whereas a barrier remains for K+.
Figs. 2(b and c) present merged snapshots of the MD simulations showing the difference between the disruption of the hydration shells of the two ions. The hydration shell of the Na+ ion is only perturbed and deformed during the intercalation process, whereas the K+ ion has to expel at least one water molecule from its shell to fit in the interlayer distance. Furthermore, the remaining shell is still sterically disrupted, hence the higher energy barrier for intercalation. This con-firms the trend of the different energy barriers in the Gibbs free-energy profiles in Fig. 2(a), which then connects and explains well the higher experimental intercalation energy for potassium in Fig. 1(c).
These results deviate from the results of Andersen et al. [48], where only two water molecules were included in the hydration shell. Their computations were based on the work by Zak et al. [49] who measured a 50% increase in the vertical lattice parameter and suggested that one or two water molecules per K atom are also intercalated in the MoS2. To test if their assumption is accurate, we also decreased the hydration of the MoS2 to 50%, mimicking the 50% vertical lattice parameter increase. The simulation snapshots in Figure S6 (a) and (c) show the perturbation of the hydration shell upon interaction of the ion. The hydration shell of the ions is more deformed than those in the case of a fully hydrated MoS2. The hydration shell around both ions adopts a planar configuration containing four water molecules, which exceeds the two water molecules reported by Zak et al. [49]. The Gibbs free-energy curves for these 50% MoS2 hydration cases in the absence of an externally applied electric field are shown in Fig. 3(a). Here, a switch in energy barrier trend can be observed: as the sodium ion has a stronger hydration shell, it presents a larger energy barrier for intercalation compared to the intercalation energy barrier of the potassium ion which stays almost the same as for 100% MoS2 hydration. Figs. 3(b) and (c) show that the intercalation energy barrier of both ions drastically decreases if an external electric field is applied. The difference between the experimental and computational models stems from practical limitations in atomistic simulations, where a small, idealized system is used to represent a local region of the larger experimental structure, allowing key intercalation trends to be captured within feasible computational resources.

Fig. 4(a) shows the XRD patterns of the intercalated and non-intercalated MoS2. Furthermore, this can also indicate irreversible changes in the crystal structure [45]. This slight broadening can better be observed in Fig. 4(b), which also shows a slight shift of the peak at the (002) crystal plane orientation to smaller angles, which corresponds to an interlayer expansion due to the intercalation [60].
Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 4(c)) was carried out to confirm the pres-ence of vacancies indicated by XRD. Bulk MoS2 has four characteristic modes in the Raman spectrum E2 2g, E1g, E1 2g and A1g, at ∼32 cm−1 at ∼286 cm−1, at ∼384.5 cm−1 and at ∼405.5 cm−1, respectively [61]. Figure S8 shows all the mentioned characteristic modes except E2 2g due to the limitation of low-frequency measurements of the instrument. The peaks appearing between ∼430 cm−1 and ∼470 cm−1 are due to the near-the-zone-edge longitudinal and acoustic phonons and their combinations [62]. The two main peaks, E1 2g and A1g, are characteristic of different vibrations of the material: E1 2g is activated by the in-plane vibrations of the Mo and S atoms, while A1g is activated by out-of-plane vibrations of the S atoms [61,63].
Fig. 4(c) shows the E1 2g and A1g modes stacked for intercalated and non-intercalated electrodes. The A1g mode was measured at 405.7 cm−1 for all samples, while for the intercalated samples, the E1 2g shows a shift to lower frequencies compared to the non-intercalated electrode. The increased separation between the E1 2g and A1g modes indicates a compressive strain in the MoS2 structure due to the presence of monosulfur defects [64]. The creation of these monosulfur defects is a consequence of the unused electrode preparation process, hence, this difference in the spectra can also be used for the estimation of the defect concentration in MoS2 [65,66]. For a structurally pristine MoS2, the difference between the E1 2g and A1g peaks is 21 cm−1 [61], whereas this value has already increased to 24 cm−1 for our MoS2 electrode. This suggests that monosulfur defects are created in the electrode (from now denoted as VS-MoS2) during the sonication step of the sample preparation process. The further blue-shift of the E1 2g peaks of the intercalated samples compared to the VS-MoS2 electrode indicates an increased concentration of monosulfur vacancies as a consequence of the intercalation process and confirms our findings in the XRD patterns [64,67].
3.4. XPS analysis Fig. 5(a) shows the Mo 3d XPS spectra of VS-MoS2, Na+-intercalated and K+-intercalated VS-MoS2. The monosulfur vacancies in the MoS2 structure identified with Raman spectroscopy are also confirmed with the presence of undercoordinated Mo sites (MoUC) in the Mo 3d spec-tra [68,69]. In these fitted Mo 3d spectra, the area (Table S6) of the MoUC atoms is increased for the intercalated VS-MoS2 compared to the VS-MoS2. This also correlates with the results from the Raman spectroscopy, as the concentration of these undercoordinated Mo sites in the XPS spectra increases with the same tendency as the concen-tration of the monosulfur defects increases in the Raman spectra. In all three fits, a small peak at a ∼234.5 eV and ∼235.5 eV can be observed, which corresponds to the oxidation state of Mo6+ in MoO3, which can be present due to the exposure to air and water in the ink during the sample preparation process and in the electrolyte during the electrochemical intercalation [46,70].
For VS-MoS2, the two main peaks, Mo 3d5∕2 and 3d3∕2for the VS-MoS2 are located at 229.1 eV and 232.4 eV, respectively, which agree with the literature values [45,71]. Fig. 5(a) also shows the shift in the binding energy for the intercalated VS-MoS2 electrodes with respect to the VS-MoS2 electrode. However, these peaks are down-shifted for the Na+-intercalated and K+-intercalated VS-MoS2 by 0.5 eV and 0.7 eV, respectively, which indicates the presence of excess electrons compared to the VS-MoS2. This also suggests that electrons were donated from the intercalants (Na+ and K+ ions) to the VS-MoS2 [45]. The same downshift in energy was observed for the S 2p3 spectra of the three materials (see Figure S10 (a)).

These levels are known to induce measurable structural and electronic changes, supporting the observed modifications in our system.
To study the effect of the intercalation on the electronic structure of the VS-MoS2 further, Figs. 5(b) and (c) assess the effect of intercalation on the valence band, hence, high-resolution XPS measurements were taken from 20 eV to −15 eV. The value of the bandgap can be changed through intercalation of alkali metal ions and, consequently, electron doping [48]. The intercalation of the alkali metal ions changes the slope of the spectra and, hence, changes the energy level difference between the Fermi level and the valence band (EF-EV). With a linear extrapolation to the valence band tail (near 0 eV binding energy) in the XPS spectra, the value of E𝐹-E𝑉 was determined, where E𝐹 is the Fermi level energy and E𝑉 is the valence band energy, respectively [75].
The high electron dopant density for the Na+-intercalated and K+-intercalated VS-MoS2 is a consequence of the synergy between the sulfur defects and donated s-electrons of the alkali metal ions. The change in the electronic properties of lithiated and sodiated defective MoS2 has already been investigated with density functional theory (DFT) by Barik et al. [76]. According to the DFT calculations, the sulfur defects create a midgap state and reduce the bandgap significantly. The adsorption of the intercalants (lithium and sodium in their case) is enhanced as the midgap state coming from the d-orbital of the Mo atom and the s-orbital of the alkali metal atom forms a strong hybridization. This results in an enhanced conductivity and changes the semiconducting nature of the defective MoS2 to metallic with the lithiation/sodiation. Our experimental results correlate well with these calculations in the case of the Na+-intercalated VS-MoS2. However, for the K+-intercalated VS-MoS2 the electron dopant density is even higher, which can be due to the presence of potassium’s empty 𝑑-orbital. The separation of light (Li+ and Na+) and heavy alkali metal ions (K+, Rb+ and Cs+) are based on the presence of this empty 𝑑-orbital, as it gives the possibility of further hybridization between the heavy alkali metal’s 𝑑-orbital and the transition metal’s 𝑝-orbital. This hybridization and the charge transfer then create a low work function due to a larger dipole moment than for light alkali metals [77]. This behavior is similar to what Yu et al. found with regards to the intercalation of sodium and potassium ions in Cu4Se4 [78,79]. Intercalation of alkali-metal ions into Cu4Se4 nanosheets induces a surface phase transition, with K+ intercalation occurring at a higher voltage ( 0.756 V) than Na+ ( 0.659 V), indicative of stronger charge transfer [78]. This stronger interaction leads to a larger surface dipole and therefore a more pronounced decrease in work function for K+-intercalated Cu4Se4 compared to the Na+-intercalated counterpart [78].
4. Conclusions In this work, we have studied the intercalation mechanisms of Na+ and K+ ions into MoS2 and their effect on the structural and electronic properties of the host material. We have found that the intercalation energy strongly depends on the perturbed hydration shell of the alkali metal ion in an aqueous environment at the interface with the MoS2. Furthermore, we have shown that the intercalation process increases the concentration of monosulfur defects in the MoS2 structure. However, the presence of these defects and the donated electrons from the alkali metal ions have a synergistic effect on the electronic material properties, resulting in increased conductivity. The difference between the level of electron dopant density with regard to light and heavy Applied Surface Science 714 (2025) 164284 6 E. Mádai et al.
alkali metal ions can be attributed to the presence of the empty orbitals, which allow further hybridization. These results also have shown that MoS2 is a highly tunable material regarding not only its structural properties, regarding its flexibility in the vertical dimension, but also its electronic properties through changing the valance band structure; and that the structure engineered on the atomic scale has a large influence on the macroscopic properties.

args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Applied Surface Science (Volume 714, Article 164284, 2025) by researchers from Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), Netherlands. The study investigates the effects of alkali metal (Na+ and K+) intercalation on the structural and electronic properties of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2).

**Background/Motivation**: MoS2 is a 2D transition metal dichalcogenide with a tunable bandgap and layered structure but has limited intrinsic conductivity. Intercalating alkali metal ions electrochemically can enhance conductivity and modify the electronic structure. The study addresses a gap in holistic comparisons linking atomistic mechanisms to macroscopic property changes.

**Methods**:
- Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS (DelftBlue supercomputer) with REBOMOS potential for MoS2, SPC/E water model, and transferable ion force field; umbrella sampling was used to study intercalation mechanisms
- Experimental: Electrodes prepared from MoS2 nanopowder (90 wt%), Carbon Black (5 wt%), and PVA (5 wt%) dropcast on glassy carbon; electrochemical intercalation via chronoamperometry in 1 mM KHCO3 or NaHCO3
- Characterization: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), Scanning Electron Microscopy with EDS, XRD (Bruker D8 Advance), Raman spectroscopy (WiTec Alpha300R, in situ measurements), and XPS (PHI 5400)

**Key Results**:
1. **Hydration shell as energy barrier**: The hydration shell of ions serves as an energy barrier to intercalation, undergoing structural change during intercalation. The energy barrier is almost twice as high for K+ as for Na+ (despite Na+'s larger hydration energy), because K+ must expel at least one water molecule from its shell to fit in the interlayer distance.
2. **Electric field effects**: Applying 0.01 V/Å lowers the intercalation barrier by ~half; at 0.02 V/Å the barrier vanishes for Na+ but remains for K+. Intercalation potentials were determined: -1.4 V vs RHE for K+, -1.3 V vs RHE for Na+.
3. **Structural changes**: XRD showed weakened (002) peak intensity, broadening, and shift to smaller angles (interlayer expansion) in intercalated samples. Raman spectroscopy showed increased separation between E1₂g and A1g modes (from 21 cm⁻¹ for pristine to 24 cm⁻¹ for VS-MoS2, further increasing after intercalation), indicating monosulfur vacancy formation—a consequence of both electrode preparation (sonication) and the intercalation process.
4. **Electronic properties**: XPS Mo 3d binding energies shifted down by 0.5 eV (Na+) and 0.7 eV (K+), indicating electron donation from intercalants. These shifts correspond to intercalation levels of approximately x≈0.3–0.5 in AxMoS2. Electron doping is higher for K+ intercalation due to potassium's empty d-orbital, which allows further hybridization with the transition metal's p-orbital.
5. **Synergistic effect**: Sulfur defects and donated s-electrons work synergistically to enhance conductivity, with the defect-induced midgap state hybridizing with alkali metal s-orbitals.

**Comparison with prior work**: The results deviate from Andersen et al.'s first-principles calculations (which assumed only 1-2 water molecules per K atom), as the current study found hydration shells adopt a planar configuration containing four water molecules in 50% hydration conditions.

**Conclusions**: The intercalation process increases monosulfur defect concentration, and the combined effect of defects plus donated electrons from alkali metals results in increased conductivity, with potassium effects being more pronounced than sodium. MoS2 is shown to be highly tunable in both structural (vertical flexibility) and electronic (valence band structure) properties, with atomic-scale structure engineering significantly impacting macroscopic properties.
args.key_excerpts: "It is demonstrated that the hydration shell of ions serves as an energy barrier to intercalation as it undergoes a structural change during the intercalation. When alkali metal ions are intercalated into MoS2, they introduce more defects and enhance conductivity. Notably, these effects are more pronounced for potassium than for sodium."

# K Intercalation-Assisted Co-Doped MoS2 Nanoflowers for an Efficient Hydrogen Evolution Reaction

### Minkai Qin

### Menghui Qi

### Ruxue Fan

### Jiadong Chen

### Xiaoyun Shi

### Binbin Lin

### Lingling Xi

### Yong Wang

Email: chemwy@zju.edu.cn.

Received 2023 Feb 28; Accepted 2023 Jun 19; Revised 2023 Jun 18; Collection date 2023 Oct 23.

This article is licensed under CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0

## Abstract

2D transition metal disulfides have emerged as promising
Pt-alternative
electrocatalysts for hydrogen generation. However, the sluggish water
dissociation kinetics and limited active sites hinder their performance
in alkaline media. Herein, we propose a two-step hydrothermal method
to synthesize K intercalation-assisted Co-doped MoS2 nanoflowers.
These nanoflowers exhibit an overpotential of only 67 mV at a current
density of 10 mA cm–2, which exceeds that of pristine
MoS2 (143 mV). We demonstrated that the intercalation of
K enlarges the interlayer spacing of MoS2 nanosheets and
facilitates the doping of Co. The incorporation of Co effectively
improves the surface charge transfer efficiency of MoS2 and accelerates water splitting with an energy barrier of 0.12 eV.
This work offers an approach to activate the inert MoS2 basal plane by chemical intercalation and atomic doping coengineering.
It can be extended to develop other functional materials beyond water
splitting.

**Keywords:** molybdenum disulfides, heteroatomic doping, chemical intercalation, hydrogen evolution reaction, hydrophilicity

![graphic file with name pc3c00033_0008.jpg](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/d53a399fcd74/pc3c00033_0008.jpg)

![graphic file with name pc3c00033_0008.jpg](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/d53a399fcd74/pc3c00033_0008.jpg)

![graphic file with name pc3c00033_0007.jpg](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/d53a399fcd74/pc3c00033_0007.jpg)

![graphic file with name pc3c00033_0007.jpg](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/d53a399fcd74/pc3c00033_0007.jpg)

## Introduction

Hydrogen, with its impressive gravimetric
energy density, is considered
an ideal fuel to address energy challenges and is a crucial ingredient
for essential industrial chemicals. It has the potential for use in
a broad range of applications.*−* Among various H2 generation
technologies, electrochemical water hydrolysis enabled by renewable
energy shows great promise for ecofriendly hydrogen production. Pt-based
catalysts are currently the state-of-art electrocatalysts for electrocatalytic
hydrogen evolution.*,* However, due to their rarity and
exorbitant cost, large-scale implementation of water splitting remains
extremely challenging.*,* As a promising alternative, 2D
transition metal disulfides have garnered considerable attention as
cost-effective and Earth-abundant electrocatalysts for hydrogen production.*,*

Molybdenum disulfides (MoS2) is a material with
stacked
layers bound together by van der Waals force, possessing a near zero
free energy of H adsorption similar to Pt-like catalysts.*,* However, both experimental and theoretical research studies have
shown that the inert basal plane and large bandgap limit the electron
transfer rate, hindering the improvement of intrinsic activity.*,* To overcome this obstacle, extensive efforts have been made to enhance
intrinsic conductivity and activate the inert plane. Doping MoS2 with transition metals such as Pt,*,* Mn,*−* Co,*,* and W*,* can endow new properties to metal-rich orbitals and adjust the electronic
structure of MoS2, thus improving its HER performance.
Nevertheless, the layered structure of MoS2 tends to stack
and aggregate, and the constraints of
its relatively narrow interlayer spacing and low hydrophilicity are
often overlooked. These constraints limit the movement of hydronium
ions and may passivate the highly active marginal sites. Furthermore,
insufficient exposure of the active sites on the MoS2 edge
leads to the overall low active density and limits the electrocatalytic
activity of MoS2. Therefore,
an effective method to improve its catalytic activity is to expose
more edge sites through structural design.*,* In addition to adjusting the electronic structure, expanding MoS2’s interlayer spacing through electrochemical intercalation
of alkali metal ions or small molecules into the van der Waals gap
may also expose additional HER active sites located in the interlayers,*−* thus achieving high HER activity under alkaline conditions.

In this work, K intercalation-assisted Co-doped MoS2 was
synthesized through a two-step hydrothermal method. The intercalation
of K resulted in a nanoflower structure composed of MoS2 nanosheets, which maximized the exposure of active sites at the
edges of MoS2. This led to a significant increase in the
catalyst active site density. Furthermore, K intercalation improved
the hydrophilicity of Co-doped MoS2, promoting interface
utilization efficiency between the catalyst and electrolyte. Co-doping
with K intercalation improved the surface charge transfer efficiency
of MoS2 and eliminated the slow reaction kinetics caused
by the low conductivity of the molybdenum disulfides. The resulting
Co-2K-MoS2 demonstrated excellent HER performance with
an overpotential of 67 mV at a current density of 10 mA cm–2 and a Tafel slope of 56.51 mV dec–1. This K intercalation-assisted
Co doping method significantly optimized the performance of MoS2-based electrocatalysts, demonstrating high stability in durability
tests, and it has great potential for use in cathodic electrolysis
reactions.

## Results and Discussion

A two-step hydrothermal method
was developed for synthesizing Co-2K-MoS2, which involves
the intercalation of K into MoS2 followed by Co incorporation.
The synthesis of MoS2 nanoflowers
involved the use of ammonium molybdate tetrahydrate and thiourea as
sources of Mo and S, respectively, while potassium nitrate was employed
as the intercalation agent. The K-MoS2 nanoflowers were
obtained by subjecting the mixture to a hydrothermal process in a
50 mL Teflon-lined steel autoclave at 220 °C for 18 h in a drying
oven. Co-2K-MoS2 was then obtained by subjecting the K-MoS2 nanoflowers to a further hydrothermal process.

### 1. Schematic Illustrations of the Synthesis Processes of K-MoS2 and Co-2K-MoS2.

[![1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/470a39f3b8e9/pc3c00033_0006.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=12382405_pc3c00033_0006.jpg)

![1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/470a39f3b8e9/pc3c00033_0006.jpg)

The phase structures and crystallinity of the
catalysts were determined
by X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern measurements. As shown in [Figure](#fig1)a, the peaks located
at 14.12, 32.90, 39.51, 58.76 can be assigned to the (002), (101),
(103), and (110) crystalline planes of MoS2 (JCPDS card
01-075-1539), in addition to the typical diffraction peaks of carbon
paper. It is worth noting that the (002) lattice plane peak position
was always affected by the interlayer distance according to Bragg’s
law. So compared to the peak position of MoS2 and Co-MoS2, the peak of K-MoS2 and Co-2K-MoS2 shifts
to a smaller angle, indicating the expanding interlayer spacing. All
investigated samples exhibited broadened diffraction peaks due to
the formation of structural defects, which are conducive to high-performance
electrocatalysis. The morphology of the Co-2K-MoS2 was
examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission
electron microscopy (TEM). Flower-like structures were observed in
the hydrothermal environment ([Figure](#fig1)b,c), each composed of randomly grown nanosheets that
greatly increase the specific surface area of MoS2 and
enlarge the contact area with the electrolyte solution. MoS2 is a typical layered material, and interlayer expansion can modulate
the band gap energy and electronic structure,*,,* favoring catalytic performance. Compared
to the pure MoS2, Co-2K-MoS2 exhibited a layer
spacing of 0.64 nm, reducing ion transport resistance in the layer
spaces ([Figure](#fig1)d and [Figure S1](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf)). The lattice spacing of Co-2K-MoS2 was 0.27 nm, corresponding to the characteristics of the
MoS2 (101) lattice plane, and no significant traces of
lattice change were observed ([Figure](#fig1)e). Co doping was successfully achieved by replacing
Mo ([Figure](#fig1)f), and
energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) elemental mapping confirmed the
existence of Co and K in the crystalline domains ([Figure](#fig1)g). Co atoms were uniformly
distributed on MoS2, likely entering the lattice of MoS2 as Mo substitutes, and no Co clusters were observed. The
content of Mo, S, Co, and K of Co-2K-MoS2 was confirmed
by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES)
analysis, which shows a Mo to S mass ratio of 0.60, while the comparative
MoS2 sample had a ratio of 0.78. Co-doped MoS2 has a smaller proportion of Mo due to Co substitution.

### 1.

[![1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/a46ec6f438cd/pc3c00033_0001.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=12382405_pc3c00033_0001.jpg)

![1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/a46ec6f438cd/pc3c00033_0001.jpg)

Structure characterizations
of Co-2K-MoS**2**. (a) XRD patterns for MoS2, 2K-MoS2, Co-MoS2, and Co-2K-MoS2. (b, c) SEM images of Co-2K-MoS2. (d) HRTEM images
and (e, f) HAADF-STEM image of Co-2K-MoS2, where the Co
site is outlined by a white circle. Blue Mo,
yellow S, and green Co. (g) Corresponding energy dispersive X-ray
spectroscopy (EDS) elemental mappings of Co-2K-MoS2.

The geometric HER activity of the catalysts, as
prepared, was evaluated
using the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) method in a three-electrode
system immersed in 1 M KOH media with 95% *iR* compensation.
Prior to the electrochemical test, the pH of the electrolyte and the
reference electrode potential were adjusted for reliability of the
measured electrochemical data. As depicted in [Figure](#fig2)a, the pristine MoS2 catalyst
exhibited the highest overpotential, reaching up to 143 mV at a current
density of 10 mA cm–2, serving as the control. While
K intercalation and Co doping alone improved the HER performance to
some extent, the enhancement was relatively limited. However, it is
noteworthy that the combination of K intercalation and Co doping significantly
improved the performance of Co-2K-MoS2, achieving an overpotential
only 67 mV at a current density of 10 mA cm–2. Additionally,
electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was utilized to investigate
the charge transfer resistance of the electrode samples. As demonstrated
in [Figure](#fig2)b, the impedance
spectra can be divided into two sections: semicircles at the high
frequency and intermediate frequency regions, corresponding to the
solid electrolyte impedance and charge transfer impedance, respectively.*,* An evident semicircle of Co-MoS2 was observed in the
high frequency region, resulting from its long diffusion path. The
semicircle at the intermediate frequency region is indicative of the
HER electrocatalytic kinetics. The Nyquist plots illustrate that Co-2K-MoS2 has the smallest charge transfer resistance (*R*
ct). The intercalation of K and Co doping in MoS2 drastically reduced the *R*
ct values from
116.9 to 5.4 Ω, implying the enhanced conductivity of Co-2K-MoS2 and the facilitated electron transfer.

### 2.

[![2](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/9cf9693435c5/pc3c00033_0002.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=12382405_pc3c00033_0002.jpg)

![2](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/4ead/12382405/9cf9693435c5/pc3c00033_0002.jpg)

Electrochemical HER performance.
(a) Polarization curves, (b) Nyquist
plots, and (c) Tafel slopes. (d) The overpotentials of Co-2K-MoS2 at different current densities in 1.0 M KOH. (e) Change in
the LSV curve of Co-2K-MoS2 after 3000 CV cycles. (f) Chronopotentiometry
measurement of Co-2K-MoS2 at a constant current density
of 10 mA cm–2 in 1.0 M KOH. (g) H2 amount
of the calculated and measured value. (h) Comparison of Tafel slope
and overpotential for Co-2K-MoS2 and previously reported
HER catalysts in alkaline electrolytes.

By comparison of the Tafel slope of various catalysts,
it is evident
that molybdenum disulfides acted as the active site for 2K-MoS2 and pure MoS2, with Tafel slopes of approximately
90.96 and 127.3 mV dec–1, respectively. Co-MoS2 and Co-2K-MoS2 exhibited a smaller Tafel slope
with 76.12 and 56.15 mV dec–1 due to the optimization
of MoS2’s surface electronic structure by the incorporation
of Co, indicating a shift in active sites ([Figure](#fig2)c). Moreover, the synergistic effect of K
and Co further improved the kinetics of the hydrogen evolution reaction.
The overpotential changes of catalysts under different current densities
(10 and 100 mA cm–2) were statistically analyzed
in [Figure](#fig2)d, with
Co-2K-MoS2 demonstrating superior HER activity. Impressively,
the overpotentials of 67 and 138 were achieved at current densities
of 10 and 100 mA cm–2 (η10 = 67,
η100 = 138 mV). Cyclic stability is a vital criterion
for catalyst evaluation, as it determines its industrial application
prospects. [Figure](#fig2)e illustrates the LSV curves before and after 3000 cycles of voltammetry
(CV) scanning at 5 mV s–1. There were no significant
differences after 3000 CV cycles, indicating that Co-2K-MoS2 has good long-term durability under alkaline conditions. [Figure](#fig2)f depicts the cyclic
stability of Co-2K-MoS2 at a constant current density of
10 mA cm–2. After continuous testing for 18 h, no
obvious activity attenuation was observed, indicating excellent stability.
Moreover, a series of characterizations were carried out to uncover
the state of morphology and structure of MoS2 after the
chronoamperometry tests, and the results indicated the structural
and morphological stability of Co-2K-MoS2 ([Figure S2](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf)). The faradaic efficiency of Co-2K-MoS2 was tested in a homemade gastight electrochemical cell, and
the measured amount of H2 generated during the HER process
dovetailed well with the theoretical value, suggesting a nearly 100%
faradaic efficiency ([Figure](#fig2)g). Furthermore, it is noteworthy that Co-2K-MoS2 outperforms various previously reported HER catalysts in alkaline
media ([Figure](#fig2)h and [Table S1](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf)).

## Mechanism Insight

To investigate the active origin
of the Co-2K-MoS2 catalyst,
we conducted further experiments to understand the effect of K intercalation
and Co incorporation on the chemical properties and electronic structures
of catalysts. The experiments showed that the structure of MoS2 did not change significantly with different contents of K,
as indicated by the diffraction peaks assigned to 2H MoS2 ([Figure S3](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf)). However, K doping did result
in the formation of MoS2 nanosheets with complete and smooth
edges during the hydrothermal synthesis. With increasing K content,
MoS2 nanosheets gradually assembled into flower-like structures
which were closely arranged and exposed more active sites at the edge
of the MoS2. With the further increase of K content, the
content of flower-like MoS2 increases to cover the structure
of carbon paper ([Figure](#fig3)a–d). Excessive stacking of these structures, however, hindered
the transfer of electrons and negatively impacted the electrochemical
performance. Our energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy elemental mappings
of 2K-MoS2 further confirmed the successful intercalation
of K ([Figure S4](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf)).

To evaluate the HER performance of the as-prepared
catalysts (MoS2, 1K-MoS2, 2K-MoS2, and 3K-MoS2), we measured and compared their performance
([Figure S5a](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf)). The results showed that 2K-MoS2 exhibited
better performance than MoS2, while the catalytic activity
of 3K-MoS2 was inferior to that of MoS2. This
was attributed to the excessive amount of K, which began to cover
the active sites of MoS2. Our experiments confirmed that
K intercalation transformed the surface nature and improved the interaction
between the catalyst and water. Furthermore, we observed that the
HER performance of the catalyst increased first and then decreased,
which was consistent with the change in morphological characteristics
caused by the addition of K. The intercalation of K modulated the
charge transfer impedance and increased the electrochemical surface
area, as confirmed by the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)
and CV measurement ([Figures S5 and S6](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf)).
These results indicate that the K element plays an auxiliary role
in the formation of MoS2 nanoflowers and exposes more active
sites of MoS2.

The hydrophilicity of the catalyst
is a crucial factor influencing
its electrochemical performance determining the contact area between
the electrocatalyst surface and water during the HER process. To determine
the influence of K doping on the surface wettability of K-MoS2 electrocatalyst, the contact-angle was measured. As a control
group, the water contact-angle of carbon paper in air was 136.2°,
showing hydrophobic properties ([Figure S7](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf)). The contact angles of MoS2, 1K-MoS2, 2K-MoS2, and 3K-MoS2 with water in the air were 102.5°,
104.5°, 88.0°, and 99.7°, respectively ([Figure](#fig2)e–h), and these values
correlated well with the electrocatalytic activity measurement results.
These findings indicate that K intercalation in MoS2 nanoflowers
significantly enhances hydrophilicity and reduces hydrogen evolution
overpotential to a certain extent, but excessive K may cover the active
site of MoS2.

Although the intercalation of K improves
the hydrophilicity and
layer spacing of MoS2, further optimization of its surface
electronic structure is necessary to enhance the charge transfer efficiency.
Therefore, we applied a doping method to create new catalytic sites
and elevate reaction kinetics by introducing Co. Appropriate amounts
of Co were loaded onto MoS2 and K-MoS2, and
their corresponding XRD patterns are shown in [Figure S8](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf). No obvious diffraction peak of the Co species was
observed except for the significant diffraction peak of MoS2. Furthermore, the HER performance of pure MoS2 and different
Co-K-MoS2 samples was measured, As shown in [Figure S9a](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf), Co-MoS2 exhibited higher
HER performance compared with that of pure MoS2, indicating
that the introduction of Co can effectively improve the catalytic
activity of MoS2. Different Co-K-MoS2 samples
showed significant volcanic performance curves, and Co-2K-MoS2 showed the highest HER performance, consistent with the hydrophilic
results of the catalysts. The corresponding Tafel slopes of these
catalysts were also calculated as shown in [Figure S9b](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf). The Tafel slope of MoS2 loaded with Co, especially
Co-2K-MoS2, was significantly lower than that of pure MoS2, indicating that Co can optimize the surface electronic structure
of MoS2 and improve the kinetics of the hydrogen evolution
reaction. Moreover, the morphology of the nanosheet was maintained
in the case of Co doping, as shown in [Figure S10](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf).

The Raman spectra revealed two distinct peaks at 379.2 cm–1 and 402 cm–1, corresponding to
the in-plane Mo-S
phonon mode (E2g) and the out-of-plane Mo-S mode (A1g) of the typical MoS2-layered structure, respectively. [Figure](#fig4)a shows a slight
red shift in the A1g mode of K-MoS2 and Co-2K-MoS2 compared to the samples without K intercalation, indicating
a weakened interlayer mechanical coupling strength and confirming
that K intercalation promotes spacing expansion. X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS) was conducted to study the effects of Co and K
doping on the valence state and chemical composition of MoS2. An XPS survey spectrum of different samples in [Figure S11](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf) confirms the presence of Mo, S, Co, and K in the
compound. From the Mo XPS of pristine MoS2 and the other
samples, different signals appear when the K and Co species are simultaneously
intercalated or doped into MoS2. At first, the small peak
that appeared at 226 eV was assigned to the S 2s in the Mo spectra.
Moreover, the Mo 3d spectrum of Co-2K-MoS2 can be deconvolved
into four peaks ([Figure](#fig4)b). The two main peaks at 229.5° and 232.5° correspond
to Mo 3d5/2 and Mo 3d3/2 in Mo­(IV), respectively,
indicating that Mo mainly originates from the Mo-S bond. Additionally,
there are two peaks derived from Mo­(VI) in Co-2K-MoS2,
indicating that Co substitution in the nearby lattice produces a unique
chemical environment of Mo, with the
coexistence of Mo­(IV) and Mo­(VI). The uneven surface charge distribution
of molybdenum disulfides facilitates water activation on the catalyst
surface. However, the characteristic peak of Mo­(VI) is not found in
the Co-MoS2 sample without K intercalation, confirming
that K intercalation benefits Co doping and that the content of Co
species in Co-MoS2 is low, making the presence of Mo6+ undetectable. As shown in [Figure](#fig4)c, the S2– of MoS2 is at 162.8 eV, while the position of S2‑ of Co-MoS2 is shifted to the left due to Co replacing part of Mo. The
right-shifted S2‑ in 2K-MoS2 can be attributed
to the interaction between S and K. Moreover, S 2p of Co-2K-MoS2 is deconvolved into six peaks, of which the double peak of
162.3 eV is assigned to the S2– species of the MoS2 basal plane, and the peak of 163.6 eV corresponds to bridging
disulfide-type sulfur S2
2–, which is
generally regarded as sulfur vacancies. And the other two peaks located
at 168.7 eV were assigned to the sulfate. The Co 2p spectrum is mainly
deconvolved into four peaks ([Figure](#fig4)d), corresponding to Co2+ and its satellite
peaks, indicating that Co2+ is dominant. Compared to Co-MoS2, the signal of Co significantly increased for Co-2K-MoS2, indicating that K intercalation accelerates Co doping. Moreover,
the relative contents of Co in the Co-2K-MoS2 and Co-MoS2 were compared through various methods, and it is obvious
that the Co content in the Co-2K-MoS2 is higher in the
Co-MoS2, which further proves that the K intercalation
accelerates the Co doping ([Table S2](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf)).

For all we know, the initial structure and chemical
composition
of as-prepared catalysts may undergo a reconstruction in the electrode–electrolyte
interface with an applied bias. A series
of Raman spectra were obtained for Co-2K-MoS2 as a function
of the applied potential (vs Ag/AgCl) during a reduction sweep. The
results showed that the in-plane Mo-S phonon mode (E2g)
and the out-of-plane Mo-S mode (A1g) did not change and
shift, indicating that the structure remained stable during the HER
process. Based on these measurements and analyses, theoretical investigations
were performed by density functional theory (DFT) calculations to
explore the origin of activity. The computational model of 2H MoS2 was constructed, and four different models were compared
([Figure](#fig5)b). First,
the 2H MoS2 structures with and without K intercalation
were constructed and compared. As shown in [Figure S12](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf), the interlayer expanded with K intercalation during the
structure optimization. Moreover, the formation energies of S vacancy
and Co substituted Mo/S were also calculated. As shown in [Figure](#fig5)c, the formation
energy of the S vacancy is 1.512 eV. Also, there are two sites for
Co substituted. One is the sublayer Mo site and the other is the S
site. According to the calculated results, the formation energy of
Co substituted Mo is 0.4378 eV, which is smaller for the Co substituted
S site (4.920 eV). Thus, the model of Co substituted Mo is more favorable.
In general, the reaction pathway of alkaline HER typically follows
a Volmer-Heyrovsky or Volmer-Tafel step, and the Volmer step (H2O + e– = H\* + OH–) is
generally considered to be the rate-determining step, as the initial
adsorption and cleavage of water molecules are usually sluggish.*,* The incorporation
of Co was found to facilitate the adsorption of H2O ([Figure](#fig5)d). Both Co-substituted
Mo and Co-substituted S models showed stronger water adsorption energies
(−0.847 and −1.275 eV, respectively) compared to the
K-MoS2 basal plane (−0.085 eV) and S-vacancy (−0.123
eV). The weaker adsorption of H2O for K-MoS2 is caused by the steric hindrance effect of S and the electron–electron
repulsion effect between the O and S atoms. To better understand the
discrepancy of adsorption energy and determine the surface electronic
features of catalysts, the d-band center was calculated. As shown in [Figure S13](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf), the d-band center of Co-2K-MoS2 with Co-substituted
Mo is found to be −1.253 eV, which was higher than that of
K-MoS2 with S vacancy (−1.767 eV), demonstrating
that the local electronic environment was modulated with the Co dopant
and the upshift d-band center benefits stronger affinity to adsorbates.
And it should be noted that the adsorption site of H2O
is the Co site for Co-2K-MoS2 with Co-substituted S, and
the corresponding d-band center of Co was calculated to be −1.119
eV. The result explains the difference of adsorption energy of H2O in the model of Co-substituted S and Mo. Moreover, atomic
level modification had a significant influence on Δ*G*
H. As shown in [Figure](#fig5)e, the Δ*G*
H of Co-substituted
Mo is 0.392 eV, indicating favorable conditions for hydrogen generation.
In addition, the incorporation of Co significantly reduced the energy
required for water splitting (H2O = H\* + OH\*), particularly
for Co-substituted Mo, where it was lowered by 0.12 eV ([Figure](#fig5)f). Partial substitution of
Co atoms for Mo atoms was found to dramatically activate the basal
plane by optimizing the H2O adsorption ability and accelerating
water dissociation. The corresponding adsorption configurations for
the water splitting step for the four different models are shown in [Figures S14–S17](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/prechem.3c00033/suppl_file/pc3c00033_si_001.pdf). Overall, on the one hand,
the intercalation of K expands the interlayer distance, facilitating
reaction diffusion. On the other hand, the doping of Co creates new
catalytic sites and optimizes the surface electronic structure, thereby
enhancing the reaction kinetics. These factors together contribute
to the excellent performance observed ([Figure](#fig5)g).

## Conclusion

In summary, this work has successfully developed
a facile approach
for synthesizing K intercalation-assisted Co-doped MoS2 nanoflowers with exceptional electrocatalytic activity for water
splitting. The nanoflowers exhibited an overpotential of 67 mV at
a current density of 10 mA cm–2, surpassing the
performance of the pristine MoS2 (143 mV). Through a series
of experiments and calculations, it is revealed that K intercalation
not only enlarged the interlayer spacing of MoS2 and facilitated
Co doping but also enhanced hydrophilicity and water adsorption. Furthermore,
the incorporation of Co optimized the surface electronic structure
and shifted the d-band center, thereby further enhancing water adsorption
and accelerating water splitting with a low energy barrier of 0.12
eV. This work presents a new avenue for designing and activating MoS2-based electrocatalysts using chemical intercalation and doping
coengineering strategies, which could also be applied to develop other
high-performance catalytic applications in other types of transition
metal dichalcogenides.

## Methods

### Materials

Urea, sodium citrate, and cobalt nitrate
hexahydrate were all purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Ammonium molybdate
tetrahydrate, ethyl alcohol, and potassium hydroxide were purchased
from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. Carbon paper was purchased
from Shanghai Heusen Electric Co. Ltd. Ultrapure water was produced
from a Millipore Milli-Q grade.

### Preparation of MoS2

Typically, 1 mmol of
(NH4)6Mo7O24·4H2O and 35 mmol of thiourea were dissolved in 40 mL of ultrapure
water and then stirred at room temperature to form a uniform solution.
Then the carbon paper was soaked in the solution and both of them
transferred into a Teflon-lined. Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave
was heated in an oven at 220 °C for 18 h. After cooling to room
temperature, the surface impurity was washed away with ultrapure water.
The obtained MoS2 was dried in a vacuum drying oven for
further use.

### Preparation of *x*K-MoS2

One mmol of (NH4)6Mo7O24·4H2O, 35 mmol of thiourea, and *x* mmol of KNO3 (*x*: 1, 2 and 3) were dissolved
in 40 mL of ultrapure water and then stirred at room temperature to
form a uniform solution. Then the carbon paper was soaked in the solution
and both of them transferred into a Teflon-lined. Teflon-lined stainless-steel
autoclave was heated in an oven at 220 °C for 18 h. After cooling
to room temperature, the surface impurity was washed away with ultrapure
water. The obtained catalysts are named 1K-MoS2, 2K-MoS2 and 3K-MoS2, respectively.

### Preparation of Co-*x*K-MoS2

One mmol amount of Co­(NO3)2, 3 mmol of urea,
and 5 mg of sodium citrate were dissolved in 40 mL of ultrapure water
and then stirred to form a uniform solution. The obtained MoS2 and *x*K-MoS2 were soaked completely
in the above solution and then transferred into a Teflon-lined. The
Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave was heated in an oven at 120
°C for 12 h. After the mixture was cooled to room temperature,
the surface impurity was washed away with ultrapure water. The obtained
catalysts were labeled as Co-MoS2, Co-1K-MoS2, Co-2K-MoS2, and Co-3K-MoS2.

### Characterization

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
images were acquired from a Hitachi SU-8010 microscope. High-resolution
transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) was performed on a Titan
G2 80-200 ChemiSTEM at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. The ESCALAB
250Xi analyzer with an aluminum anode (Al 1486.6 eV) An X-ray source
was used to obtain the chemical state and composition of catalysts.
The D/Tex-Ultima TV wide-angle X-ray diffractometer equipped with
Cu Kα radiation (λ=0.15406 nm) was adapted to acquire
the crystal structure. Inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission
spectrometry (ICP-AES) on a PerkinElmer Optima 8000 instrument was
used to obtain the elements content.

### Electrochemical Measurement

The CHI 760E electrochemical
workstation (CH Instruments, Inc., Shanghai) was used to evaluate
the electrochemical performance. The Hg/HgO electrode was used as
the reference electrode, and a graphite rod was adapted as the counter
electrode. The Hg/HgO electrode was calibrated by using a Pt electrode
as the working and counter electrode under a H2-saturated
electrolyte through CV measurements. In general, the potentials were
converted to the potentials versus the reversible hydrogen electrode
(RHE) based on the following Nernst equation: *E*
(RHE) = *E*
(Hg/HgO) + 0.0591 ×
pH + 0.098V, unless otherwise stated. The 95% *iR* compensation
was adopted before the electrochemical test. Linear sweep voltammetry
(LSV) was carried out with a scan rate of 5 mVs–1 and the Tafel plots of the overpotential vs log­(j) derived from
polarization curves. The double layer capacitance (*C*
dl) values were obtained via CV measurements between 0.67
and 0.77 V. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried
out in the frequency range from 105 to 10–2 Hz.

### In-Situ Raman Spectroscopy Measurement

In-situ Raman
spectra were recorded on a LabRAM HR Evolution with a laser of 514
nm. And the electrolytic tank was homemade by Teflon. Both the cathode
and anode compartments were covered by round quartz windows to protect
the laser emitter and signal acceptor. The Ag/AgCl electrode with
an inner reference electrolyte of 1.0 M KCl and a Pt wire serves as
the reference electrode and the counter electrode, respectively.

### Computational Section

Density functional theory (DFT)
calculations were performed with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE)
exchange-correlation function in a projector augmented wave pseudopotentials
implementation using the Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP).*,* And the theoretical calculations were carried out by DMOL3 code
for hydrogen-binding free energy.*,* Calculations
were performed on the (001) surface for 2H MoS2, and a
vacuum of 10 Å was accepted along the *z*-axis.
The cutoff energy is 400 eV, and the Gaussian electron smearing method
with σ= 0.05 eV was adopted. During structure optimization,
the geometry optimization was performed when the convergence criterion
on forces was < 0.02 eV Å–1 and the energy
difference was smaller than 10–5 eV.

This is a scientific research article from Precision Chemistry (American Chemical Society) published on PMC (PMID/PMC 12382405), titled "K Intercalation-Assisted Co-Doped MoS2 Nanoflowers for an Efficient Hydrogen Evolution Reaction" by Minkai Qin, Menghui Qi, Ruxue Fan, Jiadong Chen, Xiaoyun Shi, Binbin Lin, Lingling Xi, and Yong Wang (email: chemwy@zju.edu.cn). Received Feb 28, 2023; Accepted Jun 19, 2023; Collection date Oct 23, 2023. Licensed under CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0.

KEY FINDINGS:
The researchers developed a two-step hydrothermal method to synthesize K intercalation-assisted Co-doped MoS2 nanoflowers as a Pt-alternative electrocatalyst for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in alkaline media. The Co-2K-MoS2 catalyst achieved an overpotential of only 67 mV at a current density of 10 mA cm⁻², compared to 143 mV for pristine MoS2, and a Tafel slope of 56.51 mV dec⁻¹.

MECHANISM:
- K intercalation expands the interlayer spacing of MoS2 nanosheets (to 0.64 nm layer spacing), facilitates Co doping, enhances hydrophilicity (reducing water contact angle from 102.5° to 88.0° for 2K-MoS2), and promotes formation of nanoflower structures exposing more edge active sites.
- Co doping replaces Mo atoms (Co-substituted Mo is energetically favorable with formation energy 0.4378 eV vs 4.920 eV for Co-substituted S), optimizes the surface electronic structure, shifts the d-band center upward (−1.253 eV), improves water adsorption energy (−0.847 eV), and lowers the water-splitting energy barrier by 0.12 eV.
- The combination of K intercalation and Co doping synergistically reduced charge transfer resistance (Rct) from 116.9 Ω to 5.4 Ω.
- DFT calculations confirmed the Volmer step (water dissociation) as rate-determining; Co incorporation facilitates H2O adsorption and dissociation.

PERFORMANCE:
- Overpotentials of 67 mV (η10) and 138 mV (η100) at 10 and 100 mA cm⁻² in 1 M KOH.
- Excellent long-term durability: no significant activity loss after 3000 CV cycles and 18 hours of chronopotentiometry at 10 mA cm⁻².
- Nearly 100% faradaic efficiency (measured H2 matched theoretical value).
- Outperforms previously reported HER catalysts in alkaline media.

EXPERIMENTAL METHODS:
- Synthesis: Ammonium molybdate tetrahydrate and thiourea (Mo and S sources) with KNO3 as intercalation agent, hydrothermally processed at 220°C for 18 h in Teflon-lined autoclave; then Co(NO3)2, urea, and sodium citrate at 120°C for 12 h.
- Characterization: XRD, SEM, HRTEM, HAADF-STEM, EDS, ICP-AES, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, in-situ Raman, and DFT calculations (VASP with PBE functional).
- Electrochemical testing: CHI 760E workstation, Hg/HgO reference electrode, graphite rod counter electrode, 95% iR compensation, LSV at 5 mV s⁻¹, EIS from 10⁵ to 10⁻² Hz.

CONCLUSION: This work presents a coengineering strategy combining chemical intercalation (K) and atomic doping (Co) to activate the inert basal plane of MoS2, which can be extended to other transition metal dichalcogenides and functional materials beyond water splitting.

Funding: "Pioneer" and "Leading Goose" R&D Program of Zhejiang (2022C01151), National Natural Science Foundation of China (21802120 and 21872121). Minkai Qin and Menghui Qi contributed equally to this work. Authors declare no competing financial interest.

## Abstract

Although doping with alkali atoms is a powerful technique for introducing charge carriers into physical systems, the resulting charge-transfer systems are generally not air stable. Here we describe computationally a strategy towards increasing the stability of alkali-doped materials that employs stoichiometrically unbalanced salt crystals with excess cations (which could be deposited during, e.g., _in situ_ gating) to achieve doping levels similar to those attained by pure alkali metal doping. The crystalline interior of the salt crystal acts as a template to stabilize the excess dopant atoms against oxidation and deintercalation, which otherwise would be highly favorable. We characterize this doping method for graphene, N b S e 2, and B i 2⁢S e 3 and its effect on direct-to-indirect band gap transitions, 2D superconductivity, and thermoelectric performance. Salt intercalation should be generally applicable to systems which can accommodate this “ionic crystal” doping (and particularly favorable when geometrical packing constraints favor nonstoichiometry).

This is the Physical Review Letters article page for "Nonstoichiometric Salt Intercalation as a Means to Stabilize Alkali Doping of 2D Materials" (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.129.266401), published on 23 December 2022 in Phys. Rev. Lett. Vol. 129, Issue 26, article 266401. The paper was authored by Yuanxi Wang (Penn State / University of North Texas), Vincent H. Crespi (Penn State), Marvin L. Cohen (UC Berkeley / Lawrence Berkeley National Lab), and Amir Nourhani (University of Akron, corresponding author). The article was received 1 March 2021, revised 11 August 2022, and accepted 30 September 2022. It has 3 citations (per Dimensions) and is available via CHORUS with an accepted manuscript download option.

The abstract describes a computational strategy to increase the stability of alkali-doped materials by using stoichiometrically unbalanced salt crystals with excess cations (potentially deposited during in situ gating) to achieve doping levels similar to pure alkali metal doping. The crystalline interior of the salt crystal acts as a template to stabilize excess dopant atoms against oxidation and deintercalation. The method is characterized computationally for graphene, NbSe2, and Bi2Se3, examining effects on direct-to-indirect band gap transitions, 2D superconductivity, and thermoelectric performance. The approach is described as generally applicable to systems that can accommodate "ionic crystal" doping, particularly favorable when geometrical packing constraints favor nonstoichiometry.

PhySH subject headings include: Dopants, Electronic structure, 2-dimensional systems, Graphene, and Density functional calculations. Full article text, supplemental material, and references require a subscription or institutional login.
