In this work, high-quality edge-contacted FETs are realized using monolayer MoS 2 grown by chemical vapor deposition (CVD), which can be clearly verified from the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image. By using well-controlled plasma etching technology to form clean edge-contact regions, the etched areas are less susceptible to various molecules, free radicals, adsorbates, and air exposure generated during the plasma process. Specifically, nickel/gold (Ni/Au) contacts were evaporated under high vacuum at a slow deposition rate to serve as ohmic contacts. The edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FETs exhibited a linear current–voltage relationship at a cryogenic temperature of 20 K. The extracted Schottky barrier of the edge-contact devices was as low as 32 meV, and the contact resistance was 1.25 kΩ·μm. Furthermore, the edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FETs with _L_ ch = 120 nm on HfO 2 dielectric demonstrated high on-state current of 436 μA/μm and transconductance of 123 μS/μm at _V_ ds = 1 V, far exceeding previously reported edge-contact 2D devices.

## Results

The manufacturing process of the edge-contact FET is depicted in Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F1)B. Monolayer MoS 2 film was grown by using CVD method on a glass substrate [[38](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B38)]. The as-grown monolayer MoS 2 films were then transferred onto an HfO 2/Si substrate using polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) as an adhesion/supporting layer by a wet transfer method. Moreover, it is crucial to note that the as-grown high-quality monolayer MoS 2 is a prerequisite for obtaining high-performance devices [[39](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B39)–[41](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B41)]. The isolation region was etched using inductively coupled plasma (ICP) to obtain a long ribbon of monolayer MoS 2. An annealing process was conducted to eliminate organic residues to achieve a high-quality monolayer MoS 2 channel. The contact regions of FETs were patterned using electron beam lithography, while the channel MoS 2 regions were covered with a PMMA photoresist. Before depositing the contact metal, monolayer MoS 2 of the contact regions was etched by pure argon (Ar) plasma [the control group was treated with oxygen/argon (O 2/Ar) plasma, which will be discussed later]. More importantly, the entire etching process was carried out in a clean room with relatively low humidity, and contact metal was deposited immediately after the etching process. This process is to avoid the reaction of numerous dangling bonds (Mo-bonds and S-bonds) of MoS 2 in the contact regions with various molecules, free radicals, oxygen, and steam in the air to form molybdenum oxide, which reduces the quality of the edge contact [[42](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B42)], which will be further discussed in the following sections. The source/drain contact metal of Ni/Au is evaporated under a high vacuum of 2 × 10−7 torr at a slow rate of 0.01 nm/s, because the low damage metal deposition under high vacuum is also a prerequisite for obtaining high-quality edge contact [[43](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B43),[44](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B44)]. See Fig. [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#supplementary-materials) for device fabrication process flow.

To further verify the monolayer MoS 2 edge-contact structure more intuitively, the cross-sectional TEM characterization of the local contact regions of MoS 2/Ni was performed, as shown in Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F1)C. It is evident that the successful construction of monolayer MoS 2 edge contact has been achieved. The edges of the monolayer MoS 2 on a 9-nm-thick HfO 2 substrate are connected to the deposited metal Ni, visually indicating the formation of edge contact. The corresponding energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDXS) mapping shows the element distribution, and the elemental map of metal Ni is connected to those of Mo and S between metal Ni and the edge of the etched monolayer MoS 2, proving the formation of edge contact, as shown in Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F1)D.

In addition to the direct observation of the microscopic morphology, we further characterized the material properties of monolayer MoS 2 before and after the etching process for the edge-contact structure by spectroscopic analysis, which was used to confirm that the monolayer MoS 2 in the contact regions had been completely removed prior to contact metallization. Raman and photoluminescence (PL) spectra of the monolayer MoS 2 in the contact regions were characterized before and after the etching process, as depicted in Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F2)A and B. As shown by the black line in Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F2)A, the Raman spectra exhibit the E 1 2g and A 1g peaks with a position difference of 19.5 cm−1, confirming that the as-grown MoS 2 is monolayer, consistent with previous reports [[39](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B39),[40](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B40)]. The Raman spectrum of the etched monolayer MoS 2 in the contact regions completely disappeared from the E 1 2g and A 1g mode after the etching process. Similarly, the PL spectrum of the etched monolayer MoS 2 in the contact regions was also completely absent after the etching process, indicating that monolayer MoS 2 in the contact region had been fully removed.

In order to visually understand the electrical transport properties of edge contacts constructed under different etching conditions, the 2 batches of devices were compared side by side, except that different etching processes (Ar plasma or O 2/Ar plasma) were used. Figure [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F2)C shows the transfer characteristics (_I_ d–_V_ g curves) of the edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 transistors with _L_ ch = 1 μm at _V_ ds = 0.1 V by using the O 2/Ar plasma and Ar plasma process, respectively. The edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FET by using Ar plasma shows a 10 times higher on-state current than by using O 2/Ar plasma at the same channel length, which may be attributed to the oxidation of the edges of the etched MoS 2 by using O 2/Ar plasma. The output characteristics (_I_ d–_V_ d curves) of the transistors are shown in Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F2)D. The edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FET by using Ar plasma exhibits ohmic contact behavior with _I_ ds of 97 μA/μm at _V_ ds = 1 V, while the device using O 2/Ar plasma exhibits Schottky behavior with _I_ ds of 8 μA/μm at _V_ ds = 1 V. The electrical transport properties of devices fabricated under O 2/Ar etching conditions deteriorated substantially, confirming the significant impact of the channel edge dangling bonds on the edge-contact quality.

To further examine the edge-contact quality for the Ar plasma process, we performed low-temperature measurements of edge-contact FETs with a 200-nm short channel. We present the transfer characteristics of devices with _L_ ch = 200 nm from 300 K to 20 K, as shown in Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F3)A. It can be observed that the _I_ d–_V_ g curves at different temperatures cross around _V_ bg = 1.7 V, which is common in 2D devices and illustrates the transition of the channel from insulating to metallic properties with gate control. Figure [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F3)B compares the output characteristic curves of the edge-contact device with _L_ ch = 200 nm at room temperature of 300 K and cryogenic temperature of 20 K (see Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#supplementary-materials)). The monolayer MoS 2 edge-contact FET exhibited a linear output curve with a high output currents of 380 and 525 μA/μm at supplied drain–source voltage of 1 V and 2 V, respectively, demonstrating ohmic contact at room temperature. It is clearly shown that the saturated output current density increases from 524 μA/μm at 300 K to 710 μA/μm at 20 K under the same voltage bias of _V_ ds = 2 V and _V_ bg = 6 V, accompanied by current saturation. As depicted in Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F3)B, the output characteristic curves remain nearly linear even at 20 K, demonstrating quasi-ohmic contact. The low-temperature quasi-ohmic contact phenomenon observed in our FETs is similar to that seen in other top contacts, such as graphene contacts [[45](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B45)] and h-BN/MoS 2 stacks contacts [[46](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B46)], and is crucial to achieving high electrical performance. To evaluate the potential of edge**-**contact monolayer MoS 2 transistors at scaled channel lengths, a 120-nm short-channel high-performance edge-contact FET was demonstrated. The corresponding scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image is shown in the inset of Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F4)B. Figure [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F4)A shows the transfer characteristics of the edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FET at _V_ ds = 0.1 and 1 V. The device exhibits high on-state current, low sub-threshold swing (SS) of 150 mV/dec, and an on/off ratio of 6 × 10 7. Owing to the low SBH of the edge contacts and high-quality HfO 2 dielectric layer for MoS 2 transistors, the peak transconductance _g_ m of the device reaches 123 μS/μm at _V_ ds = 1 V. As shown in the output characteristic curves of Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F4)B, high output current of 605 and 436 μA/μm is obtained at supplied drain–source voltage of 2 and 1 V, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, the output current of 436 μA/μm at _V_ ds = 1 V in this work represents the highest output current density for monolayer MoS 2 edge-contact FETs to date, more than 4 times higher than previous studies as shown in benchmark figure of Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F4)C. Table [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#supplementary-materials) lists the specific comparisons of different electrical parameters. Furthermore, through statistical analysis of the measurement results of several edge-contact devices with different channel lengths (_L_ ch = 120, 150, 160, 180, and 200 nm), the repeatability of high output current in short-channel edge-contact FETs at _V_ ds = 1 V can be confirmed, as shown in Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F4)D. Obviously, the output current of all edge-contact devices remains at a high level, verifying the high-quality edge contacts in this work.

Essentially, the high output current and on-state current of edge-contact FET can be attributed to the low _R_ c generated by the well-constructed bonded edge interface. By extensively analyzing the output current with different channel lengths, the _R_ c for the edge-contact FETs is extracted as shown in Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F4)E. Contact resistance extracted from devices with channel lengths below 200 nm is more accurate, as the contact resistance either dominates the total resistance or is at least comparable to the channel resistance. The _R_ c value of edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FETs is 1.25 ± 0.46 kΩ·μm, better than the values of edge-contact MoS 2 FETs reported in the literatures [[29](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B29),[30](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B30),[32](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B32),[33](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B33),[37](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B37),[47](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#B47)], as depicted in Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#F4)F. Furthermore, a scaled contact length (_L_ c) device with _L_ c = 120 nm and _L_ ch = 220 nm was also successfully demonstrated experimentally to show the potential of device scaling (Fig. [S3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0593#supplementary-materials)).

## Discussion

We have reported the high-performance edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FET by using CVD grown monolayer MoS 2, with channel length reduced to 120 nm. The plasma etching by pure Ar improves the edge dangling bonds and thus improves the edge-contact quality. Edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FETs exhibit good ohmic contact at both room temperature and cryogenic temperatures, and have a record-low contact resistance of 1.25 kΩ·μm among all edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FETs. Record-high output current of 436 μA/μm and transconductance of 123 μS/μm with a steep SS of 150 mV/dec are achieved on an edge-contact monolayer MoS 2 FET with _L_ ch = 120 nm on 9-nm HfO 2 dielectric. For edge contacts, the core advantage is that it can be immune to the deterioration of performance caused by the reduction of top contact length and can build stacked nanosheet structures, which is crucial for achieving multi-layer TMD channel stacked device structures to break through the physical gate length limitations of traditional semiconductor devices while improving device performance. Due to the limitation of experimental equipment and materials, the width of source–drain metal electrodes demonstrated in this work needs to be further reduced to 10 nm in the future, edge-contact devices for multi-bridge channels need to be explored and validated, and device reliability under this structure needs to be further explored. In addition, novel metallic materials and deposition techniques can also be employed in subsequent studies to achieve further reduction of contact resistance and achieve the robustness of the device’s mechanical structure.

## Materials and Methods

### CVD growth of monolayer MoS 2 and material characterization

Monolayer MoS 2 was grown on molten glass. The growth was carried out using a furnace with 2 temperature zones, with temperatures of 250 and 860 °C in each zone. The sulfur powder was loaded onto the quartz boat and placed in zone I, while the MoO 3 precursor and the molten glass were loaded into a porcelain boat and placed in zone II. Ar gas was always supplied during the growth process. At 860 °C, the growth time of MoS 2 was about 35 min. MoS 2 was transferred to the target substrate through wet method. The basic morphology of MoS 2 was observed using an optical microscope. The thickness of MoS 2 was basically determined by Raman and PL.

### FET fabrication

The grown MoS 2 was transferred by wet method onto the high-quality HfO 2 dielectric deposited by atomic layer deposition. Generally, the thickness of HfO 2 used is about 9 nm. To obtain a regular strip-shaped MoS 2, the electron beam lithography (Raith eLine) and Ar/CF 4 plasma etching (by reactive ion etching) were used. Subsequently, monolayer MoS 2 was annealed at 250 °C for 1 h in Ar atmosphere. After electron beam lithography and etching, monolayer MoS 2 in the contact area was removed by reactive ion etching. The contact metal (Ni/Au) was then deposited under high vacuum conditions.

### Electrical measurement

The direct-current electrical measurements were conducted using a Lakeshore probe station and an Agilent B1500A semiconductor parameter analyzer. All measurements are conducted in a vacuum of 10−4 torr to reduce the influence of moisture and oxygen in the measurement environment.

This webpage presents a research article published in the journal "Research" (an SPJ/AAAS journal) on January 17, 2025 (Vol 8, Article ID: 0593, DOI: 10.34133/research.0593), titled "High-Performance Edge-Contact Monolayer Molybdenum Disulfide Transistors." The paper is authored by Jiankun Xiao, Xiong Xiong, Xinhang Shi, Shiyuan Liu, Shenwu Zhu, Yue Zhang, Ru Huang, and Yanqing Wu (corresponding author).

KEY FINDINGS:
- The researchers developed high-performance edge-contact monolayer molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) field-effect transistors (FETs) using chemical vapor deposition (CVD)-grown monolayer MoS2 and well-controlled plasma etching techniques.
- Pure argon plasma etching improves edge dangling bonds and edge-contact quality, compared to oxygen/argon plasma which degrades performance (10x higher on-state current with Ar plasma vs O2/Ar at same channel length; Ar plasma gave ohmic behavior of 97 μA/μm vs Schottky behavior of 8 μA/μm for O2/Ar at Vds=1V).
- Record-low contact resistance (Rc) of 1.25 kΩ·μm among all edge-contact MoS2 devices, achieved even at cryogenic temperatures (20 K) with quasi-ohmic contact.
- Record-high on-state current of 436 μA/μm and transconductance of 123 μS/μm at Vds = 1 V on a 120-nm channel length (Lch) device on 9-nm HfO2 dielectric.
- Schottky barrier height as low as 32 meV at drain-source voltage of 0.1 V.
- On/off ratio of 6 × 10^7, sub-threshold swing (SS) of 150 mV/dec.
- Output current of 436 μA/μm at Vds=1V represents the highest output current density for monolayer MoS2 edge-contact FETs to date, more than 4x higher than previous studies.
- Edge contacts are crucial for ultimate device pitch scaling in stacked nanosheet transistors and can eliminate Fermi pinning via covalent bonds between 2D MoS2 and metals.

METHODS:
- Monolayer MoS2 grown via CVD on molten glass (2-zone furnace at 250°C and 860°C, ~35 min growth time).
- Transferred to HfO2/Si substrate via wet transfer using PMMA.
- Device fabrication: electron beam lithography, Ar/CF4 plasma etching for isolation, annealing at 250°C for 1 hour in Ar, pure Ar plasma etching for contact regions.
- Ni/Au contacts evaporated under high vacuum (2×10^-7 torr) at slow rate (0.01 nm/s).
- Electrical measurements via Lakeshore probe station and Agilent B1500A analyzer in vacuum of 10^-4 torr.

FUTURE WORK: Reducing source-drain metal electrode width to 10 nm, exploring multi-bridge channel edge-contact devices, and further reducing contact resistance with novel metallic materials.

FUNDING: Supported by Natural Science Foundation of China (grants 92364203, 92464303, 62090034, 62425402, 62104012), National Key Research and Development Program of China (2022YFB4400100, 2021YFA1202903), Beijing Natural Science Foundation (4242057), and Technology Innovation Program of Hunan Province (2021RC5008). Authors declare no competing interests.

Comparative analysis of the common physical mechanisms underlying all methods that reduce contact resistance in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors such as molybdenum disulfide (MoS2). Please deeply research the following physical concepts and explain how each contributes to contact resistance reduction across DIFFERENT contact strategies (semimetal contacts, pure metal contacts, phase engineering, doping, edge contacts, van der Waals contacts): 
1. Fermi level pinning effect (Fermi level pinning) - how metal induced gap states (MIGS) pin the Fermi level in the bandgap and create a Schottky barrier.
2. Schottky barrier height (SBH) formation and modulation - how the barrier at the metal-MoS2 interface is set and tuned.
3. Interface state density (interface states, gap states) and the role of dangling bonds, defects, and chalcogen vacancies.
4. Orbital hybridization between metal orbitals and MoS2 orbitals (e.g., Mo d orbitals vs S p orbitals) at the interface - how strongly bonded vs weakly bonded interfaces affect the contact.
5. Charge transfer and doping at the interface - how charge transfer doping reduces the tunneling barrier and widens the depletion region behavior.
6. The role of the van der Waals gap in suppressing MIGS and reducing Fermi level pinning.
7. The role of work function matching and band alignment (CBM pinning).
Please also research whether ANY paper has PROPOSED a UNIFIED theoretical framework that explains most of these low-resistance contact methods through a common mechanism. Look for frameworks such as: (a) minimizing metal-semiconductor orbital hybridization / chemical bonding strength (weak hybridization = low pinning), (b) the 'MIGS elimination via vdW gap' framework, (c) the 'contact metal phase/metallicity' framework, (d) the 'Fermi level depinning via reduced interface state density' framework, (e) first-principles DFT studies comparing many metals on MoS2 to extract a universal descriptor (e.g., metal work function, metal d-band, interfacial charge transfer). SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Semantic Scholar record for the scientific paper "The unusual mechanism of partial Fermi level pinning at metal-MoS2 interfaces" by Cheng Gong, Luigi Colombo, Robert M. Wallace, and Kyeongjae Cho, published in Nano Letters on March 27, 2014 (DOI: 10.1021/nl403465v, Corpus ID: 20629763).

The paper's central finding is that the mechanism of Fermi level pinning at metal-MoS2 contacts is unique for metal-2D-semiconductor interfaces, and remarkably different from the well-known Bardeen pinning effect, metal-induced gap states (MIGS), and defect/disorder-induced gap states—all of which apply to traditional metal-semiconductor junctions.

The record includes 6 figures/tables, 733 citations, and 33 references. Notable citing papers include studies on defect-dominated charge transport in MoS2/metal contacts (Bampoulis et al., 2017), tunable Schottky barriers at MoSe2/metal interfaces (Huang et al., 2017), Fermi level pinning in monolayer molybdenum dichalcogenides (Kim et al., 2017), universal Fermi-level pinning in transition-metal dichalcogenides (Sotthewes et al., 2019), and the mechanism of Fermi level pinning for metal contacts on molybdenum dichalcogenide (Wang et al., 2024). Key references include foundational works on metal-graphene interfaces (Gong et al., 2010), metal contacts to MoS2 (Neal et al., 2012), and tuning electronic properties of monolayer MoS2 on transition metal substrates (Chen et al., 2013).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The mechanism of the Fermi level pinning at metal-MoS2 contact is shown to be unique for metal-2D-semiconductor interfaces, remarkably different from the well-known Bardeen pinning effect, metal-induced gap states, and defect/disorder induced gapStates, which are applicable to traditional metal-semiconductor junctions."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: The Unusual Mechanism of Partial Fermi Level Pinning at ... ---
URL: https://cgong.weebly.com/uploads/1/2/1/2/121277864/2014-nano_letter-the_unusual_mechanism_of_partial_fermi_level_pinning_at_metal%E2%88%92mos2_interfaces.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper published in Nano Letters (2014, Vol. 14, pp. 1714-1720) by researchers from The University of Texas at Dallas and Texas Instruments, investigating the mechanism of Fermi level pinning at metal-MoS2 interfaces using density functional theory (DFT) calculations.

**Key findings:**
- The study examined six metals (Al, Ag, Ir, Au, Pd, Pt) with work functions spanning 4.2-6.1 eV in contact with monolayer MoS2.
- Schottky contacts were found for all metals, with all forming n-type contacts except platinum, which formed a p-type Schottky contact.
- The Fermi levels in the metal-MoS2 complexes were found to be partially pinned, varying within a 0.5-0.64 eV window in the band gap, rather than strictly pinned at a single energy level.
- The partial Fermi level pinning results from two synergistic interface behaviors: (1) metal work function modification via interface dipole formation due to charge redistribution, and (2) production of gap states predominantly of Mo d-orbital character, caused by weakened intralayer S-Mo bonding due to interface metal-S interaction.
- The FL shift relative to the CBM of MoS2 shows a linear dependence on metal work function with a slope of 0.71 (well below 1), indicating partial pinning.
- This mechanism is fundamentally different from traditional pinning mechanisms: Bardeen's surface states theory, metal-induced gap states (MIGS), and defect/disorder-induced gap states (DIGS) are all not applicable to these pristine metal-MoS2 interfaces.

--- SOURCE 1: Ultralow contact resistance ---
URL: https://www.congsu.net/research/ultralow-contact-resistance

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes a research breakthrough in reducing contact resistance between metal electrodes and monolayer 2D semiconductor materials (specifically MoS2), published in Nature (2021). 

The content explains the context: as transistors shrink, channel materials must become thinner to maintain gate control, and Moore's Law is hitting physical limits with silicon. Two main strategies exist: redesigning Si-based transistor structures (like FinFET, moving toward gate-all-around designs) or switching to 2D materials like MoS2 which are intrinsically monolayer and free of dangling bonds. However, the main obstacle to using monolayer 2D semiconductors has been the Schottky Barrier — contact resistance between metal electrodes and the semiconductor — which was previously impossible to eliminate due to Fermi level pinning.

The researchers discovered that using bismuth (Bi), a semimetal, as the contact electrode with monolayer MoS2 achieves ultra-low contact resistance close to the quantum limit, comparable to traditional semiconductors like Si, GaN, and InGaAs. This is achieved through a mechanism called "Gap State Saturation," leveraging the bond saturation of the Bi surface and its zero density of states as a semimetal. The Schottky Barrier is eliminated entirely, allowing monolayer devices to surpass silicon performance when benchmarked by ON current per cross-sectional area.

The paper is authored by P.-C. Shen, C. Su, Y. Lin, A.-S. Chou, and colleagues, published in Nature 593, 211–217 (2021), titled "Ultralow contact resistance between semimetal and monolayer semiconductors." The research was covered by MIT News, NTU News, and UC Berkeley News. Notably, the authors clarify that while media coverage describes this as a "1-nm node technology breakthrough," they did not actually fabricate an ultra-short channel device meeting 1-nm node standards in this work — rather, they solved one of the biggest problems enabling such technology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In our paper, we discovered that the contact between bismuth (Bi), a semimetal, and monolayer MoS2 has an ultra-low resistance close to the quantum limit, on par with the performance of the traditional semiconductors like Si, GaN, and InGaAs."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper (published in Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics, June 2023) investigating electrical contact properties between semimetal electrodes (bismuth and antimony) and monolayer 2D transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) semiconductors. The study used first-principles density functional theory (DFT) simulations on six TMDC semiconductors (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2, MoTe2, and WTe2) with two semimetal contact materials (Bi and Sb).

Key findings:
- Bi and Sb work functions align well with TMDC conduction band edges, resulting in predominantly Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts.
- Semimetal/TMDC contacts have significantly larger interlayer distances than metal/TMDC counterparts, leading to only weak metalization of TMDC upon contact formation.
- This weak metalization generates semimetal-induced gap states (SMIGSs) extending below the conduction band minimum, providing an effective mechanism to reduce or eliminate n-type Schottky barrier height (SBH) while preserving the electronic structures of the 2D TMDC.
- The authors propose a modified Schottky-Mott rule accounting for SMIGS, interface dipole potential, and Fermi level shifting, which shows improved agreement with DFT-simulated SBH.
- Sb/TMDC contacts generally exhibit lower tunneling-specific resistivity than Bi counterparts, indicating better charge injection efficiency with Sb contacts.
- The findings highlight Bi and Sb as promising companion electrode materials for advancing 2D semiconductor device technology.

Paper details: Authors include Su Tong, Li Yueyan, Wang Qianqian, Zhao Weiwei, Cao Liemao, and Ang Yee Sin. DOI: 10.1088/1361-6463/acc53f; arXiv:2212.03003; 12 pages, 7 figures.

--- SOURCE 6: [PDF] 1T phase as an efficient hole injection layer to TMDs transistors ---
URL: https://krasheninnikov.de/publ/Hu_2018_2D_Mater._5_031012.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Scientific Paper: "1T Phase as an Efficient Hole Injection Layer to TMDs Transistors: A Universal Approach to Achieve p-Type Contacts"

**Publication:** 2D Materials (IOP Publishing), Volume 5, Article 031012 (2018). DOI: 10.1088/2053-1583/aac859. Received 21 February 2018, accepted 29 May 2018, published 13 June 2018.

**Authors:** Xiaohui Hu, Yifeng Wang, Xiaodong Shen (Nanjing Tech University, China), Arkady V. Krasheninnikov (Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf, Germany / Aalto University, Finland), Litao Sun (Southeast University, China), and Zhongfang Chen (University of Puerto Rico, USA).

### Purpose/Motivation
The paper addresses the challenge of achieving p-type contacts in transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) field-effect transistors (FETs). Most experimentally reported TMD FETs are n-type; p-type TMD FETs remain scarce due to fabrication difficulties. The authors investigate why MoS₂ FETs with metallic 1T-MoS₂ electrodes (first demonstrated by Kappera et al., 2014, Nat. Mater.) exhibit excellent performance with low contact resistance, and whether this approach can be extended to other TMDs.

### Methodology
- Density functional theory (DFT) calculations using the VASP package
- Projector-augmented-wave (PAW) method with GGA-PBE exchange-correlation functional
- Van der Waals corrections via Grimme's DFT-D2 method
- 500 eV plane-wave energy cutoff; 32×32×1 k-point sampling; 16 Å vacuum region
- Six different 1T/2H MoS₂ interfacial stacking configurations examined (ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA)
- Lattice constants of 1T and 2H MoS₂ are identical (3.18 Å), allowing strain-free interface construction

### Key Results
1. **Stability:** All six 1T/2H MoS₂ interfaces are energetically favorable (negative interlayer binding energies). ABC/ACB stackings are less stable (−0.10 eV/f.u.) with larger interfacial distances (6.75–6.83 Å) compared to BAC/BCA/CAB/CBA stackings (−0.15 to −0.17 eV/f.u., 6.14–6.24 Å).

2. **p-type contacts:** All 1T/2H MoS₂ interfaces form p-type contacts, with p-type Schottky barrier heights (SBH) of 0.44–0.67 eV—significantly lower than the n-type SBH values of Au/MoS₂ (0.88 eV) and Pd/MoS₂ (0.85 eV) contacts. This explains the low contact resistance observed experimentally.

3. **Pure vs. locally introduced 1T phase:** Pure 1T-MoS₂ electrodes yield a lower p-type SBH (0.49 eV) than locally introduced 1T-MoS₂ (0.57 eV), supporting Kappera et al.'s expectation of greater performance enhancement with pure 1T phase electrodes.

4. **Mechanism:** Upon interface formation, the VBM of 2H-MoS₂ becomes dominated by Mo d_z² orbitals (rather than d_xy and d_x²−y²) and shifts from the K point to the Γ point, decreasing the band gap and enabling p-type SBH. Charge redistribution (depletion and/or accumulation) at the interface creates electric dipoles and electrical polarization, affecting binding energy and SBH values.

5. **Electric field modulation:** A positive electric field (from 2H to 1T) decreases p-type SBH and increases n-type SBH; a negative field has the opposite effect. Significantly low p-type SBH values can be achieved under appropriate positive electric fields.

6. **Universality:** The approach extends to other TMDs—WS₂, WSe₂, and MoSe₂—where p-type SBH values (0.41, 0.66, and 0.74 eV respectively) are lower than their corresponding n-type SBH values (0.99, 0.69, and 0.78 eV). The work function of 1T-TMDs is closer to the VBM of 2H-TMDs, confirming 1T phases as efficient hole contacts.

### Conclusions
The metallic 1T phase serves as a universal, efficient hole injection layer for 2H-TMDs, providing a practical route to achieve p-type contacts in TMD transistors. The SBH can be tuned via stacking patterns and external electric fields, opening new avenues for contact engineering in 2D TMD-based electronics.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We investigated the carrier injection at the 1T/2H MoS₂ interface and found that although the Schottky barrier height (SBH) values of 1T/2H MoS₂ interfaces can be tuned by controlling the stacking patterns, the p-type SBH values of 1T/2H MoS₂ interfaces with different stackings are lower than their corresponding n-type SBH values, which demonstrated that the metallic 1T phase can be used as an efficient hole injection layer for 2H-MoS₂."
</key_excerpts>

The study investigates the use of reverse sputtering (Ar+ ion bombardment via RF-generated plasma) to reduce contact resistance (Rc) in molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) field-effect transistors (FETs).

Key findings and methodology:
- MoS₂ FETs suffer from Schottky barriers at the metal-MoS₂ interface, causing high contact resistance. The study explores inducing a phase transition from semiconducting 2H-MoS₂ to metallic 1T-MoS₂ via reverse sputtering at the contact interface.
- Multilayer MOCVD-grown MoS₂ (~2.5 nm thick, ~4 layers) was transferred onto SiO₂/Si substrates. Devices were fabricated with nickel (Ni) top-contacts (TOP-FETs) where only the contact regions were sputter-treated, and bottom-contact (BOT-FETs) control devices where the entire MoS₂ was exposed.
- Characterization via PL, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS confirmed that reverse sputtering induces sulfur vacancies (VS) and a 2H-to-1T phase transition in MoS₂. XPS showed the S/Mo ratio decreasing from ~2.0 (pristine) to 1.80 (200 W treatment), with full 2H-to-1T conversion observed after sputtering.
- Optimal results were achieved at 75 W reverse sputtering for 10 s: Rc decreased from 1126 kΩ·μm (pristine) to 413 kΩ·μm (a reduction to less than 50% of untreated devices), and output current increased approximately 150-fold.

- Excessive sputtering power (200 W) caused oxidation to MoOₓ and severe degradation. Insufficient power (25 W) produced too few sulfur vacancies and increased Rc. The 75 W condition represented the optimal balance between phase conversion and material damage.
- The mechanism involves sulfur vacancies creating heavily n-doped regions that narrow the Schottky barrier, plus the formation of conductive 1T-MoS₂ that enhances electron injection from Ni contacts.

The authors conclude that reverse sputtering is a scalable, CMOS-compatible, and clean method for optimizing contact resistance in MoS₂ FETs, with potential for broader application in 2D material-based microelectronics. --- SOURCE 8: Tunable phase stability and contact resistance of monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides contacts with metal | npj 2D Materials and Applications ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41699-018-0059-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in npj 2D Materials and Applications (volume 2, Article number 13, 2018) by Bin Ouyang, Shiyun Xiong, and Yuhang Jing, titled "Tunable phase stability and contact resistance of monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides contacts with metal."

**Topic/Purpose:** The paper investigates how interfacial charge transfer between monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (MX2) and metal contacts can be used to tune contact resistance in MX2/metal-based transistors. The large contact resistance between MX2 and metal is a key bottleneck limiting the development of high-performance 2D material-based FET devices.

**Methodology:**
- Computational framework based on density functional theory (DFT) using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional and projector augmented-wave method (VASP)
- Bader charge analysis for quantifying interfacial charge transfer
- Lattice misfit criterion (<2% threshold) used to screen MX2/metal combinations
- Considered five types of MX2 (MoS2, MoSe2, WS2, WSe2, MoTe2) and 3d/4d transition metals plus non-transition metals (Al, Ga, In)
- Considered 2H→T (1T, 1T', 1T") phase transformations in the screening process
- Three metal surface orientations (001, 110, 111) and three rotation angles (-30°, 0°, 30°) considered
- Spin-orbit coupling included for accurate band edge estimation

**Key Findings:**
1. The 1T phase always has much higher energy compared to other phases, so interfacial charge will not induce 2H→1T transition.
2. 28 MX2/metal systems with strong interface interaction were identified using the lattice misfit criterion.
3. Seven MX2/metal systems were identified that can potentially form zero Schottky barrier contacts via phase engineering: 1T"-MoSe2/Sc, 1T"-WS2/Zr, 1T"-WS2/V, 1T"-WSe2/Sc, 1T"-WSe2/Ti, 1T"-MoTe2/Cr, and 1T'-MoTe2/Nb.
4. Phase transitions to T phases (1T' or 1T") occur in MoSe2-Sc, WS2-Zr, WS2-V, WSe2-Ti, WSe2-Sc, Nb-MoTe2, and Cr-MoTe2 systems, where more charge is transferred from metal into the MX2 monolayer.
5. Higher metal work functions generally make it harder for metals to lose electrons, but interface coherency also plays a significant role (e.g., Ti transfers more charge than W despite having a slightly higher work function).

**Three Types of MX2/Metal Contacts Proposed:**
- Type 1: Little orbital overlapping → both sizable tunnel barrier and Schottky barrier (high contact resistance)
- Type 2: Strong orbital overlapping → metallization eliminates tunnel barrier, but sizable Schottky barrier remains (tunable with gating)
- Type 3: Phase transformation (2H→1T'/1T") → both tunnel and Schottky barriers vanish (zero contact resistance, ohmic contact)

**Contact Properties:**
- For MoS2 and MoSe2 with 2H phase, n-type doping creates low-resistance interfaces (e.g., V/MoS2 and Mo/MoSe2)
- For WS2 and WSe2, hole barriers are always lower than electron barriers
- MoTe2/Ru and MoTe2/Rh have zero hole Schottky barriers (electrons transfer from Te to metal)

**Conclusions:** The research demonstrates a wide tunable space for interfacial charge transfer and structural phase transition of MX2 through metal selection and interface orientation design, providing a realistic theoretical reference for contact behavior and potential solutions for overcoming the bottleneck of 2D transistors.
</summary>

"With the lattice misfit criterion applied to screen combination of MX2s and metals, it has been found out that both phase stability of MX2 and contact nature between MX2 and metal will be sensitively affected by interfacial charge transfer."

Corresponding author: Antonio Di Bartolomeo (adibartolomeo@unisa.it).

The study presents multilayer MoS2 Schottky Barrier Field Effect Transistors (SB-FETs) configured with back-gate and van der Pauw contacts. --- SOURCE 1: Fermi Level Pinning Dependent 2D Semiconductor Devices ---
URL: https://d-nb.info/1252551819/34

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive review article published in Advanced Materials (2022) by Xiaochi Liu, Min Sup Choi, Euyheon Hwang, Won Jong Yoo, and Jian Sun, titled "Fermi Level Pinning Dependent 2D Semiconductor Devices: Challenges and Prospects." The paper addresses the critical challenge of Fermi level pinning (FLP) at metal contacts to two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) semiconductor devices, such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs).

KEY TOPICS AND FINDINGS:

1. **Introduction and Motivation**: 2D vdW materials (e.g., MoS2, WSe2, MoTe2) offer high mobility, tunable carrier concentration, ultrathin body, and efficient electrostatic control, making them promising for future nanoelectronics. However, they face fabrication challenges including high contact resistance, strong FLP at metal interfaces, and lack of substitutional doping capabilities.

2. **Origins of FLP**: Unlike conventional 3D semiconductors (Si, III-V), FLP in 2D devices stems from four main differences: (1) unavailability of efficient doping techniques, (2) vdW gaps at the 2D-metal interface acting as tunneling barriers, (3) hybridized/metalized compounds formed under contacting metals, and (4) nonuniform carrier density due to current crowding. FLP contributors are classified as metal-induced gap states (MIGS), interface dipoles, and disorder-induced gap states (DIGS).

3. **Intrinsic contributors**: MIGS arise from d-orbital (metal)/p-orbital (chalcogen) hybridization. Metal-TMD interactions are classified into three categories based on interaction strength: weak vdW gap contacts, medium interaction with negligible gap, and strong chemical bonding leading to metallization. Interface dipoles from charge redistribution also modify band alignment and cause FLP.

4. **Extrinsic contributors**: Defects in 2D materials (0D vacancies/adatoms/antisites, 1D grain boundaries, 2D ripples/folds/wrinkles) strengthen FLP through DIGS. Transition metal vacancies and subsurface metal-like defects (~10^11 cm^-2 density) were found to be more responsible for FLP enhancement than surface chalcogen vacancies. DIGS reduce the pinning factor by ~30-40% at defect sites compared to pristine surfaces. Measured pinning factors include: MoS2 pristine 0.3 vs defect 0.11; WSe2 pristine 0.28 vs defect 0.09; MoTe2 pristine 0.11 vs defect 0.04.

5. **FLP mechanisms confirmed**: Main mechanisms include: (1) interface dipole formation due to transition metal vacancies, metal-like defects, and substitutional impurities; (2) metallization and overlap states from metal-2D interactions; (3) external damages and charge impurities from fabrication/transfer processes. The pinning factor S has empirical relation with optical dielectric constant: 1/(1-S) ∝ 0.1(ε∞-1)^2.

6. **SBH extraction methods**: The Arrhenius method (based on thermionic emission) is most commonly used but fails for ambipolar devices and low-temperature measurements (<100 K). A Landauer transport model incorporating tunneling (WKB approximation) provides more self-consistent SBH values. Short-channel (<100 nm) devices are preferred for accurate extraction.

7. **Impacts on device performance**: 
   - FLP causes unipolar (unadjustable) transistor polarity—MoS2 shows n-type behavior regardless of contact metal work function (Sc 3.5 eV to Pt 5.9 eV) with pinning factor ≈0.1
   - High contact resistance (10-10^4 kΩ·µm for 3D metal contacts; ~10 kΩ·µm even for Al with no d-orbital) versus required <0.1 kΩ·µm for optimal performance
   - Reduced effective field-effect mobility, DIBL effects requiring high dc bias, and high power consumption
   - FLP and SBH are thickness-dependent—pinning weakens with increasing layer number (pinning factor increases from 0.11 to 0.15 from monolayer to bulk MoS2)

8. **Contact strategies**: Conventional thin-film contact techniques are incompatible with 2D TMDs. Strategies focus on both suppressing FLP (weakening metal-TMD interaction, minimizing fabrication-induced disorders, reducing contact dimensionality) and utilizing strong FLP (e.g., pinning Fermi level inside conduction band for Ohmic contacts). Surface charge transfer doping is explored as an alternative to incompatible substitutional doping techniques.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In general, the untunable contact conditions and the associated high contact resistance originated from FLP are the roadblock to the development of 2D electronic device."
</key_excerpts>

The paper is titled "Revealing the weak Fermi level pinning effect of 2D semiconductor/2D metal contact: A case of monolayer In₂Ge₂Te₆ and its Janus structure In₂Ge₂Te₃Se₃" and was authored by Jing Li, Wenhan Zhou, Lili Xu, Jialin Yang, Hengze Qu, Tingting Guo, Biao Xu, Shengli Zhang, and Haibo Zeng.

- The MoS₂/Ti interface shows a much higher density of delocalized states at the Fermi level than MoS₂/Au, with significant S-Ti mixing and contributions from Mo4dxy and S3sp states, turning tunneling into resonant (ohmic) transport.

The work function of MoS₂ (5.2 eV) is larger than most metals, so contact transparency is maximized when metal Fermi-level states align with Mo4dz2 states near the conduction band bottom. Ti satisfies macroscopic criteria (high conductivity, chemical/thermal/electrical stability) and is already widely used in modern microelectronics. The authors propose general criteria for selecting optimum contact materials beyond Ti, including favorable interface geometry/bonding, high density of delocalized states at the Fermi level across the interface, and minimized or non-existent tunnel barriers.
</summary>

URL: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10153225/1/Regoutz_Manuscript_A_Balliou_REVISED_2.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Low-cost High Gain MoS2 FETs from Amorphous Low Mobility Film Precursors

This scientific paper by Angelika Balliou and colleagues (Institute of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology, NCSR Demokritos, Athens, Greece, and University College London) reports the fabrication of a novel MoS2-based ionic liquid-gated thin-film transistor (TFT) that overcomes key limitations in MoS2 electronics.

### Key Achievement
The authors demonstrate a low-cost, high-performance P-type MoS2 MOSFET fabricated from amorphous, low-mobility film precursors deposited via hot-wire chemical vapor deposition (HW-CVD) at room temperature. Key performance metrics include:
- **ON-current**: 1.5×10⁴ A for holes (normalized 1.25×10¹⁰ A/m)
- **Field-effect mobility**: 64.3 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹ at room temperature
- **Contact resistance**: 2.6 kΩ·μm (a record low competing with phase-engineered crystalline monolayer MoS2 contacts)
- **Ion/Ioff ratio**: ≈10⁴
- **Threshold voltage**: -2.49 V
- **Transconductance**: 2.4 mS

### Methodology
1. **Precursor films**: 46 nm-thick amorphous, porous MoS2 films grown via RT HW-CVD (Mo wire heated at 450°C, H₂/H₂S flow at 1.3 Torr), which are low conductivity and highly porous.
2. **Annealing**: Mild 5-minute annealing at 550°C under N₂ induces local crystallization, structural rearrangement, and thermally-induced P-type doping, reducing contact resistance by ~4 orders of magnitude (from 200.86 GΩ·μm to 14.14 MΩ·μm) and increasing planar conductivity ~5 orders of magnitude.
3. **Ionic liquid gating**: A copper phthalocyanine/butanol (CuPc/bu) ionic liquid droplet serves as both top gate and dielectric through electric double layer (EDL) formation, simultaneously acting as ionic dopant and passivation layer. A PMMA/PGMEA capping layer protects the droplet from evaporation.
4. **COMSOL finite element modeling**: Simulated heat transfer during annealing revealed differential heating—"cooler" zones near Au electrodes and "hotter" zones at channel centers—favoring local crystallization of the channel region.

### Key Findings
- **P-type conduction achieved**: The annealed MoS2 matrix undergoes thermally-induced P-type doping (confirmed via XPS showing Fermi level shifts), and local N-doping near Au contacts creates P-N junctions, enabling complementary logic applications.
- **Mobility enhancement**: Mobility increased by more than 8 orders of magnitude (from 1.93×10⁻⁷ cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹ back-gated to 64.3 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹ liquid-gated), attributed to ionic liquid screening of Schottky barriers and charged impurities, plus 3D ion accumulation in the porous matrix.
- **Optoelectronic functionality**: The CuPc-containing ionic liquid enables photoswitching and non-volatile memory functionality (synaptic-like "learning" behavior) in a single cell.
- **Characterization**: As-grown films confirmed amorphous via XRD, Raman, and UV-vis (no excitonic A/B bands); annealing transitions the material to crystalline/2H phase with bandgap increasing from 1.27 eV to 1.96 eV; MoS2 dielectric constant determined as εr=28.

### Significance
This is reported as the first low-cost, high-gain MoS2 MOSFET based on amorphous low-mobility film precursors that enables high-performance, multifunctional, stackable MOSFETs on processing-sensitive, plastic, and/or flexible substrates. The approach uses CMOS-compatible, low-energy, low-thermal-budget processes, making it suitable for mass production and the disposable portable electronics market.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"With this technique, we achieve a low-lying contact resistance (Rc) of 2.6 kΩ·μm, which competes with the Rc values obtained on monolayer MoS2 with engineered contacts."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D metal-semiconductor contact interface suppresses tunneling barrier and Fermi level pinning simultaneously ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12274-024-6877-x

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in Nano Research (Springer) on August 1, 2024, titled "sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D metal-semiconductor contact interface suppresses tunneling barrier and Fermi level pinning simultaneously." The paper addresses a key challenge in 2D electronics: while van der Waals (vdWs) stacking of 2D materials weakens Fermi level pinning (FLP) in metal/semiconductor contacts due to dangling-bond-free surfaces, the inherent vdWs gap creates a considerable tunneling barrier that limits carrier injection.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers induced a sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D carbon-based metals via surface defect engineering, which enabled large orbital overlap to form an efficient carrier channel and overcome the tunneling barrier. They constructed 36 metal/semiconductor contacts by selecting:
- 2D carbon-based X3C2 metals (X = Cd, Hg, Zn)
- 2D MSi2N4 semiconductors (M = Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti, V, Zr)

KEY RESULTS: For vdWs contacts, although Ohmic contacts formed at the interface, the highest tunneling probability (PTB) was only 3.11%. However, when MSi2N4 with surface nitrogen vacancies formed interface covalent bonds with X3C2, the PTB was significantly improved to as high as 48.73%. Simultaneously, weak FLP and Ohmic contact were maintained at the covalent-bond-based surface, attributed to the protection of MSi2N4 band-edge electronic states by the outlying Si-N sublayer.

CONCLUSION: The work provides a promising path for advancing 2D electronic and photoelectronic devices by simultaneously suppressing tunneling barriers and Fermi level pinning through sp2-to-sp3 hybridization transformation enabled by surface defect engineering. The article is subscription content (paywalled) and has 771 accesses with 1 Altmetric mention. Authors include Wenchao Shan, Anqi Shi, Zhuorong Zhong, Xiuyun Zhang, Bing Wang, Yongtao Li, and Xianghong Niu from multiple Chinese institutions. The reference list cites 57 prior works spanning foundational studies on Fermi level pinning, Schottky barriers, van der Waals contacts, and MoSi2N4/WSi2N4 material systems.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Van der Waals (vdWs) stacking of two-dimensional (2D) materials can effectively weaken the Fermi level pinning (FLP) effect in metal/semiconductor contacts due to dangling-bond-free surfaces. However, the inherent vdWs gap always induces a considerable tunneling barrier, significantly limiting carrier injection."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D metal ... ---
URL: https://www.sciopen.com/local/article_pdf/10.1007/s12274-024-6877-x.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in Nano Research (2024, 17(11): 10227–10234) investigating a novel strategy to simultaneously suppress tunneling barriers and Fermi level pinning (FLP) in 2D metal-semiconductor contacts by inducing an sp2 to sp3 hybridization transformation in 2D carbon-based metals via surface defect engineering.

**Study Design:**
- Authors: Wenchao Shan, Anqi Shi, Zhuorong Zhong, Xiuyun Zhang, Bing Wang, Yongtao Li, and Xianghong Niu (from Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Yangzhou University, and Henan University)
- Received 16 May 2024, revised 25 June 2024, accepted 10 July 2024
- Constructed 36 metal/semiconductor contacts using 2D carbon-based metals X3C2 (X = Cd, Hg, Zn) and 2D MSi2N4 semiconductors (M = Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti, V, Zr)
- Used density functional theory (DFT) via VASP software with PBE functional, and non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) method via Nanodcal for transport calculations

**Key Findings:**
1. **vdWs contacts**: Although Ohmic contacts can be formed with weak FLP, the inherent van der Waals gap induces large tunneling barriers. The highest tunneling probability (PTB) was only 3.11%. Tunneling barrier heights ranged from 4.11–5.00 eV with widths of 1.86–2.22 eV.

2. **Covalent contacts**: By inducing surface nitrogen vacancies in MSi2N4 and transforming carbon atoms in X3C2 from sp2 to sp3 hybridization, covalent C–Si bonds form across the interface. This creates large orbital overlap forming an efficient carrier channel. The PTB significantly improved to up to 48.73% (Zn3C2/MoSi2N4), with all covalent contacts exceeding 25%.

3. **Dual benefit**: The outlying Si-N sublayer of MSi2N4 protects the band-edge electronic states (contributed by the M-N inner sublayer), so weak FLP and Ohmic contacts are maintained even with strong covalent interfacial bonding.

4. **Transport properties**: Quantum transport calculations showed covalent contacts achieve completely Ohmic behavior with transport channels at the Fermi level, whereas some vdWs contacts exhibited Schottky barriers (0.5–0.9 eV). I–V curves confirmed Ohmic characteristics for both types, but covalent contacts produced higher currents (up to ~3 µA vs ~1 µA under 0.2 V bias for Hg3C2/CrSi2N4).

**Materials Properties:**
- X3C2 metals: lattice constants 7.26 (Cd3C2), 7.20 (Hg3C2), and 6.59 (Zn3C2) Å; work functions 4.33, 4.33, and 4.58 eV respectively
- MSi2N4 semiconductors: indirect band gaps ranging from 0.5 to 2.1 eV
- Lattice mismatch controlled within 5% using supercell matching modes

**Conclusions:**
The work demonstrates an effective strategy to simultaneously suppress tunneling barriers, maintain weak FLP, and achieve Ohmic contacts in 2D metal-semiconductor interfaces, offering a promising path for advancing 2D electronic and photoelectronic device performance.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"For vdWs contacts, although Ohmic contacts can be formed at the interface, the highest tunneling probability (PTB) is only 3.11%. As expected, the PTB can be significantly improved, as high as 48.73%, when MSi2N4, accompanied by surface nitrogen vacancies, forms an interface covalent bond with X3C2."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Interfacial Properties of Monolayer and Bilayer MoS2 Contacts with Metals: Beyond the Energy Band Calculations ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4772071

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Scientific Reports (Sci Rep, 2016 Mar 01;6:21786, doi:10.1038/srep21786) by Hongxia Zhong, Ruge Quhe, Yangyang Wang, and colleagues from Peking University, MIT, Washington University in St. Louis, and Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications. The paper provides a comprehensive ab initio study of interfacial properties of monolayer (ML) and bilayer (BL) MoS2 contacts with six metals (Sc, Ti, Ag, Pt, Ni, and Au).

Key findings:
1. The study used DFT (VASP with PW91 GGA functional and vdW corrections) and NEGF-based quantum transport simulations (ATK 11.8 package) to study MoS2-metal interfaces.
2. Equilibrium distances (dS-M) range from 1.557–3.405 Å, increasing in the order Ti < Sc < Ni < Pt < Ag < Au, with binding energies in the reverse order. Ti and Sc show strong adhesion (Eb = 1.181–1.848 eV/sulfur atom), Ni/Pt/Ag medium (0.503–0.830 eV), and Au weak (0.307–0.354 eV).
3. The extensively used energy band calculation scheme fails to reproduce observed Schottky barrier heights (SBHs) in 2D MoS2-Sc interfaces. Instead, ab initio quantum transport device simulations better reproduce observed SBHs, highlighting the importance of higher-level theoretical approaches.
4. Quantum transport simulations give n-type electron SBHs of 0.150 eV (ML) and 0.185 eV (BL) for MoS2-Sc interfaces, while energy band analysis artificially predicts an Ohmic contact.
5. Many-electron effects are strongly suppressed in channel 2D MoS2 due to charge transfer from electrodes, which screens electron-electron Coulomb interactions. The transport gap is determined by the DFT band gap rather than the quasiparticle band gap.
6. BL MoS2-metal contacts generally have reduced SBHs compared to ML due to interlayer coupling, leading to higher electron injection efficiency.
7. Tunneling probabilities from metal to MoS2 were estimated as 100%, 100%, 74.33%, 53.21%, 19.68%, and 4.74% for Sc, Ti, Ni, Pt, Ag, and Au contacts respectively.
8. Five types of MoS2-metal contacts were classified based on Schottky and tunneling barriers, with Sc forming the highest quality Ohmic contact.
9. ML MoS2 is n-type doped by Sc, Ti, Ag, Au, and Ni contacts, and p-type doped by Pt, enabling fabrication of p-n junctions.
10. The study demonstrates partial Fermi level pinning with a slope of 0.64 for the linear relation between Fermi level shift and work function difference.
</summary>

"Although many prototype devices based on two-dimensional (2D) MoS2 have been fabricated and wafer scale growth of 2D MoS2 has been realized, the fundamental nature of 2D MoS2-metal contacts has not been well understood yet."

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] MoS2 Transistors with Low Schottky Barrier Contact by Optimizing the ... ---
URL: http://www.cityu.edu.hk/phy/appkchu/Publications/2022/22.90.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the journal Energies (MDPI) on August 25, 2022, titled "MoS2 Transistors with Low Schottky Barrier Contact by Optimizing the Interfacial Layer Thickness." The study investigates the electronic transport characteristics of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) field-effect transistors (FETs) with two different contact structures: a copper (Cu) metal–MoS2 channel and a Cu metal–TiO2-MoS2 channel. The research addresses the problem of large Schottky barrier height (ΦB) and contact resistance that hamper high-power MoS2 transistor fabrication.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers systematically varied the thickness of a TiO2 interfacial layer (0, 1, 1.5, and 2.2 nm) between the metal and MoS2. Multilayer MoS2 flakes were exfoliated onto SiO2/Si substrates, Ti layers of 0.2–1 nm were deposited by electron beam evaporation and re-oxidized to form TiO2. Cu/Au (15/50 nm) source/drain electrodes were formed via thermal vaporizer deposition. Devices were characterized using AFM, XPS, Raman spectroscopy, SEM, and electrical measurements on a probe station.

KEY RESULTS: The metal-interlayer-semiconductor (MIS) structure with a 1.5 nm thick TiO2 layer achieved the smallest Schottky barrier of 22 meV (compared to 168 meV without the TiO2 layer) and a minimum contact resistance of 4 kΩ·µm (versus 8.2 kΩ·µm without the interlayer). Field-effect mobility values for TiO2 thicknesses of 0, 1, 1.5, and 2.2 nm were 27, 44, 58, and 11 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹, respectively—with the 1.5 nm device more than doubling the mobility compared to the control. When the TiO2 thickness exceeded the optimal value (e.g., 2.5 nm), contact resistance increased to 46 kΩ·µm due to large tunneling resistance.

MECHANISM: The TiO2 interlayer reduces Fermi level pinning by preventing penetration of the metal electron wavefunction into the semiconductor (per metal-induced gap state theory), and dipole formation at the interlayer–semiconductor interface reduces ΦB. The MIS structure involves a trade-off between Schottky barrier resistance (RSB) and tunneling resistance (RT)—thicker interlayers reduce RSB but increase RT. The TiO2 layer also acts as a dielectric shield, increasing charge density at the TiO2–MoS2 interface and isolating the device from moisture and oxygen.

CONCLUSION: The authors conclude that optimizing the interfacial layer thickness provides a viable approach to contact engineering for 2D semiconductor devices, with the MIS structure offering a potential solution for contact problems in MoS2-based transistors. Funding was provided by the Natural Science Foundation of Henan Province, the Key Scientific and Technological Project of the Technology Department of Henan Province, the Science Fund of the Educational Department of Henan Province, City University of Hong Kong Donation Research Grant, and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Innovative Collaborative Research and Development Program.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Modifying the Power and Performance of 2-Dimensional MoS2 Field Effect Transistors ---
URL: https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0057

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access review article published in the journal *Research* (Vol 6, Article ID 0057) on March 8, 2023, titled "Modifying the Power and Performance of 2-Dimensional MoS2 Field Effect Transistors." The paper reviews the evolution of transistors and examines 2D semiconductors (particularly transition metal dichalcogenides/TMDs like MoS2) as a promising solution to overcome quantum confinement limits at sub-5-nm technology nodes.

Key topics covered:

1. **Historical context of Moore's Law**: The semiconductor industry has evolved through "happy scaling era" (Dennard scaling) to more complex engineering approaches including copper interconnects (post-65nm), SiGe strain engineering, high-κ metal gates (HKMG at 45nm), and structural revolutions like Fin-FET and GAA/MBC-FET. At 3nm nodes, Fin aspect ratios exceed 12:1, posing manufacturing challenges.

2. **Ideal 2D Transistor**: 2D TMDs (MX2) offer atomically thin channels, tunable bandgap, and carrier mobility through element composition, layer number, and strain. They enable MBC-FET and complementary FET (CFET) structures via van der Waals stacking. Key performance metrics include low subthreshold swing (SS), low off-state current, high on-state current (Ion), and well-controlled threshold voltage (Vth).

3. **Mobility and Scattering**: Carrier mobility in TMDs is affected by intrinsic phonons, surface optical (SO) phonons, Coulomb impurities (CI), and defects (Matthiessen's Law). Theoretical room-temperature mobility of monolayer MoS2 is ~410 cm²/V·s, but experimental values are much lower. Key strategies to boost mobility include thiol chemistry for defect passivation, screening effects via high-κ dielectrics, boron nitride (BN) sandwiching, and optimized CVD single-crystal growth. Monolayer TMDs (~0.7nm) offer one-decade higher mobility than SOI at similar thickness.

4. **Dielectric Integration**: 2D materials lack out-of-plane dangling bonds, hindering ALD dielectric growth. Four interfacial modification strategies are discussed: (I) surface treatment (plasma, ozone, electron beam), (II) self-oxidative metal interface layers (Al, Mg, Y), (III) native oxide interface layers (HfS2, Bi2O2Se), and (IV) vdW heterogeneous interface layers (organic PTCDA molecules, Sb2O3 inorganic molecular crystals, layered dielectrics like CaF2 and SrTiO3 achieving EOT down to 0.6nm). Requirements for advanced nodes: EOT < 1nm, gate leakage < 10⁻² A/cm², and Dit < 10¹⁰ cm⁻²eV⁻¹.

5. **Ohmic Contacts**: At ultrashort channels, contact resistance (RC) dominates total resistance. Schottky barrier height, Fermi level pinning (FLP) via metal-induced gap states (MIGS) and surface defects are the main challenges. Conventional metal evaporation on MoS2 introduces defects that pin the Fermi level near midgap states, making carrier injection barriers insensitive to metal work function.

The paper concludes by summarizing the past decade of 2D semiconductor development and prospects for future semiconductor technology roadmaps toward industrial applications.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper, published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society (2014, Vol. 136, pp. 7853-7856) by researchers from UC Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Daisuke Kiriya, Mahmut Tosun, Peida Zhao, Jeong Seuk Kang, and Ali Javey), demonstrates air-stable surface charge transfer doping of MoS2 using benzyl viologen (BV).

KEY FINDINGS AND METHODOLOGY:
- BV, which has one of the highest reduction potentials of all electron-donor organic compounds, was used as a surface charge transfer donor for MoS2 flakes. - Doping achieved a high electron sheet density of ~1.2 × 10^13 cm^-2, corresponding to the degenerate doping limit for MoS2. The extracted electron mobility was 24.7 cm² V^-1 s^-1.
- BV-doped samples exhibited excellent stability in both ambient air and vacuum—minimal change in transfer characteristics even after 9 days of air exposure, contrasting with previously used potassium doping which requires high-vacuum conditions.
- Raman spectroscopy confirmed doping: the A1g peak shifted to a lower wavenumber (softening of A1g vibrations at high electron concentrations), and the full width at half maximum broadened from 5.2 to 8.2 cm^-1, while the E2g peak remained unchanged.
- BV dopants could be reversibly removed by immersion in toluene, allowing control of carrier sheet density through immersion time and enabling potential patterned doping via lithographic masking.
- Contact resistance (extracted via transfer line method) was reduced by a factor of ~3 after BV doping (from 3.3 kΩ·μm undoped to 1.1 kΩ·μm at VGS = 40 V), attributed to Schottky barrier thinning from degenerate doping. At low gate fields, reduction was greater than 100×. Temperature-dependent measurements showed increased conductance at lower temperatures, confirming ohmic contact formation via tunneling current injection.
- As a proof of concept, top-gated MoS2 transistors were fabricated with BV-doped n+ source/drain contacts self-aligned with respect to the top gate (gate used as mask for selective doping of underlapped regions). These devices showed on/off current ratio increase from ~10^4 to ~10^6, on-current increase of more than 5 orders of magnitude at VDS = 50 mV, a subthreshold swing of ~77 mV/decade (approaching the theoretical limit of 60 mV/decade), and electron mobility of ~20 cm² V^-1 s^-1.

EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS:
- Devices fabricated using mechanically exfoliated few-layer MoS2 on p+ Si/SiO2 substrate with Ni/Au (30/30 nm) contacts.
- BV solution prepared by dissolving benzyl viologen dichloride in Milli-Q water with toluene bilayer, reduced with sodium borohydride; doping done by drop-casting or 12-hour immersion, followed by N2 drying.
- Energy level offset: MoS2 conduction band edge at ~0 V vs SHE, while BV reduction potentials are −0.79 V (BV0/BV+) and −0.33 V (BV+/BV2+), enabling electron transfer from BV to MoS2.

CONCLUSION: This work introduces a highly stable and effective air-stable n-doping scheme for MoS2 based on surface charge transfer, representing an important advance enabling patterned doping of TMDCs and exploration of novel device architectures.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper published in Nano Letters (2014, Vol. 14, pp. 1714-1720) by researchers from The University of Texas at Dallas and Texas Instruments, investigating the mechanism of Fermi level pinning at metal-MoS2 interfaces using density functional theory (DFT) calculations.

**Key findings:**
- The study examined six metals (Al, Ag, Ir, Au, Pd, Pt) with work functions spanning 4.2-6.1 eV in contact with monolayer MoS2.
- Schottky contacts were found for all metals, with all forming n-type contacts except platinum, which formed a p-type Schottky contact.
- The Fermi levels in the metal-MoS2 complexes were found to be partially pinned, varying within a 0.5-0.64 eV window in the band gap, rather than strictly pinned at a single energy level.
- The partial Fermi level pinning results from two synergistic interface behaviors: (1) metal work function modification via interface dipole formation due to charge redistribution, and (2) production of gap states predominantly of Mo d-orbital character, caused by weakened intralayer S-Mo bonding due to interface metal-S interaction.
- The FL shift relative to the CBM of MoS2 shows a linear dependence on metal work function with a slope of 0.71 (well below 1), indicating partial pinning.
- This mechanism is fundamentally different from traditional pinning mechanisms: Bardeen's surface states theory, metal-induced gap states (MIGS), and defect/disorder-induced gap states (DIGS) are all not applicable to these pristine metal-MoS2 interfaces.
- The gap states are localized at Mo atoms (not the contacting S atoms), mediated through the S atoms which weaken the intralayer S-Mo bonding when metal-S bonds form.
- When interface separation is increased to 6.0 Å, all contacts obey the conventional Schottky-Mott model, suggesting that inserting buffer materials between metals and MoS2 could unpin the Fermi levels and form Ohmic contacts.

**Methodology:**
- DFT calculations performed using VASP with PAW method and LDA exchange-correlation functional.
- MoS2 lattice constant kept constant (3.12 Å optimized); metals (111) surfaces strained to match.
- Vacuum region of ~27 Å; Monkhorst-Pack k-point sampling of 4×4×1 (ionic) and 20×20×1 (electronic).
- Energy cutoff of 400 eV; calculated LDA band gap of pristine monolayer MoS2 is 1.88 eV.

**Computational details/parameters:**
- Binding energies: s-electron metals (Ag, Al, Au) interact weakly (physisorption), while d-electron metals (Pd, Ir, Pt) interact strongly (chemisorption).
- Interface distances range from 2.17 Å (Pd) to 2.92 Å (Au).
- The work was supported by the Center for Low Energy Systems Technology (LEAST) under STARnet/FCRP program sponsored by MARCO and DARPA.
</summary>

"At metal−MoS2 interfaces, the Fermi level is partially pinned as a result of two interface behaviors: first by a metal work function modification by interface dipole formation due to the charge redistribution, and second by the production of gap states mainly of Mo d-orbitals character by the weakened intralayer S−Mo bonding due to the interface metal−S interaction."

--- SOURCE 15: Ohmic contact - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohmic_contact

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Wikipedia article defines and explains the physics, fabrication, and technological significance of ohmic contacts in semiconductor devices. An ohmic contact is a non-rectifying electrical junction between two conductors that exhibits a linear current-voltage (I-V) curve consistent with Ohm's law. Low-resistance ohmic contacts allow charge to flow easily in both directions without rectification blocking or excess power dissipation.

KEY PHYSICS: The formation of metal-semiconductor ohmic contacts depends on the Schottky barrier height. While the Schottky-Mott rule predicts barrier height based on the difference between metal work function and semiconductor electron affinity, most interfaces deviate from this rule due to Fermi level pinning caused by metal-induced gap states. Practically, high work function metals form the best contacts to p-type semiconductors, while low work function metals work best for n-type. High-quality ohmic contacts are difficult to form in important semiconductors like silicon and gallium arsenide due to Fermi level pinning.

FABRICATION: The fundamental steps are semiconductor surface cleaning (via sputter-etching, chemical etching, reactive gas etching, or ion milling), contact metal deposition (via sputter deposition, evaporation, or CVD), patterning, and annealing. Surface cleanliness is critical, with native oxide removal using hydrofluoric acid for silicon and bromine-methanol for GaAs. Heavy doping near the junction narrows the depletion region, allowing electron tunneling through the barrier in both directions. Layered structures with diffusion barriers are commonly used. Contact resistance is measured using a four-point probe or the more accurate transmission line method.

TECHNOLOGICALLY IMPORTANT CONTACTS: Aluminum was originally the most important silicon contact metal but was replaced by silicon-doped aluminum and eventually silicides (e.g., titanium-tungsten disilicide) made by CVD. Compound semiconductor contacts (GaAs, III-V, II-VI) are considerably more difficult due to arsenic loss and volatility. A table lists common contact materials for Si, Ge, GaAs, GaN, InSb, ZnO, CuInGaSe2, HgCdTe, and diamond. Transparent contacts (typically indium tin oxide) are needed for LCDs, laser diodes, and photovoltaics.

SIGNIFICANCE: Contact resistance creates RC time constants that limit device frequency response, causes power dissipation through Joule heating in low-frequency circuits and solar cells, and electromigration and delamination at contacts limit device lifetime. Establishing contact fabrication methodology is critical for developing any new semiconductor technology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"An ohmic contact is a non-rectifying electrical junction: a junction between two conductors that has a linear current-voltage (I–V) curve as with Ohm's law."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Mini Review article titled "Brief Review of van der Waals Contact for Two-Dimensional Electronics" published in Applied Science and Convergence Technology (ASCT) 2026, Vol. 35(1), pp. 33-38, published online January 30, 2026. The article is authored by Jisu Jang (Department of Electric Engineering, Display and Semiconductor Engineering, Pukyong National University) and Ji Hoon Park (Departments of Metallurgical Engineering and Smart Green Technology Engineering, Pukyong National University), with correspondence to jsj@pknu.ac.kr. The work was supported by a Research Grant of Pukyong National University (202508110001). DOI: 10.5757/ASCT.2026.35.1.33.

The review addresses the challenge of Fermi-level pinning at metal-2D semiconductor interfaces, which causes uncontrollable Schottky barriers and limits 2D semiconductor transistor development (especially for low-power and complementary n- and p-type devices). The solution presented is van der Waals (vdW) contacts, where the metallic contact is placed on top of the 2D semiconductor with a vdW gap decoupling the metal-semiconductor interaction, thereby alleviating Fermi-level pinning.

Key concepts covered:
- Schottky barrier height (ϕB) determined by metal work function and semiconductor electron affinity per the Schottky-Mott rule, with pinning factor S = |dϕB/dϕm| ranging from 0 (fully pinned) to 1 (unpinned)
- Fermi-level pinning origins: interfacial chemical reactions, fabrication-induced defects, native vacancies in 2D TMDs, and local strain from lattice mismatch

The review categorizes vdW contacts into two classes:

1. The van der Waals gap does not inherently impede current for top contacts.
2. The limited surface area for side contacts does not necessarily need to be a problem.
3. For top contacts, current is mostly determined by edge injection—most current is injected from the metal into the semiconductor at the edge where the metal stops, meaning contact resistance does not scale with surface area as long as there is a few nanometers of overlap region in the direction of transport.
4. A doping gate can provide the required carrier concentration to achieve low contact resistances, and surprisingly, an electrostatic doping gate in ON state lowers contact resistance even further than expected from carrier concentration alone.
5. High contact resistances found in experiments are predicted to be the result of defects (e.g., poor metal-semiconductor contact) or non-ideal material choices (e.g., large Schottky barriers).

All 2D metals gave very high n-type Schottky barrier heights for WS2, and all 3D metals tested were still several 100 meV. --- SOURCE 1: Contact Resistance Optimization in MoS2 Field-Effect Transistors through Reverse Sputtering-Induced Structural Modifications ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12022942

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces (March 11, 2025) by researchers from AMO GmbH, RWTH Aachen University, Eindhoven University of Technology, and AIXTRON SE. The study investigates the use of reverse sputtering (Ar+ ion bombardment via RF-generated plasma) to reduce contact resistance (Rc) in molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) field-effect transistors (FETs).

Key findings and methodology:
- MoS₂ FETs suffer from Schottky barriers at the metal-MoS₂ interface, causing high contact resistance. The study explores inducing a phase transition from semiconducting 2H-MoS₂ to metallic 1T-MoS₂ via reverse sputtering at the contact interface.
- Multilayer MOCVD-grown MoS₂ (~2.5 nm thick, ~4 layers) was transferred onto SiO₂/Si substrates. Devices were fabricated with nickel (Ni) top-contacts (TOP-FETs) where only the contact regions were sputter-treated, and bottom-contact (BOT-FETs) control devices where the entire MoS₂ was exposed.
- Characterization via PL, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS confirmed that reverse sputtering induces sulfur vacancies (VS) and a 2H-to-1T phase transition in MoS₂. XPS showed the S/Mo ratio decreasing from ~2.0 (pristine) to 1.80 (200 W treatment), with full 2H-to-1T conversion observed after sputtering.
- Optimal results were achieved at 75 W reverse sputtering for 10 s: Rc decreased from 1126 kΩ·μm (pristine) to 413 kΩ·μm (a reduction to less than 50% of untreated devices), and output current increased approximately 150-fold.
- Two-probe mobility (μ₂ₚ) nearly doubled for the 75 W sample (0.81 ± 0.20 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ vs. 0.48 ± 0.10 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ for pristine). On/off ratios of 10⁶ were maintained for pristine, 25 W, and 75 W samples, degrading to 10⁵ at 200 W.
- Excessive sputtering power (200 W) caused oxidation to MoOₓ and severe degradation. Insufficient power (25 W) produced too few sulfur vacancies and increased Rc. The 75 W condition represented the optimal balance between phase conversion and material damage.
- The mechanism involves sulfur vacancies creating heavily n-doped regions that narrow the Schottky barrier, plus the formation of conductive 1T-MoS₂ that enhances electron injection from Ni contacts.

The authors conclude that reverse sputtering is a scalable, CMOS-compatible, and clean method for optimizing contact resistance in MoS₂ FETs, with potential for broader application in 2D material-based microelectronics. Funding was provided by EU Horizon 2020/Horizon Europe programs, German BMBF projects (NEUROTEC, NEUROTEC 2, NeuroSys), and the German Research Foundation (DFG).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"MoS₂–FETs exposed to optimized reverse sputtering conditions in the contact area show Rc values reduced to less than 50% of their untreated counterparts."
</key_excerpts>
