--- SOURCE 2: Semimetal contacts to monolayer semiconductor ---
URL: http://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023JPhD...56w4001S/abstract

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper (published in Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics, June 2023) investigating electrical contact properties between semimetal electrodes (bismuth and antimony) and monolayer 2D transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) semiconductors. The study used first-principles density functional theory (DFT) simulations on six TMDC semiconductors (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2, MoTe2, and WTe2) with two semimetal contact materials (Bi and Sb).

Key findings:
- Bi and Sb work functions align well with TMDC conduction band edges, resulting in predominantly Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts.
- Semimetal/TMDC contacts have significantly larger interlayer distances than metal/TMDC counterparts, leading to only weak metalization of TMDC upon contact formation.
- This weak metalization generates semimetal-induced gap states (SMIGSs) extending below the conduction band minimum, providing an effective mechanism to reduce or eliminate n-type Schottky barrier height (SBH) while preserving the electronic structures of the 2D TMDC.
- The authors propose a modified Schottky-Mott rule accounting for SMIGS, interface dipole potential, and Fermi level shifting, which shows improved agreement with DFT-simulated SBH.
- Sb/TMDC contacts generally exhibit lower tunneling-specific resistivity than Bi counterparts, indicating better charge injection efficiency with Sb contacts.
- The findings highlight Bi and Sb as promising companion electrode materials for advancing 2D semiconductor device technology.

Paper details: Authors include Su Tong, Li Yueyan, Wang Qianqian, Zhao Weiwei, Cao Liemao, and Ang Yee Sin. DOI: 10.1088/1361-6463/acc53f; arXiv:2212.03003; 12 pages, 7 figures.
</summary>

"As Bi and Sb work functions energetically aligns well with the TMDC conduction band edge, Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts are prevalent."

--- SOURCE 3: [PDF] arXiv:2212.03003v1 [cond-mat.mtrl-sci] 6 Dec 2022 ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.03003

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) study investigating the electrical contact properties between semimetal electrodes (bismuth, Bi, and antimony, Sb) and six monolayer transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) semiconductors (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2, MoTe2, WTe2), covering 12 semimetal/TMDC contact heterostructures.

Key findings:
- Recent experiments showed semimetal Bi achieves ultralow contact resistance (as low as 123 Ω·µm) with monolayer MoS2, motivating broader investigation of semimetal contacts.
- The Fermi levels of Bi (-4.12 eV) and Sb (-4.25 eV below vacuum) align closely with TMDC conduction band edges (~4 eV), enabling Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts.
- Semimetal/TMDC contacts have significantly larger interlayer distances (>3 Å) than metal/TMDC counterparts, resulting in only weak metalization of the TMDC upon contact formation.
- This weak metalization creates semimetal-induced gap states (SMIGS) that extend below the conduction band minimum, providing an effective mechanism to reduce or eliminate n-type Schottky barrier height (SBH) while preserving TMDC electronic structures.
- A modified Schottky-Mott rule was proposed: Φ(e)SBH = Wmetal − EEA − ΔV + ΔεF − ΔM, incorporating interface dipole potential (ΔV), Fermi level shifting (ΔεF), and the SMIGS energy window (ΔM), showing significantly improved agreement with DFT-simulated SBH compared to the original Schottky-Mott rule.
- Contacts exhibit both physisorptive (Te-based TMDCs, larger interlayer distances, positive ΔV) and chemisorptive (S- and Se-based TMDCs, smaller interlayer distances, low/negative ΔV) interfacial interactions.
- Sb/TMDC contacts generally exhibit lower tunneling-specific resistivity (10^-9 Ω·cm² order) than Bi counterparts, suggesting better charge injection efficiency and better thermal stability, making Sb a potentially superior semimetal contact material.
- DFT-calculated SBHs for Bi/MoS2 (0.075 eV) and Bi/WS2 (0.13 eV) differ slightly from experimental values (zero/Ohmic and 0.040 eV, respectively), likely due to defects in experimental contacted regions.
- Computational methods: VASP with projector augmented wave method, PBE-GGA exchange-correlation, DFT-D3 vdW corrections, 500 eV kinetic energy cutoff, 6×6×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-sampling, and ≥15 Å vacuum spacing.

The work provides a theoretical foundation and design blueprint for semimetal-enabled high-performance 2D semiconductor nanoelectronics, with potential applications in valleytronics and multiferroics. Funding came from the Singapore Ministry of Education Academic Research Fund Tier 2 Grant and SUTD-ZJU IDEA Visiting Professor Grant.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Recent experiment has uncovered semimetal bismuth (Bi) as an excellent electrical contact to monolayer MoS2 with ultralow contact resistance."

--- SOURCE 4: Antimony Semimetal Contact with Enhanced Thermal ... ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (IEDM 2021, DOI: 10.1109/IEDM19574.2021.9720608) from TSMC researchers studies antimony (Sb) semimetal as a novel contact material for two-dimensional (2D) MoS2 electronics, addressing the thermal stability limitations of previously studied semimetals like tin (Sn) and bismuth (Bi).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Sb contacts achieve near-zero Schottky barrier height and contact resistance of 0.66 kΩ·µm on monolayer (1L) MoS2
- Short-channel Sb-contacted MoS2 FETs demonstrate on-state current above 600 µA/µm at VDS=1V and 1000 µA/µm at VDS=2V
- Sb has a melting point of 630.6°C, substantially higher than Bi (271.5°C) and Sn (231.9°C)
- Sb-contacted devices remain fully operational after annealing at 400°C, versus only 300°C for Bi-contacted devices—a key advantage for back-end-of-the-line (BEOL) compatibility
- Sb-contacted 1L MoS2 FET retains 80% and 64% of pristine performance after annealing at 300°C and 400°C, respectively
- Bi-contacted devices decay significantly after 300°C annealing and fail completely at 400°C
- LCH=50nm devices show ION ~600 µA/µm at VDS=1V with nearly zero drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL)

METHODOLOGY:
- 1L MoS2 grown by CVD, transferred onto 100nm SiNx/Si substrate
- He-ion-beam lithography for S/D patterning; 20nm semimetal (Bi or Sb) capped with 15nm Au via e-beam evaporation and lift-off
- PMMA encapsulation with 200°C hard baking for 30 min in N2 glovebox
- Progressive thermal annealing at 200°C, 300°C, and 400°C
- Characterization via Raman spectroscopy, AFM, TEM, EDS mapping, UPS
- DFT simulations (VASP with PBE/PAW/GGA) for interface analysis and Bi-Sb alloy predictions

ALLOY STRATEGY (DFT-predicted):
- Bi-Sb alloy could balance thermal stability and low contact resistance
- BEOL compatibility requires melting point ≥400°C, needing >20% Sb ratio
- Preferred design space: 40%-100% Sb ratio (alloy remains semimetal; 4%-40% Sb makes it a semiconductor/topological insulator)
- Bi0.5Sb0.5 predicted to offer lower barrier height (0.10 eV) than pure Sb while maintaining good conductivity and 540°C melting point

CONCLUSION: Sb semimetal offers the best balance of thermal stability and low contact resistance among semimetals for 2D electronics, making it a promising BEOL-compatible contact solution for beyond-silicon technology. Funding from Ministry of Science and Technology (Grants MOST-109-2622-8-002-003; MOST 110-2119-M-A49-001-MBK).
</summary>

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13045353

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in ACS Nano (2026 Feb 24;20(12):9817, DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.5c19217) titled "Bismuth Confinement: A Strategy for Low Resistance and Good Thermal Endurance of Integrated Contacts to MoS2." The work was conducted by researchers from National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), Taiwan Semiconductor Research Institute, and the National Institutes of Applied Research in Taiwan. Corresponding authors are Iuliana P. Radu (TSMC) and Chao-Hsin Chien (NYCU).

**Core Problem:** Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are promising for advanced nanoelectronics due to atomically thin bodies enabling excellent electrostatic control. However, achieving low contact resistance (RC) requires semimetals like bismuth (Bi) or antimony (Sb), which have low melting points and are thermally unstable, limiting their compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) integration that requires annealing at 400°C in H2 environments. Refractory metals are thermally stable but induce prohibitively high RC (>1 kΩ·μm).

**Key Innovation:** The authors demonstrate a "confinement strategy" using AlOx and/or TiN barriers to encapsulate Bi contacts. This enables RC values below 200 Ω·μm while preserving device performance after forming gas annealing at 400°C for up to 10 minutes.

**Key Findings:**
- Unconfined Bi melts at ~273°C and forms spherical droplets when annealed; Sb rapidly sublimates at 400°C in forming gas within 1 minute.
- AlOx capping stabilizes Sb films up to 800°C (above its 671°C melting point) and Bi up to 450°C without outgassing, melting, or agglomeration.
- Device-level demonstration: Monolayer CVD MoS2 transistors with Bi contacts on 8 nm HfO2 gate dielectric (EOT~2nm) with TiN back gate, fully encapsulated in low-temperature ALD AlOx. After 400°C forming gas annealing (10 min), devices retained RC below 200 Ω·μm with nearly ohmic injection and ION over 60 μA/μm at LCH=100 nm.
- On-current after line-resistance subtraction exceeds 1 mA/μm at VDS=1V, ranking among the highest reported for monolayer MoS2.
- Intrinsic mobility improved slightly from 27 to 32 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹ after annealing (attributed to partial defect passivation).
- TCAD simulations extracted Schottky barrier height of 70 meV and van der Waals gap of 2 Å at the MoS2/Bi interface, confirming near-ohmic contact that did not degrade through annealing.
- Fab-relevant integration test: Bi deposited by PVD in SiO2 trenches (<40 nm wide), encapsulated by conformal 200°C ALD TiN barrier and W plug. Cross-sectional TEM/EDX confirmed Bi remains fully confined without diffusion or outgassing after 400°C annealing in N2, forming gas, and vacuum environments.
- A remaining grand challenge identified: selective dielectric etch that stops on 2D TMDs (to be addressed in subsequent publications).

**Keywords:** two-dimensional semiconductors, semimetal contacts, contact resistance, back-end-of-line (BEOL) integration, monolithic 3D integration, thermal stability
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Low contact resistance on monolayer MoS2 field-effect ... ---
URL: https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10531719

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article from ACS Nano (Manuscript ID nn-2024-07267z.R3, submitted 29-Jul-2024) by researchers from Purdue University and the University of Texas at Dallas, led by Zheng Sun, Seong Yeoul Kim, and Joerg Appenzeller. The study investigates contact engineering for monolayer MoS2 field-effect transistors (FETs) to achieve low contact resistance using CMOS-compatible metal contacts.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Ni Contacts (Covalent Type):** Ultra-high vacuum (UHV, 3×10^-11 mbar) deposited Ni contacts achieved a record-low contact resistance of ~500 ohm·μm for ML MoS2 FETs — 5 times lower than Ni deposited under high vacuum (HV, 3×10^-6 mbar) conditions. This was achieved across 60 UHV-Ni and 64 HV-Ni FETs fabricated with four channel lengths (85nm, 185nm, 385nm, 985nm) using the transfer length method (TLM). The best UHV-Ni device reached 470 μA/μm at VDS=1V, VGS=2.5V.

2. **Bi Contacts (van der Waals Type):** Contact resistance for Bi-contacted MoS2 FETs showed no dependence on vacuum deposition conditions (more than 150 Bi-contacted FETs tested: 40 UHV-Bi and 112 HV-Bi). Bi achieves high on-currents (~400 μA/μm) with on/off ratios of ~10^8, but does not chemically react with MoS2 regardless of vacuum conditions.

3. **Interface Chemistry (XPS Analysis):**
   - UHV-Ni deposition showed stronger Ni/MoSx bonding species (20% intensity vs 17% for HV-Ni) with more metallic properties
   - HV-Ni deposition resulted in MoO3 formation (thermodynamically favored due to ΔG°f,MoO3=-266.67 kJ/mol vs ΔG°f,MoS2=-112.95 kJ/mol), reducing Ni-MoS2 bonding
   - Bi showed no detectable chemical reaction with MoS2 under either condition; Bi2O3 was detected only for HV deposition
   - Thermodynamic data support these observations (ΔG°f,Bi2S3=-46.87 kJ/mol, higher than ΔG°f,MoS2)

4. **Thermal Stability:**
   - Bi/Au contacts showed excellent thermal reliability up to 400°C with no contact resistance degradation (Au capping prevented Bi evaporation; annealing in high vacuum prevented oxidation). This contrasts with prior reports of degradation at 200°C.
   - Ni contacts degraded after 100°C annealing (on-current dropped from 200 to 125 μA/μm; contact resistance increased from 2000 to 3000 ohm·μm), attributed to Ni diffusion into the channel and oxidation of diffused Ni
   - Bi remained concentrated at contact corners after 400°C annealing without chemical reaction with MoS2

**Methods:** CVD-grown ML MoS2 on SiO2 substrates, local bottom gate structures with HfO2 dielectrics (2.8nm and 5.5nm), e-beam lithography, monochromatic XPS (Al Kα, 1486.7 eV), STEM/EDS analysis, and annealing at 100-400°C in high vacuum.

**Conclusion:** The work demonstrates that interface engineering through UHV deposition of covalent-type metals (Ni) can achieve competitive contact resistance (~500 ohm·μm) comparable to vdW-type contacts, while Bi contacts offer superior thermal stability but no dependence on deposition vacuum conditions. The study provides the first statistically meaningful correlation (120+ FETs) between interface chemistry and contact resistance for ML MoS2 FETs.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Stable and scalable 1T MoS2 with low temperature-coefficient of resistance | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-30867-y

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Scientific Reports (volume 8, article number 12463, 2018) by Chithra H. Sharma, Ananthu P. Surendran, Abin Varghese, and Madhu Thalakulam. The paper demonstrates a controllable and scalable method for engineering the metallic 1T phase of MoS2 from the semiconducting 2H phase using forming-gas (10% H2 + 90% Ar) microwave plasma treatment on mechanically exfoliated samples. 

Key methodology and results:
- The technique allows lithographically defining 1T regions on 2H samples using aluminum masking, enabling monolithic integration of metallic and semiconducting phases.
- HR-TEM analysis confirmed extended 1T regions with areal coverage exceeding 70% over the 2H phase, with no signatures of distorted phases (1T′ or 1T″). The nearest Mo-Mo separation was measured at 3.19 Å.
- Raman spectroscopy showed characteristic J1, J2, and J3 peaks of the 1T phase, accompanied by photoluminescence quenching indicative of metallic phase formation. A new peak at 180 cm⁻¹ not previously reported was also observed.
- The phase transition occurs via gliding of Mo and S planes, induced by momentum transfer from plasma ions.
- Stability: 1T samples showed temporal stability exceeding 27-30 days at ambient conditions and thermal stability up to 300°C, well above standard device fabrication temperatures.
- Electrical transport: Two-probe and four-probe measurements on back-gated FET geometry from 4K to 300K showed Ohmic I-V characteristics with no gate voltage dependence (signature of metallic state). The 2H regions showed Schottky behavior and n-type FET characteristics with mobility of 16.4 cm²/V-s at 300K and 84 cm²/V-s at 4K.
- Extracted parameters for the 1T phase: sheet resistance of 108 Ω/□, carrier concentration of ~2.3 × 10¹⁵ cm⁻² (two orders of magnitude higher than 2H MoS2), and temperature coefficient of resistance α = −1.1057 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ (negligible temperature dependence from 4K to 300K).
- The sample satisfies the Ioffe-Regal criterion (kF·l ~ 239) confirming metallic conduction, ruling out hopping-mediated or activated transport.
- Stability verified over ~90 days post-processing (including ~30 days in ambient conditions) with minimal resistance variation.

The conclusion states this method enables extended, low-disorder 1T regions suitable for monolithic 2D circuits, unlike prior methods (intercalation, electron-beam irradiation, argon plasma) that yielded nanoscale patches or unstable phases.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Tuning the Schottky barrier height in single- and bi-layer graphene-inserted MoS2/metal contacts | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-67150-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Scientific Reports (volume 14, article number 20905, 2024) titled "Tuning the Schottky barrier height in single- and bi-layer graphene-inserted MoS2/metal contacts." The study, authored by Xumei Zhao, Caijuan Xia, Lianbi Li, Anxiang Wang, Dezhong Cao, Baiyu Zhang, and Qinglong Fang, uses first-principle density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate how inserting single- and bi-layer graphene affects the electronic properties and Schottky barrier of MoS2/metals contacts (Mg, Al, In, Cu, Ag, Au, Pd, Ti, and Sc).

Key findings:
- Charge transfer occurs mainly at the graphene/metal interface, with smaller transfer at bi-layer graphene interfaces or graphene/MoS2 interfaces. Bader charge analysis shows weak interactions for Mg/Al/In (0.035-0.052 e), medium for Cu/Ag/Au (0.069-0.073 e), and strong for Pd/Sc/Ti (0.101-0.208 e) with graphene.
- A tunneling barrier exists at the graphene/MoS2 interface that hinders electron injection, but tunneling transmission probabilities remain high (88-97.8% for single-layer; 85.1-96.4% for bi-layer).
- The Schottky barrier height (Φ_SB,N) decreases upon graphene insertion. With single-layer graphene insertion: MoS2 contacts with Mg, In, Sc, and Ti achieve negative n-type Schottky barriers of -0.116 eV, -0.116 eV, -0.014 eV, and -0.116 eV respectively (indicating ohmic contacts); while Al, Cu, Ag, Au, Pd show positive barriers of 0.111, 0.146, 0.199, 0.462, and 0.332 eV respectively.
- With bi-layer graphene insertion: negative n-type Schottky barriers of -0.086 eV (Mg), -0.114 eV (In), -0.059 eV (Pd), -0.008 eV (Sc), and -0.0636 eV (Ti) are observed; while Al, Cu, Ag, Au show positive barriers of 0.492, 0.492, 0.230, and 0.359 eV respectively.
- Graphene preserves the intrinsic semiconductor properties of MoS2 (maintaining band gaps of ~1.3-1.6 eV with only band shifts), effectively isolating the MoS2 layer from the metal.
- Computational details: VASP code, PAW method, PBE-GGA functional with Grimme van der Waals correction, 450 eV cutoff energy, 11×11×1 k-mesh, 15 Å vacuum layer, energy convergence of 1.0×10^-5 eV, force convergence of 0.02 eV/Å.

The study provides practical guidance for designing high-performance transition metal dichalcogenide nanoelectronic devices by demonstrating that graphene insertion into MoS2/metal contacts can reduce or eliminate Schottky barriers, transitioning contacts to ohmic behavior.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results reveal that the charge transfer mainly occurs at the interface between the graphene and metal layers, with smaller transfer at the interface between bi-layer garphene or between graphene and MoS2. And the tunneling barrier exists at the interface between graphene and MoS2, which hinders electron injection from graphene to MoS2."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Research - 2D Materials - Schottky-barrier Injection ---
URL: https://www.purdue.edu/discoverypark/nanotechnology/membership/Appenzeller/research_2d_sbfet.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the Purdue University Appenzeller research group's Nanotechnology program, specifically describing their research on Schottky-barrier injection in 2D materials. The research focuses on making good electrical contacts to emerging 2D materials and separating contact effects from intrinsic material properties. Key findings include:

1. **MoS2 Schottky-barrier Transistor with Scandium Contact**: The group studied contacts to MoS2 using low work function metals (scandium ΦM=3.5 eV, titanium ΦM=4.3 eV) and large work function metals (nickel ΦM=5.0 eV, platinum ΦM=5.9 eV). They extracted Schottky barrier heights of ~230 meV (platinum), ~150 meV (nickel), ~50 meV (titanium), and ~30 meV (scandium). The work provided evidence that MoS2-to-metal interfaces are strongly impacted by Fermi level pinning near the conduction band, similar to III-V materials and silicon. Using scandium contacts on 10-nm-thick exfoliated MoS2 flakes covered by a 15 nm Al2O3 film, they achieved high effective mobilities of 700 cm²/(V·s) at room temperature (Nano Letters, 2013, 13, 100-105). Authors: Saptarshi Das and Ashish Penumatcha.

2. **Tunability of Short-Channel Effects in MoS2 Schottky-barrier Transistors**: MoS2 FETs show electrical performance governed by an unexpected dependence on effective body thickness, which depends on intercalated water molecules in the layered structure. The doping state of MoS2 FETs strongly depends on environment (air/vacuum). Device characteristics can be tuned by controlling the effective body thickness via intercalation and engineering the interlayer barrier (Nano Letters 15, 301-306). Author: Feng Zhang.

3. **Black Phosphorus Schottky-barrier MOSFET and Modeling**: Black phosphorus (BP) is a layered 2D material with phosphorus atoms in a puckered arrangement held together by weak van der Waals forces. BP has high mobility (200-1000 cm²/V-s) and a direct tunable bandgap, making it attractive for RF and optoelectronic applications, as well as tunnel FET development. The group used a Landauer model to fit transfer characteristics of BP Schottky-barrier MOSFETs and extracted both electron- and hole-Schottky barrier heights for Permalloy and Palladium contacts to black phosphorus. This model can be extended to other 2D-material SB-MOSFETs (Nature Communications 6, 6:8948). Authors: Ashish Penumatcha and Ramon Salazar.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Through analysis of experimental results, we found for many 2D materials of interest, such as transition metal dichacolgenides (TMDs) and black phosphorus, that the metal-to-semiconductor contacts are Schottky-barrier type."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Multilayer MoS2 Schottky Barrier Field Effect Transistor ---
URL: https://d-nb.info/1365289796/34

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific paper published in IEEE Open Journal of Nanotechnology (Volume 6, 2025, pp. 51-57, DOI: 10.1109/OJNANO.2025.3553692) by researchers from the University of Salerno (Italy) and Universität Konstanz (Germany). The paper was received December 21, 2024, revised in February and March 2025, accepted March 16, 2025, and published March 20, 2025. Corresponding author: Antonio Di Bartolomeo (adibartolomeo@unisa.it).

The study presents multilayer MoS2 Schottky Barrier Field Effect Transistors (SB-FETs) configured with back-gate and van der Pauw contacts. The devices were fabricated using a dry-transfer technique with MoS2 flakes (~16.7 nm thick, ~20 layers, ~137 μm² area) encapsulated between two hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) layers on a SiO2/Si substrate (300 nm SiO2 as gate oxide). Au(53nm)/Ti(7nm) contacts were patterned via e-beam lithography.

Key findings:
- IV characteristics showed non-linear, asymmetric, rectifying behavior across all six contact combinations, confirming Schottky barriers at Ti/MoS2 interfaces despite Schottky-Mott theory predicting ohmic contacts (due to Fermi level pinning from defects and metal-induced gap states).
- Rectification ratios varied from a few units to 10³ depending on the contact pair, attributed to local inhomogeneities from fabrication and different flake coverage areas.
- Transfer curves showed n-type behavior (electrons as majority carriers) with prominent "kinks" at a transition voltage (Vtr ~ -12V to -15V) marking the transition between thermionic emission and tunnelling conduction regimes.
- A hierarchy of Schottky barrier heights was established: φb,D < φb,E ≤ φb,G < φb,F.
- A band model combining thermionic emission and tunnelling (including Fowler-Nordheim tunnelling, confirmed by linear fits in Fowler-Nordheim plots) was developed to explain the device operation, which can be broadly applied to other SB-FETs.
- At negative gate voltages, thermionic emission dominates; at positive gate voltages, tunnelling dominates, causing barrier-height differences to become less influential and output curves to symmetrize.
- The higher the drain barrier, the slower the transition from sublinear to ohmic behavior in the IV curves.

The study concludes that lead local inhomogeneities and different flake coverage affect Schottky barrier heights, which critically determine conduction mechanisms in SB-FETs. The proposed band energy model aids in understanding and optimizing 2D material transistors with Schottky-type contacts.

Experimental equipment: Lake Shore probe station with Keithley 4200-SCS semiconductor characterization system, NaioAFM (Nanosurf AG) for height profiling, all measurements at room temperature, ambient pressure, and dark conditions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A hierarchy of the Schottky barrier heights at the contacts is established, and a band model is developed to elucidate the underlying conduction mechanisms. This model combines thermionic emission and tunnelling to explain the operation of the studied MoS2 devices and can be broadly applied to other SB-FETs."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research letter published in Nano Letters (2017, Vol. 17, pp. 4781-4786, DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.7b01536) from researchers at Columbia University, Harvard University, Kyung Hee University, Yonsei University, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Sungkyunkwan University, and the National Institute for Materials Science.

**Main Topic:** The paper reports a new low-temperature Ohmic contact scheme for monolayer MoS2 using cobalt (Co) electrodes with a monolayer of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) inserted between the metal and the semiconductor.

**Key Findings:**
- The monolayer h-BN serves a dual function: it modifies the work function of Co (reducing it from ~5.0 eV to ~3.3 eV, confirmed by XPS) and acts as a tunneling barrier.
- This design breaks the metal-TMDC interaction, eliminating interface states that cause Fermi level pinning.
- A flat-band Schottky barrier of only 16 meV was measured (vs. 38 meV for Co directly on MoS2).
- Contact resistance of 3 kΩ·μm was achieved at a carrier density of 5.3 × 10^12/cm² at 1.7 K.
- Ohmic contacts were achieved at low carrier densities down to 3.5 × 10^12/cm², enabling observation of Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations at significantly lower carrier densities than previously possible.
- Hall mobility reached ~630 cm²/(V·s) at 5.3 × 10^12/cm² carrier density.

**Methodology:**
- Devices were fabricated using dry van der Waals transfer, with MoS2 and h-BN exfoliated from bulk crystals onto SiO2/Si substrates.
- 30 nm Co and 50 nm Au electrodes were evaporated under ultrahigh vacuum (~10^-10 Torr).
- Work function was verified via X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (XPS) showing Φ = 3.3 eV for Co/h-BN.
- Transport measurements included two-probe and four-probe resistance, Hall effect measurements, and magneto-transport up to 14 T at temperatures down to 1.7 K.

**Key Comparisons:**
- The h-BN/Co contact outperforms other schemes: few-layer graphene contacts (Rc ~10 kΩ·μm but only at ~10^13/cm²), Au contacts (only low resistance above 2 × 10^13/cm²), and low work-function metals like Sc and Al (non-Ohmic at low temperature).
- Co without h-BN showed nonlinear I-V behavior at low temperature.
- Other metals (Sc, Ti, Al, Ag) with h-BN tunnel barriers did not achieve low-T Ohmic contact, confirming the critical role of the strong h-BN/Co work-function interaction.
- Co evaporated under ordinary high vacuum (~10^-8 Torr) gave roughly 5 times higher contact resistance.

**Conclusions:** The Co/h-BN contact scheme provides the best reported contacts to monolayer MoS2 to date, particularly well suited for studies at low temperature and low carrier density, and may prove useful for electron injection in a wide range of other systems.

--- SOURCE 7: Metal-induced gap states - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal-induced_gap_states

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Wikipedia article explains metal-induced gap states (MIGS) in solid-state physics. MIGS are electron states that exist near the surface of a semiconductor when a metal is deposited on it (e.g., by thermal evaporation). These states have energies that fall within the semiconductor's bandgap, which are otherwise forbidden in the bulk material. When a metal is deposited on a semiconductor, even as thin as a single atomic layer, the Fermi levels of both materials must match at the interface, which pins the Fermi level in the semiconductor and creates gap states that decay deeper into the semiconductor.

Key concepts covered include:
- Band-bending at the metal-semiconductor interface: The Fermi level matching creates band bending, with different behaviors for high/low work function metals and n-type/p-type semiconductors. Volker Heine was among the first to estimate the length of metal electron state tails extending into the semiconductor's energy gap, showing the surface state energy position is quite stable regardless of the metal used.
- Branching point: MIGS are mixtures (Fourier series) of valence and conduction band states. The branching point (E_B) divides acceptor-type from donor-type MIGS. Tersoff derived the formula E_B = 1/2[Ē_V + Ē_C], where Ē_V accounts for spin-orbit splitting and Ē_C is the indirect conduction band minimum.
- Barrier height: Charge transfer between metal and semiconductor (formulated by Linus Pauling and later revised) produces a dipole and thus the Schottky barrier height. Tersoff derived Φ_bh = 1/2[Ē_C - Ē_V] + δ_m, fitting experimental data for Au in contact with 10 common semiconductors (Si, Ge, GaP, GaAs, etc.). Garcia-Moliner and Flores provided a more rigorous derivation considering density of states and dipole contributions, defining two limits: the Bardeen Limit (high interface state density pins Fermi level) and the Schottky Limit (barrier varies strongly with metal characteristics).
- Applications: The metal/semiconductor junction has bias-dependent capacitance (going as (V_if - V)^1/2), making it useful in varactor devices.

Key researchers cited include Volker Heine (1965), C. Tejedor, F. Flores and E. Louis (1977), and J. Tersoff (1984-1985), along with the foundational work of Linus Pauling on charge transfer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Metal-induced gap states are electron states that exist near the surface of a semiconductor due to the presence of a metal on the surface. They have energies that fall within the semiconductor's bandgap thus are forbidden in the bulk of the semiconductor."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Direct Visualization of Metal-Induced Gap State Distribution and Valley Band Evolution at Metal Versus Semimetal MoS2 Interfaces ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12120976

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in ACS Nano (2025 May 15;19(20):19408, DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.5c03676, PMCID: PMC12120976, PMID: 40372765) by Yi-Feng Chen, Hung-Chang Hsu, Hao-Yu Chen, Liang-Yu Chen, Yan-Ruei Lin, Ming-Yang Li, Iuliana P. Radu, and Ya-Ping Chiu (corresponding author, ypchiu@phys.ntu.edu.tw) from National Taiwan University, Academia Sinica, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC).

**Purpose/Topic:** The study directly visualizes metal-induced gap state (MIGS) distribution and valley band evolution at metal versus semimetal MoS₂ interfaces using scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/S), with the goal of understanding interlayer coupling mechanisms for optimizing 2D semiconductor contact engineering.

**Methodology:** STM/S measurements were performed on monolayer MoS₂ grown on Au(111) (prototypical metal) and Bi(111) (prototypical semimetal) substrates. Both substrates have 6-fold symmetric (111) lattice orientation matching MoS₂. The study analyzed MIGS decay lengths, quasiparticle interference (QPI) patterns, constant energy contours (CEC), and dI/dV spectroscopy across substrate-contacted and substrate-free (pit) regions at spatial resolutions of ~0.3–0.4 nm.

**Key Findings:**

1. **MoS₂/Au(111) (metal contact):**
   - MIGS distribution spans nearly the entire band gap (−1.74 eV to +0.41 eV), extending from both conduction band (CB) and valence band (VB)
   - MIGS decay length within the band gap oscillates between 0.5 and 1.5 nm
   - Strong interlayer coupling at both CB and VB; the Q-valley peak at +0.80 eV vanishes in the substrate-contacted region
   - Schottky barrier height (SBH) determined to be +0.51 eV
   - Extensive MIGS distribution fixes the charge neutrality level (CNL) in the band gap, resulting in significant SBH
   - MoS₂/Au(111) showed nearly aligned stacking, while MoS₂/Bi(111) showed ~20° rotational misalignment
   - QPI analysis confirmed destruction of the Q-valley band due to strong coupling, with no characteristic 2×2 QPI signals at M points

2. **MoS₂/Bi(111) (semimetal contact):**
   - MIGS distribution is much narrower, confined to −1.46 eV to −0.57 eV, concentrated near the VBM rather than the CBM
   - Mean decay length and standard deviations (1.1 to 2.5 nm) exceed those of MoS₂/Au(111), suggesting reduced MIGS density
   - Gap state saturation shifts the CNL toward the CBM, potentially yielding zero SBH
   - The Q-valley band structure is preserved, maintaining intervalley scattering processes (evidenced by pronounced 2×2 QPI patterns at the M point)
   - CBM of substrate-contacted MoS₂ estimated at approximately −0.11 eV, characteristic of degenerate semiconductor behavior
   - The reduced band overlap between Bi(111) and MoS₂ results from Bi's characteristically low local density of states (LDOS) near the Fermi level
   - Preserved valley band structure and elevated carrier concentration support reduced intrinsic sheet resistance

**Conclusion:** The study provides direct comparative evidence that maintaining valley band structure integrity during semimetal interlayer coupling facilitates reduced intrinsic sheet resistance, explaining the superior contact transport performance of semimetal–2D semiconductor junctions. This offers insights for rational design of future 2D-based devices.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our findings demonstrate that maintaining valley band structure integrity during semimetal interlayer coupling facilitates reduced intrinsic sheet resistance. These results elucidate the mechanism underlying weak interlayer coupling at semimetal–2D semiconductor junctions and their superior contact transport performance, providing insights into the rational design of future 2D-based devices."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This arXiv paper (2606.28902) presents a method for reproducibly fabricating Ohmic bismuth contacts to MoS2 nanotubes and nanoribbons—a key challenge previously hindering development of 1D field-effect transistors and quantum devices. The central problem was wide scatter in contact resistances on the same chip due to the small, curved surfaces of the 1D nanostructures. Building on recent breakthroughs using semimetals (bismuth, antimony) for flat 2D MoS2 flakes, the authors transferred this technique to 1D morphologies and developed an optimized fabrication protocol.

**Key Results:**
- All optimized devices displayed finite room-temperature two-point resistances with a median of 340 kΩ in a large fabrication series, with all measured segments below 30 MΩ—a reduction in resistance scatter by several orders of magnitude.
- Device active region between contacts: 100–500 nm.

**Fabrication Optimizations (tested in combination):**
1. **"Spot anchoring"**: PMMA electron beam lithography resist is locally overexposed (~200x), cross-linking it into a stable negative-resist/polymer droplet that glues the nanotube to the chip, improving mechanical stability and creating a smooth surface transition to prevent gap formation during metal deposition. Electronic characterization showed no electrical difference from droplets—their main role is mechanical stabilization.
2. **Deposition pressure**: UHV chamber pumped overnight with substrate heated to 100°C, plus a titanium gettering step, achieving final pressure of ~5×10⁻⁸ mbar (vs. ~3×10⁻⁷ mbar without). Vacuum quality proved NOT critical—chip β (skipping vacuum optimization) still gave surprisingly good contacts, consistent with earlier findings that Bi contacts are insensitive to vacuum conditions.
3. **Substrate heating** to 100°C during contact deposition: This was critical—omitting it (chip α) was the only case producing diode-like (Schottky) behavior. Higher temperature improves bismuth film quality (lower melting point 271°C, forms crystallites) and may enable recrystallization or formation of the maldonite (Au2Bi) intermetallic during gold deposition.
4. **Tilted-angle (dual-angle) deposition**: Bismuth (50 nm, 0.03 nm/s) and gold (100 nm, 0.05 nm/s) each evaporated at ±15° from orthogonal to improve coverage of the curved surface. Omitting this (chip γ) caused increased resistance scatter and median, plus a stronger gate effect (partial gate shielding from better coverage).

**Materials rationale:** Bismuth was chosen over antimony (better for 2D but not for nanotubes/nanoribbons), low-work-function metals (Ti, Sc) that react with MoS2, and doping approaches (Cu, Y) unsuitable for small nanotube surfaces. Bismuth's vanishing density of states at the Fermi edge avoids metal-induced gap states and Fermi level pinning.

**Substrate findings:** SiO2-based devices showed slightly lower resistances than hBN-based devices (surprising, since hBN normally avoids dangling bonds/charges), attributed to the more complex multi-step transfer fabrication of hBN devices increasing contamination/damage risk.

**Conclusions/Outlook:** With reliable Ohmic contacts now achievable, the path toward 1D MoS2 transistors and quantum electronics is open. Remaining challenges include intrinsic surface quality (sulfur vacancies, wall curvature, deformation) and reproducibility of single-wall nanotubes (which are thermodynamically unstable; coaxial heterostructures offer a path forward).

The paper provides a comprehensive review of intercalation—the process of inserting foreign ions or molecules between weakly-bonded layers of layered materials—as a powerful tool in 2D materials research. The article is organized around the diverse roles intercalation plays rather than by material type.

**Key topics covered:**

1. **Intercalation methods** (three main approaches):
   - **Electrochemical intercalation**: Driven by external current/voltage using an electrochemical cell; intercalants act as anode, hosts as cathode. Donor-type intercalants (Li, Na, Mg) donate electrons via reaction xH + D+ + e− → HxD, while acceptor types (e.g., H2SO4) withdraw electrons. Controlled by chronopotentiometry or chronoamperometry. Notable for easy reversibility and ability to predict stoichiometry. Limitations include electrolyte reactivity, dendrite growth, and limited temperature range, which can be mitigated with solid electrolytes (perovskite, NASICON, garnet types). In-situ TEM studies show Li intercalation into black phosphorus can form amorphous LixPy alloys beyond certain lithiation.
   - **Vapor phase intercalation**: Uses heat to control intercalant transport; divided into isothermal and two-zone methods. Compatible with a variety of intercalant/host pairs including alkali metals (Na, K, Cs), transition metals (Cu, Cd, Hg), post-transition metals (Sn, Pb), pnictogens (Bi), and halogens (Br, I). Lacks in-situ stoichiometry determination; gravimetric analysis or energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy used for quantification.
   - **Liquid phase intercalation**: Host immersed in a liquid containing intercalants (solution or molten state); does not generate electric currents. Can insert organic molecules (hydrazine, DMSO, urea, etc.). Includes ion-exchange methods (used for layered double hydroxides) and zerovalent metal intercalation via redox reactions (e.g., Cu into Bi2Se3 with up to 60% yield). Liquid ammonia widely used for alkali/alkali-earth metal intercalation, with color change from dark blue to yellowish-brown indicating progress. Better than electrochemical for less conductive host/guest species but lacks compositional control.

2. **Intercalation for fabrication of 2D materials**: Intercalation-assisted exfoliation increases interlayer spacing, weakening adhesion and reducing exfoliation energy barrier. Compared to CVD (sensitive to lattice mismatch), hydrothermal (requires specific solubility/stability), and mechanical exfoliation (limited scale), intercalation enables larger-scale, more uniform production. Three fabrication approaches described:
   - Oxidation-based intercalation (mostly for graphene oxide; introduces defects and chemical groups, lowering electrical conductivity vs. pristine graphene)
   - Reduction-based intercalation of alkali metals (widely used for TMDs like MoS2, WS2, NbSe2, and graphite, h-BN; adding water generates hydrogen bubbles to exfoliate layers; electrochemical Li intercalation into BP produces elongated BP segments for nanoribbon production)
   - Ion-exchanged intercalation and exfoliation

3. **Additional sections** (described in the introduction): intercalation for electrochemical energy storage, property tuning through intercalation-induced doping (affecting electrical, catalytic, optical, magnetic properties and strongly correlated phases like superconductivity and charge density waves), intercalation effects on interlayer interactions (mechanical/optical properties, phonon dispersions, thermal/electronic transport), and intercalation-induced structural phase transitions (e.g., 2H to 1T/1T' in TMDs, black to blue phosphorene transitions).

The review concludes with an overview of opportunities and challenges in intercalation of 2D materials for applications in energy storage, optoelectronics, thermoelectrics, and catalysis.

2. **Electric field effects**: Applying 0.01 V/Å lowers the intercalation barrier by ~half; at 0.02 V/Å the barrier vanishes for Na+ but remains for K+. Intercalation potentials were determined: -1.4 V vs RHE for K+, -1.3 V vs RHE for Na+.

Electron doping is higher for K+ intercalation due to potassium's empty d-orbital, which allows further hybridization with the transition metal's p-orbital.

Al is not a good contact metal since AlOx is insulating, but can serve as a damage-free, tunable dopant.

This damage correlates with decreased mobility and degraded transistor on/off ratios (from >10^7 for bare MoS2 to <10^4 for Ni- and Au-coated MoS2). The damage level scales approximately with metal melting temperature. Interestingly, defect engineering may actually help contacts, as some of the best contacts use evaporated Ag or Au that create "just enough" defects.

3) Reactive metals (Ti, Sc, Y) chemically react with monolayer MoS2, forming metal oxides (MOx) and sulfides (MxSy). The reaction is mostly limited to the top layer of multilayer films, meaning bilayer/multilayer MoS2 could benefit from reactive metal contacts (similar to silicide contacts in silicon technology). XPS confirmed reaction byproducts including metallic Mo and sulfur-deficient MoS2-x for Ti.

4) Thin metals do NOT significantly strain MoS2, contradicting previous reports. Grazing incidence XRD (direct lattice measurement) showed <0.04 ± 0.02% average strain change, while Raman analysis overestimated strain by up to ~1.7% (for Ag-coated samples). The discrepancy arises because Raman peak shifts can be caused by factors other than strain, including disorder, decreased domain size, and plasmon coupling with MoS2 excitons. As-grown MoS2 has ~0.4-0.5% built-in biaxial tensile strain from CVD growth.

The study concludes with recommendations for improving contacts to 2D semiconductors: doping source/drain regions via charge transfer layers (like AlOx), using reacting metals on thicker (multilayer) 2D materials analogous to "raised source/drain" in Si devices, and tuning band alignment via Fermi level de-pinning, alloying, or strain. The ultimate goal is reducing contact resistance below 100 Ω·μm for 2D semiconductors.

■METHODS In this study, we have used an Agilent 5100 atomic force microscope (AFM) in N2 environment (<0.1% relative humidity) to study the metal−GeS junction using various conductive tips. The GeS sample was purchased from HQ graphene (Groningen, The Netherlands), and the clean surfaces were prepared by mechanical exfoliation using the scotch tape method prior to scanning. The GeS sample was subsequently mounted on a Mo sample holder. Hereafter, the transport properties of the nanoscale junction were investigated using the conductive mode of the AFM. In the conductive atomic force spectroscopy mode, the conductive AFM tip (grounded) is brought into contact with the semiconductor surface, and subsequently, the sample bias voltage, V, is ramped and the current, I, is recorded. The characteristic shape of the I(V) traces provides direct information on the current injection mechanism.
The experiments were done with three diﬀerent metallic AFM tips: a highly p-doped diamond tip (AD-E-2.8-SS; Adama Innovations Ltd.) with a work function of 5.1 ± 0.1 eV,37 a strongly n-type silicon tip (Hi’Res-C14/Cr-Au, MikroMasch) with a work function of 4.2 ± 0.1 eV,9,10,38 and a Pt tip (12Pt400B, Rocky Mountain Nanotechnology LLC) with a work function of 5.6 ± 0.1 eV.11,39 The tip work functions have been also conﬁrmed using the Kelvin probe force microscopy mode using a Au calibration sample. The nominal spring constants of the p-type diamond tip, n-type Si tip, and Pt tip are 0.5, 2, and 0.3 N/m, respectively. The radii of curvature of the p-type diamond tip, n-type Si tip, and Pt tip are 10 ± 5, 1.5 ± 0.5, and 15 ± 5 nm, respectively.
■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The AFM topography of a freshly exfoliated GeS sample is shown in Figure 1a. The exfoliated GeS surface contains a large number of step edges, tiny ﬂakes, and vacancies. The height of these ﬂakes and the depth of these vacancies correspond to a single GeS layer (see Figure 1b,c). The presence of these small ﬂakes and vacancies or depressions suggests that the intralayer interaction in GeS is not as strong as some other 2D materials, like graphene and molybdenum disulﬁde, where ﬂakes and vacancies are usually fully absent.
A metal nanocontact on GeS can be established by placing a metallic tip in direct contact with the GeS substrate. When the metal tip and GeS substrate are brought into contact, electrons will ﬂow from the material with the lowest work function to the material with the highest work function until the Fermi levels of both materials become equal. The alignment of the Fermi levels gives rise to a charge redistribution at the metal−semiconductor interface and the formation of the Schottky barrier, as shown in Figure 2a. The height of this Schottky barrier for ideal n-type contacts is given by the Schottky−Mott rule, ΦB = ϕtip −χ, where ϕtip is the work function of the metallic tip and χ is the electron aﬃnity of GeS. However, the presence of interface states (Figure 2a), which are induced by defects (defect-induced gap states) or metal−semiconductor orbital hybridization (metal-induced gap states), can lead to deviations from the Schottky−Mott rule. It is also very likely that there exists a very thin tunnel barrier between the metallic tip and the GeS layer (see Figure 2a). The p-type diamond, n-type Si and Pt tips have work functions that are close to the expected bulk values of 5.1 ± 0.1,37 4.2 ± 0.1,9,10,38 and 5.6 ± 0.1 eV,11,39 respectively. The bulk GeS electron aﬃnity is 3.8 eV.
Figure 2b shows three contact I(V) curves obtained, respectively, with p-type diamond, n-type Si, and Pt tips in contact with the GeS surface. Each of these I(V) curves are the result of averaging about 100 single-point curves obtained at various locations on the surface. Therefore, they represent the average behavior of the GeS surface. The curves have an asymmetric appearance. The current ﬂows nonlinearly in both voltage directions, where the current increases sharper for negative sample biases than for positive sample biases, suggesting that the negative bias is the forward-bias regime for all three junctions.

The Schottky barrier heights range from 0.36 to 0.41 eV and do not depend on the work function of the metallic AFM tip. As shown in Figure 4a, in which the Schottky barrier heights are plotted as a function of the work function of the metal tip, the experimental results strongly deviate from what is expected from the ideal Schottky−Mott rule (black dashed line). The discrepancy can be understood by the fact that the Schottky− Mott rule does not take into account the presence of interface states, which could pin the Fermi level. GeS is a two-dimensional van der Waals material and thus it is not expected to have any intrinsic surface states, i.e., dangling bonds. However, as can be seen in Figure 4b, small-scale AFM images of GeS are quite rough, with a mean-square roughness of about 0.5 nm. Moreover, current images such as the one in Figure 4c are electronically inhomogeneous, suggesting a high number of defects. In a similar way, defects were found to induce stronger FLP compared to pristine regions on TMDCs.9,11,54,57 Comparing with similar measurements on TMDCs, GeS appears to be way more defected, indicating a lower stability of the material to ambient conditions. Based on these observations, we arrive at the conclusion that the high number of defects on the exfoliated GeS is responsible for the strong Fermi-level pinning and the weak dependence of the Schottky barrier on the work function.
■CONCLUSIONS We have studied the electronic transport mechanisms in metal− GeS nanocontacts. Depending on the applied potential diﬀerence between the metallic AFM tip and GeS, various current injection mechanisms are active. At small forward biases, thermionic emission is active. Direct tunneling takes over at reverse small biases and at applied potential diﬀerences exceeding about 2 V Fowler−Nordheim tunneling becomes the dominant current injection mechanism. We have found that the Schottky barrier of GeS varies from 0.36 ± 0.03 to 0.41 ± 0.03 eV for the diﬀerent AFM tips. The Schottky barrier is almost independent of the work function of the metal, which is indicative of a strong Fermi-level pinning. This Fermi-level pinning is caused by charged defects and impurities in GeS, which result in the formation of interface states. The strong Fermi-level pinning on GeS nanocontacts suggests that alternative strategies58,59 must be used to obtain low-resistance ohmic contacts for eﬃcient charge injection in GeS-based devices.

This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of Physical Chemistry C (J. Phys. Chem. C 2022, 126, 11400-11406) by researchers from the Physics of Interfaces and Nanomaterials group at the University of Twente, The Netherlands (Yuxuan Sun, Zhen Jiao, Harold J. W. Zandvliet, and Pantelis Bampoulis). The study investigates charge carrier injection in metal-GeS (germanium sulfide) nanocontacts using conductive atomic force microscopy (c-AFM) to assess GeS's suitability for field-effect-based device applications.

**Key Findings:**
- GeS is a layered monochalcogenide semiconductor with a band gap of ~1.6 eV, orthorhombic crystal structure, lattice constants of 0.365, 0.435, and 1.044 nm, and a van der Waals gap of ~0.3-0.4 nm.
- Three dominant charge carrier injection mechanisms were identified: thermionic emission (dominant at small forward biases <1 V), Fowler-Nordheim tunneling (dominant at large biases >2 V), and direct tunneling (dominant at small reverse biases).
- The Schottky barrier heights measured were 0.36 ± 0.03 eV (p-type diamond tip, work function 5.1 eV), 0.40 ± 0.03 eV (n-type Si tip, work function 4.2 eV), and 0.41 ± 0.03 eV (Pt tip, work function 5.6 eV).
- The Schottky barrier is nearly independent of the metal tip's work function, indicating strong Fermi-level pinning with a pinning factor (S) of 0.01—substantially stronger than in transition-metal dichalcogenides.
- The charge neutrality level (CNL) was located at 4.16 eV.
- The strong Fermi-level pinning is attributed to charged defects and impurities in GeS, which form interface states. AFM imaging revealed GeS surfaces are rough (mean-square roughness ~0.5 nm) and electronically inhomogeneous, with a high number of defects—more defected than typical TMDCs, suggesting lower stability of GeS in ambient conditions.
- The study concludes that simple metal selection cannot achieve ohmic contacts on GeS, and alternative strategies (e.g., 2D buffer layers or graphene interlayers) are needed for low-resistance contacts in GeS-based devices.

**Methods:** An Agilent 5100 AFM was used in N2 environment (<0.1% relative humidity). GeS samples were purchased from HQ Graphene (Groningen, Netherlands) and exfoliated using the scotch tape method. Three conductive AFM tips with substantially different work functions (ranging 4.2-5.6 eV) were used. Contact areas were estimated using the Hertz model. The ideality factors ranged from 1 to about 5.
args.key_excerpts: "Using tips of different materials (platinum, n-type-doped silicon, and highly doped p-type diamond), we found that the Schottky barrier is almost independent of the work function of the metallic tip, which is indicative of a strong Fermi-level pinning. This strong Fermi-level pinning is caused by charged defects and impurities."

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613)Abstract

Understanding the electron transport through transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMDC)-based semiconductor/metal junctions is vital for the realization of future TMDC-based (opto-)electronic devices. Despite the bonding in TMDCs being largely constrained within the layers, strong Fermi-level pinning (FLP) was observed in TMDC-based devices, reducing the tunability of the Schottky barrier height. We present evidence that metal-induced gap states (MIGS) are the origin for the large FLP similar to conventional semiconductors. A variety of TMDCs (MoSe 2, WSe 2, WS 2, and MoTe 2) were investigated using high-spatial-resolution surface characterization techniques, permitting us to distinguish between defected and pristine regions. The Schottky barrier heights on the pristine regions can be explained by MIGS, inducing partial FLP. The FLP strength is further enhanced by disorder-induced gap states induced by transition-metal vacancies or substitutionals at the defected regions. Our findings emphasize the importance of defects on the electron transport properties in TMDC-based devices and confirm the origin of FLP in TMDC-based metal/semiconductor junctions.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613)Introduction

Transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) (MX 2, where M = Mo or W and X = S, Se, or Te) are two-dimensional materials with a wide range of electronic properties, for instance, insulating, semiconducting, and semi-metallic.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref1),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref2) These layered materials are constituted of hexagonal-packed transition-metal atoms sandwiched between two layers of chalcogens, with a strong intralayer covalent bond between the different atoms. These individual trilayers are held together by van der Waals bonds. The optical and electronic properties of TMDC materials depend on their composition, stacking order, and thickness.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref2)−[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref6) Especially, the semiconducting TMDCs are interesting for (opto-)electronics because of their relatively high carrier mobility and their tunable band gap[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref7)−[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref9)

The metal–semiconductor junction (MSJ) is a critical component in electronic and optoelectronic devices. One of the most important parameters in the MSJs is the Schottky barrier height (SBH, ϕ B), the height of the potential barrier formed at the metal–semiconductor interface, which has a significant impact on the device performance. Tuning the SBH is necessary in order to reduce the contact resistance, modulating the charge carrier type in transistors, and to enhance the selectivity of carrier extraction for photovoltaic cells.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref10)−[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref14)

Because of the van der Waals interlayer bonding, it was expected that the contact metal is also weakly bonded to the TMDC layer, so that the SBH would approach the Schottky–Mott limit of weak pinning and could easily be tuned.[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref15),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref16) However, experiments and simulations showed the opposite behavior, the SBH depends only weakly on the contact metal.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref10),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref17)−[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20) This was attributed to Fermi-level pinning (FLP).[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref17),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref19)−[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref21) The origin of the FLP has been debated for a long time. There are two well-known models describing FLP; metal-induced gap states (MIGS)[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref22) and extrinsic disorder-induced gap states (DIGS).[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref23) For DIGS, the FLP originates from the electronic structure of the host semiconductor within the MSJ. On the other hand, the MIGS model predicts that the metal will dominate over the substrate in pinning the Fermi level. To reveal the MIGS effect experimentally within TMDCs, a reduction of the extrinsic factors, such as defects and stacking faults, is a prerequisite.

Several works have been conducted to find the origin of FLP and subsequently control its strength.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref10),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref17),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref19)−[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref21),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref24)−[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref26) Theoretical studies predicted that the FLP effect in the MSJ is mainly induced by two interface effects: first, due to modification of the metal’s work function by dipole formation at the interface and second, by the introduction of gap states due to the reduction of the chalcogen/transition-metal bonding strength.[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref21) Later, Guo et al. performed simulations for several TMDCs, showing that the TMDC/metal junctions largely follow the MIGS model, similar to three-dimensional semiconductors despite their different structure and bonding.[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref17) However, it is difficult to experimentally access the pinning mechanism because of the high density of surface defects, which alter the properties of these materials.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref24),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref27)−[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref29) To experimentally confirm the pinning mechanism of the TMDC-based MSJ, a defect-free MSJ has to be constructed.

Recently, nanoscopic MSJs have been obtained using conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM). In C-AFM, the tip can act as a nanoscopic metal electrode.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref6),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20),[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref30)−[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref33)_I_(_V_) characteristics recorded with a C-AFM of the Pt-coated tip/MoS 2 junction revealed variations in the SBH.[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref31),[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref32) This method was also used to investigate the effect of local defects,[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20) stacking faults,[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref6) plasma functionalization,[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref34) and charge variations due to doping[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref33),[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref35) on the charge transport across the MSJ. Because of the nanoscopic size of the contact metal, small variations at the surface can be measured. Substitution or removal of the transition metal or the chalcogen atoms lead to defect sites with different electronic properties compared to the pristine regions[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref28),[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref36)−[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref38) including small SBH and strong FLP.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref6),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20) On MoS 2, defects located at the Mo layer enhance further the FLP strength compared to pristine surface or regions with S-vacancies.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20)

In this work, we use the C-AFM to construct nanoscopic MSJs on several TMDCs, in order to investigate the exact mechanism behind FLP on TMDCs. We performed high-spatial-resolution C-AFM and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) imaging in order to characterize defects present on several TMDC surfaces (MoSe 2, WSe 2, WS 2, and MoTe 2). For the studied TMDCs, we find defects with similar appearance and influence; STM reveals that chalcogen defects have almost no influence on their surroundings, whereas transition-metal defects lead to a strong localized contrast that depends on the used set point. The barrier heights of the pristine surface can be explained by the MIGS mechanism, which normally applies to three-dimensional semiconductors. Spatially resolved Schottky barrier maps reveal a decrease of the SBH and a stronger FLP at defect sites because of DIGS. The DIGS decrease the pinning factor by approximately 30–40%. Our results provide new insights into the physics governing the contact properties and charge transport through the TMDC-based MSJ.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613)Results and Discussion

### Defects in TMDCs

[Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)a shows topographic AFM and lateral force images (see the inset of [Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)a) of a freshly cleaved MoSe 2 surface. The surface appears smooth and defect-free in both images. However, within the simultaneously recorded C-AFM image, the surface is inhomogeneous when a negative voltage is applied to the sample. Multiple dark circular features (with radii ranging between 3 and 4 nm) appear (see [Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)b). The current recorded at these features is higher than that for the pristine surface. The density of the features varies between 10 10 and 10 11 cm–2 dependent on the sample and location. Imaging a region without round depressions requires a high magnification of a small area. [Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)c shows an example of a high-resolution STM image where the atomic structure of WSe 2 is observed, revealing the expected hexagonal pattern with a unit cell of (0.33 ± 0.02) nm. The structure is consistent with the semiconducting 2H phase. In addition to the observed hexagonal pattern, several missing atoms are observed. At these positions, Se atoms are missing, inducing Se vacancies. The electronic influence on the surrounding of the Se vacancies is small (<1 nm in radius), excluding them from being the origin of the dark round features in the C-AFM image (see [Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)b). Besides, the density of the Se vacancies (10 12 to 10 13 cm–2) is 2 orders of magnitude higher compared to that of the dark circular features (10 10 to 10 11 cm–2) observed in the C-AFM.

Large-scale STM images reveal the presence of dark depressions similar to the ones observed in the C-AFM ([Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)d). High-resolution STM images show a depression without disrupting the atomic lattice, confirming that the effect is purely electronic (see the [Supporting Information](http://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/acs.jpcc.8b10971/suppl_file/jp8b10971_si_001.pdf)). The average defect density of 10 10 to 10 11 per cm–2 is comparable to the density found in the C-AFM images. The appearance and density of the defects are very similar to the defects observed on MoS 2.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref24) In these studies, the origin of the dark round features was attributed to metal-like defects or impurities located underneath the outermost S layer. Mo-vacancies and antisite (Mo-substitutional) defects occur on the subsurface without a structural modification of the top S layer. These defects ionize the sulfur atoms. Coulomb repulsion around these sulfur atoms leads to electron depletion and causes the appearance of the dark disk observed in both C-AFM and STM.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20),[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref39) We note here that the observed defects are intrinsic in nature, as the samples have not gone through any treatment (except exfoliation) prior to scanning. In addition, similar features with similar densities were found in other types of TMDCs, such as WS 2[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref6),[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref40) and WSe 2,[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref29),[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref41),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref42) attributed to impurity atoms (such as Re, Na, and Li) present in the crystal.[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref29),[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref43) Therefore, we suggest that the dark circular features originate from metal-like defects (Mo/W vacancies or substitutionals), which change the electronic landscape of their surroundings. Next to the dark circular defects, bright defects are observed in the STM image ([Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)d). These defects are attributed to trapped electron states around a donor on the surface chalcogen atom layer.[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref28),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref44) However, these defects are not observed in the C-AFM images.

A closer look at the metal-like defects reveals that they fall into two categories: defects with current amplitudes of approximately −150 and −50 pA (at a bias voltage of 1.2 V), as shown in [Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)e. These differences are caused by the position of the metal-like defect. When located in the top MoSe 2 trilayer, the electronic influence is larger compared to defects located in the second MoSe 2 trilayer, as observed previously for MoS 2 and conventional semiconductors.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20),[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref45),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref46) These results suggest that the conductance of MoSe 2 can be influenced by metal-like defects in the first and second trilayers.

Similar defects are found in the C-AFM images on WS 2, WSe 2, and MoTe 2 (see the [Supporting Information](http://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/acs.jpcc.8b10971/suppl_file/jp8b10971_si_001.pdf)). These defects have similar appearances as the metal-like defects on MoS 2[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20) and MoSe 2 (see [Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)b). Earlier studies emphasized the similarities between the defect types in the different TMDCs.[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref47)−[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref49) The energies needed to create defects within the different types of semiconducting TMDCs are comparable[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref38),[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref50),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref51) as well as the structural conformations.[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref52) Therefore, we conclude that the defects observed with C-AFM on the studied TMDCs are all metal-like defects.

### SBHs on Pristine and Defected Regions

Because it is now possible to distinguish between defected and pristine regions (note here that the pristine regions still contains chalcogen defects), the local electron transport through nanoscopic MSJ between a Pt tip (ϕ M = 5.64 eV) and the semiconducting TMDC can be investigated. For zero charge transfer in the MSJ (Schottky limit), the electron SBH is given by the difference between the work function of the metal (ϕ M) and the electron affinity of the semiconductor (χ S)1

A characteristic _I_(_V_) curve for the MoSe 2-based MSJ is shown in [Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)a. The measured _I_(_V_) curve on the pristine region shows a diode-like behavior, as expected for a MSJ.[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref53) The negative sample bias is defined as the forward bias regime. For larger negative voltages, the SBH lowers and the current increases exponentially with the voltage. The current in the MSJ under forward bias is described by the thermionic emission model and is given by[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref54)2where _V_ is the applied bias, _k_ B is the Boltzmann constant, _T_ is the temperature, η is the ideality factor, this is the deviation of the current transport from ideal thermal emission, and _q_ is the electron charge. The defected region shows a slightly higher current at the reverse bias (see [Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)a). This is a result of a change in the SBH and ideality factor. The SBH for the defected region is (0.24 ± 0.04) eV with an ideality factor of 1.5. As the SBH is lower, more current can pass through the junction.

The advantage of using a sharp AFM tip as the metal electrode in the MSJ is the ability to record individual _I_(_V_) curves at every point of the surface. [Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)b shows a spatially resolved current map extracted from a 128 × 128 grid of individual _I_(_V_) curves at a bias voltage of −0.15 V. A clear difference is found between the defects and pristine region, as already observed in the C-AFM image (see [Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)b[a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fn1)). We can now extract the SBH for each of the individual curves and construct a SBH map ([Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)c). Significant inhomogeneities in the barrier height are observed. Interestingly, the SBH remains constant on the pristine regions of the MoSe 2 surface, whereas directly above the defects, a decrease of the barrier height is measured.

The histogram in [Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)d is constructed of the current values within a specific part of the SBH map (marked with the dashed box in [Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)c). It reveals three peaks: corresponding to the pristine region [at (0.37 ± 0.03) eV], the defected region [(0.24 ± 0.04) eV], and a third peak at (0.30 ± 0.02) eV. A closer look at the current and SBH maps confirms the presence of defects located in the second trilayer, in line with the C-AFM images of [Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig1)b. Recent calculations showed that the influence of defects on the SBH decreases as the dopant-interface distance increases.[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref57) Therefore, defects in the second trilayer have a weaker influence on the SBH compared to defects in the first trilayer.

We have also observed defect-induced reduction of the SBH for WS 2, WSe 2, MoTe 2 (see the [Supporting Information](http://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/acs.jpcc.8b10971/suppl_file/jp8b10971_si_001.pdf)), and MoS 2.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref20) However, the absolute values of the SBH on the pristine and defected regions differ between the different TMDCs (using the same tip). This is a result of the different electron affinities and electronegativities of the various TMDC semiconductors. According to the Schottky–Mott rule (see [eq [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#eq1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#eq1)), the SBH decreases linearly with increasing electron affinity. Although a decreasing trend is found, it is not linear and the experimentally found SBH values do not match with the prediction of the Schottky–Mott rule.

### Metal-Induced Gap States

The discrepancy between the predicted and measured SBHs has also been found in other studies for conventional as well as layered semiconductors.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref6),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref19),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref24),[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref58)−[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref60) The Schottky–Mott rule assumes that there is no charge transfer between the metal and the interface states of the semiconductor. However, other studies suggested that charge transfer should also be included for the metal/two-dimensional (2D) material MSJ.[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref21),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref60) Generally, FLP is characterized using two different methods: (1) the Schottky–Mott approach and (2) the electronegativity concept. In the case of the Schottky–Mott approach, the SBH is given by6where _S_ is the Schottky pinning parameter (_S_ = dϕ B/dϕ M), χ is the electron affinity of the semiconductor, and ϕ CNL is the charge neutrality level with respect to the vacuum level which is given by7where _b_ is the _y_-intercept of the ϕ B versus ϕ M graph. _S_ is dependent on the density of interface states per unit area _N_ and their extend into the semiconductor δ as8with ε 0 ε r being the absolute permittivity of the interface. When _S_ = 1, the Schottky–Mott limit is recovered (no pinning, _N_ ≈ 0, no gap states) and the SBH is given by [eq [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#eq1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#eq1), whereas for _S_ = 0, the SBH is described by the Bardeen limit of strong pinning. In the Bardeen limit, the metal Fermi level is pinned by the interface states at ϕ CNL.

In the electronegativity concept, the SBH is determined using9with _S_′ the experimentally obtained pinning factor (_S_′ = dϕ B/d _X_[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref61),[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref62)), _X_ M the electronegativity of the metal, _X_ TMDC the electronegativity of the TMDC, and ϕ CNL′ the charge neutrality level with respect to the vacuum level. The difference between the concepts is the use of a surface property (work function and electron affinity) for the Schottky–Mott concept and a bulk property (electronegativity) for the electronegativity concept.

In order to determine the pinning factors and charge neutrality levels of the different TMDCs, the dependence of the ϕ B on the tip work function and electronegativity should be systematically studied. Therefore, we have performed the same measurements with two additional AFM tips: a PtSi tip (ϕ M ≈ 4.9 eV, _X_ M ≈ 2.08, contact area 5.7 nm 2) and a highly n-doped Si tip (ϕ M ≈ 4.15 eV, _X_ M ≈ 1.9, contact area 1.5 nm 2). For both tips, similar maps are obtained as for the Pt tip. [Figure [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig3)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig3)a shows the extracted SBH map for a PtSi tip on MoSe 2. A decrease of approximately 33% in the SBH is observed compared to the results obtained with the Pt tip on MoSe 2 for both the defects [(0.14 ± 0.03) eV] and the pristine region [(0.24 ± 0.02) eV]. This is attributed to the lower work function and electronegativity of the PtSi tip. In addition, defects in the second trilayer are no longer observed. The absolute value of the SBH decreases (as well as the absolute difference) making it no longer possible to resolve the presence of defects in the second trilayer.
