Measurements performed with a Pt tip on MoTe 2 ([Figure [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig3)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig3)b) reveal a lower SBH as compared to the same measurements on MoSe 2 ([Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig2)c). The distinct difference between the SBHs is in line with the different electron affinities and electronegativities of MoSe 2 and MoTe 2, where χ MoSe 2> χ MoTe 2[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref63),[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref64) and _X_ MoSe 2>_X_ MoTe 2. According to the Schottky–Mott rule ([eq [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#eq1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#eq1)), the MoTe 2 should have a lower SBH. However, the absolute change in the SBHs cannot be explained using the Schottky–Mott rule, as charge transfer is not included in the model.

To explain the discrepancy between the obtained SBH values and the Schottky–Mott rule, the pinning factors and charge neutrality levels of the studied TMDCs have to be obtained. [Figure [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig3)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#fig3)c plots the experimentally obtained SBHs for the pristine region of the studied TMDCs versus the metal work function of the used tips. The SBHs for all of the TMDCs depend linearly on the work function of the metal, despite the different interactions between the TMDCs and the various tips.[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref59) In all four cases (see [Table [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#tbl1)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#tbl1)), a strong FLP is observed, implying a strong interaction between the metal contact and the TMDC.[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref17),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref21),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref60) The observed pinning factor of the pristine surface of WSe 2 (_S_ = 0.28) and MoTe 2 (_S_ = 0.11) is in good agreement with the theoretically predicted pinning factors.[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410613#ref17)

args.summary:
This is a scientific research article published in the Journal of Physical Chemistry C (2019 Feb 14; 123(9): 5411, DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.8b10971) titled "Universal Fermi-Level Pinning in Transition-Metal Dichalcogenides." The authors are Kai Sotthewes, Rik van Bremen, Edwin Dollekamp, Tim Boulogne, Krystian Nowakowski, Daan Kas, Harold J. W. Zandvliet, and Pantelis Bampoulis from the University of Twente (MESA+ Institute for Nanotechnology) and RWTH-Aachen University.

The paper investigates the origin of Fermi-level pinning (FLP) in transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMDC)-based metal/semiconductor junctions. The researchers studied four TMDCs (MoSe2, WSe2, WS2, and MoTe2) using high-spatial-resolution conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM) and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to distinguish between defected and pristine regions.

Key findings include:
1. Metal-induced gap states (MIGS) are identified as the origin of the strong Fermi-level pinning, similar to conventional 3D semiconductors.
2. Two types of defects were observed: chalcogen vacancies (which have minimal electronic influence) and metal-like defects (transition-metal vacancies/substitutionals) that create dark circular features with radii of 3-4 nm and densities of 10^10 to 10^11 cm^-2.
3. The Schottky barrier heights (SBH) on pristine regions are explained by MIGS, inducing partial FLP. For MoSe2, the pristine SBH was approximately 0.37 eV with an ideality factor of 1.1.
4. Defect regions show reduced SBH and stronger FLP due to disorder-induced gap states (DIGS), which decrease the pinning factor by approximately 30-40%.
5. Pinning factors (S) for pristine regions range from 0.11 (MoTe2) to 0.30 (MoS2), and for defected regions from 0.04 (MoTe2) to 0.11 (MoS2).
6. The study used three different AFM tips (Pt with φM = 5.64 eV, PtSi with φM ≈ 4.9 eV, and n-doped Si with φM ≈ 4.15 eV) to systematically determine pinning factors and charge neutrality levels.
7. Charge neutrality levels were found to be located near the conduction band for all TMDCs, consistent with n-type Schottky barriers.
8. The results confirm that TMDC-based MSJs follow the MIGS model, and the findings emphasize the importance of defects on electron transport properties in TMDC-based devices.
args.key_excerpts: "We present evidence that metal-induced gap states (MIGS) are the origin for the large FLP similar to conventional semiconductors."

Mul-tiple n-type transistors with high electron motilities and on/off ratios, such as MoS2, MoSe2, and ReS2,[7] have been demon-strated; however, their p-type counterparts have been scarce despite years of effort. The fundamental issue in controlling device polarity is the presence of strong Fermi-level pinning at the metal–2D semiconductor interfaces.[8] This pinning can largely be attributed to the difficulty in creating an atomically clean metal–2D semiconductor interface; conventional metallization process causes chemical and/or physical damage to the 2D semiconductors and cre-ates associated defect-induced gap states that eventually pin the Fermi level at the charge neutrality level.[8,9] Such a pinning can also occur due to defects, such as vacancies[10,11] and strain.[12] Therefore, the Schottky barrier is fixed once pinning, setting the transistors into a particular polarity (i.e., mostly n-type).

However, the polarity control of 2D transistors remains a challenge because of the lack of a high-work-function electrode that completely eliminates Fermi-level pinning at metal–semiconductor interfaces. Here, a creation of clean van der Waals contacts is demonstrated, wherein a metallic 2D material, chlorine-doped SnSe2 (Cl–SnSe2), is used as the high-work-function contact, pro-viding an interface that is free of defects and Fermi-level pinning. Such clean contacts made from Cl–SnSe2 can pose nearly ideal Schottky barrier heights, following the Schottky–Mott limit and thus permitting polarity-controllable transistors. With the integration of Cl–SnSe2 as contacts, WSe2 transistors exhibit pronounced p-type characteristics, which are distinctly different from those of the devices with evaporated metal contacts, where n-type transport is observed. Finally, this ability to control the polarity enables the fabrication of functional logic gates and circuits, including inverter, NAND, and NOR.

However, an aggressive plasma etching process is required to create strong coupling between the edges of 2D materials and metals, which neces-sitates careful investigation into side effects, such as chemical impurities and contamination. Alternatively, the creation of van der Waals (vdW) contact via metal transfer has been explored, allowing for a highly tunable Schottky barrier depending on the work function of the metal used.[8,14] However, the approach suffers from poor atmospheric contamination, and requires an inert-gas processing environment, which hence increases the fabrication complexity. On the other hand, recently, the use of vdW 2D metals as contacts has been shown to provide atomi-cally clean interfaces at metal–semiconductor junctions;[15–18] these clean interfaces from vdW 2D metals could potentially prevent Fermi-level pinning, thus promising excellent control over the Schottky barrier and the resulting device polarity. Several attempts have been made to use 2D metals as vdW con-tacts on various 2D semiconductors, such as highly p-doped WSe2,[15] NbSe2,[16] 1T-TaS2,[17] and degenerately doped semi-conducting SnSe2.[18] Although all of these studies have shown improvement in contact properties (e.g., contact resistance, FET mobility) through the use of 2D metals, the underlying mecha-nism remains elusive; these improvements could have resulted from Fermi-level depinning, doping effects, or interactions within the contact interface, yet such aspects have not been investigated, which limits further development. Furthermore, to obtain the p-type transistors, a high-work-function vdW 2D metal that can completely eliminate the Fermi-level pinning is strongly desired. However, the lack of suitable 2D metal makes high-quality p-type vdW contacts extremely challenging, further hindering the construction of complementary circuits; func-tional applications that rely on control over the device polarity, such as CMOS logic gates, are yet to be achieved using vdW 2D metal contacts.
Here, we report the creation of clean van der Waals contacts that use 2D metal Cl–SnSe2 as the high-work-function elec-trode and exhibit the Fermi-level depinning at the metal–semi-conductor interface. Such clean contacts made from Cl–SnSe2 lead to near-ideal Schottky barrier heights (SBHs), following the Schottky–Mott limit and thus allowing tunability over the carrier polarity, which has not been achieved in other reported vdW 2D metal contacts for 2D transistors. We also demonstrate a complementary logic inverter with the ability to control the polarity of WSe2 transistors, achieving a high voltage gain of 40 (at a bias voltage of 5 V). This allows us to design and fabricate more complex logic functions, such as NAND and NOR gates.

Theo-retical studies have suggested that the use of vdW 2D metals is an ultra-clean and damage-free approach to solving this pinning issue.[21,22] However, the lack of a high-work-function vdW 2D metal has limited the hole injection in 2D semicon-ductors, which presents a challenge for the development of p-type transistors. Inspired by this, we explore Cl–SnSe2 as a promising 2D metal for hole injection into 2D semiconductor-based transistors. Recently, we synthesized metallic SnSe2 via substitutional doping of Cl atoms;[23,24] in contrast to pristine SnSe2, Cl–SnSe2 exhibits metallic behavior with high conduc-tivity comparable to that of few-layer graphene.[25] Furthermore, owing to its high work function (≈4.7 eV) and pinning-free sur-face, Cl–SnSe2 is expected to provide efficient hole injection and thus p-type transport, as shown in the right panel of Figure 1a.
Single crystals of Cl-doped SnSe2 were synthesized via melt-solidification process (see Methods). Figure 1b illustrates the atomic lattice structure of Cl–SnSe2, where Cl atoms replace Se atoms in the parent SnSe2. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Figure S1a, Supporting Information) for Cl–SnSe2 and pristine SnSe2 are nearly identical, indicating that the structural integ-rity of SnSe2 is maintained. Such a high crystallinity was also confirmed from Raman spectra (Figure S1b, Supporting Infor-mation), where no noticeable change in peak-to-peak distance or full width at half-maximum (FWHM) of the Eg peak was observed in Cl–SnSe2. Moreover, a slight redshift (≈1.0 cm−1) of A1g peak, which is an indication of a n-type doping in other sub-stitutionally doped materials,[26,27] was observed in Cl–SnSe2.
Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) measure-ments were performed to elucidate the band structure of the Cl–SnSe2 (Figure 1c). The energetic difference between the valence band maximum and Fermi level is ≈1.30 eV. The right inset in Figure 1c shows clear and sharp peak around the Fermi level, which corresponds to a partly filled conduction band originating from hybridized orbitals of Sn and Se atoms.[23] These hybridized states around the Fermi level would lead to degenerate semiconductor and therefore a metal-like behavior, in contrast to intrinsically semiconducting SnSe2. In addition, the carrier density of Cl–SnSe2, estimated from the Hall effect measurement, is ≈1014 cm−2 (Figure S2, Supporting Informa-tion), which is more than two orders of magnitude higher than those obtained for undoped 2D semiconductors (on the order of 1012 cm−2 or even less). More importantly, the estimated work function of Cl–SnSe2 is 4.71 eV (left panel of Figure 1c), which is close to the valence band of multilayer WSe2 (5.11 eV; Figure S3, Supporting Information), indicating that p-type behavior could be obtained for FET devices constructed using Cl–SnSe2, as will be shown in the following sections.
Metallic Cl–SnSe2 must also exhibit ohmic contact with low resistance between Cl–SnSe2 and 3D metal to ensure optimized charge injection within the 3D metal/2D metal contact system. The FET performance of 12.5-nm-thick Cl–SnSe2 was investi-gated using a transfer line method (TLM) device with varying channel lengths (Figure 1d). The device structure consisted of a Ti/Au local bottom gate, a 16-nm h-BN gate dielectric, and Pd as source/drain metal electrodes. The transfer characteristic of a device with a channel length of 1 µm (Figure 1e) exhibited negligible current modulation by the gate voltage, and metallic behavior with excellent conductivity that resulted from degen-erate states, consistent with our UPS results. Figure 1f presents the total resistance normalized by channel width (RT) as a func-tion of channel length (L) for the same device. Through TLM analysis, the contact resistance (Rc) and the sheet resistance of the channel (Rsh) were obtained from the y–axis intercept and slope, respectively, of the linear fit to the data (Figure 1f). The Pd/Cl–SnSe2 junction exhibits a low contact resistance of ≈0.083 ± 0.059 kΩ µm at VGS = 0 V, which guarantees highly efficient carrier injection at the 3D metal/2D metal junction. The four-probe measurements also give Rc = 0.35 ± 0.18 kΩ µm at VGS = 0 V, thus corroborating the contact resistance estimated from TLM analysis (Figure S4, Supporting Informa-tion). Notably, this contact resistance value is comparable to or lower than values obtained using a phase-engineered (0.2–0.3 kΩ µm),[28] 3D metal/graphene (2–102 kΩ µm),[29,30] and 3D metal/2D 1T′-WTe2 contacts (0.4–1.03 kΩ µm),[31,32] which shows the great potential of our Cl–SnSe2 as a vdW 2D metal contact. The inset in Figure 1f shows the linear output char-acteristics of corresponding devices, suggesting well-defined ohmic contacts (i.e., low-resistance contacts) between Cl–SnSe2 and Pd. The metallicity of Cl–SnSe2 is further supported by the sheet resistance–temperature (Rsh–T) plot (Figure 1g), where the obtained sheet resistance of Cl–SnSe2 is almost independent of temperature. Together, the data in Figure 1 demonstrate that we have produced a high-work-function, degenerately doped semi-conductor Cl–SnSe2, which can serve as a 2D metal electrode for pinning-free high-performance 2D devices. Below, by fabricating WSe2 devices as the main example, we reveal unique potential and excellent pinning-free nature of this 2D metal.
Figure S5, Supporting Information shows the fabrication steps for WSe2 FETs with Cl–SnSe2 contacts: (a) multilayer WSe2 onto an h-BN-capped local bottom Au gate, (b) align-ment and transfer of Cl–SnSe2, (c) removal of polycarbonate film from Cl–SnSe2/WSe2, and deposition of Pd metal pads for electrical characterization (see Methods). Such an integra-tion of a 2D metal electrode can create atomically clean inter-faces at metal–semiconductor junctions because this process prevents damage caused by direct metallization, as illustrated in Figure S5d, Supporting Information. Moreover, Cl–SnSe2 acts as a physical buffer layer protecting the underlying WSe2 from possible contaminations (e.g., chemicals, polymers, and mechanical strain) that can occur in subsequent fabrication. By contrast, the conventional processes for metal integration typically result in substantial damage to the underlying 2D semiconductors and introduce interface disorders such as defect, metal diffusion, and chemical bonds (Figure S5f, Supporting Information).[8,9,33] We explored this picture experimentally by first comparing the physical properties of differently constructed contact inter-faces. Cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of Pd/WSe2 (upper panel of Figure 2a) show apparent damage to the topmost WSe2 layers, which we believe is the main reason for Fermi-level pinning, as reported in previous studies.[8,33] By contrast, the Cl–SnSe2/WSe2 interface remained intact and free of defects, featuring an atomically clean interface (Figure S6, Supporting Information for lower-magnification Adv. The image further shows that the spacing between two dissimilar materials is nearly indistin-guishable from that in the natural van der Waals structure of WSe2, suggesting that the Cl–SnSe2/WSe2 interface becomes a true van der Waals contact. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was also conducted to investigate the chemical states of the Cl–SnSe2/WSe2 interface. The spectra obtained from Cl–SnSe2/WSe2 (Figure 2b) show features almost identical to those of pristine WSe2, suggesting that Cl–SnSe2 in contact with WSe2 does not introduce any chemical reactions, defects, or strains at the interface or within the WSe2. The Raman spec-trum of the WSe2/Cl–SnSe2 heterojunction (Figure 2c) shows no peaks associated with nonstoichiometric WxSey, further confirming a clean interface and agreeing well with our TEM and XPS results. Such a clean interface of 2D metal/2D semi-conductor contacts could offer a nearly ideal Schottky barrier height dictated by the metal work function, which is crucial for the rational design and fabrication of 2D transistors.[34] To this end, the effect of Cl–SnSe2 contacts on the electrical properties of WSe2 transistors was investigated using charge-transport measurements. Figure 2d shows a schematic (upper) and optical (lower) image of the fabricated device; two different contacts of both evaporated Pd (denoted by a black box) and Cl–SnSe2 (red box) are formed on the same WSe2 flake for a reliable comparison. For the Cl–SnSe2 contact, the device exhib-ited predominantly p-type characteristic (Figure 2e; Figure S7a, Supporting Information for log-scale plot of the same data, Supporting Information) with nonlinear IDS–VDS output curve (Figure S7b, Supporting Information), as expected from the energy band offset between the Fermi level of Cl–SnSe2 and the valence-band energy level of multilayer WSe2 (Figure S8, Supporting Information). By contrast, for the evaporated Pd contacts, with a higher work function (5.2 eV) than that of Cl–SnSe2, the device consistently exhibited n-type behavior (Figure 2f; Figure S7a, Supporting Information for log-scale plot of the same data) with a linear IDS–VDS relationship (Figure S7c, Supporting Information). This is similar to that in previously reported multilayered WSe2 transistors, where direct metalliza-tion was employed to form the contacts.[14,20] This observation indicates that the Fermi level is pinned closer to the conduction band edge of WSe2, and thus a low electron barrier is formed at the interface between Pd and WSe2. Besides, devices fabricated with Au metal also exhibited a similarly controllable polarity (Figure S9, Supporting Information). For a clear estimation, we also tested 20 devices to obtain the statistical variation in car-rier polarity (Figure 2g). Here, the carrier polarity was charac-terized by the current ratio of I3V (IDS at VGS = 3 V) to I−3V (IDS at VGS = −3 V), which represents the majority carrier type. There is a clear and distinguishable trend showing that only the Cl–SnSe2-contacted devices exhibited predominantly p-type characteristics, with I3V/I−3V ratios exceeding values of 10−2. The observed distinction could be explained by the presence (or absence) of a pinning effect, which mainly originates from the interface morphology of contacts, as discussed later in the text.

The device retained its original polarity (p-type) under ambient conditions for a 3-month period, except for a slight threshold voltage shift that may be caused by ambient water and/or oxygen, which clearly suggests the stability of our Cl–SnSe2 contacts.
To gain insight into the distinctly opposite polarities that result from different contact types, we investigated a range of different metals (Ti, Au, Pd, and Cl–SnSe2) with varying work functions within the framework of the Schottky–Mott model, which allows us to distinguish between the effect of Fermi-level pinning and the doping effect as a mechanism. Figure 3a–d shows the IDS–VGS transfer curves of multilayer WSe2 FETs with contacts composed of a series of metals. As shown in Figure 3a–c, all devices with evaporated metals exhibited similar n-type characteristics, regardless of the metal work function, indicating that the effect is not specific to a particular metal. By contrast, for the device with Cl–SnSe2 contact (Figure 3d), the majority charge carrier switched, and well-behaved p-type characteristic was observed with clear metal–insulator transi-tion behavior,[36] suggesting an optimized vdW metal contact.

Furthermore, the S parameter was determined to be 0.03, indicating that the Fermi level is strongly pinned at the metal–semiconductor inter-face.[38] By contrast, for the device with Cl–SnSe2, the Schottky barrier type is tuned from electrons to holes, and the Schottky barrier for hole injection was measured to be ≈350 ± 26 meV, in good agreement with the value expected for the WSe2/Cl–SnSe2 junction (Figure S8, Supporting Information). This result indi-cates that Cl–SnSe2 forms a nearly ideal interface with WSe2 without pinning and thus largely follows the Schottky–Mott rule (S = 1); this S value is comparable to the values obtained using the transferred metal,[8] 1T-WTe2,[32] and degenerately n-doped SnSe2.[18] Such a near-ideal interface was further verified by the enhanced subthreshold swing (SS) value and minimal hyster-esis, which are strongly related to the interfacial contamination (Figure S14, Supporting Information).[33,39,40] The schematics of the band diagrams are shown in Figure S15, Supporting Infor-mation, depicting the cases of evaporated metal and Cl–SnSe2 contacts, respectively.
The observed opposite behaviors between the different types of contacts could be explained by the presence (or absence) of the Fermi-level pinning effect, which originates mainly from interface disorders due to aggressive fabrication processes or chemical reaction at the metal–2D semiconductor inter-face.[8,9,33] Previously, scanning transmission electron micro­ scopy experiments[8,9,33] demonstrated that direct metalliza-tion can induce damages that significantly modify the original levels, leading to Fermi-level pinning and thus large deviations from the Schottky–Mott limit. This principle is consistent with the observations on our devices, which predominantly show a particular polarity (i.e., the n-type) irrespective of the work functions of the evaporated metals. By contrast, 2D metal Cl–SnSe2 does not interact with adjacent WSe2, thus forming a vdW interface, which is thought to be a near-ideal interface, and preventing the creation of defects that otherwise lead to Fermi-level pinning. Consequently, the SBH can possess an intrinsic value, thereby contributing to p-type characteristics in the WSe2 devices.
In addition to WSe2, we also confirmed the formation of a clean contact interface on MoS2. Using the same methodology, multilayer MoS2 devices were fabricated with different metal contacts, after which variable-temperature I–V measurements were performed. For MoS2 devices using evaporated metals, we consistently observed n-type behaviors, with electron barriers of 90–141 meV and a slope S = 0.05, suggesting strong Fermi-level pinning (Figure 3g; Figure S16a–c, Supporting Informa-tion). By contrast, for the device with the Cl–SnSe2 contact, we observed ambipolar characteristics, with the electron current being higher than the hole current (Figure S17, Supporting Information). Our measurement further revealed that the SBH for electrons was ≈420 ± 37 meV and the SBH for hole injection was ≈780 ± 26 meV (Figure S16d,e, Supporting Information), consistent with the Schottky−Mott theory and our FET char-acteristics. These results also confirm the high quality of the Cl–SnSe2 vdW contacts.
The ability to precisely control the carrier type of an indi-vidual device enables the implementation of CMOS logic gate circuits on a single material; this strategy can generate homogeneous CMOS structures within a single compatible process, in contrast to heterogeneous types prepared from two different channel materials (n- and p-type),[41,42] which necessi-tates distinct synthesis and processing. Given the two discrete polarities (p- and n-type) with high on/off ratios, multilayer WSe2 transistors were selected as the building blocks. First, we fabricated a complementary inverter, the simplest logic gate, as shown in Figure 4a. The inverter consisted of two WSe2 FETs placed in series, where one was created using evaporated Pd contacts (n-FET) and the other was fabricated with Cl−SnSe2 contacts (p-FET). Plots of IDS versus VGS for both FETs are shown in Figure 4b, featuring highly symmetric characteris-tics centered around VGS = 0 V. Figure 4c shows the voltage transfer characteristics of the inverter under different voltage bias (VDD). The voltage swing of the inverter features clear logic outputs with a sharp voltage transition, achieving a high gain of ≈40 at VDD = 5 V. Such a high voltage gain is crucial for robust logic operation in integrated circuits.[34] The static peak energy consumption of the corresponding device is also presented in Figure S18, Supporting Information. The perfor-mance of the inverter is sufficient for the construction of more complex circuits. To this end, we also constructed NAND and NOR logic gates by integrating four WSe2 transistors, as shown in the circuit diagram in Figure 4d. Successful operation of both NOR and NAND was observed from logically valid outputs (Figure 4e,f). Thus, these results prove the practicality of vdW 2D contacts for multifunctional integrated circuitry.
3. Conclusion In conclusion, we have demonstrated the creation of clean and p-type vdW contacts, where high-work-function 2D metal Cl–SnSe2 is in contact with 2D semiconductors, to enable con-trol over the polarity of transistors. Through detailed inves-tigations, we found that these vdW contacts can resolve the Fermi-level pinning issue in typical metal contacts, leading to near-ideal Schottky barrier heights and thus p-type characteris-tics in WSe2 transistors. Notably, the Schottky barrier heights of these devices also largely obey the Schottky–Mott limit, indica-tive of optimized metal–semiconductor contacts. We further confirmed that this vdW contact is applicable to MoS2, yielding ambipolar FET characteristics. Finally, the ability to control the polarities of WSe2 devices allows us to construct various func-tional logic gates, such as a complementary inverter, NAND, and NOR. From an industrial perspective, reliable perfor-mance and scalability of vdW 2D contact devices achieved by our method should be further optimized; high-quality growth and scalable synthesis of vdW heterostructures must be addressed.[43] We believe our demonstration of vdW 2D contact paves the way for other synthetic processes of vdW 2D contact to be explored for industrial goal of next-generation electronics.

Experimental Section Synthesis of Cl–SnSe2: Cl–SnSe2 (SnSe1.96Cl0.04) was synthesized via a solid-state reaction, following a procedure described elsewhere.[23] Briefly, this procedure was as follows: Stoichiometric amounts of Sn, Se, and anhydrous SnCl2 powders were mixed: (2 − x)Sn + xSnCl2 + 2(2 − x) Adv. Mater. 2022, 2109899 www.advmat.de www.advancedsciencenews.com 2109899 (7 of 8) © 2022 The Authors. Advanced Materials published by Wiley-VCH GmbH Se → 2SnSe2−xClx. The reaction was performed via a two-step process: the mixture was heated to 250 °C for 24 h, followed by annealing at 400 °C for 48 h. Finally, the sample was melted at 750 °C for 24 h, and then slowly cooled to 550 °C at a rate of 2 °C h−1 to grow single crystals.
Device Fabrication: A Ti (1 nm)/Au (10 nm) local bottom gate was first prepared onto a Si/SiO2 substrate as the back-gate electrode. Afterward, through the use of a polyvinyl alcohol film, h-BN (15–20 nm) and multilayer WSe2 flakes (8–12 nm) were transferred on top of the predeposited gate electrodes. The h-BN serves as a gate dielectric that greatly suppresses substrate-induced doping and preserves the intrinsic electronic properties of WSe2.[8] Using a poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) stamp covered with a polycarbonate (PC) film,[44] Cl–SnSe2 flakes were successively picked up from the substrate and placed onto WSe2 at an elevated temperature of 170 °C. The PC film was removed using chloroform, followed by acetone and isopropyl alcohol. Finally, the top electrodes were defined using e-beam lithography followed by electron-beam metal deposition. For comparison, devices with evaporated metal contacts were fabricated on the same flake via the same procedure. To fabricate the NAND and NOR logic gates, two individual samples were wire-bonded, and measured in air ambient (Detailed information on the sample preparation is provided in Figure S19, Supporting Information).
Materials and Device Characterization: The thicknesses of h-BN, Cl–SnSe2, and WSe2 flakes used in this study were measured by atomic force microscope (AFM) (XE 100, Park Systems). The thickness profile of all devices is provided in Figure S20, Supporting Information. XRD (D8 Advance, BRUKER) and Raman spectroscopy (LabRAM HR Evolution, Horiba Jovin-Yvon) with a laser excitation wavelength of 532 nm were used to characterize the crystallinities and qualities of WSe2, MoS2, and Cl–SnSe2. Cross-sectional TEM images of the contact interfaces were obtained using an image aberration-corrected TEM (HF-3300, Hitachi). XPS and UPS measurements were performed to estimate the band alignments of WSe2 and Cl–SnSe2 using VersaProbe with micro-focused and monochromatic Al Ka (1486.6 eV) and He I (21.22 eV) discharging excitation sources, respectively. All electrical measurements of the devices were conducted using a semiconductor parameter analyzer (4200-SCS, Keithley) in vacuum (≈10−3 Torr) at 293–353 K.
Statistical Analysis: The statistical analysis was conducted using Origin 9.0 software. The sample size of statistical analysis in Figure 3f,g is 24. The extraction details of Schottky barrier heights are consistent with Figure 3e. All data were raw and expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). The sample size (n) for each statistical analysis was given in each figure legend.

args.summary:
This research article (published in Advanced Materials, 2022, DOI: 10.1002/adma.202109899) from the Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST) and collaborators demonstrates Fermi-level pinning-free WSe2 transistors using 2D van der Waals (vdW) metal contacts made from chlorine-doped SnSe2 (Cl-SnSe2), enabling polarity-controllable transistors and functional CMOS logic circuits.

**Background/Problem:** Precise control over transistor polarity (n- or p-type) is critical for CMOS circuits. However, 2D transistors suffer from strong Fermi-level pinning at metal–semiconductor interfaces due to damage caused by conventional metallization, fixing transistors into mostly n-type polarity. High-work-function 2D metals capable of eliminating this pinning were previously lacking.

**Key Innovation:** The team synthesized Cl-SnSe2 (SnSe1.96Cl0.04) via a melt-solidification process, creating a metallic 2D material with a high work function of 4.71 eV. Cl atoms substitute Se atoms while maintaining the structural integrity of SnSe2. UPS measurements confirmed degenerate (metal-like) states near the Fermi level, with carrier density ≈10^14 cm^-2 (two orders of magnitude higher than undoped 2D semiconductors). The Pd/Cl-SnSe2 junction exhibited a low contact resistance of ≈0.083 ± 0.059 kΩ·µm at VGS = 0 V.

**Key Results:**
- Cl-SnSe2-contacted WSe2 transistors exhibited predominantly p-type characteristics, while evaporated metal (Pd, Au, Ti) contacts consistently produced n-type behavior regardless of work function
- Cross-sectional TEM showed atomically clean Cl-SnSe2/WSe2 interfaces, whereas evaporated Pd caused visible damage to topmost WSe2 layers (the cause of Fermi-level pinning)
- XPS and Raman confirmed no chemical reactions, defects, or strains at the Cl-SnSe2/WSe2 interface
- Hole and electron mobility of WSe2 devices: 15.7 and 33.0 cm² V^-1 s^-1, respectively; hole mobility improved to 150 cm² V^-1 s^-1 with ~4-nm-thick WSe2
- Schottky barrier height (SBH) for hole injection in WSe2 with Cl-SnSe2 contact: ≈350 ± 26 meV, following the Schottky–Mott limit (pinning factor S = 1)
- Evaporated metal contacts showed strong Fermi-level pinning (S = 0.03) with electron barriers of 190–250 meV
- The approach also works on MoS2, producing ambipolar FET characteristics with electron SBH ≈420 ± 37 meV and hole SBH ≈780 ± 26 meV
- Devices with Cl-SnSe2 contacts maintained p-type polarity under ambient conditions for 3 months
- Contact resistance for Cl-SnSe2 contacts: 114.1 kΩ·µm (higher than evaporated contacts due to larger SBH, attributed to its high barrier)

**Demonstrated Circuits:** The polarity control enabled fabrication of a complementary inverter (combining Pd-contacted n-FET and Cl-SnSe2-contacted p-FET) achieving a high voltage gain of ≈40 at VDD = 5 V, plus functional NAND and NOR logic gates using four WSe2 transistors.

**Conclusion:** The Cl-SnSe2 vdW 2D metal contacts resolve Fermi-level pinning, enable near-ideal Schottky barrier heights following the Schottky–Mott limit, and provide a pathway toward next-generation 2D electronics with controllable polarity for CMOS integration.
args.key_excerpts: "Here, a creation of clean van der Waals contacts is demonstrated, wherein a metallic 2D material, chlorine-doped SnSe2 (Cl–SnSe2), is used as the high-work-function contact, providing an interface that is free of defects and Fermi-level pinning."

Chemical Trend of Transition Metal Doping in WSe2 Dan Han1,2,3 Wenmei Ming,3 Haixuan Xu,4 Shiyou Chen1,* Deyan Sun2, and Mao-Hua Du3* 1Key Laboratory of Polar Materials and Devices (Ministry of Education) and 2Department of Physics, East China Normal University, Shanghai 200241, China 3Materials Science and Technology Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN 37831, USA 4Department of Materials Science and Engineering, The University of Tennessee Knoxville, TN 37996, USA *Communicating authors: Mao-Hua Du (mhdu@ornl.gov) Shiyou Chen (chensy@ee.ecnu.edu.cn) 2 Abstract Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are promising nanoscale materials with a wide range of applications. Chemical doping is a powerful tool for tailoring physical and chemical properties of TMDs for targeted functionalities. As one of the most important TMDs, WSe2 has great potential for applications in field effect transistor (FET) and complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) technologies for its bi-polar dopability. However, the precise control over the type and density of free carriers remains challenging. In this work, first-principles calculations were performed to study intrinsic defects and transition metal (TM) dopants in WSe2. Our results show that TM doping can effectively control the Fermi level in WSe2 with no significant compensation by intrinsic defects. Nb and Ta are effective p-type dopants capable of generating a high free hole density in WSe2. While n-type doping is possible by Re (under the Se-rich condition) and Cu (under the W-rich condition), the doping efficiency is reduced due to the lower attainable dopant concentration and higher ionization energies. The chemical trend in the attainable concentration of various substitutional TM dopants in WSe2 is largely determined by the competition between the dopant incorporation in WSe2 and the formation of the secondary phase TMSe2. Such competition is strongly affected by the different crystal environments of the TM ion in TMSe2 and WSe2, which determine the crystal field splitting and electron filling of TM d levels and consequently the formation energy of the TM dopant. 3 1. Introduction Layered transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have been extensively studied for their novel properties and a wide range of applications, including field-effect transistors (FETs)[1,2], batteries[3,4], supercapacitors[5,6], photovoltaics[7,8] and catalysis[9,10]. In particular, the atomic-scale thickness without surface dangling bonds and sizable band gaps render TMDs promising nano-electronic materials.[11-16] The ability to dope two-dimensional (2D) TMDs both n- and p-type with high carrier density and mobility as well as air and thermal stability is essential to the development of FET and complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technologies.[17-19] However, this has not been realized in 2D TMDs; thus, inhibiting further technology development. Among many TMDs, WSe2 appears promising for FET and CMOS applications due to both p- and n-type dopability. WSe2 has an indirect bandgap of 1.4 eV.[20,21] Both p-type and n-type conductivities have been reported for undoped bulk WSe2 with carrier densities on the order of 1015 or 1016 cm-3.[21-25] Chemical doping has been shown to improve p- and n-type conductivities.[26,27] Nb and Ta doping enhanced p-type conductivity in bulk and monolayer WSe2[26-29] while Re, In, and Cu doping led to n-type conductivity. [22,27,30,31] Although these results demonstrated bipolar doping of WSe2, the efficiencies of n- and p-type doping are asymmetric. Degenerate doping of WSe2 crystals by Nb with a hole density > 1019 cm-3 has been reported whereas the highest electron density in n-type WSe2 by substitutional doping is only on the order of 1017 cm-3.[27] Surface charge transfer doping by chemisorption and 4 physisorption of metal atoms and organic molecules is another approach to modulate the carrier type and carrier density in WSe2. [1,32-40] N-type degenerate doping by K in few-layer WSe2 has been reported.[34] However, the application of the surface charge transfer doping may be limited due to the relatively poor air and thermal stability as well as the incompatibility with conventional semiconductor technologies.[41] Despite the critical importance of chemical doping in functionalization of 2D TMDs, the underlying mechanisms that determine the doping efficiency is still poorly understood. Theoretical studies of TM dopants in WSe2 have been limited to neutral dopants;[42,43] the critical information on dopant formation energies, dopant-induced charge transition levels, and Fermi level pinning by dopants is still lacking. In this paper, we investigated intrinsic point defects and a series of dopants (Nb, Ta, Re, Ru, Os, Cu, Ag and In) in bulk WSe2 using first-principles calculations. The results show that the formation energy of a TM dopant in WSe2 can be substantially lower than those of intrinsic defects; thus, the TM doping can determine the Fermi level. We also found a large variation in the minimal formation energy of TM dopants in WSe2. The different ligand environments of TM dopants in WSe2 and TMSe2 secondary phases play an important role in the competition of dopant stability in WSe2 and in secondary phases, which determines the minimal dopant formation energy and the attainable dopant concentration. 2. The van der Waals interaction was included using the DFT-D2 method[50] to account for the important inter-layer coupling in WSe2. To calculate the formation energy of a defect, a 6×6×1 hexagonal supercell (a = b = 19.957 Å and c= 12.768 Å) containing 216 atoms and a Γ point centered 1×1×2 k-point mesh were used. The atomic positions were relaxed until the forces were less than 0.01 eV/Å. The calculated band gap of bulk WSe2 at the PBE level is 0.90 eV, which is underestimated due to the well-known band gap error in PBE calculations. The band gap was corrected by using the hybrid HSE06 functional[49] with the fraction of the Hartree-Fock exchange adjusted to 20%. The maximally allowed TM chemical potential (TM-rich limit) corresponds to the borderline between forming single-phase WSe2:TM and segregated phases of WSe2 and TMSe2. Below we discuss the trend of minimal formation energies of substitutional TM dopants at the TM-rich and Se-rich limits. We focus on the TM-rich and Se-rich limits because these conditions promote the substitution of W by TM dopants. Our calculations find that, at the Se-rich limit, the maximal chemical potential of a TM dopant (Nb, Ta, or Re) is limited by the formation of the secondary phase TMSe2. It can be shown that, at the Se-rich and TM-rich limits, the formation energy (Eq. 1) of a TM dopant is given by (6) 𝛥𝐻(𝑇𝑀𝑊) = (E𝐷― 𝜇𝑇𝑀,𝑏𝑢𝑙𝑘) ―𝛥𝐻(TMSe2) +𝐶.
Here, is the total energy of the supercell that contains the TM dopant, is E𝐷 𝜇𝑇𝑀,𝑏𝑢𝑙𝑘 the chemical of potential of TM in bulk TM, and is the enthalpy of 2 (TMSe ) H  formation of TMSe2. The last term C in Eq. 6 is unrelated to the dopant: C = ― Eℎ , where is the chemical potential of W +𝛥𝐻(WSe2) + 𝜇𝑊,𝑏𝑢𝑙𝑘+𝑞(𝜀𝑉𝐵𝑀+ 𝜀𝑓) 𝜇𝑊,𝑏𝑢𝑙𝑘 in bulk W metal. The binding strengths between the TM dopant and its ligands in WSe2 and in the secondary phase TMSe2 are reflected in and , (E𝐷― 𝜇𝑇𝑀,𝑏𝑢𝑙𝑘) 2 (TMSe ) H  respectively, in Eq. 6. Therefore, the formation energy of the substitutional dopant in Eq. 6 is largely determined by the competition of the TM-Se coupling in WSe2 and TMSe2, which in turn is strongly affected by the different crystal field splitting of the TM d levels in different crystal environments. It should be emphasized that the existence of a stable secondary phase for a TM dopant does not necessarily mean that 15 the TM doping would be difficult. For example, the calculated enthalpy of formation in Table S1 shows that NbSe2 and TaSe2 are chemically more stable than ReSe2 [58]; however, the doping of Nb and Ta in WSe2 is energetically more favorable than the doping of Re based on the calculated dopant formation energies in Fig. 3. (This result also agrees with the experimental observation.[27]) Therefore, what determines the formation energy of a TMW is the competition between the TM-Se bonding in WSe2:TM and that in TMSe2. A TM atom in TMSe2 and a substitutional TM dopant in WSe2 both form six TM-Se bonds. However, the six Se nearest neighbors to the TM atom in WSe2 could have a different symmetry from those in TMSe2, which strongly affects the formation energy of TMW as shown below.
NbSe2 and TaSe2 share the same crystal structure with WSe2 (space group P63/mmc). [See Figure 4(a)] The TM ions in NbSe2, TaSe2 and WSe2 all have the trigonal prismatic coordination and the d levels undergo the same crystal field splitting as shown for NbSe2 as an example in Figure 5. Nb4+ and Ta4+ are both d1 ions. Taking Nb4+ as an example, the single d electron in Nb4+ in WSe2 and in NbSe2 occupies the same low-lying level. Thus, the incorporation of Nb4+ in WSe2 competes 2 z d favorably with Nb4+ in NbSe2. On the other hand, ReSe2 has a P-1[59] crystal structure [Figure 4(b)] and Re4+ (a d3 ion) has a distorted octahedral environment, in which the three d electrons of Re4+ occupy the low-lying non-bonding dxy, dxz, and dyz orbitals (t2g) in the majority spin channel (see Figure 5), opening up an sizable band gap (1.29 eV[60]) between t2g and eg levels. When Re4+ substitutes a W4+ ion in WSe2, one of the three d electrons is forced into the higher-lying orbital. Thus, the change of the 2 2 , x y xy d  16 crystal environment of Re4+ from ReSe2 to WSe2 incurs a relatively high energy cost [a relatively high value of in Eq. 6], resulting in a higher (E𝐷― 𝜇𝑇𝑀,𝑏𝑢𝑙𝑘) ―𝛥𝐻(TMSe2) formation energy of in WSe2.
0 W Re Figure 4. Crystal structures of secondary phases of (a) NbSe2 and TaSe2 (P63/mmc), (b) ReSe2 (P-1), and (c) RuSe2 and OsSe2 (Pa-3). A TM ion has a trigonal prismatic coordination in (a) and a distorted octahedral coordination in (b) and (c). Green and grey balls represent Se and TM ions, respectively.
Figure 5. Schematic of crystal field splitting and electron filling for Nb4+ and Re4+ in WSe2 and their respective secondary phases NbSe2 and ReSe2. We further studied Ru and Os dopants, which have one more d electron than Re. 17 The results show that the substitutional and are amphoteric dopants in W Ru W Os WSe2, acting as donors when the Fermi level is low and as acceptors when the Fermi level is high. Doping WSe2 with Ru or Os is expected to result in Fermi level pinning deep inside the band gap with very low carrier density. Thus, Ru and Os are not good n- or p-type dopants in WSe2. RuSe2 and OsSe2 have the pyrite crystal structure (space group Pa-3[61,62]) as shown in Figure 4(c), in which Ru and Os have a nominal oxidation state of 2+ (due to the formation of Se-Se dimers in the pyrite structure) and a distorted octahedral coordination. The six d electrons in Ru2+ and Os2+ fill the low-lying t2g level.[63] On the other hand, Ru2+ and Os2+ in WSe2 ( and ) fill the 2-W Ru 2-W Os high-lying levels and are not even thermodynamically stable. [The (-/2-) 2 2 , x y xy d  levels of and are above the CBM.] This explains the high formation W Ru W Os energies of and as shown in Figure 3.
W Ru W Os We have also studied TM dopants (Nb, Ta, Re, Ru, Os) at interstitial sites. These interstitial TM dopants were found to have significantly higher formation energies in WSe2 than the substitutional dopants; thus, they are not shown in Figure 3. The only TM dopants that we found have relatively low formation energies for interstitials are Cu and Ag, which are stable at the hollow site as shown in Figure 1(c). CuW and AgW have significantly higher formation energies than Cui and Agi and are shown in Figure S1.[58] Importantly, under the W-rich condition, the formation energy of Cui is comparable to that of ReW as shown in Figure 3. These results suggest that the n-type doping by Re and Cu should be performed under the Se-rich and W-rich conditions, respectively. There is indeed a report that showed Cu doping turning slightly p-type 18 WSe2 to slightly n-type.[31] However, the calculated ionization energy of Cui is significant (0.32 eV below the CBM), which makes it difficult to obtain high free electron density in WSe2:Cu. The high ionization energy of Cui is the result of significant s-d coupling between Cu and the adjacent W ions, which produces a bound state below the CBM. Our calculations show that Agi has a significantly higher formation energy than Cui, which is likely due to the larger ionic radius of Ag+ (1.15 Å) than Cu+ (0.77 Å). We have also studied In dopant in WSe2 motivated by the experimental result that In doping turns p-type WSe2 to n-type.[30] However, our results show that In is not an effective dopant in WSe2 because of the high formation energies for both substitutional and interstitial In and the compensation between Ini (donor) and InW (acceptor) (Figure S1).[58] 4. Conclusion Intrinsic defects and TM dopants (Nb, Ta, Re, Ru, Os, Cu, Ag) in bulk WSe2 are investigated using first-principles calculations. All intrinsic defects have relatively high formation energies and consequently low concentrations. VSe is the dominant intrinsic defect and acts as a deep electron trap in p-type and semi-insulating WSe2. Thus, 𝑉0 Se intrinsic defects are not expected to introduce a significant amount of free carriers in undoped WSe2. All the TM dopants studied in this work have lower formation energies than those of intrinsic defects. NbW and TaW have the lowest formation energies and shallow acceptor levels, which can lead to a high level of p-type doping. In comparison, the most important n-type dopants, ReW and Cui, have relatively higher formation 19 energies and deeper ionization energies, which can lead to n-type doping but with lower free electron density. Our results show that the n-type doping is most effective by Re-doping under the Se-rich condition and by Cu doping under the W-rich condition. The large variation in the minimal formation energy of various substitutional TM dopants is related to the secondary phases TMSe2 because the maximal TM chemical potential (which corresponds to the minimal dopant formation energy) is capped by the heat of formation of TMSe2. We find that the minimal formation energy of a substitutional TM dopant in WSe2 is determined by the competition between the TM dopant incorporation in WSe2 and the formation of the secondary phase TMSe2, which in turn is strongly affected by the different crystal environments of TM dopants and consequently different crystal field splitting and electron filling in TM d levels in WSe2 and their secondary phases. Our results and insights on the TM doping efficiency in bulk WSe2 should also be relevant to the understanding of TM doping in monolayer and few-layer WSe2 and other TMDs. args.summary:
This is a scientific research paper titled "Chemical Trend of Transition Metal Doping in WSe2" by Dan Han, Wenmei Ming, Haixuan Xu, Shiyou Chen, Deyan Sun, and Mao-Hua Du, from East China Normal University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and the University of Tennessee Knoxville. The study uses first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate intrinsic defects and transition metal (TM) dopants (Nb, Ta, Re, Ru, Os, Cu, Ag, In) in bulk WSe2, a promising material for field-effect transistors (FETs) and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technologies due to its bipolar dopability.

Key findings:
1. Intrinsic defects in WSe2 have relatively high formation energies and low concentrations; the Se vacancy (VSe) is the dominant intrinsic defect acting as a deep electron trap in p-type and semi-insulating WSe2.
2. Nb and Ta are effective p-type dopants with low formation energies and shallow acceptor levels (both at Ev + 0.12 eV), capable of generating high free hole densities (>10^19 cm^-3), consistent with experiments.
3. Re (under Se-rich conditions) and Cu (under W-rich conditions) enable n-type doping, but with reduced efficiency due to lower attainable dopant concentrations and higher ionization energies. ReW has a (+/0) level at Ec – 0.20 eV; Cui has an ionization energy of 0.32 eV below the CBM.
4. Ru and Os are amphoteric dopants that pin the Fermi level deep in the band gap with very low carrier density; they are not effective n- or p-type dopants.
5. In is not an effective dopant due to high formation energies and donor-acceptor compensation.
6. The chemical trend in attainable dopant concentration is largely determined by competition between dopant incorporation in WSe2 and formation of secondary phases (TMSe2). This competition is strongly affected by the different crystal environments of TM ions in TMSe2 versus WSe2, which determine crystal field splitting and electron filling of TM d levels.
7. For example, Nb4+ (d1) and Ta4+ (d1) have the same trigonal prismatic coordination in WSe2 and their secondary phases, favoring incorporation. Re4+ (d3) in ReSe2 has a distorted octahedral environment (P-1 structure) where three d electrons occupy t2g orbitals, but in WSe2 one electron is forced into a higher-lying orbital, increasing the formation energy.

Calculated maximum dopant densities (at T = 1000°C growth temperature): NbW = 3.17×10^21 cm^-3, TaW = 1.83×10^21 cm^-3, ReW = 1.14×10^18 cm^-3 (the density of W in WSe2 is 1.65×10^22 cm^-3). These results are consistent with experimental observations (hole density 5.2×10^19 cm^-3 in WSe2:Nb, electron density 6.3×10^17 cm^-3 in WSe2:Re).

Computational methods: VASP code, PBE exchange-correlation functional with HSE06 band gap correction, DFT-D2 van der Waals correction, 6×6×1 hexagonal supercell (216 atoms), calculated band gap of 1.39 eV (HSE06) matching experimental 1.40 eV, in-plane/out-of-plane dielectric constants of 16.11 and 7.93.

## Abstract

The semiconductor industry has been facing obstacles in designing low-power (LP) nanoelectronic devices due to the lack of accurate theoretical simulations and low-resistance contacts of heterojunctions. Here, based on experimental data, we discover that the generalized gradient approximation using the Fritz Haber Institute pseudopotential accurately describes the lattice constants and electronic properties of monolayer M o⁢S i 2⁢N 4. It is further confirmed that this method is also applicable to characterize the electrical contact properties and device transport characteristics of metal/M o⁢S i 2⁢N 4 heterojunctions (where metal includes S c,B i,A g,A l,T i, graphene, C r, F e,C u,C o,A u,P d,N i, and P t). Calculations show that various bulk metal/M o⁢S i 2⁢N 4 heterojunctions exhibit _n_-type Schottky barrier contact features, and it is possible to achieve 100% carrier injection for M o⁢S i 2⁢N 4 with S c,A g,T i,P d, and P t contacts. Using the Schottky-Mott rule and quantum transport simulation, a strong Fermi-level pinning effect at the metal/M o⁢S i 2⁢N 4 interfaces is observed, and S c is identified as the best metal electrode. The 5.1-nm _p_-_i_-_n_ field-effect transistor (FET) with S c electrodes can meet the off-state current requirement of the 2013 International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors standard for high-performance and LP FET devices. By employing a high-_k_ gate, the on-state current for the undoped LP device can be improved by 2 orders of magnitude, and its high on:off ratio is up to 3 × 1 0 6. These findings provide insights into the metal/M o⁢S i 2⁢N 4 interface behaviors and provide a theoretical reference for designing M o⁢S i 2⁢N 4-based nanoelectronic devices by selecting suitable electrodes with low contact resistance.

Please follow these guidelines to create your summary:

1. Identify and preserve the main topic or purpose of the webpage.
2. Retain key facts, statistics, and data points that are central to the content's message.
3. Keep important quotes from credible sources or experts.
4. Maintain the chronological order of events if the content is time-sensitive or historical.
5. Preserve any lists or step-by-step instructions if present.
6. Include relevant dates, names, and locations that are crucial to understanding the content.
7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.
- For product pages: Keep key features, specifications, and unique selling points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

This is a scientific paper page from Physical Review Applied (published by the American Physical Society) describing a first-principles computational study of metal-semiconductor contacts and quantum transport simulations for 5.1-nm monolayer MoSi2N4 devices.

**Publication details:** Published 30 May 2024 in Phys. Rev. Applied 21, 054062 (Vol. 21, Iss. 5). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevApplied.21.054062. Received 17 February 2024, revised 2 May 2024, accepted 6 May 2024. The article has 50 citations on Dimensions and an altmetric score of 1.

**Authors:** Zhanhai Li, Jianing Han, Shengguo Cao, Zhenhua Zhang (corresponding author, zhzhang@csust.edu.cn), and Xiaoqing Deng (corresponding author, xq_deng@163.com), all from the Hunan Provincial Key Laboratory of Flexible Electronic Materials Genome Engineering, Changsha University of Science and Technology, Changsha 410114, China.

**Key findings from the abstract:**
- The generalized gradient approximation (GGA) using the Fritz Haber Institute pseudopotential accurately describes the lattice constants and electronic properties of monolayer MoSi2N4, based on experimental data.
- This method also characterizes electrical contact properties and device transport characteristics of metal/MoSi2N4 heterojunctions, where the metals studied include Sc, Bi, Ag, Al, Ti, graphene, Cr, Fe, Cu, Co, Au, Pd, Ni, and Pt.
- Various bulk metal/MoSi2N4 heterojunctions exhibit n-type Schottky barrier contact features, with 100% carrier injection achievable for MoSi2N4 with Sc, Ag, Ti, Pd, and Pt contacts.
- A strong Fermi-level pinning effect was observed at metal/MoSi2N4 interfaces using the Schottky-Mott rule and quantum transport simulations, and Sc was identified as the best metal electrode.
- The 5.1-nm p-i-n field-effect transistor (FET) with Sc electrodes meets the off-state current requirement of the 2013 International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors standard for high-performance and low-power FET devices.
- By employing a high-k gate, the on-state current for the undoped low-power device improves by 2 orders of magnitude, with a high on:off ratio of up to 3 × 10^6.

**Physics Subject Headings (PhySH):** Quantum transport, 2-dimensional systems, Metals, Nanotechnology, Schottky barriers, Semiconductor compounds, Transistors, Density functional calculations.

**Access note:** The full article text, supplemental material, and references require subscription/login authorization, but the abstract is freely available. There are 43 citing articles listed.

IEEE ELECTRON DEVICE LETTERS 1 MoS2 Field-Effect Transistors With Graphene/Metal Heterocontacts Yuchen Du, Lingming Yang, Jingyun Zhang, Han Liu, Kausik Majumdar, Paul D. Kirsch, and Peide D. Ye, Fellow, IEEE Abstract—For the ﬁrst time, n-type few-layer MoS2 ﬁeld-effect transistors (FETs) with graphene/Ti as the heterocontacts have been fabricated, showing more than 160-mA/mm drain current at 1-µm gate length with an ON-OFF current ratio of 107. The enhanced electrical characteristic is conﬁrmed in a nearly 2.1 times improvement in ON-resistance and a 3.3 times improvement in contact resistance with heterocontacts compared with the MoS2 FETs without graphene contact layer.
Temperature-dependent study on MoS2/graphene heterocontacts has been also performed, still unveiling its Schottky contact nature. Transfer length method and a devised I–V method have been introduced to study the contact resistance and Schottky barrier height in MoS2/graphene/metal heterocontacts structure.
Index Terms—MoS2, graphene, heterocontacts, MOSFET, Schottky barrier height.
I. INTRODUCTION G RAPHENE and other two-dimensional (2D) materials are the rapidly rising stars on the horizon of materials science, condensed-matter physics, and solid state devices.
They stand for a brand new family of materials that are one or few atomic layer thick, and offer many new research directions towards nanoscience and nanotechnology. However, the gapless nature of monolayer graphene has restrained its wide electronic device applications, in particularly for logic circuits [1]. Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), another type of 2D materials, recently attracted wide attentions due to their appropriate bandgap and reasonable mobility. Owing to its unique structural and electronic properties, TMDs provide us novel material systems to explore interesting phenomena, such as 2D interfaces, which might be not available to be investigated in the traditional Si and III-V semiconductors.
As one of the most studied TMDs, MoS2 has a bandgap between 1.3-1.8 eV, depending on the number of layers, and reasonable mobility [2], [3]. The on-state performance of the MoS2 FETs is mainly limited by the large contact resistance at MoS2/metal interfaces [4]–[9]. Recent attempts to improve MoS2 contacts had been concentrated on the following areas using: (1) low work function contact metal [10], (2) gas doping of MoS2 ﬂakes [11], and (3) molecular or solid doping on Manuscript received February 28, 2014; revised March 19, 2014; accepted March 20, 2014. K. Majumdar and P. D. Kirsch are with SEMATECH, Albany, NY 12203 USA.

However, the fundamental reason for the large contact resistance is the result of Fermi level pinning on MoS2 near conduction band edge due to S-vacancy defect level and charge neutral level location [14], [15]. All above experiments have just partially touched the issue and barely resolved the issue completely. Graphene contacts on MoS2 [9], which has a 2D to 2D interface, might provide a new angle to solve this technical challenge. In this letter, graphene is used in between metal contact and n-type few-layer MoS2 ﬁlm to enhance the electronic coupling between metal and MoS2 and boost the electron injection into MoS2. For the ﬁrst time, well-performed graphene/metal hetero-contacts MoS2 FETs were fabricated. The feasibility using graphene/ metal hetero-contacts to reduce contact resistance (Rc) and improve on-resistance (Ron) of the devices is demonstrated.
II. EXPERIMENT MoS2 ﬂakes with 5-6nm thickness were mechanically exfo-liated from bulk ingot (SI Supplies) by standard scotch tape technique, and then transferred to a heavily p-doped silicon substrate with a 90 nm SiO2 capping layer. The copper substrate was etched using 1M FeCl3 solution. After rinsing in DI water for several times, the PMMA/graphene layer was transferred onto the target substrate. Graphene is fully etched from the channel.

III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Output and transfer curves of a hetero-contacts FET are plotted in Fig. 2(a) and (b) to demonstrate its effectiveness to improve device performance by inserting monolayer graphene between metal and MoS2 contacts. The output curves of a reference sample are also shown in Fig. 2(a) in black. For the device contact without graphene, shown in Fig. 2(a), on-current at Vds = 4 V, and Vbg = 30 V is equal to 48.5 mA/mm. As the monolayer graphene applied in the hetero-contacts, on-current is improved to be 161.2 mA/mm at the same source/drain and gate bias. Ron determined from linear region as shown in Fig. 2(a) as dashed lines are used to have a direct comparison. Comparing to Ron of 42.8 ·mm for the reference device, hetero-contacts device shows a much lower Ron of 20.6 ·mm. In order to have a more accurate comparison, metal contacts with and without graphene on the same ﬂake have also been fabricated. Similar values of Ron and similar amount of reduction in Ron have been achieved. The results further veriﬁed the feasibility of using graphene/metal hetero-contacts to improve on-resistance of the devices. With similar channel resistance of two devices, the nearly 2.1 times dropping in Ron is directly related to the reduction of Rc by inserting monolayer of graphene into contact. In Fig. 2(b), the transfer curves of hetero-contacts FETs are plotted with source/drain biases of 0.2 V. The exhibiting hysteresis from forward and backward sweeps is due to the charge injection at the interface between MoS2 and the substrate and the charge transfer from/to neighboring adsorbates [16]. The 107 current on/off ratio is achieved on hetero-contacts devices. Extrinsic ﬁeld-effect mobility of hetero-contacts FETs is calculated to be 32.3 cm2/Vs, which is extracted from the forward I-V transfer curves by the relation, μ = d Ids d(Vbg) × L w × Cox × Vds (1) where dIds d(Vbg) is the transconductance, L is the channel length, W is the channel width, and Cox is the backgate capacitance per unit area. Using Rc of hetero-contacts device ∼3.7 ·mm, intrinsic ﬁeld-effect mobility of 50.4 cm2/Vs is obtained.
A devised I-V method has been used to quantitatively investigate the Schottky barrier height of hetero-contacts of MoS2/graphene/metal [17]. The barrier height is calculated from the current Is, determined by extrapolating the semilog Id versus Vd curve to Vd =0 V. Schottky barrier height Is is calculated from Is according to φB = K BT q In( A × A∗× T 2 Is ) (2) where A is the area, A∗is the Richardson constant, and T is the temperature. Due to the uncertainty of A∗[17], the effec-tive Schottky barrier height cannot be accurately calculated directly, however, instead of calculating the exact value of Schottky barrier height, exponential function of barrier height can be readdressed. Normalized exponential Schottky barrier height versus backgate voltage has been plotted in Fig. 3(a) to demonstrate the Schottky barrier deduction with graphene con-tact. Moreover, transfer length method (TLM) with separations of 0.5 μm, 1 μm, 1.5 μm, and 2 μm are used to accurately extract the contact resistance of MoS2/graphene/metal hetero-contacts. Contact resistance without graphene has also been extracted by applying TLM structure on a similar thickness ﬂake. In Fig. 3, both Schottky barrier and contact resistance show a strong gate bias dependent behavior. It is because (1) gate-tunable Schottky barrier width reduction due to the increment of backgate bias and (2) carrier concentration enhancement from backgate bias doping, where all lead to reduce the effective Schottky barrier height and generate more injected electrons from Fermi level at metal to conduction band of MoS2. To exclude the large absolute errors, high bias regions are appropriate to have direct comparison in the contact resistance. Contact resistance with monolayer graphene is 3.7±0.3 ·mm at Vbg = 30 V, which decreased from a value of 12.1±1.2 ·mm at the same backgate voltage without the graphene layer. This nearly 3.3 times reduction in contact resistance may possibly be attributed to the gate-induced electron injection from graphene layer to MoS2. The total carrier density summed over graphene and MoS2 hetero-contact exceeds the single MoS2/metal contact, where the monolayer graphene can be seemed as a "charge pumping" layer. It seems that 2D graphene to MoS2 interface is fundamentally different from metals to MoS2 interfaces.

This IEEE Electron Device Letters paper (DOI: 10.1109/LED.2014.2313340) reports the first fabrication of n-type few-layer MoS2 field-effect transistors (FETs) with graphene/Ti heterocontacts. The work was conducted at Purdue University (Birck Nanotechnology Center) in collaboration with SEMATECH, with authors Yuchen Du, Lingming Yang, Jingyun Zhang, Han Liu, Kausik Majumdar, Paul D. Kirsch, and Peide D. Ye.

Key findings:
- The graphene/metal heterocontact devices achieved drain current of 161.2 mA/mm at 1-µm gate length (vs. 48.5 mA/mm for reference devices without graphene), with an ON-OFF current ratio of 10^7.
- Contact resistance (Rc) was reduced from 12.1±1.2 Ω·mm (without graphene) to 3.7±0.3 Ω·mm (with graphene) at Vbg = 30 V — a nearly 3.3× improvement.
- On-resistance (Ron) improved from 42.8 Ω·mm to 20.6 Ω·mm — a nearly 2.1× reduction.
- Extrinsic field-effect mobility was 32.3 cm²/Vs; intrinsic mobility was 50.4 cm²/Vs at 300 K, decreasing to 28.7 cm²/Vs at 400 K due to electron-phonon scattering (temperature exponent ν = 1.87).
- The contact resistance improvement is attributed to gate-enhanced electron injection from Ti-doped n-type graphene into the MoS2 conduction band; the back-gate modulates not only the channel Fermi level but also the contact (graphene) Fermi level, with graphene acting as a "charge pumping" layer.

Methods: MoS2 flakes (5–6 nm thick) were mechanically exfoliated onto p-doped Si with 90 nm SiO2. Monolayer CVD graphene was transferred via PMMA method with H2/N2 annealing at 450°C. Contacts were formed by e-beam evaporation of 20nm/60nm Ti/Au. Transfer length method (TLM) and a devised I-V method were used to extract contact resistance and Schottky barrier height.

Temperature-dependent studies (300–400 K) confirmed the Schottky contact nature of the MoS2/graphene heterocontacts. Off-state current increased with temperature (activation energy Ea = 0.23 eV, corresponding to donor-level depth from natural material defects), causing the on/off ratio to drop at higher temperatures. The 2D graphene-to-MoS2 interface was found to be fundamentally different from metal-to-MoS2 interfaces, offering a new route toward Ohmic contacts on MoS2 and other 2D materials.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper published in Nano Letters (2014, Vol. 14, pp. 1714-1720) by researchers from The University of Texas at Dallas and Texas Instruments, investigating the mechanism of Fermi level pinning at metal-MoS2 interfaces using density functional theory (DFT) calculations.

**Key findings:**
- The study examined six metals (Al, Ag, Ir, Au, Pd, Pt) with work functions spanning 4.2-6.1 eV in contact with monolayer MoS2.
- Schottky contacts were found for all metals, with all forming n-type contacts except platinum, which formed a p-type Schottky contact.
- The Fermi levels in the metal-MoS2 complexes were found to be partially pinned, varying within a 0.5-0.64 eV window in the band gap, rather than strictly pinned at a single energy level.
- The partial Fermi level pinning results from two synergistic interface behaviors: (1) metal work function modification via interface dipole formation due to charge redistribution, and (2) production of gap states predominantly of Mo d-orbital character, caused by weakened intralayer S-Mo bonding due to interface metal-S interaction.
- The FL shift relative to the CBM of MoS2 shows a linear dependence on metal work function with a slope of 0.71 (well below 1), indicating partial pinning.
- This mechanism is fundamentally different from traditional pinning mechanisms: Bardeen's surface states theory, metal-induced gap states (MIGS), and defect/disorder-induced gap states (DIGS) are all not applicable to these pristine metal-MoS2 interfaces.
- The gap states are localized at Mo atoms (not the contacting S atoms), mediated through the S atoms which weaken the intralayer S-Mo bonding when metal-S bonds form.
- When interface separation is increased to 6.0 Å, all contacts obey the conventional Schottky-Mott model, suggesting that inserting buffer materials between metals and MoS2 could unpin the Fermi levels and form Ohmic contacts.

**Methodology:**
- DFT calculations performed using VASP with PAW method and LDA exchange-correlation functional.
- MoS2 lattice constant kept constant (3.12 Å optimized); metals (111) surfaces strained to match.
- Vacuum region of ~27 Å; Monkhorst-Pack k-point sampling of 4×4×1 (ionic) and 20×20×1 (electronic).
- Energy cutoff of 400 eV; calculated LDA band gap of pristine monolayer MoS2 is 1.88 eV.

**Computational details/parameters:**
- Binding energies: s-electron metals (Ag, Al, Au) interact weakly (physisorption), while d-electron metals (Pd, Ir, Pt) interact strongly (chemisorption).
- Interface distances range from 2.17 Å (Pd) to 2.92 Å (Au).
- The work was supported by the Center for Low Energy Systems Technology (LEAST) under STARnet/FCRP program sponsored by MARCO and DARPA.
</summary>

**Topic:** The study investigates how subsurface metal-like defects affect charge transport and Fermi level pinning in MoS2/metal contacts, which is critical for the development of MoS2-based electronic devices.

**Key Findings:**
- Natural MoS2 contains subsurface metal-like defects (likely Mo-vacancies or antisites) with a density of ~10^11 cm^-2 that induce negative ionization of the outermost sulfur atom complex, while S-vacancies occur at higher densities (~10^13 cm^-2) but have only minor influence (~1 nm radius).
- Using conductive AFM (C-AFM), lateral force microscopy (LFM), and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) with nanocontacts (<6 nm^2 contact area), the researchers found that subsurface metal-like defects (NOT S-vacancies) drastically decrease the metal/MoS2 Schottky barrier height compared to pristine regions.
- The Schottky barrier height decreases by 30-50% at defects in the first MoS2 trilayer and 10-15% for defects in the second trilayer.
- The pinning factor (S) is ~0.1 at defect locations and ~0.3 at pristine regions, while the charge neutrality level (ϕ_CNL) is 4.34 eV (pristine) and 4.4 eV (defects), with pinning occurring just below the conduction band (<0.25 eV).
- The pristine surface pinning factor matches theoretical predictions, while the defect-site pinning factor matches previous experimental values, suggesting that prior observations of strong Fermi level pinning (S ~ 0.1) in large-contact studies were due to subsurface metal-like defects, not S-vacancies as previously assumed.

**Methodology:**
- Measurements performed with three different AFM tip materials (boron-doped diamond ~5.1 eV work function, PtSi ~4.9 eV, and n-doped Si ~4.1-4.2 eV).
- Schottky barrier heights extracted using thermionic emission model from I(V) curves recorded in a 128×128 grid.
- Contact areas ranged from 1.5 to 5.7 nm^2 depending on tip material.
- The Schottky barrier height at pristine regions was ~0.53 eV (diamond tip), versus the predicted 1 eV from the Schottky-Mott rule, demonstrating partial Fermi level pinning.

**Conclusions:** Subsurface metal-like defects (located in the Mo-plane) provide low-resistance conduction paths in MoS2-based nanodevices and will play an increasingly prominent role as device junction contact areas decrease in size. The exact origin of these defects remains unknown and requires further study.

This webpage is an Academia.edu topic page for "Fermi level pinning" (FLP), describing the phenomenon where the Fermi level of a semiconductor becomes fixed or "pinned" at a certain energy level due to surface states or defects, affecting electronic properties and charge carrier behavior. The page catalogs 14 papers organized into three key research themes.

Theme 1: Formation of interface states and chemical interactions governing FLP at metal-semiconductor contacts in III-As and 2D semiconductor nanostructures. Notable findings: misfit dislocations act as intrinsic defect centers inducing FLP at GaInAs/GaAs heterointerfaces (Kavanagh, 2022); photoluminescence and XPS quantified band bending and FLP in InGaAs nanowires linking surface oxidation/defects to Fermi level fixation (Linhart, 2022); Kelvin probe microscopy established universal FLP at ≈4.8±0.1 eV relative to vacuum in III-As ternary alloys due to excess surface arsenic (Davydov, 2022); ground-state charge transfer complexes reduce FLP-induced interfacial charge transfer in molecular donor-acceptor junctions (Generalov, 2021); graphene buffer layer insertion breaks FLP at Au-2D SnO contacts (Tian, 2023).

Theme 2: Flux pinning and vortex dynamics in iron-based superconductors. Studies use Dew-Hughes and Kramer scaling models, SQUID-on-tip microscopy, angular-dependent magnetoresistance, and AC susceptibility to characterize pinning forces, vortex dynamics, anisotropic pinning energies, and spacer layer effects in Fe-based superconductors (Koblischka 2015, Gurevich 2016, Grimaldi 2021/2022, Poccia 2023).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper by Yuzheng Guo (Cambridge University), Dameng Liu (Tsinghua University), and John Robertson (Cambridge University) investigating the Schottky barrier heights (SBHs) of two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Key findings include:
1. **Strong Fermi level pinning**: Despite van der Waals interlayer bonding, TMDs exhibit strong Fermi level pinning with a pinning factor S ≈ 0.3 for both top and edge contact geometries on MoS2 (S=0.28 for monolayer, S=0.33 for bulk), indicating moderate pinning that follows the Metal-Induced Gap State (MIGS) model similar to 3D semiconductors.
2. **Contact geometries studied**: Twelve metals (Sc, Mg, Al, Ti, Cr, Mo, Ru, Co, Ni, Pd, Pt, MoO3) covering a wide work function range (3.5-6.6 eV) were tested for both top (on-top) and edge contact geometries (armchair non-polar, zigzag S-terminated, zigzag Mo-terminated) on four TMDs (MoS2, MoSe2, MoTe2, WS2).
3. **Edge vs. top contacts**: The p-type SBH is approximately 0.7 eV lower for edge contacts than top contacts, attributed to anisotropy of bonding and crystal field effects rather than interfacial dipoles. The CNL for a1 states (top contacts) lies ~0.7 eV higher than e-symmetry states (edge contacts), suggesting edge contacts could enable p-type contacts on MoS2.
4. **MIGS model applicability**: TMDs follow the MIGS model despite 2D bonding because contact metal atoms bond strongly to chalcogen atoms (bond lengths similar to edge contacts), and chalcogens can over-coordinate without disrupting intra-layer M-X bonds.
5. **Pinning factors for other TMDs**: S values are similar for MoS2 (0.28), WS2 (0.28), and MoSe2 (0.29), but lower for MoTe2 (0.16) due to its narrower band gap and larger optical dielectric constant.
6. **Defect effects**: Experimental pinning factors (S=0.1 from Das et al.) show stronger pinning than defect-free MIGS predictions, attributed to defects (particularly chalcogen vacancies) that cause additional Fermi level pinning and shift pinning energy toward anion vacancy defect levels.
7. **MoO3 contacts**: O-deficient MoO3 (work function 6.6 eV) provides a valuable method for hole contacts, with the O-rich interface giving much more p-type SBH closer to the valence band.
8. **Practical implications**: Fermi level is pinned near the conduction band for MoS2 (favoring n-type devices), explaining why most MoS2 MOSFETs are n-type. The pinning factor relationship with optical dielectric constant follows Monch's empirical formula for 3D semiconductors, with TMDs slightly below the 3D line.

The paper concludes that the contact problem for 2D TMDs follows the standard MIGS model despite van der Waals interlayer bonding, providing a framework to understand TMD contacts as a whole. Funding was provided by EPSRC grant EP/J011592.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific paper published in IEEE Open Journal of Nanotechnology (Volume 6, 2025, pp. 51-57, DOI: 10.1109/OJNANO.2025.3553692) by researchers from the University of Salerno (Italy) and Universität Konstanz (Germany). The paper was received December 21, 2024, revised in February and March 2025, accepted March 16, 2025, and published March 20, 2025. Corresponding author: Antonio Di Bartolomeo (adibartolomeo@unisa.it).

The study presents multilayer MoS2 Schottky Barrier Field Effect Transistors (SB-FETs) configured with back-gate and van der Pauw contacts. The devices were fabricated using a dry-transfer technique with MoS2 flakes (~16.7 nm thick, ~20 layers, ~137 μm² area) encapsulated between two hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) layers on a SiO2/Si substrate (300 nm SiO2 as gate oxide). Au(53nm)/Ti(7nm) contacts were patterned via e-beam lithography.

Key findings:
- IV characteristics showed non-linear, asymmetric, rectifying behavior across all six contact combinations, confirming Schottky barriers at Ti/MoS2 interfaces despite Schottky-Mott theory predicting ohmic contacts (due to Fermi level pinning from defects and metal-induced gap states).
- Rectification ratios varied from a few units to 10³ depending on the contact pair, attributed to local inhomogeneities from fabrication and different flake coverage areas.
- Transfer curves showed n-type behavior (electrons as majority carriers) with prominent "kinks" at a transition voltage (Vtr ~ -12V to -15V) marking the transition between thermionic emission and tunnelling conduction regimes.

- At negative gate voltages, thermionic emission dominates; at positive gate voltages, tunnelling dominates, causing barrier-height differences to become less influential and output curves to symmetrize.
- The higher the drain barrier, the slower the transition from sublinear to ohmic behavior in the IV curves.

The study concludes that lead local inhomogeneities and different flake coverage affect Schottky barrier heights, which critically determine conduction mechanisms in SB-FETs. The proposed band energy model aids in understanding and optimizing 2D material transistors with Schottky-type contacts.
