Meanwhile, the evolution of Se (3 *d*) XPS spectra shows that, in addition to WSe2, SeO2 components emerged after annealing at high temperatures (150 °C and 200 °C, Fig. [1e](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig1)). A distinct redshift in the binding energy observed in the Se (3 *d*) peak and O (1 *s*) after NO treatment at different temperatures indicates p-type doping in WSe2, as shown in Fig. [1e](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig1) and Supplementary Fig. [3](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#MOESM1).

To further evaluate the effect of the doping temperature on the WSe2 crystallinity, we have analyzed Raman spectra under the same conditions as XPS (Fig. [1f](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig1)). The spectra of 1L-WSe2 films show good crystallinity for treatment temperatures up to 150 °C, as evident from the absence of a significant peak broadening in the *A*1g and *E*2g vibrational modes. However, after NO treatment at 200 °C for 2 h, a notable drop in intensity suggests partial oxidation and loss of crystallinity. Based on Raman and photoluminescence characterizations (Supplementary Fig. [4](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#MOESM1)), we conclude that NO doping does not compromise the macroscopic crystal structure of WSe2, despite the considerable oxidation indicated in the XPS analysis.

We also examined the electrical behavior of 1L-WSe2 films treated under 150 °C for 2 h, as shown in Supplementary Fig. [5](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#MOESM1). Most devices exhibited no current conduction, despite only part of the 1L-WSe2 being oxidized, as confirmed by XPS. This insulating behavior resembles that observed in devices subjected to a pure oxygen treatment[56](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#ref-CR56 "Hung, T. Y. T., Pang, C.-S., Liu, X., Zemlyanov, D. & Chen, Z. Atomically Thin p-doping Layer and Record High Hole Current on WSe2. In 2019 Device Research Conference (DRC) 121–122 (IEEE, Ann Arbor, MI, USA, 2019)."). These findings underscore the significance of optimizing the doping temperature for incorporating nitrogen into monolayer WSe2 to achieve the desired electrical characteristics while minimizing oxidation.

To reduce the oxidation impact, we chose an intermediate NO treatment temperature between 100 °C and 150 °C. Specifically, we employed a gentler doping process (120 °C for 30 minutes) for our statistical study on monolayers, while bilayer WSe2 samples underwent higher doping temperatures and extended durations (130 °C for 2 h). It is important to note that in bilayer WSe2, the bottom layer can still function as a channel even if the top layer becomes oxidized. The yield under these conditions is higher than 90%, indicating an optimized doping temperature and time.

### Unipolar transport and Schottky barrier realignment

Understanding the physics and chemistry involved in the formation of a doping band around mid-gap, along with a shift in the Fermi level toward the valence band, enables us to explain the positive threshold voltage shift of the hole branch, the realignment of the SB, and the p-type unipolarity following NO doping, as illustrated in Fig. [2a](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig2). Note that the SB at the metal-semiconductor interface is significantly influenced by Fermi-level pinning, which results from either metal-induced gap states (MIGS) or defect-induced gap states (DIGS) pinning. MIGS are a result of the metal electron wave functions penetrating the semiconductor at the interface, creating a continuum of states and pinning the Fermi level within the bandgap. DIGS pinning occurs when the Fermi level is pinned at the energy level with the highest density of defect states. These two pinning mechanisms compete at the metal/semiconductor interface, with the Fermi level typically fixed at the overall charge neutrality level (Fig. [2a](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig2)). It is important to note that NO molecules can diffuse into the channel region beneath the source/drain contacts near the edge. If the density of doping states surpasses the influence of MIGS and DIGS, the resulting Fermi-level is primarily determined by the doping density, as illustrated in the band diagram at the metal contact interface (Fig. [2a](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig2) left).

**Fig. 2: Doping-band induced unipolarity and Schottky barrier realignment.**

![Fig. 2: Doping-band induced unipolarity and Schottky barrier realignment.](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-025-59423-9/MediaObjects/41467_2025_59423_Fig2_HTML.png)

[Full size image](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9/figures/2)

**a** Schematic of a 2D field-effect transistor (FET) with a monolayer semiconductor (WSe2) channel, platinum (Pt) metal contacts, and a local bottom gate (LBG) after nitric oxide (NO) doping. The energy band diagram at the semiconductor-contact interface shows how NO doping induces Schottky barrier (SB) realignment via doping-induced pinning (left), while the diagram at the semiconductor-dielectric interface illustrates how the doping band pins the Fermi level (*E*F) in the off-state (right). Defect bands (blue for acceptor-like traps and red for donor-like traps) are displayed in the gate dielectric and Fermi window (gray) within the semiconductor channel. *V*BG denotes the back-gate voltage, ΦSB,n and ΦSB,p refer to the Schottky barrier height (SBH) for electrons and holes, respectively, and ΔΦSB represents their change upon NO doping. **b** *I*D-*V*G characteristics at *V*D = –0.1 V for one representative long-channel device (*L*CH = 780 nm) prior and post NO doping at 120 °C for 30 min. *I*D is the drain current, *V*G is the gate voltage, and *V*D is the drain-to-source voltage. The blue shaded square marks the region of reduced SBH for holes (ΦSB,p), while the red shaded square indicates increased SBH for electrons (ΦSB,n)and doping-band-induced Fermi level pinning in the bandgap.

Figure [2b](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig2) compares the characteristics of an exemplary 1L-WSe2 device before and after NO doping. Notably, the NO doping shifts the threshold voltage of the hole current branch by approximately 0.8 V, enhancing the on-state current at a maximum gate voltage of –4V  by a factor of 10. Furthermore, it is intriguing to observe a widened off-state, with the threshold voltage of the electron branch shifted more positively relative to the hole branch. To fully understand the observed suppression of the electron branch in terms of both magnitude and threshold voltage, we propose a two-fold mechanism (Fig. [2a](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig2)). Firstly, NO doping reduces the Schottky Barrier height (SBH) for holes at the source/drain, facilitating hole injection from the source into the channel, while simultaneously increasing the electron SBH, which suppresses the electron flow from the drain (left, Fig. [2a](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig2)). Secondly, the introduced doping band pins the Fermi level within the bandgap, located between the valence band and the doping band itself (shaded grey band in the WSe2 band profile, Fig. [2a](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig2) right). This slows down the band movement towards the conduction band edge, leading to a positively shifted electron threshold voltage and an increased gate voltage needed to reach the electron branch. These two combined effects of NO doping on both the contact and channel regions are evident in the significantly enhanced on-state hole current (*I*ON) and a substantial stretch of the electron current branch observed in the transfer characteristics of NO-doped 1L-WSe2 p-FETs (Fig. [2b](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig2)). We conclude, that the on-current improvement primarily stems from two key changes induced by NO doping: a favorable shift of the threshold voltage (*V*TH) toward more positive values and a reduction in the SBH for holes. The observed larger gate voltage window between the electron and hole branches, as well as the much larger *SS* for the electron branch, are both attributed to inefficient gating due to doping-band-induced Fermi level pinning in the bandgap.

### Schottky-barrier MOSFET model with doping band

To quantify the SBH reduction in NO-doped 1L-WSe2 transistors, we employed an analytic Schottky barrier MOSFET model based on the Landauer formalism (details in Methods and Supplementary Fig. [6](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#MOESM1) and Note), building upon our previous works[57](#ref-CR57 "Heinze, S. et al. Carbon Nanotubes as Schottky Barrier Transistors. Phys. Rev. Lett. 89, 106801 (2002)."),[58](#ref-CR58 "Knoch, J., Zhang, M., Appenzeller, J. & Mantl, S. Physics of ultrathin-body silicon-on-insulator Schottky-barrier field-effect transistors. Appl. Phys. A 87, 351–357 (2007)."),[59](#ref-CR59 "Penumatcha, A. V., Salazar, R. B. & Appenzeller, J. Analysing black phosphorus transistors using an analytic Schottky barrier MOSFET model. Nat. Commun. 6, 8948 (2015)."),[60](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#ref-CR60 "Prakash, A., Ilatikhameneh, H., Wu, P. & Appenzeller, J. Understanding contact gating in Schottky barrier transistors from 2D channels. Sci. Rep. 7, 12596 (2017)."), which has been adopted to extract various SBH for various 2D semiconductors[59](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#ref-CR59 "Penumatcha, A. V., Salazar, R. B. & Appenzeller, J. Analysing black phosphorus transistors using an analytic Schottky barrier MOSFET model. Nat. Commun. 6, 8948 (2015)."),[61](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#ref-CR61 "Mleczko, M. J. et al. Contact Engineering High-Performance n-Type MoTe2 Transistors. Nano Lett. 19, 6352–6362 (2019)."). Note that the common approach for extracting SBH based on temperature-dependent measurements, originally introduced by Appenzeller et al. [62](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#ref-CR62 "Appenzeller, J., Radosavljević, M., Knoch, J. & Avouris, P. H. Tunneling Versus Thermionic Emission in One-Dimensional Semiconductors. Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 048301 (2004)."),[63](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#ref-CR63 "Das, S., Chen, H.-Y., Penumatcha, A. V. & Appenzeller, J. High Performance Multilayer MoS2 Transistors with Scandium Contacts. Nano Lett. 13, 100–105 (2013)."), is not applicable to devices with SBHs smaller than 100 meV. As shown in Fig. [2b](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig2), the combination of ultra-thin 2D channel bodies, scaled gate dielectrics, and small SB heights in our nitric oxide treated devices results in an indistinct SB slope regime, making it difficult to extract the SBH using the temperature-dependent method.

To investigate the impact of NO doping on the extracted SBH, we applied the SB-MOSFET model (see the Methods section) to undoped long-channel devices and compared the results with those of devices treated with nitric oxide. For undoped long-channel devices (*L*CH = 780 nm), the hole SBH (ΦSB,p) was extracted approximately 250 meV (Fig. [3a](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig3)). Note that in the Landauer model simulation, we only consider the device characteristics in the off-state ( | *V*G | <*|V*TH | ), where the scattering from the channel is negligible[59](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#ref-CR59 "Penumatcha, A. V., Salazar, R. B. & Appenzeller, J. Analysing black phosphorus transistors using an analytic Schottky barrier MOSFET model. Nat. Commun. 6, 8948 (2015)."),[60](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#ref-CR60 "Prakash, A., Ilatikhameneh, H., Wu, P. & Appenzeller, J. Understanding contact gating in Schottky barrier transistors from 2D channels. Sci. Rep. 7, 12596 (2017)."). After NO doping (Fig. [3b](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig3)), the device exhibits a unipolar-like behavior, characterized by a high hole current branch and a delayed, stretched electron branch, along with a substantial reduction of ΦSB,p from approximately 250 meV to 50 meV. This significant SBH reduction for holes implies a corresponding increase of the SB for electron injection (ΦSB,n from 1.35 eV to 1.55 eV) and is thus expected to decrease the electron branch current according to the comparison of the red solid lines in Fig. [3a](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig3) and red dashed line in Fig. [3b](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig3). Note that due to the use of an ultra-thin ~6 nm HfO2 gate dielectric in our experiment (with an extracted screening length of only Λ ~3 nm), a measurable electron tunneling current (red dashed line in Fig. [3b](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#Fig3)) is expected according to the conventional SB model[57](#ref-CR57 "Heinze, S. et al. Carbon Nanotubes as Schottky Barrier Transistors. Phys. Rev. Lett. 89, 106801 (2002)."),[58](#ref-CR58 "Knoch, J., Zhang, M., Appenzeller, J. & Mantl, S. Analysing black phosphorus transistors using an analytic Schottky barrier MOSFET model. Nat. Commun. 6, 8948 (2015)."),[60](/articles/s41467-025-59423-9#ref-CR60 "Prakash, A., Ilatikhameneh, H., Wu, P. & Appenzeller, J. Understanding contact gating in Schottky barrier transistors from 2D channels. Sci. Rep. 7, 12596 (2017)."), even with the large ΦSB,n of 1.55 eV. It is worth noting that the determination of the SBH is subject to some uncertainty due to the ultra-scaled screening length.

Rep. 11, 6610 (2021)."), \({\Delta V}\_{{TH}}\) is the experimentally observed *V*TH shifts in the hole branch. This is a scientific article published in Nature Communications (volume 16, article 4160, 2025) titled "Uncovering the doping mechanism of nitric oxide in high-performance P-type WSe2 transistors." The research, led by Hao-Yu Lan and Zhihong Chen, reveals the doping mechanism of pure nitric oxide (NO) in wafer-scale grown monolayer and bilayer tungsten diselenide (WSe2) transistors for high-performance p-type 2D semiconductor devices.

Key findings:
- NO doping induces acceptor doping bands near the mid-gap of WSe2, which realign the Schottky barrier (SB) and enable p-type unipolar transport
- Density Functional Theory (DFT) simulations and an analytical Schottky barrier MOSFET model (based on Landauer formalism) show SB height reduction from ~250 meV to ~50 meV after NO doping
- Monolayer WSe2 transistors achieved: on-state current of 300 μA/μm (at V_DS=-1V, V_OV=-0.8V), contact resistance of 875 Ω·μm, peak transconductance of 400 μS/μm, and subthreshold swing of 70 mV/dec
- On/off ratios preserved >10^9 with minimal variability and good stability over 24 days
- Bilayer WSe2 achieved on-state current of 448 μA/μm and contact resistance of 390 Ω·μm
- Se vacancies (V_Se) at ~6×10^12 cm^-2 density serve as NO bonding sites (confirmed by STM and matching doping density calculations)
- XPS analysis shows NO treatment introduces W-N species at lower binding energies and WO3 at higher energies; SeO2 appears at higher temperatures
- Optimized doping conditions: 120°C for 30 minutes for monolayers, 130°C for 2 hours for bilayers, with yield >90%
- NO doping shifts hole branch threshold voltage by ~0.8V, enhancing on-state current 10-fold
- Combined with scaled high-κ dielectric (6nm HfO2, EOT ~1.5nm), this doping technique is presented as promising for realizing high-performance p-type 2D transistors for next-generation ultra-scaled electronics

## Abstract

Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors are promising in channel length scaling of field-effect transistors (FETs) due to their excellent gate electrostatics. However, scaling of their contact length still remains a significant challenge because of the sharply raised contact resistance and the deteriorated metal conductivity at nanoscale. Here, we construct a 1D semimetal-2D semiconductor contact by employing single-walled carbon nanotube electrodes, which can push the contact length into the sub-2 nm region. Such 1D–2D heterostructures exhibit smaller van der Waals gaps than the 2D–2D ones, while the Schottky barrier height can be effectively tuned via gate potential to achieve Ohmic contact. We propose a longitudinal transmission line model for analyzing the potential and current distribution of devices in short contact limit, and use it to extract the 1D–2D contact resistivity which is as low as 10−6 Ω·cm2 for the ultra-short contacts. We further demonstrate that the semimetal nanotubes with gate-tunable work function could form good contacts to various 2D semiconductors including MoS2, WS2 and WSe2. The study on 1D semimetal contact provides a basis for further miniaturization of nanoelectronics in the future.

In such semimetal-semiconductor junctions, the clean and intact vdW interface as well as the suppressed metal-induced gap states (MIGS) in semiconductors can effectively eliminate the Fermi level pinning. The small DOS could also enable an efficient modulation on work function of CNTs by external electric field. Therefore, the gate-tunable Schottky barrier height (SBH) at such 1D/2D interface can be predicted. All these specific properties indicate that the individual semimetal SWCNT has great potential as an ultimate scaled contact in 2D electronics.

In this work, we propose a 1D semimetal contact by integrating two SWCNT electrodes with the same chirality on 2D semiconductors, which successfully reduces the contact length of 2D FETs to sub-2 nm. We demonstrate that such mixed-dimensional semimetal-semiconductor (Sm-S) junctions are more tightly contacted than the 2D–2D ones and can be switched between Schottky and Ohmic contact by tuning gate potential. A longitudinal transmission line model (LTLM) was developed to describe the potential and current distribution of devices in short contact limit. The 1D-2D interfacial contact resistivity, as well as the contact resistance, were measured as 10−6 Ω·cm2 and 50 kΩ·μm in Ohmic contact mode, which leads the way in ultra-short contacts to 2D semiconductors. Furthermore, the MoS2, WS2 and WSe2 FETs with 1D semimetal contacts all exhibited high on/off ratio exceeding 106 and on-state current of several microampere, indicating the generality of SWCNT contacts. This work indicates that FETs composed of 1D semimetal contacts and 2D semiconductors are prospective for future integrated circuits in the post Moore’s law era.

## Results

### 1D semimetal contact

Figure [1a, b](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1) sketch the fabrication process of the 2D FETs with 1D semimetal contacts. The ultralong CNTs (centimeters in length) were grown with iron as catalyst and ethylene as carbon source by chemical vapor deposition (CVD)[45](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#ref-CR45 "Huang, L. et al. Cobalt ultrathin film catalyzed ethanol chemical vapor deposition of single-walled carbon nanotubes. J. Phys. Chem. B 110, 11103–11109 (2006)."),[46](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#ref-CR46 "Wang, X. et al. Fabrication of ultralong and electrically uniform single-walled carbon nanotubes on clean substrates. Nano Lett. 9, 3137–3141 (2009).") (Fig. [1a](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1)). Suspended CNTs were obtained across the trenches on patterned silicon wafer (Fig. [1b-i](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1)). Evaporated sulfur particles were deposited on the surface of CNTs to assist the optical imaging[47](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#ref-CR47 "Jian, M. et al. Volatile-nanoparticle-assisted optical visualization of individual carbon nanotubes and other nanomaterials. Nanoscale 8, 13437–13444 (2016).") and precise manipulation of CNTs under optical microscope, as shown in Fig. [1b-ii](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1) and Supplementary Fig. [1](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1). The entire individual ultralong CNT on Si substrate can be efficiently tracked with the optical microscope (Supplementary Movie [1](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM4)), and the metallic ones can be screened out in combination with resistance monitoring. Two suspending segments from a same metallic SWCNT across two neighboring trenches were picked by the W tips and then transferred onto a mechanically exfoliated 2D MoS2 in parallel as the source and drain electrodes, respectively (Fig. [1b-iii](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1)). The specimen was then annealed at 300 °C under 400 mTorr Ar atmosphere for 1 h to remove the sulfur particles while achieving clean and tight mixed-dimensional vdW interface. More comparative experiments have further verified that the sulfur-assisted transfer technique does not affect the transport properties of both SWCNT and MoS2, which can be found in Supplementary Note [1](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1) and Supplementary Figs. [5](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1), [6](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1). Finally, the patterned Ti/Au (5 nm/50 nm) electrodes were fabricated by using e-beam lithography, electron beam evaporation and lift off procedures (Fig. [1b-iv](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1)).

Further characterizations were performed on the as-fabricated device. The 1D–2D interface between the SWCNT and MoS2 was confirmed by a cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) image and the corresponding element spatial distribution captured by the electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS), as shown in Fig. [1c](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1). Figure [1d](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1) is a scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of such a device, in which the two parallel and straight bright lines are the metallic SWCNT electrodes. The two 1D contacts defined a rectangular channel for the MoS2 FET (orange dotted box). The electrodes in the blue and green dotted boxes were fabricated for further analysis on the interface contact resistivity. Figure [1e](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1) displays the Raman spectra of MoS2 and the two SWCNTs on Si/SiO2 substrate. More information about the Raman experiments can be found in Supplementary Fig. [4](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1). The CNTs exhibit the prominent radial breathing mode (*RBM*) peaks around 146 cm−1, verifying their single-walled structure and their same chirality. On Si/SiO2 substrate, the quantitative relationship between the *RBM* peak and SWCNT diameter can be expressed as \({\omega }\_{{{{{{\rm{RBM}}}}}}}=248/{d}\_{{{{{{\rm{CNT}}}}}}}\)[48](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#ref-CR48 "Jorio, A. et al. Structural (n, m) determination of isolated single-wall carbon nanotubes by resonant Raman scattering. Phys. Rev. Lett. 86, 1118–1121 (2001)."), and the diameter of CNT can be calculated to be 1.7 nm. The absence of *D* peak around 1350 cm−1 indicates the high quality of the CNT structure.

To present the geometry and electronic structures of the mixed-dimensional heterojunction, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed on a (5,5) CNT/MoS2 heterostructure. The junction atomic structure, differential charge density and electrostatic potential distribution are presented in Fig. [1f](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1). Comparative calculations were also conducted on a graphene/MoS2 heterojunction (Supplementary Fig. [7](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1)). As shown by the variation of the relative energy as a function of interlayer distance, the most stable structure shows a vdW gap of 3.06 Å for CNT/MoS2 and 3.42 Å for graphene/MoS2, respectively. The obviously small vdW gap of such 1D–2D junction can be attributed to CNT’s tubular structure. Since the tunneling probability of electrons decreases exponentially with the increase of barrier width, the smaller vdW gap indicates a smaller tunneling resistance. Figure [1g](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig1) shows projected density of states (PDOS) of the heterostructure. The small and nearly constant DOS endows the CNT with gate-tunable work function, and efficiently suppresses the MIGS in MoS2. Therefore, the gate-tunable SBH at the CNT/MoS2 interface can be predicted. Without external electrical field, the Fermi level of CNT is 0.35 eV lower than the conduction band (CB) edge of MoS2, indicating an *n*-type Schottky barrier. While with applied electrical field of 0.2 V/Å, the Ohmic contact can be achieved (Supplementary Fig. [9](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1)), the corresponding width *w*t and height *Φ*t of the potential barrier are calculated to be 1.87 Å and 4.03 eV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. [10](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1)). This contributes to a small tunnelling resistivity of 2.882 × 10−9 Ω·cm2 (see details in Supplementary Note [7](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1)). These results present the potential of 1D semimetal contact for 2D FETs.

### Electrical transport measurements

Electrical transport measurements indicate that the ultra-short contact length of such 1D semimetal contacts can achieve improved performances of 2D FETs. Comparative transistors were made on the same MoS2 flake with CNT contacts (smaller than 2 nm in diameter, electrodes A and B) and Ti/Au contacts (2 µm in contact length, electrodes 1 and 2), respectively. Transfer characteristics (black curve in Fig. [2a](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig2)) of the individual SWCNT (electrodes C and D) present a conduction current about 5 µA and on/off ratio less than 5 under a bias voltage of 0.1 V, revealing good metallicity. The four-layered (4 L) MoS2 transistor with CNT contacts exhibits n-type conduction with an on/off ratio exceeding 107 and on-state current of 4 µA, both of which are one order of magnitude larger than those of the device using Ti contacts. Supplementary Fig. [19](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1) also shows the better switching performance of CNT contacts by comparing the devices using CNT, Ni and Au contacts. The linear and symmetrical output characteristics (Fig. [2b](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig2)) indicate that Ohmic contact with negligible Schottky barrier can be acquired at the CNT-MoS2 interface under positive *V*g. In contrast, the *I*–*V* curves of the device using Ti contacts show obvious nonlinearity (Fig. [2c](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig2)), implying the presence of barriers. This can be further verified by temperature-dependent transfer characteristics. As temperature lowering, the on-current of CNT-MoS2 FET increases due to the enhanced mobility of MoS2, whereas the current of Ti- MoS2 FET decreases for the weakened thermal emission current (Fig. [2d](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig2)). Furthermore, the barrier heights \({\varPhi }\_{{{{{{\rm{B}}}}}}}\) at the CNT-MoS2 and Ti-MoS2 interfaces have been extracted as a function of *V*g from the slops of ln(*I*ds/*T*3/2) ~ *q*/*kT* (Fig. [2e](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig2)) following the 2D thermal emission theory[10](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#ref-CR10 "Yu, L. et al. Graphene/MoS2 hybrid technology for large-scale two-dimensional electronics. Nano Lett. 14, 3055–3063 (2014)."), and the results are presented in Fig. [2f](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig2). It can be seen that the \({\varPhi }\_{{{{{{\rm{B}}}}}}}\) at CNT-MoS2 interface changes significantly in the lower *V*g regime and the tuning efficiency of the barrier decreases at higher *V*g. In comparison, the barrier height at CNT-MoS2 interface can be modulated more efficiently than that at Ti-MoS2 interface. Ohmic contact can be achieved for the CNT contact at *V*g = 35 V, where the barrier height drops to 0. The FET composed of monolayer (1L) MoS2 behaves similarly, which can be found in the Supplementary Fig. [13](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1).

### LTLM and extraction of contact resistance

The contact resistance *R*c (Ω·µm) is a critical parameter for quantitative evaluation of the 1D semimetal contact. It is a combination of the interface contact resistivity \({r}\_{{{{{{\rm{c}}}}}}}\) (Ω·cm2) and the channel sheet resistivity \({\rho }\_{{{{{{\rm{TMD}}}}}}}^{2{{{{{\rm{D}}}}}}}\) (Ω·☐−1) for 3D or 2D metal contacts according to the conventional transmission line model. In the case of the 1D semimetal contact, the current is efficiently injected into the channel (Supplementary Fig. [16e](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1)), and the contact resistance in short contact limit should be expressed as \({R}\_{{{{{{\rm{c}}}}}}}={r}\_{{{{{{\rm{c}}}}}}}/{l}\_{{{{{{\rm{c}}}}}}}\) (see details in Supplementary Note [7](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1)). The contact length \({l}\_{{{{{{\rm{c}}}}}}}\) is defined as the diameter of CNT (the feature size of contact geometry).

Due to the micron-scale 2D FET device size (on the same order of magnitude as the mean free path of electrons in metallic SWCNT), the resistance of CNT electrodes is not negligible, and the potential/current distribution in the channel is not uniform. Thus, the commonly used four-probe method or transfer length method is not applicable for the measurement of the 1D contact resistance. Considering the symmetric conditions of our devices, an LTLM can be developed to describe the potential and current distribution of devices in short contact limit (details can be found in Supplementary Note [6](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#MOESM1)). The 1D–2D heterostructure can be modeled as a resistor network, as sketched in Fig. [3a](/articles/s41467-022-35760-x#Fig3). The total resistance of the device \({R}\_{{{{{{\rm{tot}}}}}}}\) (two-probe resistance between Source and Drain) includes three parts in series: the contact resistance \({R}\_{1}\) between CNT and Ti, the interconnect resistance \({R}\_{2}\) of the CNT wires on SiO2 substrate, and the resistance \({R}\_{3}\) of the heterostructure region. They can be expressed as:

$${R}\_{{{{{{\rm{tot}}}}}}}={R}\_{1}+{R}\_{2}+{R}\_{3}$$

(1)

where \({R}\_{1}=2{R}\_{{nc}}^{{{{{{\rm{CNT}}}}}}}+{R}\_{{{{{{\rm{Q}}}}}}}^{{{{{{\rm{CNT}}}}}}}\), \({R}\_{2}=2{\rho }\_{{{{{{\rm{CNT}}}}}}}^{{{{{{\rm{on}}}}}}\,{{{{{\rm{Si}}}}}}{{{{{{\rm{O}}}}}}}\_{2}}{L}\_{{{{{{\rm{in}}}}}}}\), \({R}\_{3}={R}\_{{{{{{\rm{H}}}}}}}+{R}\_{{{{{{\rm{Q}}}}}}}^{{{{{{\rm{CNT}}}}}}}\). \({R}\_{{{{{{\rm{Q}}}}}}}^{{{{{{\rm{CNT}}}}}}}\), \({R}\_{{{{{{\rm{nc}}}}}}}^{{{{{{\rm{CNT}}}}}}}\), \({\rho }\_{{{{{{\rm{CNT}}}}}}}^{{{{{{\rm{on}}}}}}\,{{{{{\rm{Si}}}}}}{{{{{{\rm{O}}}}}}}\_{2}}\), \({L}\_{{{{{{\rm{in}}}}}}}\) is the quantum resistance of CNT, the interfacial resistance between CNT and Ti, the resistivity of the CNT wire, and the interconnect length of CNT wire, respectively. \({R}\_{{{{{{\rm{H}}}}}}}\) is the equivalent resistance of the heterostructure:

$${R}\_{{{{{{\rm{H}}}}}}}=\sqrt{2{R}\_{{{{{{\rm{t}}}}}}}{\rho }\_{{{{{{\rm{l}}}}}}}}/\left(1-{{{{{{\rm{e}}}}}}}^{-\frac{W}{{L}\_{T}}}\right)$$

(2)

Therefore, good contacts can be accessed for a variety of device design requirements including the threshold voltage and conduction type by employing semiconductors with different band edge positions. ## Discussion

In summary, we report the 1D semimetal contacts to 2D semiconductors, which successfully reduce the contact length to sub-2 nm. The FETs with such 1D contacts exhibited enhanced performance. The potential and current distribution of devices in short contact limit was modeled by the as-proposed LTLM and the 1D–2D interface contact resistivity was thus measured as low as 10−6 Ω·cm2. The low contact resistance can be attributed to the formation of Ohmic contact and the smaller vdW gap at the 1D-2D interface. The SWCNTs demonstrated their ability to form good contact with various semiconductors, which strongly supports the miniaturization of low-power electronic devices and the extending of Moore’s Law in the future.

## Methods

### Synthesis of ultralong CNT

The ultralong CNTs are grown using a CVD system. The catalyst strips are prepared by electron beam deposition of 0.2 nm Fe onto the silicon substrate and then slicing. The furnace temperature is set to 970 °C for CNT growth. The H2 and C2H4 with flow rate of 200 sccm and 1 sccm are selected as reducing gas and carbon source, respectively. A pre-prepared Si/SiNx substrate with seven 200 μm-wide trenches is placed behind the catalyst strip to collect the CNTs grown in suspension. args.summary:
This is a scientific article published in Nature Communications (volume 14, article number 111, 2023) reporting on the development of one-dimensional (1D) semimetal contacts to two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors for field-effect transistors (FETs).

**Key Findings:**
- The researchers constructed 1D semimetal-2D semiconductor contacts using individual metallic single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) as electrodes, pushing contact length into the sub-2 nm region.
- These 1D-2D heterostructures exhibit smaller van der Waals gaps (3.06 Å for CNT/MoS2 vs 3.42 Å for graphene/MoS2) than 2D-2D ones, and the Schottky barrier height can be effectively tuned via gate potential to achieve Ohmic contact.
- A longitudinal transmission line model (LTLM) was developed to analyze potential and current distribution in short contact limit, extracting 1D-2D contact resistivity as low as 10^-6 Ω·cm² and contact resistance of 50 kΩ·μm for ultra-short contacts.

**Methodology:**
- Ultralong CNTs (centimeters in length) were grown by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) with iron catalyst and ethylene as carbon source at 970°C.
- Sulfur particle deposition assisted optical imaging and precise manipulation of CNTs.
- Two segments from the same metallic SWCNT were transferred onto exfoliated 2D materials (MoS2, WS2, WSe2) as source/drain electrodes, followed by annealing at 300°C.
- DFT calculations on (5,5) CNT/MoS2 heterostructures confirmed the small vdW gap and gate-tunable Schottky barrier.

**Results:**
- MoS2 FETs with CNT contacts showed n-type conduction with on/off ratio exceeding 10^7 and on-state current of 4 µA, one order of magnitude better than Ti-contact devices.
- Ohmic contact was achieved at Vg = 35V where barrier height drops to zero.
- All three channel materials (MoS2, WS2, WSe2) exhibited on/off ratios exceeding 10^6 and on-state currents of several microamperes.
- Field-effect mobilities were 85.9 cm²/V·s (4L MoS2) and 69.3 cm²/V·s (1L MoS2).
- The theoretical tunneling resistivity is 2.882×10^-9 Ω·cm², suggesting potential for further reduction to 419 Ω·µm contact resistance.

**Significance:**
This work demonstrates that 1D semimetal contacts using individual SWCNTs are a promising solution for the ultimate scaling of 2D transistors, overcoming the sharp rise in contact resistance and deteriorated metal conductivity at nanoscale that plagues conventional 3D/2D metal contacts, supporting future miniaturization of nanoelectronics and extending Moore's Law.

The paper reports viable edge contact formation to hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)-encapsulated monolayer MoS2, achieving relatively low edge contact resistance, high mobility, and high on-current density comparable to top contacts. # Making electrical contact along 1-D edge of 2-D materials

Date:
:   October 31, 2013

Source:
:   City College of New York

Summary:
:   Scientists have demonstrated it is possible for an atomically thin two-dimensional material to have electrical contact along its one-dimensional edge. The contact architecture offers a new assembly technique for layered materials that prevents contamination at interfaces.

Share:
:   [Facebook](#) [Twitter](#) [Pinterest](#) [LinkedIN](#) [Email](#)

FULL STORY

---

Dr. Cory Dean, assistant professor of physics at The City College of New York, is the lead author of a paper published today in the journal *Science* that demonstrates it is possible for an atomically thin two-dimensional (2D) material to have electrical contact along its one-dimensional (1D) edge. The contact architecture offers a new assembly technique for layered materials that prevents contamination at interfaces.

Professor Dean conducted the research as a postdoctoral fellow at Columbia University, working with Professor of Electrical Engineering Ken Shepard and Professor of Mechanical Engineering James Hone, the paper's co-authors. The new method, which was developed using graphene as the two-dimensional model, resulted in the cleanest graphene produced to date.

"Two-dimensional materials such as graphene, which are just one atom thick, can have their electrical properties externally modified," Professor Dean said. "However, because the materials are extremely sensitive to the environment, any external contamination quickly degrades performance."

The need to protect the material from contamination while still allowing electrical access has been a roadblock to development of graphene-based technologies, he added. "By making contact only to the 1D edge of graphene, we have developed a fundamentally new way to bridge our 3D world to this fascinating 2D world without disturbing its inherent properties. This virtually eliminates external contamination and finally allows graphene to show its true potential in electronic devices."

"Our novel edge-contact geometry provides more efficient contact than the conventional geometry without the need for further complex processing," added Professor Shepard. "There are now many more possibilities in the pursuit of both device applications and the pure physics of clean systems."

The researchers fully encapsulated the 2D graphene layer in a sandwich of thin insulating boron nitride crystals. To do this, they employed a new technique in which the top boron nitride crystal was used to sequentially pick up the other layers in the stack. "This technique completely eliminated any contamination between layers," Professor Dean noted.

Once they created the stack, they etched it to expose the edge of the graphene layer. Then they evaporated metal onto the edge to create the electrical contact. By making contact along the edge, the team realized a 1D interface between the 2D active layer and 3D metal electrode.

Even though electrons entered only at the 1D atomic edge of the graphene sheet, the contact resistance was remarkably low, reaching 100 ohms per micron of contact width -- a value smaller than what is typically achieved for contacts at the graphene top surface.

Continuing their collaboration, the team is now working on applying these techniques to develop new hybrid materials by mechanical assembly and edge contact. They plan to draw from the full suite of available 2D layered materials, including graphene, boron nitride, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), transition metal oxides (TMOs), and topological insulators (TIs).

"With so much current research focused on developing new devices by integrating layered 2D systems, potential applications are incredible, from vertically structured transistors, tunneling based devices and sensors, photoactive hybrid materials, to flexible and transparent electronics," added Professor Hone.

This ScienceDaily article (dated October 31, 2013) reports on a breakthrough in graphene-based electronics research led by Dr. Cory Dean, assistant professor of physics at The City College of New York, published in the journal Science. The team demonstrated that it is possible to make electrical contact along the one-dimensional (1D) edge of an atomically thin two-dimensional (2D) material, rather than on its top surface. This new edge-contact architecture offers a fundamentally new assembly technique for layered materials that prevents contamination at interfaces.

Key details:
- The research was conducted by Dean as a postdoctoral fellow at Columbia University, with co-authors Professor Ken Shepard (Electrical Engineering) and Professor James Hone (Mechanical Engineering).
- Using graphene (just one atom thick) as the 2D model, the method produced the cleanest graphene to date.
- The researchers fully encapsulated the graphene layer in a sandwich of thin insulating boron nitride crystals, using a technique where the top boron nitride crystal sequentially picked up the other layers, completely eliminating inter-layer contamination.
- The stack was etched to expose the graphene edge, and metal was evaporated onto the edge to create the electrical contact, forming a 1D interface between the 2D active layer and 3D metal electrode.
- Despite electrons entering only at the 1D atomic edge, contact resistance was remarkably low, reaching 100 ohms per micron of contact width — smaller than typical contacts at the graphene top surface.
- The team plans to apply this technique to develop new hybrid materials from the full suite of 2D layered materials: graphene, boron nitride, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), transition metal oxides (TMOs), and topological insulators (TIs).
- Potential applications include vertically structured transistors, tunneling-based devices, sensors, photoactive hybrid materials, and flexible/transparent electronics.
- Journal reference: L. Wang et al., "One-Dimensional Electrical Contact to a Two-Dimensional Material," Science, 2013; 342 (6158): 614. DOI: 10.1126/science.1244358.
- The article also includes a related story about "New Techniques Produce Cleanest Graphene Yet" from the same date.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Contact Resistance Optimization in MoS2 Field-Effect Transistors through Reverse Sputtering-Induced Structural Modifications ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12022942

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces (March 11, 2025) by researchers from AMO GmbH, RWTH Aachen University, Eindhoven University of Technology, and AIXTRON SE. The study investigates the use of reverse sputtering (Ar+ ion bombardment via RF-generated plasma) to reduce contact resistance (Rc) in molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) field-effect transistors (FETs).

Key findings and methodology:
- MoS₂ FETs suffer from Schottky barriers at the metal-MoS₂ interface, causing high contact resistance. The study explores inducing a phase transition from semiconducting 2H-MoS₂ to metallic 1T-MoS₂ via reverse sputtering at the contact interface.
- Multilayer MOCVD-grown MoS₂ (~2.5 nm thick, ~4 layers) was transferred onto SiO₂/Si substrates. Devices were fabricated with nickel (Ni) top-contacts (TOP-FETs) where only the contact regions were sputter-treated, and bottom-contact (BOT-FETs) control devices where the entire MoS₂ was exposed.
- Characterization via PL, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS confirmed that reverse sputtering induces sulfur vacancies (VS) and a 2H-to-1T phase transition in MoS₂. XPS showed the S/Mo ratio decreasing from ~2.0 (pristine) to 1.80 (200 W treatment), with full 2H-to-1T conversion observed after sputtering.
- Optimal results were achieved at 75 W reverse sputtering for 10 s: Rc decreased from 1126 kΩ·μm (pristine) to 413 kΩ·μm (a reduction to less than 50% of untreated devices), and output current increased approximately 150-fold.
- Two-probe mobility (μ₂ₚ) nearly doubled for the 75 W sample (0.81 ± 0.20 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ vs. 0.48 ± 0.10 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ for pristine). On/off ratios of 10⁶ were maintained for pristine, 25 W, and 75 W samples, degrading to 10⁵ at 200 W.
- Excessive sputtering power (200 W) caused oxidation to MoOₓ and severe degradation. Insufficient power (25 W) produced too few sulfur vacancies and increased Rc. The 75 W condition represented the optimal balance between phase conversion and material damage.
- The mechanism involves sulfur vacancies creating heavily n-doped regions that narrow the Schottky barrier, plus the formation of conductive 1T-MoS₂ that enhances electron injection from Ni contacts.

The authors conclude that reverse sputtering is a scalable, CMOS-compatible, and clean method for optimizing contact resistance in MoS₂ FETs, with potential for broader application in 2D material-based microelectronics. Funding was provided by EU Horizon 2020/Horizon Europe programs, German BMBF projects (NEUROTEC, NEUROTEC 2, NeuroSys), and the German Research Foundation (DFG).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"MoS₂–FETs exposed to optimized reverse sputtering conditions in the contact area show Rc values reduced to less than 50% of their untreated counterparts."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Semimetal contacts to monolayer semiconductor ---
URL: http://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023JPhD...56w4001S/abstract

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper (published in Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics, June 2023) investigating electrical contact properties between semimetal electrodes (bismuth and antimony) and monolayer 2D transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) semiconductors. The study used first-principles density functional theory (DFT) simulations on six TMDC semiconductors (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2, MoTe2, and WTe2) with two semimetal contact materials (Bi and Sb).

Key findings:
- Bi and Sb work functions align well with TMDC conduction band edges, resulting in predominantly Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts.
- Semimetal/TMDC contacts have significantly larger interlayer distances than metal/TMDC counterparts, leading to only weak metalization of TMDC upon contact formation.
- This weak metalization generates semimetal-induced gap states (SMIGSs) extending below the conduction band minimum, providing an effective mechanism to reduce or eliminate n-type Schottky barrier height (SBH) while preserving the electronic structures of the 2D TMDC.
- The authors propose a modified Schottky-Mott rule accounting for SMIGS, interface dipole potential, and Fermi level shifting, which shows improved agreement with DFT-simulated SBH.
- Sb/TMDC contacts generally exhibit lower tunneling-specific resistivity than Bi counterparts, indicating better charge injection efficiency with Sb contacts.
- The findings highlight Bi and Sb as promising companion electrode materials for advancing 2D semiconductor device technology.

Paper details: Authors include Su Tong, Li Yueyan, Wang Qianqian, Zhao Weiwei, Cao Liemao, and Ang Yee Sin. DOI: 10.1088/1361-6463/acc53f; arXiv:2212.03003; 12 pages, 7 figures.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"As Bi and Sb work functions energetically aligns well with the TMDC conduction band edge, Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts are prevalent."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: [PDF] arXiv:2212.03003v1 [cond-mat.mtrl-sci] 6 Dec 2022 ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.03003

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) study investigating the electrical contact properties between semimetal electrodes (bismuth, Bi, and antimony, Sb) and six monolayer transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) semiconductors (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2, MoTe2, WTe2), covering 12 semimetal/TMDC contact heterostructures.

Key findings:
- Recent experiments showed semimetal Bi achieves ultralow contact resistance (as low as 123 Ω·µm) with monolayer MoS2, motivating broader investigation of semimetal contacts.
- The Fermi levels of Bi (-4.12 eV) and Sb (-4.25 eV below vacuum) align closely with TMDC conduction band edges (~4 eV), enabling Ohmic or nearly-Ohmic n-type contacts.
- Semimetal/TMDC contacts have significantly larger interlayer distances (>3 Å) than metal/TMDC counterparts, resulting in only weak metalization of the TMDC upon contact formation.
- This weak metalization creates semimetal-induced gap states (SMIGS) that extend below the conduction band minimum, providing an effective mechanism to reduce or eliminate n-type Schottky barrier height (SBH) while preserving TMDC electronic structures.
- A modified Schottky-Mott rule was proposed: Φ(e)SBH = Wmetal − EEA − ΔV + ΔεF − ΔM, incorporating interface dipole potential (ΔV), Fermi level shifting (ΔεF), and the SMIGS energy window (ΔM), showing significantly improved agreement with DFT-simulated SBH compared to the original Schottky-Mott rule.
- Contacts exhibit both physisorptive (Te-based TMDCs, larger interlayer distances, positive ΔV) and chemisorptive (S- and Se-based TMDCs, smaller interlayer distances, low/negative ΔV) interfacial interactions.
- Sb/TMDC contacts generally exhibit lower tunneling-specific resistivity (10^-9 Ω·cm² order) than Bi counterparts, suggesting better charge injection efficiency and better thermal stability, making Sb a potentially superior semimetal contact material.
- DFT-calculated SBHs for Bi/MoS2 (0.075 eV) and Bi/WS2 (0.13 eV) differ slightly from experimental values (zero/Ohmic and 0.040 eV, respectively), likely due to defects in experimental contacted regions.
- Computational methods: VASP with projector augmented wave method, PBE-GGA exchange-correlation, DFT-D3 vdW corrections, 500 eV kinetic energy cutoff, 6×6×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-sampling, and ≥15 Å vacuum spacing.

The work provides a theoretical foundation and design blueprint for semimetal-enabled high-performance 2D semiconductor nanoelectronics, with potential applications in valleytronics and multiferroics. Funding came from the Singapore Ministry of Education Academic Research Fund Tier 2 Grant and SUTD-ZJU IDEA Visiting Professor Grant.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Recent experiment has uncovered semimetal bismuth (Bi) as an excellent electrical contact to monolayer MoS2 with ultralow contact resistance."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Antimony Semimetal Contact with Enhanced Thermal ... ---
URL: https://hanwang6.github.io/Lab_Website/iedm_2021.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (IEDM 2021, DOI: 10.1109/IEDM19574.2021.9720608) from TSMC researchers studies antimony (Sb) semimetal as a novel contact material for two-dimensional (2D) MoS2 electronics, addressing the thermal stability limitations of previously studied semimetals like tin (Sn) and bismuth (Bi).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Sb contacts achieve near-zero Schottky barrier height and contact resistance of 0.66 kΩ·µm on monolayer (1L) MoS2
- Short-channel Sb-contacted MoS2 FETs demonstrate on-state current above 600 µA/µm at VDS=1V and 1000 µA/µm at VDS=2V
- Sb has a melting point of 630.6°C, substantially higher than Bi (271.5°C) and Sn (231.9°C)
- Sb-contacted devices remain fully operational after annealing at 400°C, versus only 300°C for Bi-contacted devices—a key advantage for back-end-of-the-line (BEOL) compatibility
- Sb-contacted 1L MoS2 FET retains 80% and 64% of pristine performance after annealing at 300°C and 400°C, respectively
- Bi-contacted devices decay significantly after 300°C annealing and fail completely at 400°C
- LCH=50nm devices show ION ~600 µA/µm at VDS=1V with nearly zero drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL)

METHODOLOGY:
- 1L MoS2 grown by CVD, transferred onto 100nm SiNx/Si substrate
- He-ion-beam lithography for S/D patterning; 20nm semimetal (Bi or Sb) capped with 15nm Au via e-beam evaporation and lift-off
- PMMA encapsulation with 200°C hard baking for 30 min in N2 glovebox
- Progressive thermal annealing at 200°C, 300°C, and 400°C
- Characterization via Raman spectroscopy, AFM, TEM, EDS mapping, UPS
- DFT simulations (VASP with PBE/PAW/GGA) for interface analysis and Bi-Sb alloy predictions

ALLOY STRATEGY (DFT-predicted):
- Bi-Sb alloy could balance thermal stability and low contact resistance
- BEOL compatibility requires melting point ≥400°C, needing >20% Sb ratio
- Preferred design space: 40%-100% Sb ratio (alloy remains semimetal; 4%-40% Sb makes it a semiconductor/topological insulator)
- Bi0.5Sb0.5 predicted to offer lower barrier height (0.10 eV) than pure Sb while maintaining good conductivity and 540°C melting point

CONCLUSION: Sb semimetal offers the best balance of thermal stability and low contact resistance among semimetals for 2D electronics, making it a promising BEOL-compatible contact solution for beyond-silicon technology. Funding from Ministry of Science and Technology (Grants MOST-109-2622-8-002-003; MOST 110-2119-M-A49-001-MBK).
</summary>

"Sb semimetal is studied as the contact metal for 2D materials for the first time, demonstrating one of the lowest contact resistance among previously reported approaches for MoS2 only second to Bi."

SUMMARY:

This webpage from Physics World (IOP Publishing) features a scientific article about reducing contact resistance in 2D semiconducting transistors. The article reports that researchers in the US, Korea, and Singapore have developed high-performance field-effect transistors (FETs) made from monolayer molybdenum disulphide (MoS2) films with atomically thin graphene bottom gates. The devices achieve a low contact resistance of just 2.3 kΩ·μm between MoS2 and nickel electrodes, excellent switching characteristics, and high channel conductance (over 100 μS/μm). Devices were made with channel lengths as short as 50 and 14 nm with a 5-nm gate dielectric, showing near-ideal subthreshold slope of 64 mV/decade, low threshold voltage (~0.5 V), and no significant performance degradation at 14 nm channel lengths. The research was published in Nano Letters. The page also includes Physics World site navigation, related articles, job listings, and podcast links.

Corresponding authors are Iuliana P. Radu (TSMC) and Chao-Hsin Chien (NYCU).

**Core Problem:** Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are promising for advanced nanoelectronics due to atomically thin bodies enabling excellent electrostatic control. However, achieving low contact resistance (RC) requires semimetals like bismuth (Bi) or antimony (Sb), which have low melting points and are thermally unstable, limiting their compatibility with back-end-of-line (BEOL) integration that requires annealing at 400°C in H2 environments. Refractory metals are thermally stable but induce prohibitively high RC (>1 kΩ·μm).

**Key Innovation:** The authors demonstrate a "confinement strategy" using AlOx and/or TiN barriers to encapsulate Bi contacts. This enables RC values below 200 Ω·μm while preserving device performance after forming gas annealing at 400°C for up to 10 minutes.

**Key Findings:**
- Unconfined Bi melts at ~273°C and forms spherical droplets when annealed; Sb rapidly sublimates at 400°C in forming gas within 1 minute.
- AlOx capping stabilizes Sb films up to 800°C (above its 671°C melting point) and Bi up to 450°C without outgassing, melting, or agglomeration.
- Device-level demonstration: Monolayer CVD MoS2 transistors with Bi contacts on 8 nm HfO2 gate dielectric (EOT~2nm) with TiN back gate, fully encapsulated in low-temperature ALD AlOx. After 400°C forming gas annealing (10 min), devices retained RC below 200 Ω·μm with nearly ohmic injection and ION over 60 μA/μm at LCH=100 nm.
- On-current after line-resistance subtraction exceeds 1 mA/μm at VDS=1V, ranking among the highest reported for monolayer MoS2.
- Intrinsic mobility improved slightly from 27 to 32 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹ after annealing (attributed to partial defect passivation).
- TCAD simulations extracted Schottky barrier height of 70 meV and van der Waals gap of 2 Å at the MoS2/Bi interface, confirming near-ohmic contact that did not degrade through annealing.
- Fab-relevant integration test: Bi deposited by PVD in SiO2 trenches (<40 nm wide), encapsulated by conformal 200°C ALD TiN barrier and W plug. Cross-sectional TEM/EDX confirmed Bi remains fully confined without diffusion or outgassing after 400°C annealing in N2, forming gas, and vacuum environments.
- A remaining grand challenge identified: selective dielectric etch that stops on 2D TMDs (to be addressed in subsequent publications).

**Keywords:** two-dimensional semiconductors, semimetal contacts, contact resistance, back-end-of-line (BEOL) integration, monolithic 3D integration, thermal stability
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Low contact resistance on monolayer MoS2 field-effect ... ---
URL: https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10531719

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article from ACS Nano (Manuscript ID nn-2024-07267z.R3, submitted 29-Jul-2024) by researchers from Purdue University and the University of Texas at Dallas, led by Zheng Sun, Seong Yeoul Kim, and Joerg Appenzeller. The study investigates contact engineering for monolayer MoS2 field-effect transistors (FETs) to achieve low contact resistance using CMOS-compatible metal contacts.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Ni Contacts (Covalent Type):** Ultra-high vacuum (UHV, 3×10^-11 mbar) deposited Ni contacts achieved a record-low contact resistance of ~500 ohm·μm for ML MoS2 FETs — 5 times lower than Ni deposited under high vacuum (HV, 3×10^-6 mbar) conditions. This was achieved across 60 UHV-Ni and 64 HV-Ni FETs fabricated with four channel lengths (85nm, 185nm, 385nm, 985nm) using the transfer length method (TLM). The best UHV-Ni device reached 470 μA/μm at VDS=1V, VGS=2.5V.

2. **Bi Contacts (van der Waals Type):** Contact resistance for Bi-contacted MoS2 FETs showed no dependence on vacuum deposition conditions (more than 150 Bi-contacted FETs tested: 40 UHV-Bi and 112 HV-Bi). Bi achieves high on-currents (~400 μA/μm) with on/off ratios of ~10^8, but does not chemically react with MoS2 regardless of vacuum conditions.

3. **Interface Chemistry (XPS Analysis):**
   - UHV-Ni deposition showed stronger Ni/MoSx bonding species (20% intensity vs 17% for HV-Ni) with more metallic properties
   - HV-Ni deposition resulted in MoO3 formation (thermodynamically favored due to ΔG°f,MoO3=-266.67 kJ/mol vs ΔG°f,MoS2=-112.95 kJ/mol), reducing Ni-MoS2 bonding
   - Bi showed no detectable chemical reaction with MoS2 under either condition; Bi2O3 was detected only for HV deposition
   - Thermodynamic data support these observations (ΔG°f,Bi2S3=-46.87 kJ/mol, higher than ΔG°f,MoS2)

4. **Thermal Stability:**
   - Bi/Au contacts showed excellent thermal reliability up to 400°C with no contact resistance degradation (Au capping prevented Bi evaporation; annealing in high vacuum prevented oxidation). This contrasts with prior reports of degradation at 200°C.
   - Ni contacts degraded after 100°C annealing (on-current dropped from 200 to 125 μA/μm; contact resistance increased from 2000 to 3000 ohm·μm), attributed to Ni diffusion into the channel and oxidation of diffused Ni
   - Bi remained concentrated at contact corners after 400°C annealing without chemical reaction with MoS2

**Methods:** CVD-grown ML MoS2 on SiO2 substrates, local bottom gate structures with HfO2 dielectrics (2.8nm and 5.5nm), e-beam lithography, monochromatic XPS (Al Kα, 1486.7 eV), STEM/EDS analysis, and annealing at 100-400°C in high vacuum.

**Conclusion:** The work demonstrates that interface engineering through UHV deposition of covalent-type metals (Ni) can achieve competitive contact resistance (~500 ohm·μm) comparable to vdW-type contacts, while Bi contacts offer superior thermal stability but no dependence on deposition vacuum conditions. --- SOURCE 2: Stable and scalable 1T MoS2 with low temperature-coefficient of resistance | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-30867-y

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Scientific Reports (volume 8, article number 12463, 2018) by Chithra H. Sharma, Ananthu P. Surendran, Abin Varghese, and Madhu Thalakulam. The paper demonstrates a controllable and scalable method for engineering the metallic 1T phase of MoS2 from the semiconducting 2H phase using forming-gas (10% H2 + 90% Ar) microwave plasma treatment on mechanically exfoliated samples. 

Key methodology and results:
- The technique allows lithographically defining 1T regions on 2H samples using aluminum masking, enabling monolithic integration of metallic and semiconducting phases.
- HR-TEM analysis confirmed extended 1T regions with areal coverage exceeding 70% over the 2H phase, with no signatures of distorted phases (1T′ or 1T″). The nearest Mo-Mo separation was measured at 3.19 Å.
- Raman spectroscopy showed characteristic J1, J2, and J3 peaks of the 1T phase, accompanied by photoluminescence quenching indicative of metallic phase formation. A new peak at 180 cm⁻¹ not previously reported was also observed.
- The phase transition occurs via gliding of Mo and S planes, induced by momentum transfer from plasma ions.
- Stability: 1T samples showed temporal stability exceeding 27-30 days at ambient conditions and thermal stability up to 300°C, well above standard device fabrication temperatures.
- Electrical transport: Two-probe and four-probe measurements on back-gated FET geometry from 4K to 300K showed Ohmic I-V characteristics with no gate voltage dependence (signature of metallic state). The 2H regions showed Schottky behavior and n-type FET characteristics with mobility of 16.4 cm²/V-s at 300K and 84 cm²/V-s at 4K.
- Extracted parameters for the 1T phase: sheet resistance of 108 Ω/□, carrier concentration of ~2.3 × 10¹⁵ cm⁻² (two orders of magnitude higher than 2H MoS2), and temperature coefficient of resistance α = −1.1057 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ (negligible temperature dependence from 4K to 300K).
- The sample satisfies the Ioffe-Regal criterion (kF·l ~ 239) confirming metallic conduction, ruling out hopping-mediated or activated transport.
- Stability verified over ~90 days post-processing (including ~30 days in ambient conditions) with minimal resistance variation.

The conclusion states this method enables extended, low-disorder 1T regions suitable for monolithic 2D circuits, unlike prior methods (intercalation, electron-beam irradiation, argon plasma) that yielded nanoscale patches or unstable phases.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The 1T samples show excellent temporal and thermal stability making it suitable for standard device fabrication techniques... The 1T samples exhibit Ohmic current-voltage characteristics in all temperature ranges without any dependence to the gate voltage, a signature of a metallic state."

--- SOURCE 3: Contact Resistance Optimization in MoS2 Field-Effect ... - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12022942

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces (March 11, 2025) by researchers from AMO GmbH, RWTH Aachen University, Eindhoven University of Technology, and AIXTRON SE. The study investigates the use of reverse sputtering (Ar+ ion bombardment via RF-generated plasma) to reduce contact resistance (Rc) in molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) field-effect transistors (FETs).

Key findings and methodology:
- MoS₂ FETs suffer from Schottky barriers at the metal-MoS₂ interface, causing high contact resistance. The study explores inducing a phase transition from semiconducting 2H-MoS₂ to metallic 1T-MoS₂ via reverse sputtering at the contact interface.
- Multilayer MOCVD-grown MoS₂ (~2.5 nm thick, ~4 layers) was transferred onto SiO₂/Si substrates. Devices were fabricated with nickel (Ni) top-contacts (TOP-FETs) where only the contact regions were sputter-treated, and bottom-contact (BOT-FETs) control devices where the entire MoS₂ was exposed.
- Characterization via PL, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS confirmed that reverse sputtering induces sulfur vacancies (VS) and a 2H-to-1T phase transition in MoS₂. XPS showed the S/Mo ratio decreasing from ~2.0 (pristine) to 1.80 (200 W treatment), with full 2H-to-1T conversion observed after sputtering.
- Optimal results were achieved at 75 W reverse sputtering for 10 s: Rc decreased from 1126 kΩ·μm (pristine) to 413 kΩ·μm (a reduction to less than 50% of untreated devices), and output current increased approximately 150-fold.
- Two-probe mobility (μ₂ₚ) nearly doubled for the 75 W sample (0.81 ± 0.20 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ vs. 0.48 ± 0.10 cm²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹ for pristine). On/off ratios of 10⁶ were maintained for pristine, 25 W, and 75 W samples, degrading to 10⁵ at 200 W.
- Excessive sputtering power (200 W) caused oxidation to MoOₓ and severe degradation. Insufficient power (25 W) produced too few sulfur vacancies and increased Rc. The 75 W condition represented the optimal balance between phase conversion and material damage.
- The mechanism involves sulfur vacancies creating heavily n-doped regions that narrow the Schottky barrier, plus the formation of conductive 1T-MoS₂ that enhances electron injection from Ni contacts.

The authors conclude that reverse sputtering is a scalable, CMOS-compatible, and clean method for optimizing contact resistance in MoS₂ FETs, with potential for broader application in 2D material-based microelectronics. Funding was provided by EU Horizon 2020/Horizon Europe programs, German BMBF projects (NEUROTEC, NEUROTEC 2, NeuroSys), and the German Research Foundation (DFG).
</summary>

"MoS₂–FETs exposed to optimized reverse sputtering conditions in the contact area show Rc values reduced to less than 50% of their untreated counterparts."

--- SOURCE 4: Researchers find a way to reduce contact resistance with molybdenum disulphide nanosheets ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Researchers from Rutgers University and Los Alamos National Laboratory have developed a method to reduce contact resistance in molybdenum disulphide (MoS2) nanosheets, a promising material for next-generation computer chips. Published in Nature Materials (September 5, 2014, DOI: 10.1038/nmat4080), the team developed a "lithiation" process that phase-shifts the semiconducting 2H phase of MoS2 into the metallic 1T phase by exposing it to n-butyl lithium. This enables wires to be easily connected to a fully conducting metallic contact, overcoming the high-resistance problem (0.7 kΩ μm–10 kΩ μm) typically caused when metals are deposited on the 2H phase.

Key results from the study include:
- Contact resistances decreased to 200–300 Ω μm at zero gate bias with 1T phase electrodes.
- Field-effect transistors (FETs) fabricated and tested in air exhibited mobility values of ~50 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.
- Subthreshold swing values below 100 mV per decade.
- On/off ratios of >10⁷ and drive currents approaching ~100 μA μm⁻¹ with excellent current saturation.
- The deposition of different metals had limited influence on FET performance, suggesting the 1T/2H interface controls carrier injection.
- Increased reproducibility of electrical characteristics was achieved through this phase-engineering strategy.

Remaining challenges include accurately phase-shifting only the desired portion of a sheet and the metastable nature of MoS2, which tends to revert to its semiconductor phase under certain (not yet fully understood) conditions. Possible solutions being explored include producing MoS2 flakes via exfoliation or chemical vapor deposition.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article describing a novel one-step hydrothermal method to synthesize 1T-dominant MoS2 nanosheets with long-term ambient stability for efficient electrocatalytic (hydrogen evolution reaction, HER) applications. The key innovation is the use of hydrazine hydrate (N2H4·H2O) as an intercalating agent that serves as an electron donor to stabilize the metallic 1T phase.

**Background:** Metallic 1T-phase MoS2 exhibits superior HER performance compared to the natural 2H phase due to higher electrical conductivity and more active sites, but previously reported 1T-MoS2 catalysts suffered from extreme instability, transforming back to 2H within ~2 hours at room temperature.

**Methods:** Samples were synthesized via hydrothermal treatment at 180°C for 48 hours using ammonium heptamolybdate and thioacetamide, with varying N2H4:Mo molar ratios (0:1, 1:1, 4:1, 12:1), producing samples labeled MoS2-0HZ, MoS2-1HZ, MoS2-4HZ, and MoS2-12HZ. Characterization used SEM, HR-TEM, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, and four-point-probe conductivity measurements. DFT calculations (PBEsol functional, VASP software, Tkatchenko-Scheffler dispersion correction, Hubbard-U=4.0 eV) were performed to understand the stabilization mechanism.

**Key Results:**
- The 1T phase proportion increased with hydrazine concentration: 0%, 31%, 69%, and 70% for MoS2-0HZ, MoS2-1HZ, MoS2-4HZ, and MoS2-12HZ respectively (saturation reached at N2H4:Mo = 4:1).
- The 1T-dominant MoS2-4HZ exhibited excellent ambient stability with no significant phase transformation over 3 months.
- Electrical conductivity was ~700 times higher than 2H MoS2 (sheet resistance decreased from 28.9 kΩ/square for 2H to 41.1 Ω/square for 1T-dominant).
- HER performance improved dramatically: onset potential reduced from 286 to 196 mV vs. RHE, Tafel slope decreased from 99 to 64 mV/dec, and current density was ~12 times larger than 2H MoS2 at overpotential 300 mV.
- ECSA increased with 1T phase content: 609.62, 787.23, and 970.66 cm² for 0%, 31%, and 69% 1T phase respectively.
- DFT calculations showed hydrazine intercalation is exothermic for 1T MoS2 (Eintercalation = -6.117 eV) but endothermic for 2H MoS2 (Eintercalation = +1.541 eV).
- Bader charge analysis revealed a Mo atom near the hydrazine docking position gets reduced by ~0.1 e⁻, donated from the N2H4 molecule, stabilizing the 1T phase by partially filling the 4dxy,yz,xz orbitals.
- An N-S bond forms between hydrazine and the MoS2 layer for the 1T polymorph but not for 2H.
- Hydrazine-intercalated samples showed enhanced suspension stability in water (remained suspended after 1 week vs. complete precipitation for 2H MoS2).

**Conclusions:** The one-step hydrazine-assisted hydrothermal method enables precise control of 2H/1T phase ratio with excellent stability, high conductivity, and superior HER performance, attributed to electron donation from hydrazine to adjacent Mo atoms. The strategy may be broadly applicable to developing highly efficient and stable 2D electrocatalysts. The work was conducted by researchers from the University of New South Wales, Macquarie University, The University of Newcastle (Australia), and the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (Spain).

SUMMARY:
<summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Tuning the Schottky barrier height in single- and bi-layer graphene-inserted MoS2/metal contacts | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-67150-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Scientific Reports (volume 14, article number 20905, 2024) titled "Tuning the Schottky barrier height in single- and bi-layer graphene-inserted MoS2/metal contacts." The study, authored by Xumei Zhao, Caijuan Xia, Lianbi Li, Anxiang Wang, Dezhong Cao, Baiyu Zhang, and Qinglong Fang, uses first-principle density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate how inserting single- and bi-layer graphene affects the electronic properties and Schottky barrier of MoS2/metals contacts (Mg, Al, In, Cu, Ag, Au, Pd, Ti, and Sc).

Key findings:
- Charge transfer occurs mainly at the graphene/metal interface, with smaller transfer at bi-layer graphene interfaces or graphene/MoS2 interfaces. Bader charge analysis shows weak interactions for Mg/Al/In (0.035-0.052 e), medium for Cu/Ag/Au (0.069-0.073 e), and strong for Pd/Sc/Ti (0.101-0.208 e) with graphene.
- A tunneling barrier exists at the graphene/MoS2 interface that hinders electron injection, but tunneling transmission probabilities remain high (88-97.8% for single-layer; 85.1-96.4% for bi-layer).
- The Schottky barrier height (Φ_SB,N) decreases upon graphene insertion. With single-layer graphene insertion: MoS2 contacts with Mg, In, Sc, and Ti achieve negative n-type Schottky barriers of -0.116 eV, -0.116 eV, -0.014 eV, and -0.116 eV respectively (indicating ohmic contacts); while Al, Cu, Ag, Au, Pd show positive barriers of 0.111, 0.146, 0.199, 0.462, and 0.332 eV respectively.
- With bi-layer graphene insertion: negative n-type Schottky barriers of -0.086 eV (Mg), -0.114 eV (In), -0.059 eV (Pd), -0.008 eV (Sc), and -0.0636 eV (Ti) are observed; while Al, Cu, Ag, Au show positive barriers of 0.492, 0.492, 0.230, and 0.359 eV respectively.
- Graphene preserves the intrinsic semiconductor properties of MoS2 (maintaining band gaps of ~1.3-1.6 eV with only band shifts), effectively isolating the MoS2 layer from the metal.
- Computational details: VASP code, PAW method, PBE-GGA functional with Grimme van der Waals correction, 450 eV cutoff energy, 11×11×1 k-mesh, 15 Å vacuum layer, energy convergence of 1.0×10^-5 eV, force convergence of 0.02 eV/Å.

The study provides practical guidance for designing high-performance transition metal dichalcogenide nanoelectronic devices by demonstrating that graphene insertion into MoS2/metal contacts can reduce or eliminate Schottky barriers, transitioning contacts to ohmic behavior.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results reveal that the charge transfer mainly occurs at the interface between the graphene and metal layers, with smaller transfer at the interface between bi-layer garphene or between graphene and MoS2. And the tunneling barrier exists at the interface between graphene and MoS2, which hinders electron injection from graphene to MoS2."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Research - 2D Materials - Schottky-barrier Injection ---
URL: https://www.purdue.edu/discoverypark/nanotechnology/membership/Appenzeller/research_2d_sbfet.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the Purdue University Appenzeller research group's Nanotechnology program, specifically describing their research on Schottky-barrier injection in 2D materials. The research focuses on making good electrical contacts to emerging 2D materials and separating contact effects from intrinsic material properties. Key findings include:

1. **MoS2 Schottky-barrier Transistor with Scandium Contact**: The group studied contacts to MoS2 using low work function metals (scandium ΦM=3.5 eV, titanium ΦM=4.3 eV) and large work function metals (nickel ΦM=5.0 eV, platinum ΦM=5.9 eV). They extracted Schottky barrier heights of ~230 meV (platinum), ~150 meV (nickel), ~50 meV (titanium), and ~30 meV (scandium). The work provided evidence that MoS2-to-metal interfaces are strongly impacted by Fermi level pinning near the conduction band, similar to III-V materials and silicon. Using scandium contacts on 10-nm-thick exfoliated MoS2 flakes covered by a 15 nm Al2O3 film, they achieved high effective mobilities of 700 cm²/(V·s) at room temperature (Nano Letters, 2013, 13, 100-105). Authors: Saptarshi Das and Ashish Penumatcha.

2. **Tunability of Short-Channel Effects in MoS2 Schottky-barrier Transistors**: MoS2 FETs show electrical performance governed by an unexpected dependence on effective body thickness, which depends on intercalated water molecules in the layered structure. The doping state of MoS2 FETs strongly depends on environment (air/vacuum). Device characteristics can be tuned by controlling the effective body thickness via intercalation and engineering the interlayer barrier (Nano Letters 15, 301-306). Author: Feng Zhang.

3. **Black Phosphorus Schottky-barrier MOSFET and Modeling**: Black phosphorus (BP) is a layered 2D material with phosphorus atoms in a puckered arrangement held together by weak van der Waals forces. BP has high mobility (200-1000 cm²/V-s) and a direct tunable bandgap, making it attractive for RF and optoelectronic applications, as well as tunnel FET development. The group used a Landauer model to fit transfer characteristics of BP Schottky-barrier MOSFETs and extracted both electron- and hole-Schottky barrier heights for Permalloy and Palladium contacts to black phosphorus. This model can be extended to other 2D-material SB-MOSFETs (Nature Communications 6, 6:8948). Authors: Ashish Penumatcha and Ramon Salazar.
</summary>

"Through analysis of experimental results, we found for many 2D materials of interest, such as transition metal dichacolgenides (TMDs) and black phosphorus, that the metal-to-semiconductor contacts are Schottky-barrier type."

--- SOURCE 7: Metal-induced gap states - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal-induced_gap_states

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Wikipedia article explains metal-induced gap states (MIGS) in solid-state physics. MIGS are electron states that exist near the surface of a semiconductor when a metal is deposited on it (e.g., by thermal evaporation). These states have energies that fall within the semiconductor's bandgap, which are otherwise forbidden in the bulk material. When a metal is deposited on a semiconductor, even as thin as a single atomic layer, the Fermi levels of both materials must match at the interface, which pins the Fermi level in the semiconductor and creates gap states that decay deeper into the semiconductor.

Key concepts covered include:
- Band-bending at the metal-semiconductor interface: The Fermi level matching creates band bending, with different behaviors for high/low work function metals and n-type/p-type semiconductors. Volker Heine was among the first to estimate the length of metal electron state tails extending into the semiconductor's energy gap, showing the surface state energy position is quite stable regardless of the metal used.
- Branching point: MIGS are mixtures (Fourier series) of valence and conduction band states. The branching point (E_B) divides acceptor-type from donor-type MIGS. Tersoff derived the formula E_B = 1/2[Ē_V + Ē_C], where Ē_V accounts for spin-orbit splitting and Ē_C is the indirect conduction band minimum.
- Barrier height: Charge transfer between metal and semiconductor (formulated by Linus Pauling and later revised) produces a dipole and thus the Schottky barrier height. Tersoff derived Φ_bh = 1/2[Ē_C - Ē_V] + δ_m, fitting experimental data for Au in contact with 10 common semiconductors (Si, Ge, GaP, GaAs, etc.). Garcia-Moliner and Flores provided a more rigorous derivation considering density of states and dipole contributions, defining two limits: the Bardeen Limit (high interface state density pins Fermi level) and the Schottky Limit (barrier varies strongly with metal characteristics).
- Applications: The metal/semiconductor junction has bias-dependent capacitance (going as (V_if - V)^1/2), making it useful in varactor devices.

Key researchers cited include Volker Heine (1965), C. Tejedor, F. Flores and E. Louis (1977), and J. Tersoff (1984-1985), along with the foundational work of Linus Pauling on charge transfer.
</summary>

URL: https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/a-claim-that-tsmc-has-a-1nm-process-hits-the-headlines

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Semiconductor Digest article by Dick James that debunks a media claim that TSMC had achieved a 1nm process technology. The article traces how UK website Verdict took a Nature publication and incorrectly morphed it into headlines claiming TSMC had made a 1nm breakthrough, which was then circulated widely across tech press. The actual Nature paper (published May 12, 2021, submitted July 1 of the prior year) was a joint collaboration between MIT, TSMC, UC Berkeley, National Taiwan University (NTU), and KAUST in Saudi Arabia, with 23 authors total.

The scientific work described in the paper involves using bismuth (Bi) as a semi-metal contact for molybdenum disulphide (MoS2) monolayer transistors, achieving a record low contact resistance of 123 Ω-µm and a record high on-state current density of 1,135 µA/µm. The paper addresses the challenge of contact resistance between metal electrodes and 2D monolayers - conventional metal contacts create Schottky barriers at interfaces, but bismuth suppresses gap states and spontaneously forms degenerate states in the monolayer, giving zero Schottky barrier height. The devices were fabricated by transferring MOCVD or CVD MoS2 monolayers onto silicon nitride or silicon dioxide dielectric layers on P++ Si substrates, with 20nm bismuth e-beam deposited and capped with gold. Channel lengths ranged from ~30-500 nm with widths of 2-10 µm.

The author points out that nowhere in the paper is a specific 1nm technology mentioned - the only relevant reference is an MIT press release noting that 2D monolayers could potentially reduce channel length from ~5-10 nanometers to a subnanometer scale, which is a channel length, not a technology node. The author concludes that the 1nm claim is "journalistic hyperbole" and that while finding good low-resistance contacts to 2D monolayers is a significant step forward, real products are far off. The South China Morning Post estimated the technology is at least ten years from commercialization. The article also notes this is not the first MoS2 work from this collaboration - previous papers at VLSI 2020 and IEDM 2020 explored similar topics. The author was Shannon Davis, editor of Semiconductor Digest.
